News.title: Our tiny village survived 1066 & William the Conquerer – now our homes are CRUMBLING because of thundering new invasion
News.content:
Next

AN ANCIENT village that survived the 1066 Norman Conquest is being wrecked by an invasion of lorries, locals have said.

Hundreds of HGVs plough through the picturesque village causing daily quakes that furious residents liken to “living in a washing machine”.



Pevensey Castle is over 1,700-years-old and was originally built by the Romans in AD 290.

It’s even included in The Bayeux Tapestry along with reams of embroidered linen illustrating William the Conqueror’s invasion – and is just 10 miles from the site of the Battle of Hastings.





But the historical gem is being ruined by “thundering” lorries grating and vibrating the castle wall, according to locals.

Huge lorries clatter through the Tudor streets of Pevensey Village at 30mph every day, each of them causing quakes in the stonework as they pass.



Locals are sick of the shaking and fear the traffic could even be risking pedestrians’ lives.

It’s got so bad that 500-year-old Tudor wall paintings in a local visitor centre are crumbling.

The abandoned Roman fort that once stood on the site of the castle became a stronghold for thousands of Norman troops during the invasion of 1066.



After sinking an arrow into King Harold’s eye and slaughtering thousands of English fighters the blood soaked invaders set up camp in the castle ruins.

Then in the 1070s William the Conqueror ordered a huge stone fortress to be built which still stands today.

During The Sun’s visit we watched dozens of lorries pelting round the corner of Castle Road, missing the fortress wall by centimeters.

It’s been battered so many times that a huge two metre chunk of wall has been destroyed.

Now a petition has kicked off to stop the traffic chaos.



Locals want a HGV weight restriction and the speed limit cut to 20mph.

The campaign is spearheaded by Peter Lowton, chairman of Pevensey Parish Council, who is appalled by the situation.

He told The Sun: “I think it’s shocking.



“We’re very lucky in this country to have such wonderful heritage and we should be protecting it not allowing it to disappear.

“The reality is the damage that’s been caused to the castle is obvious and there will be further damage.

“When you look at the Tudor wall paintings of The Mint House, it’s just shocking.

“They’re trying to restore the building whilst at the same time lorries are destroying it.

“Their case to get funding will rely on whether things are put in place to stop the lorries from damaging it.”



The Mint House is a Tudor inn steeped in English myths and legends of sword fights, royals, ghosts and murders.

The quakes have damaged the building so much that crumbling plastering has uncovered hidden 400-year-old wall paintings.

The half a millennium old art was crafted by travelling merchants who offered innkeepers the chance to decorate their businesses.



Restoration has already cost £600,000 and future funding relies on stopping the shakes.

During our visit we felt the wooden floor boards vibrating under foot whilst lorries almost as tall as the building trundled past.

Project manager Joe Seaman has been looking after the building since 2021 and says the condition is getting worse.

He told The Sun: “You can literally feel the building shaking as they go past, because it’s 500-years-old the surfaces vibrate and it’s not good for it at all.

“This hasn’t sprung out of nowhere, the damage has been going on for a number of years and the corner of the castle has been hit a number of times.



“Because we’re restoring the building we’re finding more and more wall paintings.”

He added: “But there’s no point us putting in £1million if it’s still going to be damaged by the road.”

The traffic isn’t just damaging the village’s Tudor relics, Joe says it’s risking pedestrian safety.

With almost 70,000 visitors to the castle each year, the road is bustling with tourists.

He continued: “It’s a constant worry that someone will come round the corner too fast, it’s an accident waiting to happen.



“We’re not saying turn the whole village into a museum, but we want people to be able to cross the road without getting run over.

“I don’t like nimbyism, but I do think when there are institutions like National Highways then maybe they should help rather than be the block.

“We’d love to work with them to find a solution, it’s not about blaming it’s about working with people.”

The street is a B road which means online sat navs send unsuspecting truckers through the village instead of on the nearby Pevensey Bypass.

Katherine, a local resident, supports the proposed speed limit cut.



She told The Sun: “It’s a complete blind spot when you try and cross next to the castle.

“It’s just lethal because you can’t see anything round the corner.”

Mark Penderton has lived in the village for 33 years and had to pay for a structural engineer after a lorry cracked his wall.

He said: “We’ve had our property damaged three times by lorries and a number of near misses.

“We hear a lot of noise and vibrations, our neighbour’s possessions vibrate on the window ledge and their car mirrors were knocked off by lorries.”



East Sussex County Council is responsible for the road and said: “We have yet to receive the petition, but the concerns raised will be considered in full once we do.”

English Heritage manage and conserve Pevensey Castle.

A spokesman told The Sun: “We are aware of concerns about large vehicles passing close to Pevensey Castle’s historic walls and the potential impact this may have.

“We take these concerns very seriously and include the external wall faces in our regular site checks.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The road is outside English Heritage’s control, but we welcome the local authority’s invitation to discuss measures to address the issue, including road speeds and restrictions on large vehicles.



“We hope these discussions will help identify practical ways to reduce any potential risk and protect this important historic monument.”

News.title: Putin builds new air defence towers near his forest palace as Ukraine steps up attacks on Russia
News.content:
Next

VLADIMIR Putin has thrown up four new missile defence towers around his secret forest palace amid mounting Ukrainian attacks.

The paranoid tyrant now has 30 air defence towers guarding his heavily fortified Valdai hideaway.



One towering missile launcher stands just 1,312 feet from the palace where Putin is believed to live with his secret lover Alina Kabaeva, 43, and their two young sons.

The latest military build-up was exposed by Radio Svoboda using satellite imagery of the sprawling estate in Russia’s Novgorod region.



Four newly constructed towers are among the closest permanent missile defence positions to the dictator’s bolthole, some 230 miles northwest of Moscow.

And locals have revealed how troops have descended on the surrounding woodland as the Kremlin continues to tighten its iron grip on the estate.



One resident said: “See that tower? They’ve brought in a lot of soldiers – they’re building things there, constantly building.”

A teacher in the nearby village of Roshchino described how the ominous air defence machinery has become a familiar presence.

They said: “That’s the air defence system – you wouldn’t recognise the sounds.

“If it’s spinning, it means there’s no immediate danger overhead.



“If it stops, it means something is flying over us.”

The latest additions come amid mounting fears of Ukrainian drone strikes penetrating deep into Russian territory.

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky previously claimed Putin had deployed nearly 90 air defence launchers to the wider Valdai area, stripping other Russian regions of vital protection.



He said: “They have moved nearly 90 air defence launchers to Valdai from other Russian regions, and a special air defence division is being formed there to ensure the peace of the Russian leadership.”

Zelensky also warned in June that the Kremlin was scrambling to protect its most prized locations.

“The Russian leadership is moving more air defence systems to Moscow, to Valdai, and to Putin’s bridge across the Kerch Strait,” he said.

The military shield has grown dramatically since 2024, when just seven air defence positions guarded the secluded fortress.

Earlier research by Radio Liberty identified 27 emplacements around the estate, including at least eight towers installed within four months.



Most were believed to house formidable Pantsir missile systems, each costing up to £16million.

At least one was understood to be an S-400 system, with a staggering price tag of up to £800million.

Combined with sophisticated radar equipment, the arsenal protecting Putin’s private sanctuary is estimated to be worth well over £1billion.



The lavish military protection dwarfs the defences guarding many Russian cities.

Moscow and its surrounding region, home to some 20 million people, reportedly have just 100 air defence emplacements between them.

Other Russian cities are understood to have even fewer, while Putin pours military resources into protecting his secluded family retreat.

The latest security frenzy follows a bitter row over the dictator’s claims that Ukraine had tried to attack his palace.

In December, Ukrainian forces launched a long-range drone strike against the Akron chemical plant in Veliky Novgorod, around 85 miles from Valdai.



The industrial site plays a key role in Russia’s explosives production.

But Putin claimed more than 90 Ukrainian drones had instead been directed towards his private residence.

He even complained to US President Donald Trump that Kyiv had attempted to target him and his family.

Western and Ukrainian intelligence dismissed the explosive accusations as false, with Trump also rejecting the Kremlin’s account.



Despite the claims being disputed, Putin pressed ahead with bolstering his palace defences.

Reports also suggested Kabaeva had refused to remain at the heavily guarded estate amid fears for her safety.

The former Olympic gymnast is believed to share the sprawling complex with Putin and their sons Ivan, 11, and Vladimir, seven.

The boys, whose existence the Kremlin has never publicly acknowledged, are reportedly being raised under the surname Spiridonov.



They are educated by private tutors rather than attending ordinary schools and are said to be keen young gymnasts.

Their secret surname is believed to honour Putin’s paternal grandfather, Spiridon Putin, who worked as a chef for some of the Soviet Union’s most notorious figures.

Putin’s hidden family life has become the subject of repeated investigations into the luxury surrounding his lakeside fortress.

The vast woodland estate is believed to contain a nuclear bunker, private hospital and separate residence for Kabaeva and the children.

Investigative outlet Proekt previously exposed an enormous private spa complex tucked away inside the grounds.



It reported: “Located about the same distance from Putin and Kabaeva’s houses is a huge spa complex with a solarium, a cryo chamber, a 25-metre swimming pool, a hammam, a sauna, a mud room, massage baths, cosmetology and dentistry areas.”

Investigators also uncovered evidence of a secret playground and karting track built for the dictator’s young sons.

Proekt reported a “constant presence of children in the residence”.

The fortress is so heavily guarded that Putin reportedly travels there aboard his own armoured train rather than relying on ordinary transport.

Proekt revealed: “For this reason, a secret, guarded station was built near his residence.”



The Kremlin’s frantic fortification comes as Ukraine ramps up retaliation attacks on Russian soil.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

In June, Moscow had been blitzed by Ukraine’s biggest attack of the war so far – with dramatic clips showing 400 drones raining hell on Vladimir Putin’s doorstep.

Extraordinary footage showed huge plumes of smoke rising over the Russian capital amid the onslaught – part of Volodymyr Zelensky’s endgame blitz.

News.title: Ex-safari park ranger, 45, jailed for RHINO POACHING after shooting dead endangered animal to sell its horn
News.content:
POACHER LOCKED UP Ex-safari park ranger, 45, jailed for RHINO POACHING after shooting dead endangered animal to sell its horn







Next

A STAR wildlife ranger, once set to becoming head of South Africa’s most prestigious safari park, has been jailed for 14 years for Rhino poaching.

Rodney Landela’s betrayal has rocked the 630 rangers who risk their lives every day hunting evil poachers in the Kruger National Park.



The 45-year-old will now be locked up in a tough South African prison with dozens of poachers he and his rangers put behind bars.

Landela was arrested after being caught red- handed shooting an endangered white rhino and dehorning it to make a profit.



The price per ounce of rhino horn in the Far East is higher than that of gold or cocaine.

He stood in the dock in Skukuza Regional Court on Saturday as his sentence was called out.

Prosecutors told the court how a patrolling KNP ranger heard three gunshots ring out in the bush and raced towards the gunfire.

Ranger Lucky Ndlovu saw two men jump into a white Toyota Hilux station wagon and flee the scene and radioed in fellow rangers and air support.



A chopper on patrol landed in the road in front of the Toyota and ordered the occupants out at gunpoint.

Ranger Ndlovu was stunned to see his highly respected boss Landela climb out of the vehicle along with Kruger State wildlife vet Kenneth Mochocho, 52.

Landela claimed he had been in the area when he heard the gunshots and was trying to find a place to get phone signal to report a poaching.

But a suspicious ranger followed his route into the bush where he found a backpack with a rhino horn inside.

He also discovered Landela’s high- powered .375 CZ Magnum hunting rifle, 3 spent .375 cartridges and an axe with rhino blood on it.



DNA taken from bloodstains on Landela’s clothes and an axe and from the vet’s vehicle and on his jacket linked both of them to the shooting.

Both were arrested but have been on bail for 10 years as the case dragged on with constant court adjournments.

On Saturday Regional Magistrate Mbogeni Ngobeni dismissed their not guilty pleas and convicted both.



They bowed their heads for sentence on two counts each of killing an endangered rhino and carrying a firearm with intent to commit crime.

The magistrate said Landela was privy as a senior ranger to extremely sensitive information which could benefit poachers.

Both men were handed 10 years behind bars for killing a rhino and four years for using a firearm, to run concurrently and the magistrates ordered no parole.

The park’s first Head Ranger, decorated British Army officer and Boer War hero Major James Stevenson-Hamilton, banned all hunting in the Kruger.

Landela was one of just four regional managers protecting wildlife in a park the size of Wales.



Affectionately known as the “Crown Prince of the Kruger”, he was once tipped to become Head Ranger of the iconic park.

But his arrest for poaching in 2016 torpedoed his shoe-in to the prized position and instead in 2021 the Kruger appointed Cathy Dreyer, 48 instead.

Lawyers for both men said they intended to appeal the judgement.



But senior KNP colleagues of the disgraced ranger are now asking how deeply involved Landela was with the deadly poaching gangs and how much he pocketed.

A senior ranger with over 20 years of experience, speaking anonymously for fear of losing his job, said: “There could not have been a person in a better position to be recruited.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“His inside information was priceless to a syndicate as he knew all the details of the anti-poaching operations.

“He also knew exactly where the rhino herds were and in his position of power could move weapons and poached horns in and out of the Kruger because he was above suspicion.”

Next

A MAJOR motorway is closed with 20-minute delays and three miles of congestion due to a “police-led incident”.

Traffic is piling up in both directions of the M27 in Hampshire between J1 and J2 near Southampton.



Drivers caught in the closure are being turned around at the rear of the queue as Hampshire Police remain at the scene.

Further delays are expected as National Highways Traffic Officers assist with traffic management.



A spokesperson for Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said: “Officers are currently on scene at an incident on the M27.

“Closures have been put in place between Junction 1 and Junction 2 on the Eastbound and Westbound carriageways.



“We ask drivers to seek alternative routes whilst officers are on scene.”

A spokesperson for National Highways added: “The M27 in Hampshire is closed in both directions between J1 and J2 near Southampton following a Police led incident.

“Hampshire Police are currently on scene. National Highways Traffic Officers are assisting with traffic management.”

In an update on X, they continued: “#M27 both directions in #Hampshire between J1 #A31 & J2 #Ower.

News.title: I was jailed on death row before Brit millionaire saved me from lethal injection hell…bungling cops made crucial mistake
News.content:
DEATH HOUSE HORRORS I was jailed on death row before Brit millionaire saved me from lethal injection hell…bungling cops made crucial mistake







Next

RYAN Matthews will never forget the five haunting words read out to him in court 30 years ago: “We sentence you to death.”

Still only a teenager, he was swiftly taken to a dark, eerie prison cell on death row where he would spend 23 hours a day waiting to die for the next five years.



But the agony of his impending execution was made worse for one reason – he was innocent and only convicted because of bungling cops.

After five gruelling years on death row, Ryan was finally spared from the lethal injection thanks to a boasting convict already behind bars and a Brit millionaire desperate for justice.



Ryan’s life was turned upside down when he was arrested aged 17 and charged for the murder of grocery store owner, Tommy Vanhoose.

Ryan and a friend, Travis Hayes, also 17, were driving in a nearby area in a car similar to the getaway vehicle.



During intense questioning, Hayes told cops he had been Ryan’s accomplice in the murder and getaway driver.

He later claimed police bullied him into making the confession and refused to testify against his friend in court.



Despite initially failing to reach a unanimous verdict, the jury returned just 20 minutes later to find Ryan guilty.

The dad-of-three told The Sun: “Once they sentence you in court and say, ‘Ryan Matthews, we sentence you to death,’ they ship you out to the Penitentiary the very next day.

“When you walk in there you can feel something hanging over the place: you’re never going home.

“I was walking along a tier towards my cell and I didn’t know what to expect. I’d never been in that situation before.”

Almost three decades on he can still remember the sharp, sudden change of atmosphere when an inmate walked to the execution chamber.



He added: “You feel it. You can really feel it in the air. It’s sad and sombre.

“When somebody goes to the death house, they come to get them a few days beforehand and they have their last meal and everything.

“The whole tier changes. There’s no energy. It’s almost quiet, apart from the fans and the television. There’s not much joking going on. It’s a very sad feeling.



“I knew a few guys who had been there before I arrived, and you could tell they weren’t right. They’d been there a long time and you could see that it had really got to them.

“I started to understand the toll that being there for so long could take.”

Ryan, now 47, spent two and a half years in the parish jail before his murder trial.

“During that time, I didn’t know how to defend myself against something I hadn’t done”, he said.

“I thought the truth would eventually come out. I thought I shouldn’t have to do much because I had nothing to do with it and didn’t even know about it.



“But as those two and a half years passed, I watched other people go to trial and saw the outcomes. I started to realise that things could go badly for me.”

Shauneen Lambe, a British barrister who sat through the trial, later began working on the case following an intervention from British Lawyer Clive Stafford Smith.

Lambe accused the original defence team of poorly representing Ryan.

Rumours then began circulating that a man named Rondell Love, serving 20 years for a murder committed six months after the Vanhoose murder, was boasting about being the real killer.

That prompted Lambe to secure three statements confirming Love’s confessions before she returned to the UK to seek further funding.



British human rights group Reprieve quickly backed the case and crucially so did millionaire House of Lords member Martha Lane Fox who had agreed a £10,000 donation to Ryan’s legal fight.

The fresh injection of cash allowed for DNA tests to be taken which proved Love had been wearing a mask collected as evidence from the crime scene.

In 2004, a retrial was granted and Ryan was exonerated at the age of 24.



Forever grateful, Ryan said: “I don’t think I should have been found guilty in the first place. It’s not as though my DNA was found on the mask.

“It was never there. You can understand why I didn’t have much faith in the system.

“It wasn’t until I was actually granted bond and allowed to go home that I started to believe things might really be changing.”

He also praised Martha for her donation as the pair finally met in 2022.

Ryan added: “Martha is a very nice lady. I heard about it when my lawyers came to see me. They told me she was willing to pay for the DNA test.



“I thought that was great. I was still locked up and I didn’t know what to expect, but I appreciated it.

“I didn’t really get the chance to think about it properly when I first came home and was exonerated.

“She probably doesn’t realise how much of a part she played in me getting out. She was very influential.”

But Martha wasn’t alone and his case had gathered so much attention in the UK that Ryan began receiving thousands of letters from behind bars.

He added: “Countless people wrote to me in prison from the UK. Thousands and thousands of letters.



“It was amazing to know that people cared enough to sit down and write to me.

“The guards must have been sick of me because I was getting thousands of letters, almost every day.”

Despite all he had been through, Ryan says he has now found a way of letting his anger go.

He said: “Humans will be humans, but being angry at them puts you in a certain place. It stagnates you, and that’s why I don’t hold on to it.

“When it first happened, yes, I was angry. But eventually, I came to understand that people are people. I don’t hold on to any anger.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

In 2019, Ryan graduated from college with a degree in applied arts and sciences before obtaining a Masters in business analytics in 2023.

He has three children – aged 21, 18 and 10 and now works in the corrugation industry.

News.title: Boy, 10, fighting for life after horror three-car crash on Scots road
News.content:
ROAD HORROR Boy, 10, fighting for life after horror three-car crash on Scots road







Next

A YOUNG child has been left fighting for his life after a horror three-car crash on a Scots road.

The vehicles collided on the A701 between Broughton and Blyth Bridge in the Scottish Borders around 12.15pm on Friday.



A white Seat Leon, black Audi Q5 and a red Jaguar F Pace were all involved in the crash.

Emergency crews were scrambled to the scene of the smash which left five people injured.



A ten-year-old boy who was in the seat was among those raced to hospital after the horror collision.

Medics say he is currently in a critical condition.



The men driving the Seat and the Jaguar were seriously injured in the collision.

A teenage boy from the Seat and a woman passenger from the Audi were also taken to hospital for treatment.

Cops locked down the road as they launched a probe into the collision.

It was reopened around 7.10pm after work was carried out.



Officers assigned to the investigation have appealed for anyone with information to come forward.

Sergeant Grant Hastie said: “I am appealing to anyone who witnessed the crash, or saw the vehicles prior, and has yet to speak to officers to come forward with any information that could assist with our investigation.

“I’d also ask that those driving in the area at the time with dash-cam footage review this to see if it has captured anything of significance.”

Anyone with information is asked to contact Police Scotland on 101, quoting incident number 1186 of 16 October, 2026.

News.title: Wheelchair-bound girl, 7, fighting for life after being shot in the face by Oregon shooter in tragedy that killed 4
News.content:
Next

A WHEELCHAIR-BOUND girl is in critical condition after being shot by the teen gunman who opened fire at an elementary school.

Three children and a 25-year-old teacher were slaughtered after Griffin John II stormed into Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday afternoon.



The 16-year-old fired through the locked doors with a pump-action shotgun before breaking into a special needs class full of terrified children.

He unloaded 15 shots across the room and still had 44 rounds left before he was gunned down by hero armed bystander Kaylub Giamanco, 36.



Seven-year-old Saylor Graham – who uses a wheelchair – was shot in the face during the horror rampage, according to the New York Post.

Kyle Giamanco, the brother of the man who stopped the shooter, told NBC outlet he knows her family and confirmed she is recovering from surgery.

Read More US News STOPPED COLD Hero bystander who took down Oregon school shooter ID'd as sick details emerge

Little Saylor was well known in the community for her bubbly personality and trademark pink glasses.

She was Silver Rail’s adopted “Sparrow” – meaning the school helped to raise money to fund her medical expenses.



Matt Sampson, Sparrow USA’s executive director, told local outlet Central Oregon Daily: “Saylor is the definition of light and joy.

“And one of those kids that, you know, when she’s in the room.

“You can’t think of anything else other than what Saylor’s doing; ‘I need to get to know her.”

“She’s just very inspirational, very joyful, very courageous, and inspirational”, he added.

According to a 2024 announcement, Saylor battles CASK, a gene mutation that impacts her physical and cognitive development.



She has also been diagnosed with dysphagia, a disorder that makes it difficult for her to swallow food and drink.

“She’s a fighter, and we’re praying that she fights through this and her family”, Sampson said.

“I want to express to her family how much we love them and how valuable they are to us,” he added.



Teacher Becky Drury, 54, also survived the shooting but suffered serious injuries, authorities said.

The 54-year-old was shot through her left arm and right hand but is “recovering in the hospital after surgery,” her mothe-r -in law Yvonne said.

Meghan Lambert, 25, and three children aged five, eight and 11, were killed in the shooting.

Meghan’s family described her as a funny, compassionate woman who “always fought for the underdog and those with special needs”.

“Meghan loved those children,” they said on Friday, adding that teaching at Silver Rail was her “dream job”.



The youngest victim has been named by police as Rhoam Summer.

“Today has been the worst day of my life,” Kelik Summer, Rhoam’s father, said in a statement on Facebook.

“My son Rhoam was killed in a school shooting. We are broken and lost, but are surrounded by friends and family who are keeping us safe.”



Amid the horror, a heroic teacher threw her phone at John before tackling him to the ground in a desperate bid to disarm the killer.

As she tried to wrestle a shotgun from his grip on the floor of the classroom, a bystander armed with a pistol ran inside and killed the teen.

The selfless teacher was not injured in the terrifying ordeal, police said.

“To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude,” Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

When Bend police arrived at the scene, John was already dead, authorities said.



The shooter’s motive remains unclear.

News.title: The Gentlemen-style drug manors taking over UK’s countryside as monsters turn castles & mansions into cannabis factories
News.content:
Next

WITH its glamourous stately homes, acres of rolling fields and ancient woodland the backdrop of the fictional world of The Gentlemen is the quintessential countryside ideal.

And while Guy Ritchie’s world of drug lords, murder and betrayal may be just another Netflix drama, experts have revealed how real-life UK criminal enterprises are actually using rural mansions and castles to house professional cannabis factories – minus the glitz and glamour.



The criminal underworld has turned its back on small, terraced-house operations in favour of large-scale slave labour to run industrial sized grows on farmland and in stately homes, just like The Gentlemen’s storyline.

But the reality of being part of this criminal network is far less glamorous than the lives of The Gentlemen’s Eddie Horniman and Susie Glass, running a vast operation for jailed mob boss Bobby Glass.



In the year ending March 2025, police and Border Force recorded 10,689 seizures involving cannabis plants, up 10 per cent from 9,710 the previous year.

Organised criminal gangs often mix their shady drugs dealing with people trafficking and force illegal immigrants to work in large-scale grows, often living in squalid conditions.

Leading illegal drugs expert Ian Hamilton, Associate Professor at York University, told The Sun how a shift in trends for illegally growing cannabis in the UK is disrupting the market.

“Cannabis growers are much more innovative than national crime agencies and law enforcement and are finding new ways of evading detection while maximising supply,” he said.



“In terms of cannabis farms, it used to be two-up, two-down terraced houses with typically Vietnamese workers who were being exploited to look after them.

“I think that still goes on, but I think they’ve morphed a bit and realised that larger, more rural properties, either commercial or residential units, offer them a good scale so they can grow far more.”

In April this year a ‘Gentlemen-style’ mansion grow was discovered in a home in north-west Wales, which once hosted the king.

The Plas Glynllifon mansion was raided by police who discovered millions of pounds worth of mature crops in 12 rooms, using dodgy electrics to power the artificial lighting and a water supply which had been diverted.

The Grade I listed manor house, near Caernarfon, Gwynedd, with more than 100 rooms, was once owned by Lord Newborough and in 1969 hosted the ball of the investiture for the Prince of Wales, now King Charles.



Meanwhile Woodlands Castle near Taunton in Somerset is a former upmarket wedding venue set on 12 acres and was found to contain 3,500 plants with a potential value of £1.4million in June 2021.

Almost every room of the large property was used for cultivating cannabis plants, with sophisticated lighting, insulation and cultivation systems on nearly every floor.

One expert told Taunton Crown Court it was the biggest growing operation he had ever seen Trung Pham, 40 at the time, claimed he had been kidnapped by the Vietnamese mafia and forced to cook and clean at the castle.



But a jury found him guilty of being concerned in the production of cannabis and he was jailed for three years.

In Stirling, in Scotland, the owner of a luxury £650,000 countryside home was horrified to find tenants had transformed it into an illicit growing operation in 2019.

John Brown had built the six-bedroomed house in Stirling, Scotland, 20 years previously and it was the first time he had rented it out as he was going abroad to work.



Two men were jailed for three years each after they admitted being concerned in the supply of Class-B drugs.

Kladji Ibrahimi, 23, pleaded guilty to committing the offence between the dates of April 1 and July 21, 2019, and Edi Vaka, 26, between April 1 and June 1 that year.

Back in 2015, Criminals turned a Downton Abbey-style mansion into a drugs factory raking in £400,000 every nine weeks.

Wendreda House in March, Cambridgeshire, had plants worth an estimated street value of almost £1 million.

The owner of the property lived in London and had not been aware of the six-month-long operation in which 1,000 plants were grown in opulent surroundings.



Flass is a Grade II listed Neo-Palladian and Italianate mansion near Maulds

Meaburn, Cumbria, which was raided by police in 2012 and found to be housing a vast cannabis farm worth £1 million.

The nine-bedroomed house was made to look like a luxurious, lived in property downstairs, but upstairs was home to the cannabis farm.

Paul Davis, 64 at the time, co-owned the property and was jailed for three years and eight months for being part of the gang running the criminal operation.



As well as the sheer size of some of these grows with hundreds of thousands of pounds worth of crops, there are other benefits attracting drugs producers to take over the countryside.

Prof Hamilton continued: “A lot of strains of cannabis that are growing now are very pungent. So even with the lengths that people go to kind of seal up their units, it still has a very strong smell about it.

“There’s also the idea that nobody is really watching much, a lot of these farms and other properties are isolated.

“They don’t have a lot of passing traffic, people generally go to a farm or estate with a purpose, and also, I think rural police forces aren’t that well-resourced, unlike the Met Police and other big urban areas.

“It’s not just law enforcement they are trying to hide from either, it’s other syndicates or organised crime groups, so an isolated property, whether it be a farm, an old mansion house, is in a lot of ways easier to protect because you can have CCTV, you can be very aware of who’s coming and who’s going, which is far harder when you’re in the middle of Birmingham, or in a residential area where there’s a lot of people traffic.



“Being able to grow at scale is particularly attractive – rather than having 10 terraced houses you can just build one large commercial unit, and that offers savings and scale – economies of scale, as it’s known.

“It’s just a lot easier to manage. It’s like why do you have a factory rather than 10 small shops? It’s just replicating that same business model.”

Professor Hamilton says UK citizens are increasingly being groomed and coerced into working for mob bosses cultivating the class-B drug, especially young people.



Professor Hamilton said: “There’s an endless supply of people being drawn in, who are groomed almost, who are very vulnerable in one way or another, either because they’re not very bright, or because they have a particular problem.

“They might be socially isolated or vulnerable in some other way, and they tend to be people who are a bit younger as well.”

But it is south Wales which claims the crown as the capital of cannabis farms, according to the fire service, which usually attend to deal the risks caused by bypassed electricity, exposed wires, water and electricity in humid conditions and overloaded circuits.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

South Wales Fire and Rescue Service attended the highest number of suspected or identified cannabis farms, responding to 90 properties over seven years.



The Home Office recorded 640 cannabis farm fires across the UK between 2019 and 2024.

News.title: France protests - live: Lyons tourist office set on fire as rallies turn violent
News.content:
Police have used tear gas and a water cannon as tens of thousands of protesters demonstrate across France against the cost of living, rising fuel prices and the state of public services

Riot police have fired tear gas on the streets of cities across France and arrested more than 160 people as thousands of protests against the cost of living, rising fuel prices and state of public services take place across the country.

In Lyons, a tourist office has been completely destroyed after it was set on fire. Tens of thousands are protesting in Paris alone with police firing tear gas and turning a water cannon on crowds in the Place de la République. In Marseille, a town hall was invaded and barricades set on fire as footage appears to show people attacking a bank.

Police said 150 protesters were arrested in Paris "primarily for carrying weapons or prohibited protective gear". President Emmanuel Macron has appealed for "calm" and called on demonstrators to show "respect for people and property".

Student protests in France have seen hundreds of thousands take to the streets since they began late last month. Protesters are demanding more investment in their schools, criticising the lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and rundown buildings.

The latest protests are about wider problems in France, including the state of the education system.

News.title: Waterford 'arson' latest: Two charged after parents and 2 children die in fire
News.content:
Waterford 'arson' latest: Two charged after parents and 2 children die in fire

Philip and Kim English, died alongside their two young sons, Callum, 12, and Jayden, nine, when their home in Co Waterford, Ireland, went up in flames

View Image Four members of the same family perished in the fire

A man and a woman have been charged following a horror arson attack that killed four members of the same family.

Parents, Philip and Kim English, died alongside their two young sons, Callum, 12, and Jayden, nine, when their home in Co Waterford, Ireland, went up in flames on Tuesday this week.

On Thursday, Gardai confirmed the arrest of a man in his 20s and a woman in his 30s. Officers said the pair have now been charged.

It comes after the fatal inferno broke out at the property in the early hours of Tuesday, killing the four family members and injuring two other children. It is understood the younger children remain in critical condition in hospital.

The incident sent shockwaves throughout the local community, with tributes describing the family as "well known" and "much loved".

Article continues below

Gardai said earlier this week it was searching for 'person or persons' in connection with the house fire, as officers said they believed the property was targeted in an arson attack.

News.title: Boy, 10, fighting for life after three-car crash with four others rushed to hospital
News.content:
Boy, 10, fighting for life after three-car crash with four others rushed to hospital

The crash between a Seat Leon, Audi Q5 and Jaguar F Pace happened in the Scottish Borders

View Image The horror crash happened on the A701 (Image: Google Maps)

A 10-year-old boy is in a critical condition after three cars collided on a main road in the Scottish Borders.

‌



‌



Emergency Services rushed to the scene on the A701 south of Blyth Bridge after the boy and four others were injured in the crash on Friday at around 12.15pm

‌



Occupants of all three cars involved - a white Seat Leon, a black Audi Q5 and a red Jaguar F Pace - were all rushed to hospital. Police said two men, the drivers of the Seat and the Jaguar, were taken for hospital after being seriously injured.

‌



Two other people, a teenage boy and a woman who were passengers in the Seat and the Audi respectively were also taken to hospital. The 10-year-old boy had been a passenger in the Seat and doctors have today (Saturday) described his condition as critical.

Teenager one of two passengers dead in horror UK plane crash as aircraft plunges into countryside READ MORE :

No details of any injuries sustained by the driver of the Audi have been released by police. The road was closed for around seven hours to allow for crash investigation work and the recovery of the vehicles.

Police are now appealing for witness and anyone with dash cam footage which may help their enquiries to come forward.

‌



Sergeant Grant Hastie said: "I am appealing to anyone who witnessed the crash, or saw the vehicles prior, and has yet to speak to officers to come forward with any information that could assist with our investigation.

"I'd also ask that those driving in the area at the time with dash-cam footage review this to see if it has captured anything of significance."

A spokesperson for Police Scotland said: "Road Policing officers are appealing for information following a serious crash south of Blyth Bridge in the Scottish Borders.

‌



"The crash happened around 12.15pm on Friday, October 16, on the A701 between Broughton and Blyth Bridge. Three vehicles were involved including a white Seat Leon, black Audi Q5 and a red Jaguar F Pace.

"Emergency services attended, and a 10-year-old boy who was a passenger in the Seat Leon was taken to hospital for treatment where he remains in a critical condition.

"Two male drivers of the Seat Leon and Jaguar F Pace were also taken to hospital for treatment to serious injuries. A teenage boy who was a passenger in the Seat Leon and a woman who was a passenger in the Audi Q5 were also taken to hospital for treatment. The road was closed to allow for enquiries to be carried out and re-opened around 7.10pm.

Article continues below

"Anyone with information is asked to contact Police Scotland on 101, quoting incident number 1186 of October 16."

News.title: Woman, 22, died of head injury after skydiving accident - inquest hears
News.content:
Woman, 22, died of head injury after skydiving accident - inquest hears

The experienced skydiver was found in a field and pronounced dead

View 2 Images Madeleine Trask

A 22-year-old woman died from a head injury after a skydiving accident, an inquest has heard. Madeleine Trask died after the incident at Langar Airfield on July 5, which saw police, firefighters and paramedics called to the scene.

‌



‌



The experienced skydiver was found in a nearby field and pronounced dead. An inquest into her death opened at Nottingham Coroner’s Court, hearing that a provisional cause of death has been given as a head injury.

‌



The hearing has now been adjourned, with a date for the full inquest yet to be set. Following Madeleine’s death, a statement released by Skydive Langar said: “We are deeply saddened to confirm that a fatal incident occurred at our centre today involving an experienced skydiver.

‌



View 2 Images The incident happened during a skydive

‌



“The entire team at Skydive Langar is devastated by this tragic loss. Our immediate thoughts, deepest condolences, and full support are with the skydivers family, friends, and everyone within our close knit community who has been affected at this incredibly difficult time.

British Skydiving - the national governing body for the activity in Great Britain and Northern Ireland - subsequently confirmed that a board of inquiry would be convened to investigate the circumstances surrounding the death.

The body said: “We recognise that incidents such as this can have a profound impact on those involved, those who witnessed the event, and the wider skydiving community.”

Article continues below

According to Madeleine’s LinkedIn profile, she started work in the café at Skydive Langar in May 2023 before working as a parachute packer from summer 2025 onwards.

News.title: Couple reveal secret as they win lottery again after record-breaking scratch card prize
News.content:
Couple reveal secret as they win lottery again after record-breaking scratch card prize

A Canadian couple for whom lottery luck has struck twice in the past six years have given some advice on how they managed to win so much money in a relatively short space of time

View 3 Images Angelina and Edward Lado have won the lottery for a second time (Image: @atlanticlottery/Instagram)

A Canadian couple spoke about what they think is the secret to their lottery success after they scored two wins in the space of just six years.

‌



‌



The duo, Angelina and Edward Lado, have won $675,000 (£357,000) on a scratch card they purchased for just $4 (£2.12) which would have been an incredible achievement on its own. And yet, in 2018, they won a massive $2.5m (£1.33m) from a game known as Multi Millionaire Scratch ‘N Win. This first victory was reportedly the record for the biggest win from a scratch card in history.

‌



When it came to this second windfall, the pair had an important choice when their numbers came up. Although Angelina and Edward won a lump sum, they also have the option of $1,000 (£530) a week for 25 years instead.

‌



As they celebrate their latest windfall, the pair have spoken about what they think their secret to success has been, and it’s something anyone can do.

View 3 Images Angelina and Edward Lado won six years ago (Image: Atlantic Lottery)

People reported that Edward said: “We play but modestly, especially now, but if you don’t play, you don’t win. We’ve purchased bigger tickets and not won anything significant on them and then Set for Life costs just $4 and we did.”

‌



Edward also spoke about how he felt when he realised the pair had won for the second time, explaining: “I thought maybe she was bluffing when she told me, I really couldn’t believe it… I told her to calm down and when I come home, we will see if it is for real.”

View 3 Images The couple's advice was the only way to win was to play (stock) (Image: Getty)

When asked what he would do with the money going forward, Edward said they were still “digesting the moment and letting it sink in” before making any firm decisions about what they would do next.

Article continues below

What they did, however, with their first win was incredibly moving. The couple had moved from South Sudan to Canada 11 years before their win in 2018.

The money they won allowed Edward to find his mother, a person whom he couldn’t remember, and it turned out she was in Uganda. At the time, he said: “I will go to find her and hopefully bring her here. It’s very hard for me to believe that is now possible.”

News.title: Pope Leo XIV lung cancer sparks warning from Vatican diplomat after 'game changer' diagnosis
News.content:
Pope Leo XIV lung cancer sparks warning from Vatican diplomat after 'game changer' diagnosis

Top diplomat and Vatican foreign secretary Archbishop Paul Gallagher said 'things have got to be sorted out' following the Pontiff's diagnosis and surgery last week

View 4 Images Pope Leo in images released by the Vatican three days after his surgery (Image: Vatican Media via AP)

A top Vatican diplomat has issued a warning about the Pope's health after saying Leo's diagnosis was a "game changer".

‌



‌



The Pope, 71, was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, last week following surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung on Tuesday. The Pontiff is due to leave Rome's Gemelli Hospital today after undergoing the procedure on Tuesday, and is set to return to public engagements by leading Sunday prayers from his apartments in Vatican City.

‌



His return will be welcomed by top officials, but the experience has left some urging caution and warning it will "make things different" at The Vatican.

‌



View 4 Images People praying under for Pope Leo outside the Gemelli hospital (Image: AP Photo/Alessandra Tarantino)

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

Major Pope Leo health update as Vatican issues statement after cancer surgery READ MORE :

Pope Leo urges Vladimir Putin for ceasefire in occupied Ukraine city days after Pontiff's lung cancer op READ MORE :

Speaking to the BBC, Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the British diplomat who has served as the Vatican's foreign minister since 2014, warned the Pope's health may have been taken "a little bit for granted". He told BBC Radio 4's The Sunday Programme, which is set to air tomorrow: "I think we were maybe taking him a little bit for granted."

‌



View 4 Images The Pope lead a mass in a makeshift chapel at the Gemelli University Hospital in Rome (Image: VATICAN MEDIA/AFP via Getty Images)

The Archbishop added the diagnosis would be a "game changer" as "things have got to be sorted out" when he returns to his duties. He said: "It's in some ways I think going to be a bit of a game changer after having the latter years of Pope Francis when he was in the wheelchair. And Pope Leo comes along and he's sporty and he seems to be in excellent health, and now we're told that he's not in excellent health and things have got to be sorted out."

Leo's predecessor, Pope Francis, was in and out of hospital during his last year as pope in 2025, having been admitted on February 14 that year for a polymicrobial respiratory infection. The infection later developed into severe bilateral pneumonia, asthmatic bronchitis, and bronchietactasis, all conditions of the lung. He died on April 21 at the age of 88.

Article continues below

View 4 Images Pope Francis suffered from several health problems towards the end of his life (Image: AP)

There was some secrecy surrounding his final months, which Leo has notably avoided in his approach to his own health difficulties. The current Pope announced last Sunday to the faithful gathered in St Peter’s Square that doctors had identified a nodule on his lung, and that it would be removed.

Since the surgery on Tuesday that confirmed the cancer diagnosis, Leo has given strong indications that he was recovering well, including by holding a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, meeting with top aides and celebrating Mass in a hospital chapel. Spare medical bulletins from his personal physician and surgeon likewise indicated a good post-operative recovery that had allowed him to carry on “normal daily activities completely on his own.”

News.title: Chancellor told boosting plane manufacturing in Budget could slash flight fares
News.content:
Chancellor told boosting plane manufacturing in Budget could slash flight fares

EXCLUSIVE: John Healey could help create the 'next generation' of air travel and deliver cheaper fares, cleaner aircraft and more accessible travel for the public, the industry claims

View 2 Images The aviation industry say investment now could help slash fares (Image: Ceri Breeze via Getty Images)

Boosting British plane manufacturing in the budget could help slash flight fares for holidaymakers, the Chancellor has been told.

‌



‌



Trade body ADS urged John Healey to help create the “next generation” of air travel, claiming it can deliver cheaper fares, cleaner aircraft and more accessible travel.

‌



The group, which represents 1,100 companies across the Aerospace, Defence, Security, and Space industries, said the sector already supports more than 113,000 jobs and generates £41.5 billion in annual turnover, but that this could soar even higher if the Government backs the industry.

‌



In their submission to the Government ahead of Mr Healey’s first Budget as Chancellor, they say investing now would help attract investment into UK factories and create jobs.

Kevin Craven, Chief Executive of ADS, the trade association for the UK's aerospace, defence, security and space sectors, representing more than 2,000 member companies, claimed it was a "pivotal moment"

He said: "Decisions on where the next generation of commercial aircraft will be designed and built are being taken now, and the UK must demonstrate it is one of the most attractive places in the world to invest and grow.

‌



View 2 Images The Chancellor has been urged to back British aviation (Image: Gary Roberts/SOPA Images/Shutterstock)

“These aircraft are expected to be 20-30% more fuel efficient, helping to reduce emissions, lower costs and make air travel more affordable for passengers. This represents a generational opportunity for the UK economy, supporting high-value jobs, investment and growth across the country.

"There is enormous opportunity to grow our sector but also high levels of risk to our current share of this global market place. We now need to see the Government back its ambition and give industry the confidence to invest.”

‌



The calls were backed by MPs from the APPG for the Future of Aviation, Travel and Aerospace, who urged the Chancellor to back British business and help create the jobs of the future.

Luke Taylor MP, Chair of the APPG said: “Our world leading aerospace industry is a key driver of economic growth and the Chancellor must use the upcoming Budget to back British aerospace with long term support for innovation and create a business environment that delivers investment.

“By working with industry to secure UK work on the next generation of single-aisle aircraft, from airframe structures to systems, power plant, undercarriage and advanced composites, the Government can deliver skilled jobs, investment and opportunities for businesses across the supply chain, as well as delivering more fuel-efficient aircraft, cleaner and quieter journeys, lower running costs and lower costs for consumers.

‌



“But that work will not come to Britain by default. We need a Budget that backs British businesses and supports them to build manufacture and deliver here."

A government spokesperson said: "This Government is leading a new age of British industrialisation, backing British businesses and British workers with the investment, skills and support needed to grow the industries of the future.

"Alongside action to reduce energy costs for manufacturers, we are creating more apprenticeship opportunities, helping more young people into work and ensuring businesses can access the skilled workforce they need to grow.

Article continues below

"As has always been the case, the Chancellor will set out the Government's plans at the Budget and we will not comment on speculation or proposals ahead of then."

News.title: More NHS staff sacked over attacks victims' records
News.content:
Further members of staff have been sacked by an NHS trust for inappropriately accessing medical records of the Nottingham attacks victims.

Nottingham students Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, and grandfather Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane, who was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.

In May, Nottingham University Hospitals (NUH) NHS Trust confirmed it had dismissed 11 members of staff and, in an update on Friday, said a total of 15 people had now been sacked as part of its investigation.

The families of Barnaby, Grace and Ian previously welcomed the action taken by the trust but called the development in May a "kick in the teeth".

Dr Manjeet Shehmar, medical director at NUH, said: "There is simply no excuse for accessing the records of a patient without a legitimate reason and I hope this sends a really clear message â we will investigate and we will take action.

"To lose a loved one in the way that the families of Ian, Grace and Barnaby have is heartbreaking enough.

"I am so sorry that they have had this further compounded by the actions of these staff members."

News.title: UK must protect against Russian 'hybrid attacks', ex-national security adviser says
News.content:
The government must do more to protect key infrastructure against "hybrid attacks" from Russia, a former national security adviser has told the BBC.

Lord Ricketts said more money should be spent on the defence budget, as well as improving the resilience of energy, transport and air traffic control.

He warned hybrid attacks were becoming "more reckless, more dangerous" and that people could end up being killed.

It comes after MI5 chief Sir Kevin McCallum said in his annual speech earlier this week that threats from foreign states, including Russia and Iran, had quadrupled in the last decade.

Lord Ricketts told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that ministers had to warn British people about what might be coming.

"Not only is [Russian President Vladimir] Putin trying to break morale in Ukraine, he's also trying to undermine morale in European countries," he said.

He said there had been a stark warning from the head of MI5 that there could be worse to come in terms of hybrid attacks in the UK or on other Nato territory.

Responding to a question about the impact of disruption by Russia, Lord Ricketts said: "I'm not saying there's going to be industrial war with tanks rolling across the north German plain.

"But yes these hybrid attacks are getting more reckless, more dangerous...people are going to end up getting killed somewhere."

Hybrid attacks tend to use non-military methods, such as hacking, in an attempt to destabilise a country.

Moscow is suspected to be behind many such attacks in Europe since the start of the war in Ukraine, but it has always denied involvement.

As well as cyber-attacks, hybrid attacks can include attempts at sabotage and efforts to spread misinformation.

Lord Ricketts's warning comes after US President Donald Trump blocked sanctions on Russia. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said the decision "only encourages him [Putin] to keep attacking" Ukraine.

The former national security adviser, who also previously ran the Foreign Office, said the UK's focus should be on putting more effort into the coalition of the willing, rather than attempting to act as a bridge between Zelensky and Trump.

"I don't think in Trump's current mood there is any influence Britain can have in the short term," he said.

A growing number of European leaders have warned that Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine.

Last month, Germany said Russia was responsible for a drone attack on an airport in Leipzig, in which an explosive failed to detonate close to Ukrainian cargo planes.

French President Emmanuel Macron warned in September that the threat of hybrid attacks by Russia against Europe and France had intensified.

News.title: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch
News.content:
Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder

Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.

Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.

Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.

"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.

"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."

Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.

News.title: Why people who have never smoked are getting hooked on vapes
News.content:
When vaping first took off at Gracey Mungulu's school, she was vocal about the fact she found it as repulsive as smoking.

"I literally used to tell people like, 'Er, why are you doing that?'" she says.

But Gracey says the habit became so common among her classmates that by the age of 16 she too had taken it up, even though the first time left her coughing rather than inhaling.

"The more you see it, the more you start trying it a bit more," Gracey says, "and then eventually I just got used to it and I was just doing it all the time."

Now 21, she buys a refillable vape every day, using it whenever her hands aren't busy with her work as a hairdresser and in a school.

Gracey is among the more than one million people in the UK who say they have never smoked but now vape, according to recent Office for National Statistics (ONS) survey data â and that number has risen year-on-year.

When vaping first came to the market it was seen as a way to help smokers quit cigarettes.

Vaping nicotine, a highly addictive substance, is less harmful than cigarettes, but the long-term effects are not yet clear, according to the NHS.

News.title: Not sure what to wear for Halloween? These outfits are set to be the most popular this year
News.content:
If you're still on the hunt for the perfect Halloween costume, then you might want to look to gargoyles, Freaky Nikki and Dolly Parton for inspiration - they are all predicted to be popular outfit choices for 2026.

"People don't necessarily want to look frightening - they want to look extraordinary," says costume designer Tamar Zaig, who runs a fancy dress hire shop in London and says she's seeing a "real appetite for escapism, glamour and a bit of dark humour" right now.

And as usual, the year's major film and TV releases, as well as news and pop culture trends, are also driving outfit choices.

So, here are some spooky ideas to try.

News.title: Two-week half terms: The school holiday no one can agree on
News.content:
Samantha Buckland is bracing herself for a tough fortnight. The single mum lives in Reigate, Surrey, and her seven-year-old son goes to a state school that has just introduced a two-week half term.

Buckland has two jobs: teaching medical students at a hospital in Brighton and working at a vintage shop in her home town. The 45-year-old receives universal credit and is worried about the cost of looking after her son while school is closed.

"What I'm trying to do is find out who I can get childcare from and work around that," she says. "I'd like to work, I need money. It's not cheap to live these days."

But money isn't Buckland's only concern. She's also trying to piece together the patchwork of childcare needed to cover the break.

There's a local holiday club, but it's only running for one of the two weeks, which Buckland says "parents are up in arms about". She'll also have to work at the hospital some days.

As a result, she's considering asking family to help, or even going to stay with a fellow mum so they can take turns with the kids.

News.title: Trial of German steakhouse heiress that sparked a huge spy scandal
News.content:
It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scandal in recent history.

Christina Block, heir to a popular chain of steakhouses, is accused of ordering an Israeli security firm to carry out the violent abduction of her children from Denmark, following a bitter custody battle with her former husband.

There are allegedly connections with at least two former secret agents, from Germany and Israel.

In the latest twist, investigators in the case stumbled across evidence that has led to Germany's former intelligence chief, August Hanning, being arrested this month for treason and espionage.

Hanning's arrest stunned the intelligence community. Although his case has nothing to do with the Hamburg trial, he has denied allegations of involvement in an earlier attempted abduction of the children.

There was enormous media interest in Germany when Christina Block and six others went on trial in a high-security courtroom in Hamburg in July last year.

Block House restaurants, specialising in steak and baked potatoes, are a feature of many German towns. Their success over the past half century has helped make Christina Block's father Eugen a multimillionaire.

Prosecutors allege that she and a family lawyer, Andreas Costard, organised the forcible abduction of two of her children, who were staying with her former husband, Stephan Hensel, at his home in Denmark.

They say the operation was carried out by a 36-year-old Israeli citizen named only as Jonathan G and five others.

The abduction took place during the New Year celebrations of 2023-24, as the two children and their father were watching a firework display, according to the indictment.

Prosecutors say several men ambushed and beat up Stephan Hensel, and dragged the boy and the girl, then 10 and 13 years old, into a car.

On the approach to the border with Germany, they are alleged to have changed vehicles, taped up the children's mouths and tied the girl's hands.

The group are then said to have travelled on to Baden-WÃ¼rttemberg in a campervan. Prosecutors say the children were held there against their will until their mother arrived to pick them up on 2 January 2024 and took them to her home in Hamburg.

News.title: Boy, 16, and 80-year-old man die in light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond
News.content:
A 16-year-old boy and an 80-year-old man have died following a light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond in Scotland.

Emergency services were called to the scene of the crash near the village of Drymen, in the Stirling Council area, at about 16:45 BST on Friday.

The boy and man were pronounced dead and their next of kin have been informed, police said.

Temporary airspace restrictions are currently in place over the area while the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) conducts its inquiries.

An AAIB spokesperson said: "A team has travelled to the accident site near Drymen, north of Glasgow, to make inquiries and gather evidence as part of the process of conducting a safety investigation."

News.title: Man jailed for Starmer-linked arson attacks is deported
News.content:
A man who plotted to carry out arson attacks on property connected to Sir Keir Starmer has been deported, the Home Office says.

Stanislav Carpiuc, 28, was one of two men convicted over the attacks, which took place in May last year and targeted a car and two houses.

The Ukrainian-born Romanian national was sentenced to two years in prison in June. The Home Office said he had been removed from the UK, without specifying where he had been sent.

The BBC revealed the attacks were ordered on behalf of Russia, with an anonymous handler known as EL promising payment to Carpiuc's accomplice, Roman Lavrynovych.

Lavrynovych, a 22-year-old Ukrainian national, was sentenced to seven years imprisonment in June.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "This was an abhorrent attack and the conviction and imprisonment of these men should send a clear message to anyone blinded by the promise of money from strangers. You will be caught and face severe consequences.

"This individual has now been deported from the UK," it added, referring to Carpiuc.

News.title: Nurse stole £750k from 99-year-old woman for cosmetic surgery and home improvements
News.content:
A nurse who stole Â£750,000 from a vulnerable 99-year-old and spent the money on cosmetic surgery and home improvements has been struck off.

Rebecca Louise Burwood exploited the resident who was living at Bryn Yr Haul Care Home in Mold, Flintshire, where she was deputy manager, for her own personal and financial gain.

She coerced the pensioner from 2017 to 2023 and also bought a car and campervan with the stolen money, as well as obtaining ownership of the woman's home.

A Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) hearing found Burwood's fitness to practise was impaired by reason of misconduct and imposed a striking-off order, meaning she will be removed from the nursing register.

The NMC hearing was told Burwood had a longstanding relationship with the woman before she moved into the home in 2018.

The panel heard the resident had no family members and was vulnerable after a fall. She was dependent on Burwood for friendship and social contact.

It found that, between 2017 and 2023, Burwood abused a position of trust and power, becoming the resident's lasting power of attorney, while also overseeing her care.

Burwood withdrew money from the woman's bank account, accepted ownership of her house and received thousand of pounds, which was used for her own benefit, including for building work and the purchase of vehicles.

Evidence presented showed more than Â£370,000 had left the resident's account over five years, with Â£160,000 of that from making large cash withdrawals at ATMs.

She also took the resident to the solicitors and got her to transfer the ownership of her Â£400,000 house.

The hearing was told there was "evidence to show Mrs Burwood used the funds for house improvements, utility bills and council tax", and there were "allegations that Mrs Burwood used some of the funds for personal cosmetic surgery".

She convinced the resident to pay Â£20,000 for a car and Â£9,000 for a campervan, which she said was purchased so the pair could go on days out.

Burwood claimed the work on her home had been so the elderly woman could live with her in the event of another outbreak of Covid - however it had been paid for before any Covid lockdown in the UK.

News.title: Why hasn't the UK had any named storms yet?
News.content:
With November already on the horizon the UK is yet to see its first named storm of the season.

Deep Atlantic lows responsible for more turbulent conditions have been steered away by dominant areas of high pressure.

This year the headlines have been about worsening drought rather than the impact of gales.

However, could this be the calm before the storms as the Met Office predict a growing chance that late autumn and early winter will turn wetter and windier as El NiÃ±o strengthens in the Pacific.

News.title: Husband calls for PM to intervene after wife detained in Egypt
News.content:
The husband of a woman who was detained by the Egyptian authorities has called for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to get involved and help with her release.

Eman el-Shazly, from Handsworth Wood, in Birmingham, was taken from her mother's house in Cairo two months ago, allegedly in relation to her sister's online activism.

Her husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, said that their family felt "very helpless" and that their "only possible solution" was for Burnham to "make a phone call to Egypt" to end the detainment.

The BBC has approached the Egyptian consulate in London for a response. The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said it was in contact with authorities in Egypt.

Moustapha said he had had "no contact whatsoever" with his wife, but had heard from her mother that her health had deteriorated due to a lack of food and medical assistance.

"It's not a five-star hotel, there's 30 individuals sleeping in a cell with one toilet and one shower," he said.

He told the BBC that his wife had travelled to Egypt to look after her elderly, sick mother, who had been undertaking 18-hour round trips to take food to el-Shazly's two brothers in detention.

News.title: DIY SOS to be 'rested' next year to save money, BBC says
News.content:
The long-running home renovation TV series DIY SOS will be "rested" next year in the light of "savings challenges", the BBC has said.

It will be replaced by a spin-off show featuring highlights from past episodes. Sources denied reports in the Sun newspaper the programme would be axed as part of a plan to make savings.

Presented by Nick Knowles, DIY SOS sees a team transform the homes of families who are facing severe illness, disability, bereavement or building disasters.

It was first broadcast in 1999 and is currently airing its 35th series on BBC One and iPlayer.

The decision comes during the corporation's drive to save Â£500m over three years. It has already cancelled several well-known TV shows including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind and Live At The Apollo.

A BBC spokesperson said: "In light of the BBC's savings challenges we have taken the decision to rest DIY SOS in 2027 and commission a new spin-off show instead from producers South Shore.

"DIY SOS Rebuilt My Life will revisit successes from the show's past and expand the brand on the BBC in a more cost-effective way next year."

News.title: Miranda's tears, joy and dance moves steal show as deadly boredom sets in on The Celebrity Traitors
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode six of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

For a show that likes to keep participants and viewers on the edges of their seats, gripped by suspense and skullduggery, it was ironic that Friday's episode of The Celebrity Traitors came down to which one of its stars would die of boredom.

The climactic final scene switched between a series of faces as we waited to see which of the famous faithful would... yawn.

Some dramatic editing and music attempted to build fevered anticipation, but this was a slow-motion, low-energy premise for a murder in plain sight.

The trio of traitors had been tasked with being as boring as possible, and yawned theatrically in one of the castle's communal rooms in the hope that their apparent fatigue would be contagious.

News.title: Third runway at Heathrow Airport would drive growth, Healey says
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey has said building a third runway at Heathrow Airport has "always been a case for growth" after Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to say if he backed the expansion.

Healey said airport expansion, including at Heathrow, had been "a big part of jobs and growth" in recent decades, speaking at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok.

His comments came after Prime Minister Andy Burnham was more sceptical, telling the BBC last month it was "a matter for London and Londoners".

Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves had put the airport's expansion at the centrepiece of an argument that Britain was open for business.

Earlier this week Heathrow's chief executive Thomas Woldbye warned that not building a third runway at the UK's busiest airport would be a "huge missed opportunity".

Healey told reporters: "The case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth."

He added: "The formal position now is that the consultation is closed, led by the Transport Department.

"We're reviewing those, and then further decisions and announcements will follow."

The third runway been debated for decades, with the project facing opposition from residents, politicians and climate campaigners.

Last year, Reeves announced the government-backed expansion, saying "a third runway is badly needed", and the government could not "duck the decision any longer".

Asked about the project in September, Burnham suggested it was an argument for London to decide.

"I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation," he added.

The Department for Transport has said it is "considering the appropriate next steps" following the public consultation on its National Policy Statement, which provides the basis for deciding whether to grant a new runway at Heathrow.

The airport's consortium of owners has said they need explicit backing from Burnham before the end of the year in order to proceed with the project.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme earlier this week, Woldbye said it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project.

He said he hoped the prime minister would "come along" with the project, adding that a third runway was "not just for Londoners".

"Benefits will be felt all over the country because our supply chain reaches all the way from the north all the way to the south of the UK," Woldbye said.

Heathrow serves more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average, if a third runway is built.

The project, which has an estimated price tag of Â£33bn, would see hundreds of homes demolished, rivers diverted and the M25 motorway rerouted through a tunnel between junctions 14 and 15.

The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has since suggested it would be delayed by four years to 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues.

News.title: Donald Trump’s White House is finally falling apart
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in
