Beyond the clashes at some demonstrations, Saturday has also seen widespread peaceful protests, with unions, teachers, healthcare workers and regular citizens taking to the streets.

French “yellow vest” protesters – who took to the streets in nationwide protests from 2018 to 2020 to protest rising fuels costs – have also signalled that they will join the protests.

The yellow vests have been “trying to make a comeback”, Birchard said, and this “seems to be the moment”.

Bruno Cautres, a researcher at the Paris-based Center for Political Research, told Al Jazeera that Saturday’s events are a “culmination of different mobilisations” including students, teachers, nurses, farmers, yellow vests.

He said the French population is frustrated by high taxes combined with a significant national debt and deficit that prevent the government satisfying their demands: “The French are asking themselves where are we going as a country? How are we going to get out of this budget crisis?”

President Emmanuel Macron appealed for calm on Friday, the eve of the protests.

“There is a constitutional right to protest and to express oneself,” he said in Brussels. “But this right comes with the need to respect. Respect for people, respect for property, and therefore a commitment not to insult or destroy.”

World.title: Why Trump’s latest White House press secretary lasted just five days
World.content:
Katie Zacharia is the shortest-serving White House press secretary after a rocky tenure, but she’s not the first to go.

United States President Donald Trump’s latest press secretary has been let go after just five days on the job, following a widely criticised first – and only – White House news conference and amid scrutiny of her credentials.

Trump told reporters on Friday that he believed the press had been harsh towards his new top spokesperson, Katie Zacharia, but that he had advised her to “reconsider” the role.

Shortly after, Al Jazeera and other media confirmed that Zacharia would be “transitioning out” of the position.

That made her the shortest-serving press secretary in US history – even shorter than the tenure of Anthony Scaramucci, the former White House communications director who was fired after 10 days on the job during Trump’s first term in office in 2017.

His sacking gave rise to the term “one Scaramucci” – or “a Mooch” – which journalists and White House observers use jokingly as a measure of time to predict how long Trump officials would last in their jobs. Now, a new unit of time – “one Zacharia” – is only half as long.

Recalling his own White House stint this week, Scaramucci wrote on X: “Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.”

Here’s what we know about Zacharia’s brief tenure:

Why was Katie Zacharia removed as White House press secretary?

The White House has not given an official reason for Zacharia’s departure, but it came amid mounting concerns about her competency and professional background.

During her first and only news conference on Tuesday, Zacharia appeared uneasy at the podium and struggled at times to get through her sentences. She fumbled her words while looking down at her notes, once confused the words “husband” and “president” and ended the briefing after 14 minutes, taking only three questions from reporters.



Scrutiny intensified after it emerged that Zacharia, who has a law degree and described herself as “an attorney”, had studied law at university but never passed the bar exam required to practice law in the US. She later claimed she had worked as a lawyer in China.

Conservative Fox News host Sean Hannity asked Zacharia during an awkward interview on Thursday: “Why didn’t you just say: ‘I never practised law’?”

Following news of her departure, Zacharia wrote on X that it had been “an honour” to work for Trump, calling him a “kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man”.

How was her one White House briefing received?

Zacharia, who took over from former press secretary Karoline Leavitt, was widely criticised as unpolished and unprepared during her appearance before the White House press corps on Tuesday this week, even by many of Trump’s allies.

During Hannity’s interview with Zacharia, he noted that she had been “widely panned” for her performance.

Conservative journalist and commentator Megyn Kelly said Zacharia needed “to present as a serious person”.

Jen Psaki, a former White House press secretary who worked under Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden, compared Zacharia’s troubled briefing to a comedy skit. “Maybe this whole White House press secretary thing isn’t really for Katie,” she said. “It’s not for everybody.”

As a fellow White House deportee, Scaramucci gave Zacharia some advice. “Speaking as the world’s leading expert on short White House tenures: turn off the news and go enjoy your family. In time you’ll realize that the Universe did you a major favor,” he wrote on X.

Who will take over White House press briefings now?

That remains to be seen.

The White House has not announced a permanent replacement, and Trump told Fox News he is “not in a hurry” to fill the role.

The vacancy leaves Trump without a top spokesperson as the US remains mired in a conflict with Iran and heads into crucial midterm elections next month.

How many press secretaries has Trump gone through?

Zacharia was the sixth person to serve as White House press secretary under Trump. He went through four of the officials during his first term and, so far, two in his second.

Zacharia’s predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, had held the position since the start of Trump’s second term in January 2025. She resigned in August to spend more time with her children.

Trump’s first-term press secretaries were Kayleigh McEnany, Stephanie Grisham, Sarah Huckabee Sanders and Sean Spicer.



McEnany and Spicer now work in media. McEnany hosts several shows on Fox News, while Spicer contributing to NewsNation and has launched his own podcast.

Huckabee Sanders currently serves as the governor of her home state of Arkansas, where she is seeking re-election on November 3.

Grisham left the press secretary position after less than a year in 2020 and became First Lady Melania Trump’s chief of staff. She resigned that role after the January 6, 2021 insurrection and has since become a major critic of the US president.

Which other Trump-appointed officials have been fired?

Zacharia joins a roll call of Trump administration officials to be pushed out during his second term.

Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece who was previously engaged to Trump’s son Donald Trump Jr, was asked to step down from her role earlier this week after reports emerged that she offered a political donor access to senior administration officials in exchange for money.

Earlier in the year, Trump fired Attorney General Pam Bondi amid controversy over her handling of files relating to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, which had become a growing political problem for the administration.

A month earlier, Trump ousted Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, after she was grilled in Congress over a $220m advertising campaign and her comments about two US citizens fatally shot by federal officers in Minnesota.

Mike Waltz was one of the first Trump administration officials to be removed during his second term. Waltz was fired as national security adviser in early May 2025 after he mistakenly invited a journalist into a messaging application in which he and other top administration officials discussed military attack plans on Yemen.

World.title: Child, four women among Palestinians injured in West Bank pogroms
World.content:
Attacks across occupied West Bank follow a religious edict by a prominent far-right rabbi permitting the seizure of Palestinian olives.

Share Child, four women among Palestinians injured in West Bank pogroms on social media

Several Palestinians have been injured by Israeli settlers, and farmers have been arrested by Israeli forces during Israeli pogroms across the occupied West Bank.

Four women and a child were among six people injured on Saturday when Israeli settlers attacked residents in Ma’in village in the Masafer Yatta area, south of Hebron, according to the Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS).

In the town of Deir Ammar, west of Ramallah, Israeli forces opened fire on farmers picking olives, forcing them to leave their land, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.

In the same area, Israeli settlers shot and injured two Palestinians. In the village of Tuqu, southeast of Bethlehem, Israeli forces fired on a Palestinian civilian vehicle.

‘Part of campaign’

In the village of Kafr Malek, northeast of Ramallah, settlers raided a farm at dawn and killed about 20 sheep, Mayor Najeh Rustum told Al Jazeera.

He added that Israeli forces had raided the village the previous night as well, firing tear gas canisters that ignited a fire in a house and caused material damage.

Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah, said settlers destroyed olive trees across the Beit Furik plain, east of Nablus, in the northern West Bank while Israeli forces arrested landowners and olive pickers.

In the village of Deir Jarir, east of Ramallah, she said, settlers under army protection fired live ammunition at farmers in the al-Hariq area to prevent them from completing the harvest and forced them off their land. Settlers also smashed the vehicle of international activist Jonathan Budlak in the village and threw stones at a farmer’s vehicle.

In the village of Burqa near Ramallah, Israeli forces and settlers prevented farmers from picking olives, Odeh said, adding that settlers attacked farmers in the Wadi al-Sha’er area, southeast of Salfit.



“What we see, whether it’s in Beit Furik, Kafr Malek, Deir Jarir or elsewhere in the occupied West Bank, is part of a campaign,” Odeh said.

She said settlers have become increasingly emboldened, publicly advertising attack campaigns on social media platforms.

“There have been 300 documented attacks since the beginning of October, and that has had a devastating impact on a very important season for Palestinian farmers,” she said, adding that danger comes from soldiers and settlers alike as military forces routinely intervene to protect settlers and attack Palestinians defending their land.

Prominent rabbi justifies attacks

The attacks follow a religious edict issued by Rabbi Dov Lior, a prominent rabbi for National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party and a leading authority among the Hilltop Youth, which is a religious Zionist group devoted to seizing Palestinian land in the West Bank.

In the edict, Lior stated that harvesting olives in the Holy Land is entirely permitted and carries an added virtue, given security dangers.

He wrote that Jews are permitted to harvest olives even in areas far from Jewish communities to publicly display ownership of the land and fulfil God’s commandment of conquering it. He claimed the land belongs to the Jewish people and Palestinians did not buy or rent it.

Odeh said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu downplays pogroms and no concrete action is taken to stop them.

“It is a matter of debate among politicians, but no one is stopping these settlers, whose names, locations and homes are known,” she said, adding that politicians permit the violence to continue because “it is politically expedient” and secures votes before elections on October 27.

World.title: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
World.content:
Donald Trump has blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens.

The sanctions were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by Trump in September.

But the US president issued an executive order on Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US "national interest", prompting a backlash from US lawmakers. Zelensky said it was unfortunate the US has decided to "completely disregard" the sanctions.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Ukraine then accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.

Trump and Zelensky have exchanged sharp words about one another. Ukraine's president declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The new US sanctions law took aim at Russia's economy, giving Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas â most significantly China and India.

It also included sanctions against senior Russian figures, including Putin, as well as Russian financial institutions and Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of vessels used to circumvent existing embargoes.

World.title: Teacher fought US school attacker before armed dad shot suspect 'multiple times'
World.content:
Some readers may find this article distressing.

A female teacher in the US state of Oregon tackled a teenage shooter who entered her classroom and tried to wrestle the gun from his grasp, police have said.

The teacher, who has not been named, threw her mobile phone before trying to disarm the 16-year-old on the floor of a classroom at Silver Rail Elementary in the city of Bend.

The attacker killed three children and a teacher after shooting his way into the building on Thursday.

He was shot dead by a father with two daughters at the school, who was driving past as the attack started to unfold and, armed with a pistol, ran in to confront the suspect.

Police said the attacker used to be a student at the school. His motive remains unclear.

He had been armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped, police said. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class.

"To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.

Police used a news conference on Friday to identify two of the four victims of the school shooting. They were five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.

Lambert's family said in a statement shared by the police that her goal was to be a teacher in the district in which she grew up and that she was "compassionate and had a huge heart".

"She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," they said.

Bryan Jolly, Summer's grandfather, said the family was devastated by his death.

"The whole thing is senseless, and a shock," he told the New York Times, saying his grandson was "was very bright and very mischievous and very fun-loving, and totally without fear".

The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said.

Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition.

World.title: Three men jailed for 158 years each for murdering Australian and US surfers in Mexico
World.content:
A Mexican judge has sentenced three men convicted of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their US friend Carter Rhoad to 158 years and nine months in jail each.

The Robinsons and Rhoad were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck on a secluded beach in Baja California in 2024 while they were on a surfing trip, the court heard during the trial.

The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the area is usually safe from the violence seen in other parts of Mexico.

The guilty verdict was handed down last week. Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom that her sons' murders had taken "the future we had imagined with them".

The convicted killers' full names were not given for legal reasons, meaning they were only identified as JesÃºs Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ãngel JesÃºs.

In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, JesÃºs Gerardo (alias "El Kekas"), was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery.

The court heard that the bodies of the victims were found dumped down a well with gunshot wounds to their heads.

At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in the beach town of Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings.

Ensenada has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers, but the chilling murders revealed how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico.

The only explanation the authorities were able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Their killings happened barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week, when their families were able to identify them.

Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California.

World.title: Brazil sees record fall in Amazon deforestation as key election looms
World.content:
Brazil's government says deforestation rates in the country's Amazon and savanna regions have fallen to record lows ahead of a presidential election run-off in which the rainforest's future is a key issue.

Left-wing President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva, when he assumed office three years ago, pledged to end deforestation by 2030 in the Amazon. It had surged under his right-wing predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro.

Lula will face Bolsonaro's son Flavio in the run-off on 25 October, with polls suggesting a neck-and-neck race. Flavio is expected to continue his father's policies if he wins, though he has pledged to fight organised crime in the Amazon.

Satellite data shows that in the year to July 2026, the deforestation rate fell by 41.8% in the Amazon - the biggest drop since records began in 1988. The fall in the Cerrado, Brazil's savanna region, was 23.8%.

The Amazon rainforest - the world's largest - is a crucial buffer in the global fight against climate change and 60% of it is located in Brazil.

World.title: Nursery owner in China jailed for life after hundreds of children poisoned
World.content:
A nursery owner and five members of her staff have been jailed after they were found to have poisoned more than 200 children with lead-tainted food.

Li Huifang, who operated the Heshi Peixin Kindergarten in Tianshui, in the Gansu province, was sentenced to life in prison for producing and selling toxic and harmful food, according to Chinese state media.

In July 2025, 247 pupils and staff at the nursery were found to have abnormally high blood lead levels after children began falling ill.

A report into the incident found that chefs at Heshi Peixin had used inedible paint to "enhance the look" of its meals to attract more students - despite the paint being being clearly marked as such.

In addition to the sentence, the Lanzhou Intermediate People's Court also ordered the confiscation of 500,000 yuan (Â£56,200; $74,700) of Li's personal assets, state broadcaster CCTV reported.

Nursery executive principal Zhi Jinglin was sentenced to 15 years in prison and fined 300,00 yuan.

Four other members of staff who worked in the nursery's kitchen received sentences of between six to eight years, according to state media.

The court found the four had been instructed by Li and Zhi to add toxic and harmful ingredients to food served to children and staff.

Food samples were later found to contain lead 2,000 times in excess of China's national safety limit.

The investigation into the poisoning began after 235 children from Heshi Peixin nursery had to be treated for lead poisoning after eating steamed red date cakes and sausage corn buns.

Investigators found that the red date cake and the corn sausage rolls had lead levels of 1052mg/kg and 1340mg/kg respectively, both of which far exceed the national food safety standard limit of 0.5mg/kg.

Lead poisoning is "particularly harmful to young children" and can "severely damage the brain and central nervous system", according to the World Health Organization.

Officials later found that dozens of provincial officials and hospital staff attempted to cover up the incident by tampering with blood tests and accepting bribes from a nursery investor.

China has since published a set of national guidelines for the provision of meals on campuses. Among the measures is the requirement for every new batch of food to be tested, and for flour, rice and cooking oil to be purchased from centralised procurement points only.

World.title: Rare pink diamond goes on display in France 100 years after amateur heist
World.content:
A rare pink diamond is going on display in France for the first time since it was stolen almost 100 years ago to the day - the last time it was shown to the public.

The nine-carat, pear-shaped gemstone known as the "Grand CondÃ©" was pilfered in an overnight raid on the ChÃ¢teau de Chantilly in October 1926 and concealed in a hollowed-out apple.

The diamond - one of few royal jewels to survive the French Revolution - was recovered a few weeks later when a hungry maid at the hotel in which the thieves were staying took a bite of the apple.

It will once again be on display in the CondÃ© Museum at the ChÃ¢teau de Chantilly until 3 January.

The museum's director Mathieu Deldicque said that while the apple story may sounds far-fetched, it was widely covered by newspapers at the time.

Deldicque has faced questions about whether the exhibition may be tempting fate, especially given the string of heists on European cultural institutions in the past 12 months, including the daring daylight robbery of jewellery from the Louvre museum in Paris.

While he declined to reveal to CNN how much the diamond was insured for, he noted that extensive academic study into the properties of the diamond had taken place to make it uniquely identifiable.

The results of this analysis, as well as previously unseen archive material about the gem's history and theft, form part of the exhibition, according to the museum.

Naturally occurring pink diamonds are exceptionally rare and often sell for tens of millions of dollars. The highest price ever fetched for one at auction was $71.2m (Â£53.6m) in 2017, according to Sotheby's.

The exact origins of the Grand CondÃ© remain a mystery.

It was first mentioned in 1740 in an inventory of Louis Henri de Bourbon, Prince of CondÃ©, drawn up following his death, the ChÃ¢teau de Chantilly said.

It then became part of the collection of Queen Marie-AmÃ©lie of Bourbon-Sicily, the wife of French King Louis Philippe I, and then her son, Prince Henri of OrlÃ©ans, the Duke of Aumale.

He bequeathed it to the Institut de France, which now owns the ChÃ¢teau de Chantilly, 50km (31 miles) north of Paris, along with thousands of artworks and manuscripts which became the MusÃ©e CondÃ© collection.

World.title: Pope discharged from hospital days after lung cancer surgery
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV has been discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital, just four days after an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung.

The 71-year-old walked unaided to his waiting car, stopping to speak to well-wishers.

The Vatican said the Pope will give the traditional Angelus prayer and blessing to a crowd in St Peter's Square on Sunday, as he did last week when he surprised the world by announcing the surgery.

On Friday, photographs were released of the Pope celebrating Mass and distributing communion in hospital for staff.

A statement from his doctors said blood tests and a chest X-ray showed "steady improvement" following his operation.

The surgery on Tuesday, which lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung. The results of further tests to check for any sign that the cancer has spread have not yet been announced.

The Pope also spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday, in their first call since June 2025. The Vatican said the call was to urge "dialogue and peace".

It came as Russia's bombardment of cities across Ukraine intensifies, with a growing number of civilian casualties and no sign of Putin being ready to halt the invasion.

The Pope also called for a humanitarian ceasefire in the Ukrainian city of Oleshkiy, occupied by Russia and under constant shelling, to allow people to be evacuated and for the urgent delivery of food and medicine. The BBC recently reported on residents there being forced to eat garden weeds to survive.

The Pope's schedule has been cleared completely until 20 October, so his reappearance in public so soon is a surprise and will be some relief for Catholics around the world.

Those close to the Pope said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America, planned for early November and which includes a visit to Peru, where he was a missionary for many years.

It is not yet clear whether he might be fit to travel or require further treatment.

World.title: Katie Zacharia leaving White House role less than five days into job
World.content:
Katie Zacharia will be leaving her post as White House press secretary, just five days after her shaky public debut.

US President Donald Trump told reporters moments before news of her exit was announced that he had told her "you don't have to do this if you don't want to" and "honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider".

Zacharia faced heavy criticism for her first press briefing on Tuesday, which lasted less than 15 minutes and included only three questions from reporters.

The 42-year-old spent the days following playing defence, fielding tough questions from news outlets about her credentials and preparedness for the job.

Trump hinted at her impending exit early on Friday afternoon, during an impromptu news conference in front of the Marine One helicopter.

"I said, 'Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don't need this'," Trump said.

"You don't have to be treated this badly," he continued, adding that he believed she had been treated "pretty nastily" by the media.

Hours later, she praised Trump as "kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and the most hardworking man" on X, writing that it had been an honour to work for him.

As the November midterm elections, which will decide who controls the US Congress, draw closer, Democrats are seizing on Zacharia's abrupt departure as a sign of failure in the Republican White House.

"The White House Press Secretary is gone. Maga extremists continue to fall apart," the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, posted on X.

Zacharia appeared visibly nervous during her inaugural White House press briefing, in which she read talking points from a notebook, answered only a few questions and referred to her husband as the president.

During the briefing, a reporter asked Zacharia - who had been called an attorney by Trump and others and who graduated from Pepperdine University's law school - about where she passed the bar exam. To practise law in the US, an attorney must be admitted to a state's bar association by passing a rigorous exam.

"When I was in China," she replied.

After intense scrutiny and digging by the media, Zacharia admitted on Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam.

She did say in a statement that she had practised international transaction law in China with the "appropriate credentials".

Questions about her legal credentials became a major talking point throughout the week, with Sean Hannity, from conservative-leaning Fox News, lobbing particularly pointed questions at her during an interview on Thursday.

When she said she had not passed the bar, he replied: "Why didn't you just say, 'I never practiced law?'"

Zacharia also described how quickly she had taken on the press secretary role - having been hired less than a week before her debut - prompting him to ask: "Am I hearing that you think the staff should have better prepped you?"

When she appeared on Fox & Friends, which Trump often watches, on Friday, Zacharia faced a similar line of questioning.

She told the show's hosts that she did not disclose to Trump that she was not an attorney because "those questions weren't asked", saying she was hired for a communications role, not a legal one.

Host Lawrence Jones then asked her: "Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?"

She avoided offering a direct answer but ended by saying: "I hope to be able to build the confidence and trust of everyone around me."

Zacharia's early exit is the quickest among Trump's White House press team.

Anthony Scaramucci left his post as White House communications director after only 10 days during Trump's first term.

"Records are made to be broken," Scaramucci wrote on X on Friday. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

Prior to her appointment as press secretary, Zacharia was a frequent fixture on right-wing US networks such as Fox and Newsmax.

She had a brief stint as a spokeswoman at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and worked as a communications adviser for Trump's social media platform Truth Social, according to her LinkedIn.

In her early career, Zacharia worked as an intern for the Republican National Committee and the White House Office of Political Affairs during the Bush administration in 2006.

World.title: Jigawa ADC crisis deepens as Rep candidate challenges replacement with Aregbesola’s aide
World.content:
The legal battle over the African Democratic Congress (ADC) primary election for the Hadejia/Auyo/Kafin Hausa Federal Constituency in Jigawa State has taken a dramatic turn before the Federal High Court as a party official, Mansur Kanya, wrote to the court denying any involvement in the disputed exercise.

The crisis began after Baffa Suleiman deposed to an affidavit under oath claiming he—and not Zakari Alhaji-Sidi—won the primary election conducted on 25 May 2025.

Mr Suleiman claimed that Mr Kanya acted as the collation officer who declared him the winner, an assertion Mr Kanya has refuted.

In a dramatic twist, Mr Kanya submitted an affidavit of facts directly countering Mr Suleiman’s claims, stating that he was in Kaduna State on a national party assignment when the Jigawa primaries took place and could not have collated the results, let alone declared Mr Suleiman the winner.

The plaintiff, Mr Alhaji-Sidi—popularly known as Zakari Kafin-Hausa—won the party’s primary election in May, but was subsequently replaced with Mr Suleiman, an aide to ADC National Secretary Rauf Aregbesola.

In Suit No. FHC/ABJ/CS/1655/2026, Mr Sidi is seeking the interpretation and enforcement of Section 29(1) of the Electoral Act 2026.

He named the ADC as the 1st Defendant, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) as the 2nd Defendant, and Mr Suleiman as the 3rd Defendant.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The latest court filing, prepared by Mr Sidi’s legal team led by Suleh Umar (SAN), was a reply to the counter-affidavits submitted by the 1st and 3rd defendants on 10 and 16 August.

Mr Sidi maintains that Certified True Copies (CTCs) of the ward and local government collation results, monitored and issued by INEC, confirmed his victory.

Conversely, he argues that Mr Suleiman relies entirely on a single document, Exhibit “BSS1,” which lacks foundational collation results from the constituency’s three local government areas, describing it as fabricated.

The filing contends that as custodians of the primary election records, the ADC failed to tender ward and local government result sheets to rebut the INEC-certified documents.

Invoking Section 167(d) of the Evidence Act 2011, Mr Sidi urged the court to presume that the defendants withheld these documents because the evidence would be unfavourable to their case.

To challenge the validity of Exhibit “BSS1,” Mr Sidi introduced Exhibit “AM2”—an official posting letter proving that Mr Kanya was assigned by the ADC to serve on the Kaduna State Appeal Committee at the time of the Jigawa primaries.

Mr Sidi also pointed to a congratulatory message sent to him by Mr Kanya, who wrote to the court to clear his name and support Mr Sidi’s position.

Addressing the ADC’s claim regarding discrepancies in his name, Mr Sidi clarified that ward officials recorded his victory using his widely known moniker, “Zakari Kafin-Hausa,” instead of his formal name, Zakari Alhaji-Sidi, which he used when purchasing nomination forms.

Mr Sidi executed an Affidavit of Reconciliation of Names (Exhibit “1”), arguing that the party cannot exploit an administrative error made by its own officials to deny him the nomination.

Citing Supreme Court and Court of Appeal precedents—including Amaechi v. INEC and Buhari v. PDP—Mr Sidi urged the court to give decisive weight to the independent statutory report generated by INEC as the neutral monitoring authority under Section 84(1) of the Electoral Act.

Mr Sidi is praying the court to discountenance the arguments of the 1st and 3rd Defendants, uphold the INEC-certified primary election monitoring results, and declare him the legitimate ADC candidate for the Hadejia/Auyo/Kafin Hausa Federal Constituency.

The matter has been adjourned to 22 October for hearing and the adoption of final written addresses.

World.title: 2027: G100 alliance talks not about consensus presidential candidate – ADC
World.content:
The African Democratic Congress (ADC) has confirmed it is in talks with other opposition parties about possible electoral alliances ahead of the 2027 general elections, but says the discussions are not aimed at producing a single presidential candidate.

The party’s National Publicity Secretary, Bolaji Abdullahi, disclosed this in a telephone interview with PREMIUM TIMES on Saturday, amid renewed calls for its presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, to step aside for Peter Obi of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC).

Mr Abdullahi said the talks, facilitated by the G100 opposition unity initiative, focus on electoral cooperation, including protecting votes.

“Discussions are going on, but it’s not about a single presidential candidate or any such thing,” he said.

“It’s about opposition political parties forming a common alliance towards the election.”

He explained that such cooperation could involve parties supporting one another in areas where they are politically stronger.

When asked whether the ADC was participating in the G100 initiative, Mr Abdullahi replied, “We are fully involved.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He cited recent visits by representatives of other opposition parties to Mr Abubakar as evidence of the consultations, adding that similar engagements had taken place with other presidential candidates.

However, he could not provide details of the progress made, saying the meetings were being conducted at the level of party chairmen and secretaries, and he had not been briefed.

He also said he was not privy to the work currently being undertaken under the G100 initiative.

G100’s broader agenda

G100 convenor Salihu Lukman has outlined a broader agenda that includes developing a framework for a common opposition presidential candidate.

Speaking in an interview on Channels Television’s Hard Copy, Mr Lukman said the initiative had brought opposition parties together, with their leadership now driving the negotiations.

He said the opposition summit held on 31 August agreed to establish five working groups, including one tasked with developing options for producing a single presidential candidate.

“One of the working groups is the one that will work on that single consensus candidate,” he said.

According to him, participating parties would nominate representatives to the group, which would operate under agreed terms of reference and develop recommendations to guide further negotiations.

Mr Lukman acknowledged that producing a united front or a single candidate was not guaranteed, but expressed confidence in the parties’ willingness to cooperate.

While the ADC emphasises electoral alliances rather than negotiations over presidential tickets, the wider G100 framework includes consideration of a common candidate.

It remains unclear whether the relevant working group has been formally constituted or whether the participating parties have adopted any recommendations on presidential candidacy.

What has happened since the summit?

The G100-facilitated summit, held at the Shehu Musa Yar’Adua Centre in Abuja on 31 August, brought together representatives of six opposition parties: the ADC, Allied Peoples Movement (APM), NDC, Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), Peoples Redemption Party (PRP) and Social Democratic Party (SDP).

The parties agreed to establish a Central Leadership Committee, alongside publicity and legal committees, to coordinate their activities.

They also proposed five working groups to develop recommendations on political cooperation, a common presidential candidate and other issues.

On 16 September, the Central Leadership Committee held its inaugural meeting and agreed on operational arrangements, including rotating the chairmanship among participating parties.

According to a statement Mr Lukman later issued, the parties were asked to nominate representatives to the committees and working groups by 18 September, with activities expected to begin later that month.

PREMIUM TIMES could not independently confirm whether all nominations were completed or whether the working groups had submitted their reports.

In a televised interview, Mr Lukman said consultations had expanded beyond the original six parties, though he did not name additional participants or announce a binding agreement.

He also said another working group would develop a minimum programme of action for participating candidates to subscribe to.

The proposed programme would draw from existing policy proposals rather than merge the parties’ manifestos.

Mr Lukman cited Mr Abubakar’s proposed domestic petroleum production subsidy as an example of a policy that could be developed into a clearer implementation framework.

Kwankwaso’s proposal

Opposition consultations have drawn fresh attention after Rabiu Kwankwaso, the NDC vice-presidential candidate, renewed calls for Mr Abubakar to abandon his presidential bid and support Mr Obi.

During an appearance on Channels Television’s Politics Today on Thursday, Mr Kwankwaso reaffirmed his position when asked whether he wanted the former vice-president to withdraw.

“Well, yes,” he replied, according to a report published by The Sun newspaper on Friday.

When PREMIUM TIMES sought clarification from Mr Abdullahi on Friday, the ADC spokesperson said the party had received no formal proposal for Mr Abubakar to step aside for Mr Obi.

He also said no when asked whether the ADC was participating in negotiations to produce a consensus presidential candidate or had authorised discussions that could affect its existing presidential ticket.

The differing accounts leave an important question unresolved: whether the proposed framework for a common candidate will become part of the formal negotiations among participating parties.

For now, the ADC has confirmed its participation in G100-facilitated talks, while its spokesperson says the discussions concern electoral cooperation rather than negotiations over presidential tickets. Mr Lukman has outlined a wider process that includes developing options for a consensus candidate, but no agreement on such a candidate has been announced.

World.title: Army explains arrest of Amnesty International’s reporter
World.content:
The Nigerian Army has attributed the arrest of Plateau State-based journalist Lawrence Zongo to alleged unauthorised access to a restricted military facility, citing security concerns over his use of Meta smart glasses.

Mr Zongo, a conflict journalist and volunteer reporter with Amnesty International, was arrested on 5 October at a military medical facility within Maxwell Khobe Cantonment, the headquarters of the Army’s 3 Division in Rukuba, Jos, Plateau State.

He had reportedly visited the facility to see relatives receiving treatment for injuries sustained in an attack in Bassa Local Government Area of the state.

Amnesty International raised the alarm over his detention on Wednesday, demanding his immediate and unconditional release.

The organisation said Mr Zongo had been held incommunicado since his arrest and that efforts to gain access to him had been unsuccessful.

“Amnesty International is deeply concerned by the arbitrary detention of our member in Plateau State, Mr Lawrence Zongo, who has been unlawfully detained incommunicado in military detention in Jos since Monday,” the organisation said.

“Mr Zongo must either be handed over to civil authorities or immediately released.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

However, the Army, in a statement on Friday, said Mr Zongo was arrested after allegedly entering the restricted facility without obtaining the required clearance from the relevant authorities.

The military also cited his use of Meta smart glasses, which it considered a potential security concern within the installation.

The Army disputed suggestions that pressure from Amnesty International and other groups forced it to release the journalist.

Circumstances of arrest and release

Conflict journalist Masara Kim provided additional details about the arrest and subsequent release in a social media post.

According to Mr Kim, Mr Zongo entered the military facility without clearance, wearing Meta smart glasses, and headed toward the hospital.

He said the journalist identified himself as an Amnesty International volunteer who had come to visit relatives receiving treatment.

Mr Kim added that military police questioned him after they were reportedly unable to verify his claim that the patients were his relatives.

These details could not be independently verified.

Mr Kim said some military personnel had vowed to charge Mr Zongo with espionage, but interventions by individuals and groups contributed to his eventual release.

He named youth leaders Dalyop Mwantiri and Ezekiel Bini among those who intervened, saying they appealed on the journalist’s behalf and undertook to produce him whenever required for further investigation.

According to Mr Usman, Mr Zongo was scheduled to be transferred to Abuja on 9 October but was released following the interventions.

He added that the investigation would continue and that the journalist could be required to assist with further inquiries.

The available information does not establish whether Mr Zongo was formally accused of an offence or whether the Army has concluded its investigation.

Amnesty raises due process concerns

Amnesty International has maintained that Mr Zongo’s detention raised serious concerns about his fundamental rights and due process.

The organisation demanded his release or transfer to civilian authorities, saying efforts to gain access to him had been unsuccessful.

READ ALSO: Army allegedly detains Plateau human rights defender

While the Army cited alleged unauthorised access to a restricted military installation and security concerns over the journalist’s smart glasses, questions remain about the legal basis for his detention and the circumstances surrounding his release.

The available accounts do not establish whether Mr Zongo was informed of the grounds for his arrest or granted access to legal representation during his detention.

The Army’s explanation and Amnesty International’s concerns highlight the need for clarity on the legal basis for the detention and the status of the investigation.

World.title: Nigeria’s health partnership with the US: National sovereignty and domestic financing, By Muhammad Ali Pate
World.content:
The MoU is legally non-binding, recognises the application of Nigerian law and permits either participant to discontinue cooperation under its terms. Implementation must remain within the country’s legal and institutional authority. Any citizen, journalist, researcher or civil-society organisation wishing to examine the instrument is encouraged to request a copy formally under the Freedom of Information Act, so that public discussion proceeds from the text itself and from the commitments and safeguards it contains.

For more than two decades, Nigeria and the United States have worked together on major public-health challenges. Through the US President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), the President’s Malaria Initiative, polio eradication, laboratory development, disease surveillance, health security and contributions through the Global Fund and Gavi, that partnership has saved lives and strengthened institutions on which millions of Nigerians depend.

Nigeria values this record of cooperation, but the next phase must serve a clear national purpose. No country of our size can indefinitely finance essential health services through external assistance. Our responsibility is to preserve the gains built with partners while expanding domestic financing, strengthening Nigerian institutions and ensuring that critical services remain available as the international financing environment changes.

A National Framework for Transition

That direction was established before the current bilateral arrangement. In December 2023, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu presciently launched the Nigeria Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative and the Health Sector Renewal Compact, bringing the Federal Government, the 36 states, the Federal Capital Territory and development partners behind a common reform agenda. Through the Sector-Wide Approach, fragmentation and duplication are being reduced, while public and partner resources are, for the first time, being aligned behind one plan, one budget and one report, with clearer responsibility for results and a deliberate transition towards national ownership.

When the United States revised its global health approach in 2025 under the then new Administration of President Donald Trump, its emphasis on country ownership, country systems and government-to-government cooperation converged with reforms Nigeria had already begun. The immediate task was to protect continuity of treatment and prevent reversals in HIV, tuberculosis, malaria and other essential services while strengthening the domestic foundations on which those services must ultimately rest.

The health MoU signed by Nigeria and the United States on 19 December 2025 was negotiated within that policy framework and should be understood in that context. Covering April 2026 to December 2030, it provides a managed transition from externally financed implementation towards stronger use of Nigerian institutions, government systems and domestic resources, while preserving essential services as Nigeria assumes a larger share of their financing and management.

Financing the Transition

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The financing structure under the MoU makes this purpose clear. Planned United States support is nearly $2 billion over five years and declines over the period, while Nigeria plans nearly $3 billion in additional domestic health financing. Nigeria’s contribution is not transferred to the United States; it remains in Nigeria and is applied to priorities determined by Nigeria, including HIV, tuberculosis, malaria, maternal and child health, laboratories, health workers, surveillance, commodities, primary healthcare and health information systems. There is no credible path out of aid dependency that does not require Nigeria to invest more of its own resources in the health of its people.

The Federal Government had already begun to translate this commitment into the budget. The 2025 federal health budget rose by nearly 60 per cent, increasing health’s share of the national budget to 5.2 per cent from just over 3 per cent. In presenting the 2026 Appropriation Bill, President Tinubu proposed ₦2.48 trillion for health and described health investment as 6 per cent of the budget net of liabilities. The 2026 Appropriation Act was subsequently signed into law with an aggregate expenditure of ₦68.32 trillion. Under the MoU, however, Nigeria’s co-investment is measured by actual expenditure: at least 6 per cent of executed annual Federal and State budgets for health, not by budget announcements alone.

The MoU is broader than medicines or vaccines. It covers outbreak surveillance and response, laboratory capacity and biosafety, frontline health workers, health commodities, data systems and strategic investments in service delivery, while supporting procurement reform and increased local manufacturing. Its performance framework includes viral suppression among people living with HIV, tuberculosis outcomes, malaria deaths, maternal and child survival, immunisation, and the speed with which public-health threats are detected, reported and controlled.

Sovereignty, Law and Public Scrutiny

Nigeria negotiated the framework through a whole-of-government process involving the ministries responsible for Health, Foreign Affairs, Finance, Budget and Economic Planning, together with relevant health agencies. The Attorney-General of the Federation reviewed and cleared it confirming that it did not undermine Nigeria’s national interest. The MoU is legally non-binding, recognises the application of Nigerian law and permits either participant to discontinue cooperation under its terms. Its implementation remains within the country’s legal and institutional authority. Any citizen, journalist, researcher or civil-society organisation wishing to examine the instrument is encouraged to request a copy formally under the Freedom of Information Act, so that public discussion proceeds from the text itself and from the commitments and safeguards it contains.

Regulatory Authority and Health Security

NAFDAC continues to exercise its statutory responsibility for medicines, vaccines and diagnostics. The MoU refers to NAFDAC’s existing regulatory-reliance framework, under which the agency may consider assessments by recognised stringent regulatory authorities while retaining responsibility for Nigeria’s own decision. Regulatory reliance reduces unnecessary duplication and accelerates access to quality-assured products; it does not remove NAFDAC’s authority to evaluate applications, inspect products and facilities, undertake risk-based testing, release vaccine lots and conduct post-market surveillance where required.

The same principle governs cooperation involving health data and pathogens. Nigeria must be able to detect an emerging pathogen, sequence it rapidly and share scientifically useful information when that serves public health. Requests for access remain subject to Nigerian law, data-protection requirements, scientific and ethical review and agreement on benefits arising from collaboration. Building domestic genomic-sequencing capacity, secure data systems and a national genomics repository strengthens sovereignty by enabling Nigeria to participate in global science from a position of competence. The bilateral MoU does not displace Nigeria’s position in the continuing multilateral negotiations on pathogen access and benefit sharing under the Pandemic Agreement.

Faith-based Service Delivery and Accountability

The MoU also provides that, to the maximum extent permitted by law, approximately ten per cent of planned U.S. support is intended for eligible faith-based health providers. The provision does not designate or confer preference on any religion or denomination. At the signing, the United States Ambassador acknowledged Nigeria’s Christian and Muslim traditions, making clear that eligible providers from both could receive support. This recognises the longstanding contribution of faith-based institutions to healthcare delivery, particularly in communities where access remains limited.

Beyond financing and service continuity, the framework changes how external support is managed and accounted for. Much previous assistance was implemented through non-governmental channels that delivered important results but sometimes limited government’s direct visibility over expenditure and made integration with national systems more difficult. To the maximum extent permitted by United States law, the new arrangement moves financing towards government-to-government and on-budget mechanisms, with audits, performance reviews and tracking of co-investment. This strengthens national oversight, reduces fragmentation and makes both countries accountable for their commitments.

The Measure of Success

The partnership will ultimately be measured in the lives and institutions it protects. People living with HIV must continue to receive treatment; deaths from malaria and tuberculosis must fall; mothers and children must receive better care; and outbreaks must be detected and contained faster. Nigeria’s laboratories, workforce, supply chains and data systems must also become stronger as Federal and State governments assume a larger and more durable share of the cost.

By 2030, the proper measure of success will not be how much external assistance Nigeria received, but how much more capable and self-reliant our health system became while that assistance declined. Nigeria will continue to work with the United States and other partners in pursuit of shared health, security and development objectives, while strengthening the domestic foundations on which lasting progress depends. The destination is clear: a health system financed increasingly by Nigeria, governed through Nigerian institutions and able to sustain better outcomes for Nigerians.

Muhammad Ali Pate is Nigeria’s coordinating minister of Health and Social Welfare.

World.title: Poland vs Nigeria: Five Players to watch as Flamingos begin World Cup campaign
World.content:
Nigeria’s Flamingos begin their quest for global glory on Saturday when they face Poland in their opening Group B fixture at the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup Morocco 2026, with several exciting young talents expected to play decisive roles in a contest that could shape the direction of both teams’ campaigns.

For Nigeria, the Asian Cup, where head coach Akeem Busari’s side demonstrated their attacking potential, offers a chance to build on their impressive performances. But Poland are no strangers to this level of competition, having reached the quarter-finals in 2024.

The European side secured their return to the final with a 2-0 w n the UEFA Women’s U-17 Championship play-off, courtesy of a brace from midfielder Zofia Buthe.

Nigeria also have their own match-winner in Harmony Chidi, who returns to the global stage with valuable experience from her previous edition; meanwhile, Queen Joseph and Oluwakemi Adegbuyi offer Busari additional attacking options.

With both teams eager to begin on a positive note, here are five players who could have a major influence on Saturday’s encounter.

Harmony Chidi — Nigeria’s captain with unfinished business

If Nigeria are to make a strong start in Morocco, much will depend on the influence of Harmony Chidi, the Flamingos captain whose pace, energy and goalscoring ability make her one of the most important players in Busari’s squad.

Chidi is not approaching this tournament as an experienced youngster discovering the demands of international football for the first time. She featured at the 2024 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in the Dominican Republic, where she scored against Ecuador at just 14 years old.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Two years later, she returns with greater responsibility, wearing the captain’s armband and carrying the expectations that come with being one of Nigeria’s most established attacking threats at this level.

Her recent numbers offer further encouragement. Chidi scored five goals during Nigeria’s World Cup qualifying campaign before adding three more during the WAFU-B U-17 Girls Cup in September. Those performances helped establish her as a central figure in the Flamingos’ preparations for Morocco.

However, her importance extends beyond the goals. Chidi brings pace and relentless movement to Nigeria’s frontline, qualities that can help maintain shape against a quick-attacking side.

Against Poland, her ability to exploit spaces behind the defence, make intelligent runs and turn promising situations into clear chances could prove decisive. Nigeria will need their captain to lead from the front, particularly if the European side begins with a compact defensive structure.

Her return also has a personal dimension. Having already experienced the World Cup as a teenager, Chidi now has a chance to show how much she has developed and help guide a new generation of Flamingos toward a deeper run in the competition.

For Nigeria, she is more than a goalscorer. She is the attacking reference point around whom much of their forward play could revolve.

Zofia Burzan — Poland’s chief attacking threat

If Nigeria have Harmony Chidi, Poland have Zofia Burzan, a midfielder whose performances during the European qualifying campaign have already shown why she deserves close attention.

Burzan was instrumental in securing Poland’s place at the World Cup, scoring both goals in the 2-0 play-off victory over England. The result booked the final European qualification spot and confirmed her ability to deliver in a high-pressure encounter.

Her influence extended beyond that decisive match. Burzan scored all four of Poland’s goals at the UEFA Women’s U-17 Championship and finished as the tournament’s top scorer. She has also contributed a goal and four assists for her club, Czarni Sosnowiec.

Those numbers underline the danger she presents to Nigeria. Although operating in midfield, Burzan has demonstrated a keen eye for goal and the ability to influence attacking moves rather than link play between the defensive and forward lines.

The Flamingos must therefore be careful not to give her too much time or space around the edge of the penalty area. If she is allowed to carry the ball forward, pick out passes, or arrive in dangerous positions, Poland could punish defensive lapses.

Nigeria’s midfield will play an important role in limiting her influence. By maintaining pressure on the ball, closing passing lanes, and preventing Burzan from receiving possession comfortably, Nigeria could disrupt Poland’s attacking rhythm.

The challenge is complicated by her proven ability to decide matches. Her brace against England was not merely a contribution to qualification; it was the difference between Poland reaching Morocco and missing out on the tournament.

Nigeria know they cannot afford to underestimate a player who has already demonstrated that she can deliver when her team needs her most.

Burzan is arguably Poland’s biggest individual threat, and how effectively the Flamingos contain her could go a long way toward determining the outcome of Saturday’s encounter.

Oluwakemi Adegbuyi — The WAFU-B MVP ready for the global stage

While Chidi provides leadership and World Cup experience, Oluwakemi Adegbuyi arrives in Morocco with momentum of her own after an outstanding performance at the WAFU-B U-17 Girls Cup.

The Robo Queens forward was named Most Valuable Player of the regional tournament after helping Nigeria win all five of their matches. She scored four goals during the competition and emerged as one of the standout performers in a team that demonstrated considerable attacking depth.

Her contribution makes her one of the players worth watching as the Flamingos move from regional competition to the more demanding environment of a global tournament.

Adegbuyi’s threat gives Busari another attacking option who can take responsibility in the final third. With Chidi likely to attract close attention from Poland’s defenders, the availability of another forward who can punish defensive mistakes could be crucial.

Nigeria will need to avoid becoming predictable in possession. If Poland concentrate on restricting Chidi’s space and limiting the supply to the captain, Adegbuyi could benefit from the openings created elsewhere in the attack.

Her movement, timing, and ability to make the most of opportunities will be key against a Polish side eager to start its campaign with a positive result.

The challenge now is to translate her impressive regional form onto the world stage. A World Cup opener carries a different level of pressure, and the quality of opposition can leave little room for hesitation in front of goal.

If Adegbuyi reproduces the confidence and attacking productivity that earned her the WAFU-B MVP award, she could become one of Nigeria’s most valuable weapons in Morocco.

Blanka Zając — Poland’s leader with a point to prove

While Burzan provides Poland with a proven goalscoring threat, captain Blanka Zając brings another important dimension to the European side: leadership and the responsibility of setting the tone for a young squad on the world stage.

Zając’s journey to captaining Poland at the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup represents a significant milestone in her development. In an interview with FIFA ahead of the tournament, she described the captaincy as a source of pride and spoke about the team’s ambition to progress as far as possible.

Her comments also reflected an understanding of how fine the margins can be in tournament football. Zając acknowledged that a single point, a goal or a small difference in the group standings could determine which teams advance.

That awareness could be particularly important against Nigeria, a side that arrives with considerable attacking confidence and will be keen to impose itself early.

As captain, Zając will be expected to help maintain Poland’s organisation, keep her teammates focused as the pressure rises, and ensure the team stays composed through the different phases of the contest.

Her leadership will be especially valuable if Nigeria enjoy periods of sustained pressure. Poland will need discipline and concentration to prevent the Flamingos from turning possession into clear scoring opportunities.

The opening match also gives Zając a chance to lead Poland into the tournament with a statement performance. The Europeans have reached the quarter-finals in 2024 and will want to show they can compete again after missing last year’s edition.

For Zając, the immediate task is to help her team navigate a difficult opening assignment. For Nigeria, limiting Poland’s ability to settle into the game and play with confidence will be an important part of their strategy.

Although Burzan may attract much of the attention because of her goalscoring exploits, Zając’s influence as captain could prove equally significant in a match where composure and collective discipline matter as much as individual brilliance.

Queen Joseph — Nigeria’s attacking spark

Another Nigerian forward who can influence the contest is Queen Joseph, whose movement and finishing make her a key option for Busari as the Flamingos seek to unsettle Poland’s defence.

The Fosla Academy attacker has already made her presence felt during Nigeria’s qualifying campaign, including scoring a hat-trick against Benin Republic. That performance highlighted her ability to capitalise on opportunities and turn attacking pressure into goals.

For a team hoping to make an early statement at the World Cup, having several players who can deliver in front of goal is a significant advantage.

Joseph’s inclusion among Nigeria’s attacking options gives Busari flexibility in how he approaches the game. The Flamingos can stretch Poland’s defensive line, create space through movement in the final third, and ensure scoring responsibility does not fall on one player alone.

The key will be how effectively Joseph combines with Chidi and Adegbuyi. Nigeria’s attacking threat could become particularly difficult to contain if the forwards interchange positions and force Poland’s defenders to make quick decisions about whom to track.

Joseph will also need to demonstrate composure when chances arrive. International youth tournaments often feature closely contested matches where one clinical finish can turn a winning start into a frustrating result.

Her qualifying performances have shown her potential. Saturday offers another chance to show she can carry that form into the biggest competition of her young career.

With Nigeria aiming to make a deeper impression in Morocco, Joseph’s contribution could prove just as important as the goals scored by the team’s more prominent names.

The battle that could decide the opener

Saturday’s meeting at the Mohammed VI Football Complex in Rabat gives Nigeria a chance to start their World Cup campaign on the front foot. Still, Poland’s experience and individual quality mean the Flamingos will need more than attacking ambition to secure a positive result.

The Nigerian trio of Chidi, Adegbuyi, and Joseph offer Busari different ways to threaten the Polish defence. Chidi brings pace, experience, and leadership; Adegbuyi arrives as a regional tournament MVP, and Joseph has already demonstrated her finishing ability during qualifying.

Poland’s hopes will rest in part on Burzan’s capacity to influence the game and Zając’s ability to lead the team through the pressure of a demanding opener.

For Nigeria, the challenge will be to combine their attacking strengths with defensive discipline, particularly when Poland attempt to use Burzan to create opportunities.

A strong start could provide the Flamingos with valuable momentum ahead of their remaining Group B fixtures against Puerto Rico and defending champions DPR Korea. With qualification at stake, every goal and every point could prove important.

The spotlight will fall on the five players, but the outcome will ultimately depend on which team executes its game plan better.

If Nigeria’s attacking talents can find their rhythm while keeping Poland’s key threats under control, the Flamingos will have a genuine opportunity to open their Morocco 2026 campaign with a statement victory.

World.title: Subsidy Return: International investors, markets have written off Nigerian opposition politicians as unserious, says Oyedele
World.content:
Nigeria’s Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, said on Saturday that international investors and markets have written off Nigerian opposition politicians calling for a return to the subsidy regime.

Mr Oyedele spoke on the sidelines of the World Bank/IMF meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.

The minister responded to questions about how the government hopes to balance the needs of the investment community with domestic concerns among citizens.

“The second point I want to make, and hopefully this will not be misinterpreted, is that, in having all those meetings (with global development and financial organisations, investors and market leaders), I concluded that the markets, including the domestic market—because that you can read from the capital markets—and the international markets, have largely, largely written off the opposition in Nigeria as being unserious. That is why they have not priced in the proposed return of subsidy,” Mr Oyedele said.

“And the reason why you know what I’m saying is right is, God forbid a bad thing, if Mr President says today, ‘we are considering subsidy’, you will see the reflection in price. So maybe it’s good that the international community and the domestic capital markets are aware of who is sincere with Nigerian people and what direction of travel they should take.”

Nigeria has introduced a series of reforms the government said focused on fixing the economy’s structure. However, the impact has been enormous for many Nigerians grappling with the cost-of-living crisis. The government introduced reforms in the foreign exchange market, abolished what it termed a wasteful, corruption-ridden subsidy regime amid fiscal pressures, and institutionalised tax reforms.

While the Nigerian government, led by President Bola Tinubu, has defended its economic policy of subsidy removal as critical to the nation’s fiscal survival, opposition politicians—such as Atiku Abubakar of the ADC and Peter Obi of the NDC—have canvassed for and promised a return to different subsidy arrangements if elected into power.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Opposition

In August, Atiku said he believed a country’s progress and wealth should be measured by citizens’ ability to buy goods and services, not by how much revenue the government collects.

“On the question of subsidy, my position has not changed and will not change: I will restore it! A nation as blessed as ours has no business abandoning its citizens to hardship. Nigeria is rich enough to look after her own,” the former vice president vowed.

Mr Obi, who on his part had earlier warned that subsidy was an “organised crime” that would be removed, made a U-turn in a BBC interview on Tuesday, 6 October, saying he would restore the subsidy if elected president.

He argued that the subsidy regime’s major problem was the corruption surrounding its implementation.

“I’ll remove the corruption and retain the subsidy,” he said.

Mr Obi also explained how he intended to tackle corruption, arguing that his anti-corruption strategy would centre on the president’s conduct and that of his immediate family.

“If you are not stealing, if you are not involved, your wife and family are not involved, you reduce it by 50 per cent,” the presidential candidate said.

Messrs Obi and Atiku are the leading opposition figures in Nigeria’s next general elections scheduled for January 2027. Previously, both opposition figures had been unequivocal about removing the petrol subsidy.

PREMIUM TIMES reported earlier on Saturday that Mr Oyedele said there will be no return to subsidy regimes, adding that the 30-day retail margin discount introduced by the government isn’t a subsidy arrangement.

“And let me be clear as well, this was a recurring question almost through all our engagements, but also with the rating agencies, with the investors, and the multilateral institutions. Every time they ask, are you reversing your plans? Are you bringing back subsidies? Let me be clear, there will be no return to fuel subsidies or multiple exchange rates,” he said.

World.title: ‘Things not as bad as people claim; Tinubu is fixing Nigeria’ — Jide Kosoko
World.content:
Veteran actor Jide Kosoko defended President Bola Tinubu’s administration amid criticism of the country’s economic situation, saying it is not as bad as critics portray.

The 72-year-old actor made the remarks during an interview on “Talk To B”, a podcast hosted by his colleague, actress Biola Adebayo. The video was posted on YouTube on Friday night.

He said Mr Tinubu was making strenuous efforts to address the country’s problems.

Kosoko, an open supporter of the president and the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC), also argued that the current administration was facing criticism for problems inherited from previous governments.

He said: “People don’t queue to make money; everybody works for their money and business. Things are not as bad as some people made us understand. People make money here and there. Some people might still be unlucky, but that doesn’t mean their time will not come. It is not turn by turn. You can have your money today; my own time can come today too. I need not wait for you. It all depends on what I do and what you do.

“The situation of things now is because the country’s previous governments really did not plan towards the population that was increasing. That was the main problem. They didn’t prepare enough for the gradual population increase. If they had met these challenges, we might not have so many problems on the ground, which Bola Ahmed Tinubu is now fixing. He’s now fixing the country.”

Hunger

Furthermore, the actor argued that some Nigerians complaining about hunger had no meaningful source of livelihood before Mr Tinubu assumed office.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He added that government policies had changed annually even before Mr Tinubu became president, but successive administrations had failed to manage the changes effectively.

“When you see people saying, I am hungry. Go and check the majority of those people saying that. Before Tinubu came, what were they doing?

“What were they eating? Every year, things change. Those that we understand, we understand. Those that we abuse, we abuse them. I don’t care”, said Kosoko.

Subsidy

Kosoko attributed Nigeria’s present predicament partly to previous governments’ reluctance to end the subsidy regime.

He conceded that his generation’s leaders failed to remove the subsidy, worsening the country’s situation. However, he noted that the same generation was now leading efforts to put things right.

He added that Nigerians would have to confront certain difficulties collectively to overcome the challenges.

“The free money being used to satisfy you and me needs to be taken back for us to face reality. The reality is that we are not buoyant enough to start enjoying what we are enjoying. We still have quite a few other things to do. If the subsidy were not removed and fuel prices were down, you would still spend the excess you pay now on necessary things.

“You are still going to use those things you could have saved from the cost of fuel for students’ school fees, to ensure your environment is good. Your business is moving. This government has taken some of those things from you. Look at NELFUND, students’ loan. If the loan is not given, whatever you will have made will go into that school for your children. It has been taken off you.”

Kosoko called on students and other beneficiaries of the Tinubu administration’s policies to share their experiences and let the citizens know the impact of the government’s programmes.

Policies

He said Nigerians should not expect the government to distribute rice, yams, and other foodstuffs directly to their homes to secure their support.

The actor admitted that the country had yet to overcome its economic challenges but insisted that the administration had introduced policies that were making a difference and attracting investment from business owners.

He appealed to Nigerians to remain patient as the country rebuilds, saying he believed the president was on the right track.

“If people like Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala confirm that we are on the right track. She has nothing to gain from such a statement. Then, we are on the right track. Many leaders in the Western world, and many people, are now partnering with Nigeria on investments and similar initiatives. Those are the things that will help us in the few periods we have left.

“The suffering we should have suffered in the past is what we’re all suffering now. If our generation is still helping ensure that this generation still enjoys it, we have little time left. But most importantly, don’t forget we have generations coming. We need to face it once and for all. It is a difficult time—no doubt about it. But we need to face it once and for all. Fix the country”, said the actor.

“Give him a second term”

Kosoko urged Nigerians to re-elect Mr Tinubu in the next presidential election, arguing that the opposition parties had little to offer compared with the incumbent.

He said Mr Tinubu understood the difficulties Nigerians faced and was open to criticism of his administration.

According to Kosoko, such criticism would help the government identify outstanding challenges and address areas that required improvement.

He added that the president had invested in developing people, some of whom had gone on to mentor others and prepare them for leadership roles.

“Let’s allow the man to finish his job. He’s doing well. Regardless of what his opponents are saying, and at any rate, there is nothing he is doing that is bad before them. They want to rubbish what he is doing so you will think they have stocks, but unfortunately, he is already there doing what he understands. I’ll keep letting people know we still need to give the president a chance to finish what he is doing.

“My appeal is this, please, my people, let’s try and allow Mr President and his team to finish what they started. Honestly, I bet we will all laugh at the end of the day. Then the problem will be, after 2031, who takes over? Because Bola Ahmed Tinubu is going now. By the time he finishes, whoever takes over must be ready for the same strong challenge to keep it moving.

“My appeal is this. He will take us out of this mess. He is only cleaning up people’s mess. We should know. If we don’t cooperate, let it happen, and join in enduring this pain, we won’t reach the promised land. But by God’s grace, we will get to the promised land.”

World.title: INTERVIEW: How Johnvents is turning Nigeria’s cocoa challenges into a global agribusiness
World.content:
Over the years, Johnvents, a subsidiary of Capitalsage Holdings, has leveraged Nigeria’s agricultural potential to develop an integrated agribusiness spanning commodity trading, agro-processing and consumer products. Its portfolio includes chocolate products, cashew kernels, soybean oil, soybean meal, animal feed and bottled water, among others.

In this interview with PREMIUM TIMES, John Alamu, founder and group managing director of Capitalsage Holdings, discusses how Johnvents is transforming Nigeria’s agribusiness landscape through investments in cocoa and cashew processing, vegetable oil production, animal feed manufacturing and other value-added products.

Mr Alamu discusses the experiences that inspired his entrepreneurial journey, the challenges of accessing finance and markets, and the company’s efforts to improve cocoa quality through farmer training, sustainable practices, and access to improved seedlings. He also highlights the need to expand domestic cocoa production, replace ageing cocoa trees and strengthen agricultural processing to reduce Africa’s dependence on raw commodity exports.

Excerpt

PT: What motivated you to go into cocoa-product manufacturing?

Mr Alamu: I started my career at the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) in Ibadan. I am also the proud son of a teacher who taught agriculture, and I graduated from the Federal University of Agriculture, Abeokuta. So, when you look at my family background, education and career, you can see that agriculture has always been part of my journey. I began my career at IITA, a research institute, as a monitoring and evaluation specialist. This allowed me to work directly with farmers. At the time, we were not working specifically on cocoa. We worked with farmers cultivating cassava, maize and other crops.

Through our research, farmers repeatedly identified several challenges, but two consistently stood out: access to finance and access to markets. The response to these challenges was often more research, and the cycle continued. I decided not to see these two major problems in the agricultural sector merely as challenges. Instead, I saw them as opportunities to explore. I had several ideas about how to take advantage of these opportunities and turn them into viable businesses. I saw them as ventures I could pursue, and I believe that’s how the company name, Johnvents, came about. Our initial business focused on training farmers in good agronomic practices, buying their produce, and selling it to the market.
