World.title: Egypt’s president says country ready to defend Saudi Arabia ‘if requested’
World.content:
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Saturday said Egypt was ready to defend Saudi Arabia “if requested”, as fighting flares between the kingdom and Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.

Since Yemen’s war reignited in July, the Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi targets, including energy facilities and Riyadh’s international airport, where 13 people were killed in a single attack last week.

The Houthis have also blockaded the Bab al-Mandab Strait, piling pressure on energy exports as Iran presses its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.

Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian military academy, Sisi said Egypt was “not looking for a role to play” in regional conflicts, but added that it was “inconceivable” for Cairo to stand by while Saudi Arabia was “harmed or its security and stability threatened”.

“Egypt, of course, with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, will carry out any measure to protect you or defend you,” he said.

He added that any deployment would require parliamentary approval and said he hoped lawmakers would convene in an emergency session to grant authorisation “if it is requested of us”.

“I’m not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone,” Sisi said. “We are speaking only about defence.”

During a visit to Egypt last month, de facto Saudi leader Mohammed bin Salman and Sisi called for free and secure navigation in the Red Sea, a vital trade route.

The conflict with the Houthis poses risks not only to Saudi Arabia’s security and energy exports, but also to Egypt, where disruption to Red Sea shipping could further reduce revenues from the Suez Canal, a key source of foreign currency.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said last month that Egypt’s Suez Canal lost about $11 billion in revenues since the Houthis began attacking commercial vessels following Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack on Israel.

Despite its longstanding military ties with Gulf states, Egypt has not joined the Mecca agreement, a mutual defence pact signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan in August, with Cairo generally favouring diplomacy over participation in regional military alliances.

Saudi Arabia has long been a key backer of Egypt, providing financial support after the 2013 ouster of Islamist late president Mohammed Morsi and during subsequent economic crises.

World.title: JAMB moves to rescue graduates stuck for years over NIN data mismatch
World.content:
Professor Segun Aina

… unveils new service

By Joseph Erunke, Abuja

Thousands of Nigerian graduates who have been unable to participate in the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) scheme for years because of discrepancies between their Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) records and National Identification Number (NIN) details may soon get relief, as JAMB prepares to introduce a service to align their biodata.

The initiative is part of measures by the examination body to remove administrative bottlenecks that have left graduates stranded despite completing their university education.

JAMB Registrar, Prof. Segun Aina, disclosed this in Abuja while receiving a delegation from Veritas University, Abuja, led by its Vice-Chancellor, Rev. Fr. Professor Hyacinth Ichoku.

Aina said the new NIN alignment service would enable eligible candidates to update their biodata to match their official identity records, potentially clearing a major obstacle preventing affected graduates from proceeding to NYSC.

He said the board had identified cases of graduates who completed their studies four or five years ago but remained unable to participate in the national service scheme because their personal details in JAMB’s records did not match those registered with the National Identity Management Commission.

The registrar estimated that thousands of candidates could be affected, describing the initiative as part of his administration’s commitment to reducing the difficulties students and graduates encounter while dealing with the board.

“I am pleased to announce that today we will be formally launching an NIN alignment service that will allow candidates to change their biodata to match their official identity and that will unlock the possibility of NYSC for thousands of people,” he said.

Aina, who described his mission at JAMB as one of building trust and reducing trauma, said the board was leveraging technology to resolve problems that had previously prevented candidates from accessing its services.

He added that candidates who had lost access to their registered email addresses or telephone numbers could now make changes and regularise their relationship with the board, unlike in the past when such situations could prevent them from carrying out transactions.

The registrar also urged universities to cooperate with JAMB in regularising admissions, warning that candidates admitted outside the board’s Central Admissions Processing System remained a particularly difficult challenge.

He said such candidates might have completed their studies but could still face recognition and documentation problems because their admissions were not processed through the approved central system.

Beyond the planned NIN alignment service, Aina disclosed that JAMB was considering incorporating life skills and critical-thinking assessments into the Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination (UTME) to give universities a broader basis for selecting candidates.

He said the proposed reform was intended to move admission decisions beyond academic performance alone and recognise candidates with practical abilities, sound reasoning and other competencies essential for success in higher education.

According to him, the board had established a committee to examine how the additional assessment components could be integrated into the UTME.

Aina argued that candidates who had already been assessed in their subject knowledge at the ordinary-level stage might not need to be evaluated solely on the same basis during the admission process.

He said the proposed approach would give universities greater flexibility to identify applicants whose critical-thinking and life-skills performance demonstrated their suitability for particular courses, even where their conventional UTME scores fell slightly below the institutions’ usual cut-off marks.

“We should be able to find institutions that will say our cut-off for this course is 200, but we will take 190 if you score over 80 per cent in the critical-thinking and life-skills component of the examination,” he said.

The registrar noted that some candidates might not be outstanding academic performers under conventional assessment methods but could possess other abilities that made them worthy of admission consideration.

He said the proposed reform would promote a more inclusive admission process by recognising candidates’ all-round capabilities rather than relying exclusively on their academic performance on examination day.

The initiative, he added, would require collaboration between JAMB and tertiary institutions to ensure that the proposed assessment components served as useful tools for admission decisions.

Aina, however, expressed concern over candidates admitted into tertiary institutions outside the central admissions system, saying the board had yet to find a solution for many who had completed their programmes but were not recognised in its records.

He described the situation as a serious challenge, noting that the consequences of administrative decisions in the admission process could affect the future of young Nigerians.

“The responsibility entrusted to you is a big one. It is not just one person that you tell to go away and come back; it is a life that can be destroyed by the work that you do,” he said.

He urged university administrators to work closely with JAMB to ensure that admissions were properly processed and documented, thereby preventing students from encountering difficulties years after graduation.

The registrar said his administration would continue to explore technology-driven solutions to eliminate avoidable obstacles and improve candidates’ experiences with the board.

He stressed that the objective was not to introduce disruptive policy reversals but to improve the implementation of existing policies and make JAMB’s operations more responsive to the needs of students.

Earlier, the Vice-Chancellor of Veritas University, Rev. Fr. Professor Hyacinth Ichoku, congratulated Aina on his appointment and pledged the institution’s cooperation with the examination body.

Ichoku said the university’s delegation visited to formally welcome the new registrar and express its support for his national assignment.

He said Veritas University was committed to maintaining a productive relationship with JAMB to strengthen admission processes and advance higher education in Nigeria.

The vice-chancellor also informed Aina of the forthcoming Pan-African University Debating Championship, which Veritas University is hosting with the endorsement of the Federal Ministry of Education, and invited him to attend.

Ichoku said students of the university had continued to distinguish themselves in national and international competitions, particularly in sports, debating and technological innovation.

He said the students’ achievements reflected the institution’s commitment to developing talent and equipping young Nigerians with skills that could make them competitive beyond the classroom.

World.title: 4 Asian countries Nigerians can visit without applying for visa before travel
World.content:
File image.

Nigerian passport holders have a limited number of options for travelling to Asia without completing a traditional visa application before departure. However, some destinations offer visa-on-arrival facilities, allowing eligible visitors to obtain entry permits at designated airports.

According to available 2026 travel information, the Maldives, Lebanon, Timor-Leste and Cambodia are among the Asian destinations reported to offer Nigerian travellers alternative entry arrangements. The conditions differ by country, and travellers should confirm their eligibility before booking flights.

Here are four destinations worth considering.

1. Maldives

The Maldives is an island country in the Indian Ocean, known for its white-sand beaches, turquoise waters and luxury resorts.

Nigerian passport holders are reported to be eligible for a tourist visa on arrival, meaning they do not generally need to obtain a tourist visa from a Maldivian embassy before travelling.

Visitors should prepare a valid passport, accommodation details, a return or onward ticket and evidence of sufficient funds, as required by the immigration authorities.

The Maldives is an option for Nigerians seeking a beach holiday, honeymoon or short leisure trip. Travellers should confirm the current requirements with Maldives Immigration before departure.

2. Lebanon

Lebanon, located on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean Sea, combines historic sites, mountain scenery and a distinctive food culture.

According to the Lebanese Consulate in Lagos, Nigerian passport holders are eligible for a free visa on arrival at Beirut Rafic Hariri International Airport. The visa is valid for one month and may be extendable, subject to the applicable conditions.

Travellers are advised to carry a passport valid for at least six months beyond their intended stay, a return flight reservation and proof of accommodation.

Before travelling, Nigerians should also check current security advisories and confirm that entry arrangements remain in effect.

3. Timor-Leste

Timor-Leste, also known as East Timor, is a Southeast Asian country occupying the eastern half of the island of Timor.

Its customs authority states that visitors can generally obtain a visa on arrival when entering by air or sea, subject to the applicable requirements. The published tourist visa fee is US$30.

Travellers should have a passport valid for at least six months, a return or onward ticket, accommodation arrangements and evidence of sufficient funds.

Nigerians planning to visit should confirm the current admission requirements with Timor-Leste’s authorities before booking their journey.

4. Cambodia

Cambodia is a Southeast Asian destination known for Angkor Wat, historic temples, cultural attractions and the capital city, Phnom Penh.

Some travel guides list Cambodia among destinations where Nigerian passport holders may obtain a visa on arrival. However, Cambodia’s official e-visa portal also offers an online tourist visa, with a published fee of US$30 and a stated processing time of three business days.

Because the available information does not conclusively establish that Nigerian ordinary passport holders currently qualify for visa on arrival, travellers should verify their eligibility directly with Cambodian immigration authorities before departure. If a prior e-visa is required, Cambodia should not be described as a destination that Nigerians can visit without applying for a visa beforehand.

World.title: Nigeria’s poor population may be world’s largest, says EU envoy
World.content:
Gautier Mignot, EU Ambassador to Nigeria and ECOWAS.

…commits €45m aid

By Folarin Kehinde

The European Union (EU) Ambassador to Nigeria and the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), Gautier Mignot, has said Nigeria probably has the highest number of people living below the poverty threshold globally, describing poverty as one of the country’s biggest challenges.

The envoy spoke in Abuja over the weekend at the 2026 International Day for the Eradication of Poverty, where he called for sustained efforts by the Federal Government, development partners and other stakeholders to address the country’s poverty crisis.

“Today, Nigeria is probably the country in the world with the highest number of people living under the poverty threshold,” he said.

Mignot also disclosed that the European Union had committed nearly €45m in humanitarian assistance to Nigeria in 2026, particularly to support conflict-affected and crisis-prone areas.

He described poverty as a major concern for Nigeria’s international partners, stressing that it required urgent attention and sustained commitment in the years ahead.

Mignot cited figures indicating that 133 million Nigerians were living in multidimensional poverty in 2022, adding that estimates from different sources suggested the situation had worsened since then.

He said the EU’s humanitarian assistance was being provided through the European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations, with particular attention to communities affected by conflict and other crises.

“Through the European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations, ECO, the European Union has committed again this year almost 45 million euros for humanitarian assistance in Nigeria, particularly in conflict-affected and crisis-prone areas”.

According to him, the EU is working with the Nigerian government, humanitarian organisations, development partners and local communities to ensure that emergency assistance is linked to long-term resilience and sustainable solutions.

He explained that humanitarian interventions address immediate needs, while poverty reduction programmes focus on creating lasting pathways out of poverty.

Speaking on the theme of the event, United for Peace and Human Rights, Safe Homes for All, the ambassador said meaningful poverty reduction was impossible without peace, security, dignity and respect for human rights.

He added that households unable to meet their basic needs could hardly feel secure or fully enjoy their fundamental rights.

Mignot acknowledged the Federal Government’s efforts to tackle poverty through social investment programmes, targeted cash transfers, livelihood support and measures to strengthen social protection systems.

He listed the National Social Safety Net Programme, the Nigeria Community Action for Resilience and Economic Stimulus, and the Renewed Hope Social Protection Programme among the initiatives aimed at supporting vulnerable Nigerians.

He also highlighted the Household Prosperity and Empowerment Social Protection Project, supported through Nigeria’s partnership with the World Bank, saying the initiative was expected to improve assistance to vulnerable households and strengthen their resilience.

The envoy said the EU was complementing these efforts through its Supporting Sustainable Social Protection Systems in Nigeria programme, which works with government institutions and implementing partners, including UNICEF, GIZ, the International Labour Organisation, ActionAid and Oxfam.

He disclosed that the programme covered Abia, Benue, Oyo, Sokoto, Kebbi, Adamawa and Borno states.

According to him, the intervention focuses on strengthening social protection policies, expanding social registers to identify more poor and vulnerable households, and improving data systems for planning and resource allocation.

Mignot said multidimensional poverty assessments helped governments identify overlapping deprivations in education, healthcare, nutrition and living standards, enabling them to target interventions more effectively.

He added that the EU had supported the review of Nigeria’s National Social Protection Policy, as well as the development of state social protection policies and a Social Protection Bill.

The ambassador also called for stronger coordination between humanitarian assistance and long-term development programmes, noting that poor households were particularly vulnerable to emergencies, including severe acute malnutrition.

He welcomed the ongoing humanitarian transition, under which Nigerian authorities at all levels are expected to progressively assume greater responsibility for funding and coordinating humanitarian assistance.

Mignot commended the minister responsible for humanitarian affairs and poverty reduction, Bernard Doro, for his efforts and reaffirmed the EU’s commitment to supporting Nigeria’s poverty reduction drive.

He said tackling poverty sustainably required a coordinated, long-term approach involving government institutions, civil society, local communities and international development partners.

“Humanitarian needs cannot wait, and poverty either,” he said, urging stakeholders to make the fight against poverty a year-round priority.

World.title: CAN at 50: Church must challenge govt, defend Nigerians — Archbishop Okoh
World.content:
Archbishop Daniel Okoh, CAN President

…As First Lady urges Christians to sustain unity

…Honours Gowon, OBJ, Osinbajo, others

By Luminous Jannamike, Abuja

President of the Christian Association of Nigeria (CAN), Archbishop Daniel Okoh, has charged the Church to challenge government failures, defend vulnerable Nigerians and resist political capture, declaring that it must not surrender its prophetic responsibility for the sake of political convenience.

Speaking at CAN’s 50th anniversary celebration in Abuja on Saturday, Archbishop Okoh said the Church must adopt a more courageous, evidence-based and constructive approach to national affairs, holding those in power accountable while supporting policies that advance the common good.

In his homily, themed “CAN at 50: A Prophetic Voice of Hope,” the CAN president said the Church must remain independent, morally alert and committed to speaking for Nigerians whose voices are often ignored.

“The Church must speak!” he declared.

Archbishop Okoh listed internally displaced persons, children denied education, unemployed youths, farmers unable to access their farmlands because of insecurity, women facing violence and victims of human trafficking among those whose plight the Church must address.

He warned, however, that speaking prophetically did not mean opposing every government policy or turning the Church into a partisan platform.

“A responsible watchman must be accurate. He should not raise alarm simply because he dislikes a policy or disagrees with a political leader,” he said.

On the relationship between the Church and government, Archbishop Okoh advocated what he called critical collaboration, urging Christian leaders to commend good policies and challenge failures without compromising their independence.

“Collaborate where common good requires it, challenge where justice requires challenge, commend where government does well and warn where government fails, while maintaining the Church’s independence,” he said.

He said the next 50 years of CAN should be marked by stronger research, advocacy, institutional maturity and collective action, with greater attention to justice, human dignity, democratic institutions, religious freedom and the welfare of vulnerable citizens.

Archbishop Okoh also urged Christians to preserve the unity that inspired CAN’s founding in August 1976, warning that denominational rivalries could weaken the Church’s collective voice.

He recalled that the Association’s early years were marked by mutual suspicion and the marginalisation of some Christian traditions, but said successive leaders had worked to build a more inclusive platform.

“At 50, all the church traditions in Nigeria are represented in CAN through the following major blocs: CSN, CCN, CPFN/PFN, OAIC and TEKAN/ECWA. The last time I checked, no one is missing on the table,” he said.

The CAN president cautioned Christians against taking that unity for granted or allowing disagreements, particularly on social media, to undermine their fellowship.

He stressed that CAN belonged to every believer, not just its elected and appointed officers, and urged members to break down remaining barriers between denominations.

Drawing on the biblical image of a watchman, Archbishop Okoh said the Church had a duty to identify threats to justice and human dignity, warn those in authority and defend citizens whose circumstances left them vulnerable.

He also called on Christians to match their prayers for Nigeria with practical action, integrity and responsible leadership.

“Nigeria can be better — Nigeria will be better! But hope requires responsibility: prayer must be accompanied by positive action, faith by integrity, leadership by accountability and freedom by responsibility,” he said.

Archbishop Okoh said the jubilee must serve as the beginning of a renewed national mission, with the Church expected to defend human dignity, demand accountability and contribute to national development.

Christians Must Sustain Unity – Mrs Tinubu

The First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu, congratulated CAN on its 50 years of service to God and humanity, urging Christian denominations to sustain their unity.

She said the anniversary theme, “Walking Together in Faith,” reflected Christ’s prayer for the unity of believers.

“I pray that, just as Christ prayed for the saints, all the Christian blocs and denominations will continue to remain united in Jesus’ name,” she said.

The golden jubilee celebration also featured awards recognising prominent Nigerians and public office holders for their contributions to the Church and society.

Honours as List

Former Head of State, General Yakubu Gowon; former Presidents Olusegun Obasanjo and Goodluck Jonathan; and former Vice-President Yemi Osinbajo were listed among recipients of the Pillar of Faith awards.

Senate President Godswill Akpabio, Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives Benjamin Kalu, Secretary to the Government of the Federation George Akume, several state governors and other public officials were listed in the Christian Icon category.

The programme also featured prayers for Nigeria and its leaders, the presentation of CAN’s history book and the launch of a proposed airport chapel project.

World.title: Neto double gives Chelsea win; marred by Martinez injury
World.content:
Chelsea’s English midfielder #14 Jordan Henderson (L) and Chelsea’s Portuguese midfielder #07 Pedro Neto (R) celebrate on the pitch after the English Premier League football match between Everton and Chelsea at Hill Dickinson Stadium in Liverpool, north west England on October 17, 2026. Chelsea won the game 2-0. (Photo by PETER POWELL / AFP) / RESTRICTED TO EDITORIAL USE. No use with unauthorized audio, video, data, fixture lists, club/league logos or ‘live’ services. Online in-match use limited to 120 images. An additional 40 images may be used in extra time. No video emulation. Social media in-match use limited to 120 images. An additional 40 images may be used in extra time. No use in betting publications, games or single club/league/player publications. /

Pedro Neto’s double condemned Everton to a first defeat of the season as Chelsea won 2-0 at the Hill Dickinson Stadium despite the loss of goalkeeper Emi Martinez to a head injury.

Neto opened the scoring inside the first minute of the second half and secured the three points during the 11 added minutes following the lengthy treatment given to the stricken Martinez.

The Argentine international was involved in a sickening head clash with Everton defender Jarrad Branthwaite and was taken to hospital.

Victory lifts Chelsea above the Toffees into the top four of the Premier League.

After a slow start, a fiery-tempered encounter sparked into life when Everton midfielder Harrison Armstrong launched into a tackle on Josh Acheampong for the first of five first-half yellow cards.

That challenge also enlivened the home crowd and spurred Everton on to their best spell of the game.

Thierno Barry was guilty of another wasteful day in front of goal as the Frenchman planted a header from Jack Grealish’s cross too close to Martinez.

Chelsea have made a habit of fast starts under Xabi Alonso, but it took until four minutes before half-time to threaten when Moises Caicedo blasted off the bar from a well-worked corner.

Everton were furious that Morgan Rogers escaped a second booking just before the break after a thunderous clash with England team-mate James Garner.

That proved to be a huge decision as the visitors this time flew out of the blocks at the start of the second period.

Jorrel Hato got to the byline and his low cross fell to Neto, who had time to control before firing low past Pickford.

Chelsea had not kept a Premier League clean sheet in 22 matches stretching back to January, but were rarely troubled by an Everton side short on forward options despite the loss of Martinez.

The treatment for the goalkeeper threatened to halt Chelsea’s momentum as they controlled the second half.

Belgian Mike Penders replaced Martinez for his first Premier League appearance but had little to do bar dealing with a few desperate Everton crosses.

At the other end Pickford made a fine save to deny Joao Pedro.

But Chelsea did get their second goal when Neto coolly stroked into the bottom corner after Jordan Henderson’s free-kick was blocked by the Everton wall.

World.title: AICL GMD, Tamuno Seeks Stronger Diaspora Investment in Africa
World.content:
The Group Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Abuja Investments Company Limited (AICL), Her Excellency, Ambassador Maureen Tamuno, has called for stronger partnerships between Africa and its diaspora to accelerate investment, facilitate skills transfer, create jobs and promote sustainable economic development across the continent.

Tamuno made the call on Thursday while delivering the keynote address at the seventh Diaspora Africa Conference, held at the Afreximbank Africa Trade Centre, Abuja, under the theme, ‘Homecoming: Bridging the Divide from Diaspora to Africa’s Future’.

She said homecoming should go beyond reconnecting with ancestral roots to building lasting relationships through productive investments, knowledge exchange, enterprise development and initiatives capable of improving livelihoods.

Drawing on her experience as Nigeria’s former High Commissioner to Jamaica, with concurrent accreditation to Haiti, Belize and the Dominican Republic, Tamuno stressed that diaspora engagement should extend beyond financial remittances to include professional expertise, international networks, entrepreneurship and technology transfer.

She identified trust, capital, skills, identity and policy as five critical bridges required to strengthen collaboration between Africans at home and abroad.

According to her, transparency, accountability and reliable institutions are essential to attracting diaspora investments. She urged governments to make investment information accessible, digitise public systems and ensure that transactions are transparent and independently verifiable.

“Patriotism should inspire an investment; it must never replace due diligence. Shared ancestry does not guarantee financial return,” she said, advocating structured investments backed by clear agreements, proper documentation and effective accountability mechanisms.

The AICL chief executive highlighted investment opportunities across the company’s portfolio, including real estate, markets, public infrastructure, transportation, entertainment and the creative economy. She invited diaspora entrepreneurs, investors and institutions to explore mutually beneficial partnerships with AICL to unlock opportunities within the Federal Capital Territory.

She also advocated a shift from the traditional emphasis on remittances for consumption towards structured investments that generate financial returns while delivering social and economic benefits.

Tamuno called for stronger collaboration in professional training, research, technology and enterprise development, noting that diaspora professionals could contribute through mentoring, knowledge exchange and partnerships without necessarily relocating permanently to Nigeria.

She further stressed the importance of including women, young people and persons with disabilities in investment opportunities, leadership, technical training and enterprise ownership, saying Africa’s development must provide inclusive opportunities for all.

To translate the conference’s resolutions into measurable outcomes, Tamuno proposed a Homecoming Partnership Compact to track progress over the next 12 months. The proposed framework would monitor partnerships established, enterprises supported, people trained and jobs sustained.

She said the success of diaspora engagement should be measured not by announcements and promises alone, but by functioning businesses, responsible investments and tangible improvements in people’s lives.

Tamuno urged Africans at home and abroad to embrace shared responsibility in building a prosperous continent, stressing that trust, mutual respect and sustained collaboration were essential to creating an Africa that future generations would be proud to call home.

“Let this seventh edition mark a movement from recognition to relationship, from relationship to responsibility, and from responsibility to results.We cannot undo the journeys that divided us. But we can choose the partnerships that shape our future.” she added.

World.title: Court Dismisses Suit Against Sokoto ADC Leadership
World.content:
Onuminya Innocent in Sokoto

The Federal High Court sitting in Sokoto has dismissed a suit filed by Umar Faruk challenging the leadership of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) in Sokoto State.

The case was dismissed yesterday by Justice Ahmad Gama for lack of merit and evidence.

Faruk, a former State Chairman of the party, and others had in July filed a suit at the court alleging that the party structure in the state was hijacked by new entrants.

He had prayed the court to restore him as the substantive Chairman of the party in the state.

After listening to counsel for both parties, Justice Gama resolved the four reliefs sought by the plaintiffs in favour of the respondents.

The court held that it lacked jurisdiction to meddle in the internal affairs of a political party.

Justice Gama further explained that Faruk and others failed to exhaust the party’s internal dispute resolution mechanism before approaching the court.

He noted that the plaintiffs failed to show that their fundamental human rights were infringed upon.

Reacting to the judgement, counsel to the respondents, Suleiman Usman, SAN, described the judgement as sound and commendable.

Usman said the judge remained neutral in his decision, adding that a litigant cannot win a case without proving it with substantial evidence.

He added that the judgement has deepened the democratic system and constitutional jurisprudence in the country.

World.title: Fintiri Demands Modern Border Surveillance in Adamawa
World.content:
Daji Sani in Yola

Adamawa State Governor, Hon. Ahmadu Umaru Fintiri, has task the Federal Government to strengthen border surveillance, security architecture, increase funding for security agencies and deepen inter-agency cooperation as part of measures to address persistent security challenges facing the country.

The governor made the call on Friday evening while delivering the keynote address at the opening ceremony of the Federal and States Security Administrators’ Meeting FSSAM) 2026, held at the Banquet Hall, Government House, Yola.

Fintiri, who was represented by his Deputy, Professor Kaletapwa Farauta, said the meeting came at a critical time when the nation is confronted with diverse security threats that require collective and innovative solutions.

He noted that Adamawa State’s location along Nigeria’s international border with Cameroon places it at the frontline of cross-border security concerns, including arms proliferation, smuggling and movement of criminal elements.

The governor therefore urged the Federal Government to prioritise the deployment of advanced surveillance technology, drones and joint border patrols to effectively monitor unmanned border routes.

He also called for the expeditious establishment of One-Stop Border Posts to improve border management, facilitate legitimate trade and curb illegal activities.

Fintiri further advocated increased operational funding, modern equipment and improved welfare packages for the personnel of the Nigeria Police Force, Nigerian Armed Forces, Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, Department of State Services and Nigeria Customs Service.

He stressed that adequate motivation and logistics remain critical to boosting the morale and operational effectiveness of security operatives across the country.

The governor also emphasized the need for stronger synergy among security agencies, warning that inter-agency rivalry and poor intelligence sharing could frustrate national security efforts.

According to him, his administration’s security approach under the Fresh Air Agenda is anchored on community-based security, recognizing that lasting peace must be built from the grassroots.

He said the creation of seven new emirates and chiefdoms was deliberately aimed at strengthening traditional institutions, bringing governance closer to the people and enhancing local intelligence gathering.

Fintiri disclosed that the state government has continued to support security agencies with operational vehicles, communication gadgets and funding for joint security operations, including Operation Farauta, to sustain peace and stability.

He however cautioned against premature declarations of victory over insurgency, noting that Boko Haram and ISWAP still exploit rural terrain, asymmetric tactics and cross-border vulnerabilities to attack soft targets.

The governor also drew attention to emerging threats such as cybercrime, digital radicalisation and vandalism of critical infrastructure including electricity facilities and telecom installations, urging participants to develop practical, measurable strategies and adopt digital freight and transit-tracking systems to secure trade routes.

World.title: When The Leader Remembers: A Lesson In Unscripted Humanity
World.content:
Rahma Abdulmajid

History is obsessed with the theatre of power. It immortalizes the roaring stadiums, the blinding camera flashes, and the hollow majesty of choreographed handshakes—but real control operates in the shadows.

True, transformative leadership is never born on a brightly lit stage. It is forged in the shadows, deep within the quiet, unscripted margins where teleprompters go dark and the roaring crowds fall silent. When the glittering costume of power is violently stripped away, only two things can remain: a hollow, echoing emptiness, or the raw, unvarnished force of pure humanity.

New Delhi was buzzing on day two of the BRICS summit. Inside the Nigerian Embassy, the energy turned electric as Vice-President Kashim Shettima arrived for a brief courtesy visit. A roaring, joyous crowd of resident Nigerians had gathered, transforming the venue into an impromptu homecoming. Excitement hung thick in the air, punctuated by rising chants and the endless, rapid-fire click of camera shutters capturing every handshake and smile.

Yet beneath that surface warmth, a subtle tension shifted the room. While everyone else basked in the moment, the vice-president’s gaze fractured. His eyes darted from face to face with a sharp, urgent intensity, searching for something vital that the rest of us had completely overlooked.

It was contagious. Soon, it wasn’t just his security detail on high alert. Even those of us in his inner circle found ourselves scanning the room, hunting for whatever phantom danger our principal was so desperately trying to find. Even inside the private quarters meant for his rest, there was no escape from the search.

The moment the commotion outside died down, his voice sliced through the polite small talk. “Where is Mr. Prakash?” The embassy officials froze, trapped in a heavy, bewildered silence. They traded blank stares, hunting for the name in their memories. Then, understanding clicked. He spoke again, steady and firm. “Mr. Prakash,” he said. “The embassy driver. Is he still here?”

Within minutes, Mr. Prakash appeared. He was an elderly, humble Indian man, his weathered face and traditional mourning haircut bearing the unmistakable scars of a life battered by time. Though he held nothing more than a modest driver’s job at an African embassy, he carried a crushing mountain of obligations alone on his narrow shoulders. He approached, his fragile gaze holding the look of someone who had just stumbled upon long-lost family.

The vice-president had just sat down to his welcome meal when he spotted Prakash. In an instant, protocol and plate were forgotten. He stood straight back up, greeting Prakash with a deep reverence that hushed the entire room. “Mr. Prakash, how have you been?” he said warmly. “Thank you for everything.”

Then, turning to the rest of us as if to permanently etch the man’s dignity into our minds, he explained, “He drove me around years ago during my visit to India as governor.” What followed was uniquely disarming: he began inquiring about Mr. Prakash’s family by name. He remembered vivid details from a brief encounter years ago—the kind of trivial history most leaders cast aside.

When Prakash, with trembling hands, pulled out a worn-out phone, desperate for a photograph to mark the improbable reunion, my principal left his meal once more and threw an arm around him like an old, dear friend. In that moment, he posed not as a Vice President, but simply as a man with his brother.

But it wasn’t the cameras that stole my breath that afternoon. It was what happened after the lenses lowered—away from the flashing lights and prying eyes. Without announcement or applause, Senator Shettima slipped a hand into his pocket, scooped out a generous wad of cash, and tucked it quietly into Mr. Prakash’s coat.

No aides were instructed. No media were invited. It was an act born purely out of kindness, deep empathy, and raw humanity. When language threatened to build a wall—because Prakash speaks little English and the Vice President speaks no Hindi—compassion found its own dialect.

He switched effortlessly to Hausa, a Nigerian local language, not for Prakash to understand literally, but to universalise the moment, to say in a tongue he knows best what the heart knows in every language: “Mene ne amfanin nasarar rayuwa idan baka taimaka wa wanda yake bukatar taimakonka ba?” Translated in English, this means, “What is the benefit of success in life if you do not help those who need your help?”

What I witnessed did not surprise me, but it deeply enriched my soul. You see, I too am a Prakash in the Vice President’s world. Over the past three years of working by his side, no living soul has recognised the heavy reality of my life like he has. When my husband died serving our nation, I was left to carry the immense weight of raising our children alone. Yet, His Excellency truly sees that sacrifice, honouring the burden I bear every single day.

To speak the absolute truth, Kashim Shettima’s quiet, unwavering remembrance of my grief over the past three years has outshone even my closest blood relatives across the eleven long years since my husband passed away. He remembers the dates others forget. He asks the questions others avoid. He carries burdens that are not constitutionally his to bear.

Seeing Vice-President Shettima evokes the presence of transformative leaders. He reminds me of Uruguay’s President José Mujica, who chose a modest farmhouse over a palace, and Nelson Mandela, whose profound friendship with Christo Brand transcended prison walls.

Their stories remind us that true leadership is never about titles, offices, or protocols. It lives in an unshakeable refusal to walk past someone in need—a stubborn conviction that every human being, no matter how small their station, is worthy of being remembered.

This noble, compassionate heart is precisely why President Bola Ahmed Tinubu chose Kashim Shettima as his running mate—to gift Nigeria a leadership defined not by noise, but by empathy; not by showmanship, but by deep, genuine service. In a world where many leaders remember only those who can repay them, it is truly revolutionary to find one who remembers a driver.

* Abdulmajid is the Personal Assistant to the President on Radio and Broadcast (Office of the Vice-President)

World.title: Witness Admits Ex-Aviation Minister, Sirika, Not Signatory to N599m Consultancy Contract
World.content:
Alex Enumah in Abuja

A witness of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) in the ongoing trial of former Minister of Aviation, Hadi Abubakar Sirika, has admitted that the ex minister was not a signatory to the award of consultancy contract by the Federal Ministry of Aviation to the tune of N599 million.

The witness, Christopher Odofin, also told the court that from the face of the documents leading to the award of the disputed contract, there was nothing implicating the former minister in the contract issues.

Odofin, an investigator with the EFCC, stated this while responding to questions from Sirika’s lawyer, a former Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Chief Kanu Agabi (SAN), during the continuation of trial of the former minister at the High Court of the Federal Capital Territory, in Maitama, Abuja.

Sirika is being prosecuted by the EFCC, alongside his daughter, Fatima and son-in-law, Hamma Jalal Sule, and a company allegedly owned by the couple, Al Buraq Global Investment Limited, on a six-count charge bordering on abuse of office and contract fraud to the tune of N2.8 billion.

According to the charge, the former minister was said to have abused his office when he allegedly conferred unfair advantage on Al Buraq Global Investment Limited by using his position to influence award of contract for the apron extension at the Katsina Airport for the sum of N1,498,300,750, among other alleged offences.

The actions, the commission claimed, were contrary to the provisions of Sections 12 and 19 of the Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Act, 2000, and Section 17(b) of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (Establishment) Act, 2004, as well as Section 315 of the Penal Code Act, Cap 532 Acts of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) and punishable under the same sections.

However, the former minister and his co-defendants pleaded not guilty to the charge preferred against them.

At Thursday’s proceeding, the EFCC’s witness when confronted with tendered prosecution’s documents admitted that the letter of contract award was not signed by the former minister and that Sirika was also not a member of the Ministerial Tenders Board of the Aviation Ministry that awarded the contract in dispute.

He told the court that on the face of the contract award document, there was nothing to show that the Director of Procurement in the ministry who signed the contract papers ought not to have signed the contract.

However, Odofin stated that the former minister was charged to court because of his oral instruction on the contract for N599 million which was beyond the threshold, alleging that the contract was awarded to Sirika’s associate.

On the voice note extracted from the phone of the former Permanent Secretary of the Aviation Ministry, Mr Abel Enitan, the witness admitted that the telephone where the voice extraction was carried out was not before the court and that there was no evidence that what was extracted from the phone was served on the owner of the phone.

He admitted that the EFCC completed its investigation as at April 26, 2024 when the charges against the defendants were filed before the court but however, told the court that he was not aware of the series of additional proofs of evidence filed by the prosecution after the charge had been filed.

He also said that he was not aware of how 11 persons listed as witnesses in the initial proof of evidence was increased to 20.

Answering questions from the counsel to the second defendant, Efut Okoi, the witness admitted that Sirika’s daughter, Fatima, charged along with him, was not the Chief Executive Officer of Al Buraq Global Investment Limited that was awarded the contract for the expansion of apron at the Katsina Airport.

He also said that the digital forensic report used in filing the charges was not prepared by him but by one Bello Gideon.

He told the court that he did not extract extrajudicial statements from officers of the Nigerian Air Force, Nigerian Airport Authority and Katina State government on the expansion of the Katsina Airport apron.

He told the court that as of the time of awarding the contract for the expansion of the apron to Al Buraq Global Investment, Abel Enitan was Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Aviation and the Chairman of the Ministerial Tenders Board.

Meanwhile, Justice Sylvanus Oriji has adjourned the case to October 20 and 28 for the continuation of cross-examination of the witness.

World.title: BETA 2026: Adunni Foundation Puts Children At Centre of Basic Education Reforms
World.content:
Funmi Ogundare

The Adunni Foundation is set to convene pupils, teachers and education stakeholders to examine reforms needed to improve Nigeria’s basic education system, with a focus on learning outcomes, teachers, infrastructure, inclusion and child safety.

The 2026 Basic Education Torchbearers Awards (BETA), themed, ‘The Child at the Centre: What Must Change in Nigeria’s Basic Education?’, will hold on October 21, at Foundation of Truth Assembly (FOTA), Eric Moore Road, Surulere, Lagos,

It will recognise top-performing pupils in the National Common Entrance Examination (NCEE) and the Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE).

Founder and Chief Executive Officer of The Adunni Foundation, Ms Motunrayo Alaka, said the event would provide a platform for stakeholders to move discussions on basic education challenges towards collective responsibility and practical action.

She said basic education should be assessed based on children’s learning experiences, knowledge acquisition and access to opportunities.

“Placing the child at the centre requires us to address learning outcomes, teachers, infrastructure, inclusion, safety and the responsibilities of every stakeholder. BETA 2026 offers an opportunity to move these concerns towards shared responsibility and action,” Alaka stated.

Speakers expected at the event include the Board Chairperson of The Adunni Foundation, Dr Yele Okeremi; Medical Director of Grachelle Multi-Specialty Hospital and Fertility Clinic, Dr Ede-Edokpolor Osazuwa; Managing Director of Speedmeals Culinary Ltd, Chef Tobias Igwe; and Miss Aanuoluwapo Ojewunmi of the Young Aerospace Professionals Initiative (YAPI).

Others are the Foundation’s Chief Executive Officer, Alaka, and Legal Consultant, Mr Aderemi Durojaiye. The Founder of CAST Public Relations, Mr Babajide Benson, will serve as compere.

The programme will also feature ‘Hope Nigeria Talks’, a platform designed to enable children to express their aspirations for education and the country they will inherit.

Another session, ‘Uniforms and Dreams: Careers That Serve Nigeria’, will connect pupils with professionals and expose them to career opportunities that education can provide.

According to Alaka, the initiative is designed to encourage children to envision their futures while helping them understand the role of education in achieving their ambitions and contributing to national development.

The maiden edition of BETA, held in 2025, honoured individuals and institutions whose contributions helped lay important foundations for basic education.

“The 2026 edition shifts attention to children and the changes required to improve their learning experiences and secure better opportunities for their future,” the founder said.

Anchored on the belief that education is independence, Alaka said BETA seeks to promote access to quality basic education and ensure that every child has the knowledge, skills and confidence to fulfil their potential and contribute meaningfully to society.

“The initiative also supports the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, particularly Goal 4, which seeks to ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all.”

She called on education stakeholders and members of the public to renew their commitment to placing children at the centre of decisions, policies and investments in basic education.

World.title: Google Opens Global Public Access to Gemini 4 Argon App
World.content:
Emma Okonji

Google, yesterday, announced that its newest AI model, Gemini 4 Argon, was now open to the public globally across the Gemini app, Google Search, AI Studio, and Antigravity, alongside a new programme giving 10,000 scientists and researchers six months of free top-tier access.

Google, in a statement, said following initial safety testing with government and cybersecurity teams, everyday users, developers, and businesses in Nigeria can now use it, while Nigerian scientists and university researchers can apply for a new programme giving 10,000 researchers six months of free top-tier access.

“For most Nigerians, a new AI model name means little unless it changes what they can do on their phones and laptops. Until now, chatbots were mostly used for quick text shortcuts like polishing an email. With this update, Gemini moves beyond the chat box. It can produce fifteen times more work in one sitting, understand 3D space from phone photos, build working visual tools on your screen, and run recurring tasks across your apps,” the statement said.

According to Google, there are five practical things users can now do with Gemini.

They include: Have Gemini put customer quotes together and handle morning inbox. Until now, chatbots only wrote text in a chat window, leaving business owners to copy and paste everything into slides and emails late at night. In the Gemini app, users can point it to a folder of rough notes and prices, and it will build a Google Slides deck, draft the email, and repeat that routine every Monday morning automatically.

The second is to create a personal rent, salary, and market budget tracker that helps tap on the phone.

Stretching a monthly salary across food, transport, family support, thrift (ajo), and house rent takes planning. Instead of a static text reply, Canvas in the Gemini app lets users ask for a clickable money tracker on the screen with sliders to log market expenses and track weekly rent savings.

The third is to turn heavy school handouts and exam topics into visual lessons that can be seen and touched.

Preparing for university exams, WAEC, or JAMB through 80-page handouts with no diagrams is tiring. Instead of summarizing a PDF into bullet points, Gemini combines 3D visuals, voice, and video to turn a tough science topic into a 3D model you can rotate on your screen or an illustrated audio story.

The fourth is to snap a photo of an empty room or shop and see how everything fits in 3D.

Older AI models treated photos as flat pictures with no sense of space. Gemini 4 Argon understands real dimensions from a normal camera shot. When moving into a flat or setting up a shop, users can have Gemini build a 3D layout on their screen to test how shelves or chairs fit before paying a carpenter.

The fifth is to map out a complete side hustle plan in one sitting without the AI cutting off.

Older chatbots usually gave five vague bullet points and stopped halfway when asked for a business plan. Google expanded how much Gemini could write in one response by fifteen times and trained it to drop robotic phrases, letting users get a complete Nigerian startup manual and naira cost breakdown in one sitting.

World.title: Tinubu’s Current East-West Road Decision Could Transform Niger Delta, Says Ugolor
World.content:
Sylvester Idowu in Warri

The Publisher of the ‘Common Good Letter’, Rev. David Ugolor, has commended President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s directive that the continuing Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway be aligned with sections of the existing East–West Road in the Niger Delta.

He maintained that the directive, if properly designed, transparently financed and effectively implemented, could become one of the most consequential infrastructure decisions affecting the Niger Delta under the present administration.

Rev. Ugolor, in a statement issued yesterday stated that a safe and durable East–West Road would connect communities, reduce transport costs, strengthen regional trade, support agriculture and industry, attract investment and save lives.

“The ‘Common Good Letter’ has consistently called on President Tinubu and the federal government to treat the East–West Road as a national economic priority.

“While we welcomed the renewed presidential attention, the decision could become a defining issue in the 2027 presidential election—but its value must ultimately be measured by completed kilometres, safe roads, transparent expenditure and economic benefits, not announcements.

“However, the information currently available to citizens remains incomplete and potentially confusing as the announcement appears to concern the alignment of part of the coastal highway with the existing East–West Road.

“It should not yet be presented as a fully funded and procured reconstruction programme until the Government publishes the governing approvals and implementation details,” he observed.

Ugolor also called on the Federal Government to clarify whether the announced directive represents a realignment of the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway onto specified sections of the existing East–West Road.

He called for a reconstruction and expansion of those sections as part of the coastal-highway contract, a new procurement requiring separate Federal Executive Council approval, a variation of an existing contract; or a coordinated programme involving existing East–West Road contractors, the Niger Delta Development Commission, state governments and the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway contractor.

“These distinctions are critical because several sections of the East–West Road are already covered by existing contracts, emergency interventions or works being undertaken by different public institutions.

“Without a publicly available implementation framework, there is a serious risk of overlapping mandates, duplicated contracts, double funding and uncertainty over responsibility for delivery,” he warned.

The Common Good Letter publisher also called on the Minister of Works, Dave Umahi,

to publish a comprehensive East– West Road and Coastal Highway Integration Plan setting out the exact alignment, sections and kilometres affected.

“The engineering justification and comparative assessment of the original and revised routes, the pavement, drainage, flood-control and climate-resilience designs as well as the estimated cost of the revised works.

“Whether the expenditure was provided for in the 2026 federal budget or will require a supplementary appropriation, whether funding will come directly from the Federal Government, borrowing, private finance, concession arrangements or a combination of these sources.

“Any Federal Executive Council and National Assembly approvals required the applicable procurement method and whether the existing coastal-highway contractor will execute the work or a competitive process will select contractors?”

“These questions require answers for the fact that all existing East–West Road contracts, contractors, contract values, payments, completion levels and outstanding obligations, how the new arrangement will affect existing contracts and prevent duplicate payments, the respective roles of the Federal Ministry of Works, NDDC, state governments and other institutions, and the timetable, milestones, warranties, performance bonds and arrangements for independent technical monitoring as well as funding must be explained.

“The reported claim that the Federal Government is providing 30 per cent of the wider coastal-highway financing while foreign banks provide 70 per cent also requires clarification.

“The government should also state whether that financing arrangement covers the newly aligned East–West Road sections, identify the financial institutions involved, disclose the material financing terms and explain any sovereign guarantees or contingent liabilities.

“Changing the route of a major public infrastructure project must also be accompanied by updated engineering studies, environmental and social assessments, cost estimates, procurement approvals, financing arrangements and safeguards for affected communities,” Ugolor added.

The Common Good Letter publisher also called on the Minister of Works to convene a public technical and accountability briefing dedicated to the East–West Road.

“The briefing should present one authoritative implementation map and contract matrix showing, at a glance, who is responsible for each section, how much has been approved and paid, the work completed, the remaining milestones and the expected completion date.

“The people of the Niger Delta should not have to reconcile contradictory announcements to understand what government is doing on their most important regional highway. As we welcome the policy direction, we now ask for the plan, contracts, financing and measurable delivery framework.

“The East–West Road must not remain a road of repeated promises, overlapping interventions and uncompleted contracts. It must become a transparent, climate-resilient economic corridor that moves people, businesses and the Niger Delta economy,” Ugolor further declared.

World.title: Weather: Brace for severe storms, heavy rain and damaging winds in KZN

SAWS has issued a Yellow Level 2 warning for severe thunderstorms in western and southern inland KwaZulu-Natal.

Heavy rain and damaging winds could cause localised flooding and damage to infrastructure and settlements.

Morning fog patches over the interior, otherwise partly cloudy and warm to hot.

Scattered showers and thundershowers are expected but isolated in the north, except in the extreme north-east.

The UVB sunburn index will be moderate.

Durban is going to be partly cloudy scattered showers and thundershowers in the afternoon.

Light south-westerly winds will blow before a shift to moderate easterly to north-easterly in the afternoon.



Temperatures will range from 21°C to 26°C.

The UVB sunburn index will be moderate.

World.title: Eskom to implement a 15-hour power outage in Gauteng on Tuesday
World.content:
Eskom will switch off electricity in part of Ga-Rankuwa for 15 hours next week as it carries out maintenance on its distribution network.

The power utility said the outage will affect customers in Ga-Rankuwa Zone 20 on Tuesday, 20 October, from 8:00 until 23:00.

Eskom published the notice in its October 2026 Gauteng Cluster Connect newsletter, compiled by its Gauteng Communication and Stakeholder Management team.



Why Eskom is cutting power in Ga-Rankuwa

According to Eskom, the interruption will allow its teams to perform essential maintenance on distribution power lines serving the area.

Unlike many planned outages that end in the late afternoon, this shutdown will stretch well into the night. Residents in Zone 20 can expect to spend the entire working day and most of the evening without electricity.

Eskom cautioned that the maintenance may not go ahead as planned if circumstances beyond its control arise. Residents should keep an eye on Eskom’s official channels for any changes to the schedule.



Tips to get through a long night without electricity

With power only expected back at 23:00, households will need to plan for both daytime and evening needs.

Residents can charge cell phones, laptops, power banks and rechargeable lamps on Monday night. Torches, candles and matches should be within easy reach before sunset, and anyone using candles or gas should never leave them unattended.

Families may want to cook supper early using gas or prepare meals that do not require electricity. Filling flasks with hot water before 8:00 can help with tea, coffee and baby bottles later in the day.



Homes that rely on electric gates, alarms or security lights should make sure backup batteries are charged, and residents may want to check in on elderly neighbours who live alone.

Eskom advised customers to treat all electrical appliances as live at all times during the outage, since power could return without notice. Switching off sensitive appliances can also protect them from power surges when supply is restored.

The utility thanked customers for their cooperation and apologised for the inconvenience.

World.title: Kaizer Chiefs confirm disappointing news
World.content:
Kaizer Chiefs have confirmed the dreaded news. South African broadcasters will not televise this afternoon’s CAF Confederation Cup showdown between Amakhosi and Red Arrows FC.

Supporters had expected to watch the game on SABC. Amakhosi have now explained why the broadcaster cannot air the match.

KAIZER CHIEFS CONFIRM SABC BLACKOUT

The club said: “This afternoon’s CAF Confederation Cup clash against Red Arrows FC will not be televised in South Africa. Unfortunately, the hosting team has been unable to provide our broadcasters, SABC with the necessary link to air the match in Mzansi.



We will keep Amakhosi faithful updated directly from the venue on X with coverage and key moments as they happen in Ndola, Zambia,” the statement concluded.

Meanwhile, SABC 2 is broadcasting Orlando Pirates’ game against African Stars.

AMAKHOSI ANNOUNCE STARTING LINE-UP

Starting line-up: Renaldo Leaner, Thabiso Monyane, Inacio Miguel, Thabo Moloisane, Bradley Cross, Paseka Mako, Reeve Frosler, Sibongiseni Mthethwa, Mduduzi Shabalala, Mfundo Vilakazi, Luke Baartman

Substitutes: Bruce Bvuma, Rushwin Dortley, Kabelo Nkgwesa, Thulani Mabaso, Asanele Velebayi, Faiz Abrahams, Etiosa Ighodaro, Flavio Da Silva, Wandile Duba.

The likes of Lebohang Maboe, Siphesihle Ndlovu, Adolf Mtasingwa and Khanyisa Mayo remain out injured.

Substitutes: Rukoro, Collin, Guiseb, Patrick, Nathan, Paul, US A, Martino, Lukas
