World.title: Decades after apartheid, South Africans seek justice for crimes of the past
World.content:
Decades after apartheid, South Africans seek justice for crimes of the past

toggle caption i AP

SHARPEVILLE, South Africa – Paulina Mathinye gestures with anguish at the rows of garbage-strewn graves, overrun with weeds, in the cemetery where her father is buried.

"Look at that, where they sleep," she says of the dozens of Black protesters buried here, all of whom were killed when police opened fire on March 21, 1960 in what became one of the bloodiest days in apartheid history.

"Why are they dirty? It's a disgrace," says the 71-year-old grandmother, who wears a floral dress and a smart sunhat.

The cemetery, like much else in this visibly poor township about an hour's drive from Johannesburg, has been left to decay. But Mathinye notes that for one day a year at least, when South Africa's political elite descend to commemorate the massacre, the graveyard is spotless. The anniversary is a public holiday known as Human Rights Day.

Sponsor Message

"I'm still angry. My anger comes out because that's the day my father was shot," says Mathinye, who was just five years old at the time.

She says her father's part in what became a turning point in the struggle against apartheid has not been sufficiently recognized by the current democratic government.

And she says she wants justice – however delayed.

toggle caption i Kate Bartlett/NPR

That's why she's signed up to take part in a potential class action lawsuit 66 years later, along with Sharpeville survivors and the families of Sharpeville victims.

At least 69 people were shot by police that day. They had been demonstrating against the country's pass laws – which restricted black people's movements and where they could live and work.

While it's unclear if any perpetrators are still alive, those taking part in the case hope it could lead to reparations.

But first, the group's lawyers must challenge an apartheid-era law that continues to block their efforts to seek legal redress. The law remains in force decades after apartheid ended and a Black-majority government took power.

In September they filed an application in the Gauteng High Court challenging the continued existence of the Indemnity Act 61 of 1961. If the court finds the law unconstitutional, and also certifies a class action for survivors and dependants of those killed, then claims for individual damages could follow.

Sponsor Message

Mathinye says the repercussions of that day in 1960 have affected her whole life.

Without her father, the main breadwinner, she couldn't finish school. That, in turn, affected the lives of her children and grandchildren.

"So we struggled a lot. And we are still struggling now, because nothing has been happening," she told NPR.

If the case goes ahead and succeeds, Mathinye says she'll use any money from reparations to fix up her modest home and pay for her four grandkids' educations.

Part of a wider trend

The Sharpeville case is just one in a new wave of legal efforts that are seeking truth, accountability and reparations for apartheid-era crimes before it's too late.

"It's crucial that these issues of deep injustice are properly dealt with and that South Africa confronts them and does not sweep them under the carpet," says Daniel Leader, an international human rights lawyer advising the South African legal team representing the Sharpeville survivors and families.

Other cases include a court ruling last year that found South Africa's first Nobel Peace Prize laureate, Chief Albert Luthuli, was beaten to death by apartheid police in 1967.

Luthuli, the former leader of the African National Congress — Nelson Mandela's party — had previously been ruled to have died after being struck by a train. The new ruling overturned the finding of an earlier inquest.

The inquest into the 1985 killings of four anti-apartheid activists known as the "Cradock Four" has also been reopened. The activists were abducted and killed by apartheid security forces near the Eastern Cape town of Cradock. Although the officers involved are all dead, the victims' families hope the inquest will establish who ordered the killings.

And the inquest into the torture and death of Steve Biko, the iconic Black Consciousness leader who died in police detention in 1977, has also returned to court.

Sponsor Message

"It's very clear that the murder of Steve Biko was exactly that, murder," Biko's son Nkosinathi told media in September at the reopened inquest. "We hope that this inquest will eventually get to this very certain, unambiguous finding."

toggle caption i Anonymous/CAPE ARGUS/AP

The original inquest in 1977 heard from members of the security branch who said Biko had fallen and hit his head in a "scuffle with security police."

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), a court-like restorative justice body set up in the 1990s to uncover the truth about human rights violations during apartheid, re-examined the Biko case.

It denied amnesty to security officers who testified, saying they hadn't been truthful. That essentially cleared the way for possible prosecutions, but they never happened.

In fact, hundreds of the TRC's recommendations for prosecutions were delayed or never pursued. Last year, President Cyril Ramaphosa established a formal inquiry to investigate whether the recommendations were deliberately shelved.

The inquiry is looking into whether there was a secret deal between the old leaders of the apartheid regime and the country's new Black leaders not to prosecute cases in the interests of reconciliation. Its findings are due in December.

Back at the Sharpeville cemetery, Paulina Mathinye and three other descendants of those killed in the massacre, pause in front of a memorial plaque before exiting the graveyard.

Vincent Thamae, from the NGO, Voices of Sharpeville which works with survivors and descendants asks that they take leave of the dead.

"We ask of those who are sleeping here to be with us as we pursue justice for them," he says.

World.title: No Kings turns its focus to voting this weekend. Here's what we know
World.content:
No Kings turns its focus to voting this weekend. Here's what we know

toggle caption i Charlie Riedel/AP

No Kings, the coalition known for organizing anti-Trump protests, is trying a different democratic tactic: increasing voter turnout.

On Saturday, grassroot groups across the country will hold over 3,000 "No Kings: Vote Early" marches and other events. Organizers say these events are a nonpartisan effort to promote early voting in the midterm elections, and will involve helping people check their voter registration, make a plan to cast their ballot and understand their voting rights.

The voting push effort marks a pivot for the No Kings coalition, which comprises hundreds of partner organizations, including the American Civil Liberties Union and Black Voters Matter.

Sponsor Message

No Kings has previously held three days of nationwide protests since the start of Trump's second term because organizers say Trump's actions in office are more akin to those of a monarch than a democratically elected head of state. Trump has previously rejected the idea that he is behaving like a monarch.

"The first three No Kings were designed to send a message," says Ezra Levin, the co-founder of Indivisible — one of the major organizations within the No Kings network. "We're done sending a message."

Now, he says, they want people to vote.

There are two main goals for the event, says Levin, the first is to help facilitate what he hopes will be the largest number of midterm early voting numbers in the country's history.

The second goal is No Kings groups getting volunteers trained as poll watchers, an endeavor Levin says is in response to efforts by the Trump administration that he views as threats to election integrity. Levin points to the failed SAVE America Act that would have required voters to show a document proving their U.S. citizenship, such as a passport or a birth certificate, when registering to vote. He also raises concerns that federal immigration officers will be sent to the polls, and President Trump's attempted restrictions on voting by mail.

Sponsor Message

What do organizers expect nationwide?

Saturday's events vary widely across the country, from block parties to cookouts to rallies. In Golden, Colo., a "Paws to the Polls" event invites people to bring their dogs on a march. Organizers in Everett, Wash., planned a "concert for democracy," featuring an environmental troubadour.

All events will share similar restrictions, Levin says, including a rule against political endorsements and inviting current candidates to speak.

Superhero capes and masks will be a staple of Cammy Dunford's event in Frisco, Texas. Dunford, a co-leader of Indivisible Frisco, plans to hold a "voting is your superpower" gathering. She will be wearing a red and blue cape (to embrace the political spectrum of voters) and will give away other superhero capes and masks.

"I don't care if you're an independent, first-time voter, Democrat, Republican," Dunford says, "if you are eligible to vote, you need to get out there and vote. Because without everybody voting, we don't have a democracy."

Early voting in Texas does not start until Oct. 19, but Dunford and a group of her neighbors put together 500 mini goodie bags to hand out — filled with QR codes linking to voting information and voting resources. They will also wave bright signs with superhero-shaped images urging people in passing cars to vote.

Dunford says that her group has two people already trained as poll monitors and is hoping to recruit more on Saturday. She says poll monitors are trained by Common Cause, a government watchdog group that equips them to answer questions from voters. They have T-shirts that identify them at the polls, she says, so voters can find them and ask questions.

At a Wyandotte, Mich., event, Christy McGillivray, the executive director of Voters Not Politicians, a nonpartisan advocacy organization, is scheduled to speak to a No Kings crowd about the history of fighting for democracy in the U.S. She says the organization of grassroots events across the country is inspiring.

Sponsor Message

"It makes people feel like they're a part of something bigger than themselves," she says. "And that's what democracy is. Democracy is about working with each other and for each other."

World.title: Sidewalk sleepers: They have nowhere else to stay while a loved one is in the hospital
World.content:
Sidewalk sleepers: They have nowhere else to stay while a loved one is in the hospital

toggle caption i Sajad Hameed for NPR

DELHI, India — At 2 a.m. on the sidewalk outside one of Delhi's best-known public hospitals, Shabana Kumar gently wakes her husband. They sleep in shifts of about an hour at a time because their 6-year-old son is a patient in the oncology ward, being treated for leukemia, a cancer of the blood and bone marrow. They are afraid that if they are both asleep, an urgent call could come about their son's condition and they might miss it.

The Kumar family lives more than 600 miles from Delhi in the state of Bihar. Arun, 32, works as a farmer. Shabana, 30, is a homemaker caring for their only son.

Sponsor Message

They made the trip to Delhi because they could not afford the cost of their child's cancer treatment in Bihar. The All India Institute of Medical Sciences, or AIIMS, subsidizes expenses for families in need.

But for many families, there is one challenge they must bear on their own — finding a place to live in Delhi during the days, weeks, even months of treatment. Like the Kumars, families who can't afford to rent lodging often set up a temporary dwelling on the sidewalk.

On a night in August, dozens of families were sleeping on blankets or sheets spread directly on the sidewalk. Some tie mosquito nets to railings to protect themselves and their kids. They keep their bags and other belongings beside them as they sleep.

toggle caption i Sajad Hameed for NPR

During the day, families move between the sidewalk and the hospital for appointments, tests, medicines and consultations. They carry their most important belongings with them while leaving less valuable items at their sleeping spot. One family member often stays behind to keep an eye on their things.

Like the family from Bihar, people who've accompanied a patient may sleep outside while the patient is housed in the hospital. In other cases, the person receiving care is seen during the day but does not have a bed, so they sleep on the sidewalk as well.

Sponsor Message

At night, the sidewalk dwellers return to the pavement, where a small ecosystem has grown around the families. Women cook rice over makeshift brick stoves. Volunteers distribute food. Nearby shops sell medicines and other necessities. Nearby tea stalls not only serve beverages but let families charge their phones.

Once strangers, they exchange information about doctors, tests and where to find a free meal or, when none is available, an affordable one they can pay for.

toggle caption i Sajad Hameed for NPR

Vishnu Singh, 38, runs a tea stall outside AIIMS.

"I see poor people sleeping here every day, so many that I cannot even count them," he said.

At AIIMS and Safdarjung Hospital, which is associated with Vardhman Mahavir Medical College, we interviewed families who had traveled from across India, often hundreds of miles from home, to seek medical care. The two hospitals stand opposite each other, treating patients with illnesses ranging from cancer and heart conditions to intestinal disorders and other serious ailments.

Some families had been there for a week, others for a month or longer. For many, returning home between hospital visits was impractical, so patients and the relatives accompanying them stayed in Delhi for the duration of their care.

The families we spoke with described their experiences spending days or weeks in Delhi while navigating appointments, tests, consultations and treatment.

toggle caption i Sajad Hameed for NPR

When treatment means living outside

It is a startling contrast — a hospital that provides critical care, that, according to its annual report, gives subsidies to thousands of poor families for treatment — and that is ringed by folks who traveled great distances to find care for a loved one and who cannot afford a place to stay.

NPR reached out to the hospital by email to ask about the issue of accommodations and the community of sidewalk dwellers. The hospital did not respond.

AIIMS' website notes that its Medical Social Service Unit provides financial assistance for medical treatment and travel costs for some patients coming from outside Delhi. It also states that the unit helps arrange accommodation for out-of-town patients and their family members and caregivers at dharamshalas, traditional charitable lodging facilities affiliated with AIIMS, or other low-cost accommodation.

Sponsor Message

The website does not say whether AIIMS pays for those accommodations or provides financial assistance specifically for the lodging costs. Shalini Yadav is one of the patients who sleeps on the sidewalk with her parents.

toggle caption i Sajad Hameed for NPR

Yadav is a second-year college student from Piprat village in Tikamgarh district, Madhya Pradesh, in central India. She had been preparing for the state civil service examination. Her plan was to become a government officer.

Now she is spending her days reading Gunahon Ka Devta (The God of Sins), a famous 1949 Hindi tragic romance novel written by Dharamvir Bharati, on the pavement outside AIIMS, waiting to find out when her treatment will begin and when she can go home.

Yadav says she has been dealing with an intestinal illness for five or six years and has already undergone two operations. Her family had sought treatment elsewhere before relatives and neighbors advised them to travel to Delhi in search of better treatment at AIIMS — a trip of roughly 370 miles. "We thought AIIMS was the best hospital in India," she said. The cost of staying in Delhi was also a burden: Her family could not afford a room and had already spent thousands of rupees on travel and other expenses.

When we interviewed her on Aug. 3, she had been there for about three weeks with her parents, Surendra Singh Yadav, 47, a farmer, and Kalpana Yadav, 45.

"We thought the facilities would be good, the doctors would be good, and everything would happen quickly. We never imagined that we would have to sleep on the road," she said.

For her, the pavement is not just uncomfortable, it is also frightening. During the day, she says, she can manage. At night, she worries about the people around her.

"There are all kinds of people here," she says. "Some are good, but some drink or use drugs. There is shouting and fighting. As a girl, I feel very uncomfortable here at night."

Sponsor Message

But the family has little choice. They cannot afford a room in Delhi, she says. "We have decided that we have to sleep on the road because there is no other option."

During the day, Yadav goes into the hospital for appointments, tests and checkups, then returns to the pavement while waiting for the next step in her treatment. Everything is on hold — her college education, her hopes of qualifying for a government job, her father's farming work.

"It feels like we are being forced to live like this," she says.

"I just pray that I can meet a doctor"

Lakhi Bai, 62, from Ramnagar in Maihar district, Madhya Pradesh, in central India, about 500 miles away, came to Delhi seeking treatment for diabetes and a condition that she says causes numbness and a loss of sensation in parts of her body.

She says she could sometimes sustain an injury without feeling pain. When we met her, she had been sleeping outside Safdarjung Hospital for about 20 days. During that time, she says, she had been going to different doctors and departments for consultations and tests but had not yet received a treatment plan.

Bai is a farmer and describes herself as a homemaker. She said she has three sons but is no longer in contact with them. She came to Delhi alone.

toggle caption i Sajad Hameed for NPR

"I cannot afford to bring someone with me," she says. "If I bring someone, I have to pay for their food and accommodation, too."

It's been a difficult period. "Sometimes I don't even get food," she says. "I sleep with an empty stomach."

Sleeping outside is also stressful. The heat is hard to endure, she said, as is rainwater.

"When it rains, water comes here," she said. "There is nowhere to go."

AIIMS did not respond to requests for comment about her account or the experiences described by other families interviewed for this story.

Sponsor Message

Bai did not know how much longer she would have to remain in Delhi. "I have no place to stay," she says. "I just pray that I can get the treatment I need and something can be done."

A month outside awaiting a child's heart treatment

In August, Balraam Singh, 35, a brick-kiln worker from Meerut, Uttar Pradesh, had been sleeping outside Safdarjung Hospital for about a month with his wife and their 7-year-old son, Munna Singh.

Munna has a heart condition that his father describes as a "hole in the heart."

They had come from about 50 miles away seeking further medical evaluation and treatment at Safdarjung Hospital.

"We came with a lot of hope that we would find a doctor and my son would be treated," he says. "But now it feels like we may have to go back without knowing what will happen next.

For Singh, who can earn $5 to $7 a day at the kiln where he works, staying in Delhi means not only a loss of income but the need to spend money on food and other daily needs.

Six months of saving for another hospital visit

Gulshan Bano, 38, had come to Delhi from Bihar with her 60-year-old mother, Asma Khatoon, and her 6-year-old daughter, Fiza. They had been sleeping outside Safdarjung Hospital for about a week when we met them in August.

Bano says her mother has had a heart condition for several years and was receiving treatment in Bihar. Her mother had undergone checkups and tests there, but the family felt she needed further evaluation and care.

toggle caption i Sajad Hameed for NPR

Relatives also advised them to seek treatment in Delhi, and the family decided to travel for further consultations and tests.

Bano said doctors have told them that her mother has a heart problem and have prescribed medication rather than recommending surgery.

Sponsor Message

The family returns to Delhi for checkups about every six months. To pay for the trips, Bano works in domestic jobs in Bihar.

"I work for months and save whatever I can, and then I come here," she says. "Whatever little money remains has to be used here."

Bano said her husband does not contribute to her mother's medical expenses and she has little choice but to keep making the journey to Delhi.

A visit can last about a month, Bano said, as the family waits for scheduled consultations, tests and follow-up care. Because they cannot afford other accommodation, they sleep outside the hospital between appointments and tests rather than return home and make another journey to Delhi.

"Where should I go?" she said. "I have to come here because my mother needs treatment."

For families like Bano's, charities and volunteers can provide some of the practical support they need while they wait outside the hospitals.

Rajiv Ranjan, who works with the Delhi-based Donate A Meal Trust, said his organization regularly helps patients and their attendants staying outside AIIMS and Safdarjung Hospital by distributing food, clothes and rations.

He said the organization has seen many families remain outside the hospitals while seeking treatment or caring for relatives inside.

"We come here for people who sleep outside while they or their family members are receiving treatment inside the hospital," he says. "They have nowhere else to stay, so we try to help with whatever we can." The group distributes about 100 meals a day, Ranjan says.

Food, however, is only one of the needs.

"People need shade from the sun, and during the rainy season they need somewhere to stay dry," Ranjan said. "Some of them take shelter under the Delhi Metro, the city's rapid-transit rail system, when it rains."

For Shalini Yadav, the 20-year-old college student from Madhya Pradesh who traveled to Delhi for treatment, the food distributions and other help have become part of life outside the hospital. She said people arrive to help in whatever way they can, but the assistance does not reach everyone.

Sponsor Message

"Sometimes we get food. When we don't, we buy it nearby. But there are many people here who don't get anything to eat."

For families, treatment means returning to Delhi again and again

Suhana Bano, 47, from Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh, has been bringing her 18-year-old son, Mohammad Sameer, to Delhi for treatment for about two years.

toggle caption i Sajad Hameed for NPR

Sameer has irritable bowel syndrome. He was in seventh grade when this digestive ailment forced him to leave school. The family first sought treatment at several hospitals in Bareilly, about 155 miles from Delhi, before traveling to Safdarjung Hospital.

Suhana Bano said the family turned to Delhi after seeking treatment locally, hoping to find the specialized care Sameer needed.

The family travels to Delhi whenever Sameer is due for a consultation or tests. Typically, they stay one to two months, Bano says. While in Delhi, the family sleeps outside Safdarjung because they cannot afford a room.

Aamar Singh, 60, a farmer from Hathras, Uttar Pradesh, had been sleeping outside AIIMS for about a week when we met him in April.

His 35-year-old daughter, Neelam, was admitted to the AIIMS intensive care unit with a respiratory problem, he said. His 40-year-old sister, Rashima, stayed outside with him. At night, they sleep alongside stray dogs that also gather on the pavement.

Singh does not know how long his daughter will remain in the ICU after being admitted for treatment and therefore does not know how long he will have to remain outside.

Food is not always available, he said, and some days they go hungry.

"Sometimes you eat, sometimes you don't," he said. "My daughter is inside, so I have to stay here. What else can I do? This is our situation."

So Aamar Singh waits on the pavement for news about his daughter until he can take her home.

Sponsor Message

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

Sajad Hameed is an India-based journalist and multimedia storyteller focusing on South Asia. He writes about politics, human rights, health, business, the economy and the impact of climate change, with particular focus on the region's evolving social and political landscape.

Rehan Qayoom Mir is an independent journalist whose work has appeared in outlets including Al Jazeera English, The Guardian, Nikkei Asia, The Progressive, Jacobin and more. He reports from across India and South Asia, with a focus on ground reporting and human-interest stories.

World.title: Trump promised a swing district blitz. He's going to a lot of very red states
World.content:
Trump promised a swing district blitz. He's going to a lot of very red states

toggle caption i Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images

📲Follow the midterms & more in the NPR App

Early in September, President Trump gathered Republicans running in competitive races for a dinner in the White House Rose Garden. Prime aged beef burgers were on the menu as the president made a pledge to spend the final month before the midterms campaigning for the approximately 30 Republican candidates in attendance.

"I'm going to go to every one of those 35 places and we're going to see if we can get everyone elected," Trump said confidently.

The White House hasn't clarified which 35 places the president was talking about that night. Since then, Trump has campaigned with fewer than a third of those candidates. Rather than focus on swing states and swing districts as the president said he would, his travel schedule has taken him to a lot of Republican territory.

Sponsor Message

Trump's itinerary is both a reflection of where he can help (and where he can't) but also of a shifting landscape where even red state Republicans need a boost.

Loading...

On the tarmac between rally stops in Arizona and Montana this week, Trump attempted to spin his visits to states he won decisively just two years ago as a matter of gratitude.

"So, I do it to thank them," Trump said. "I also do it because we have some great people there that are running and I want to make sure they win."

He went on to bemoan the drop in Republican turnout in years when he isn't on the ballot, something Trump and his team are trying to counteract with an October campaign rally blitz that has taken him to Ohio (twice), Texas (twice), Oklahoma and even Tennessee.

"What the hell am I doing in Tennessee?" Trump mused from stage to wild cheers.

Earlier this week, the president took an eight hour flight to Alaska to campaign for Republicans, Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Rep. Nick Begich, both of whom face races that are too close for comfort in a state Trump won by 13 points in 2024.

"This is worth the 8 hours in a plane," Trump said to an adoring crowd. "And don't forget I've got 8 hours going back. Give me credit for that."

Sponsor Message

In fact, he made two more stops on the way back and spent the night at the Trump hotel in Las Vegas.

The Republican National Committee has announced he'll be campaigning in Kansas Monday, which has a toss-up U.S. Senate race, something few would have anticipated even a month ago.

Loading...

Republicans are on defense in a lot of states where they've traditionally won without much trouble. Trump's team is picking locations where he can activate the Republican base in places where he's done well in the past.

"Just a lot of excitement, a lot of momentum building up on the ground here," said RNC Chairman Joe Gruters in a call with NPR from a Trump rally in Arizona. "It's turnout, turnout, turnout. How do you get the base to show up? You put the president on the ballot. You put him out there."

Trump frequently implores his supporters to vote as if he were on the ballot. It's a novel political strategy that runs counter to the norm for unpopular presidents whose parties face significant midterm headwinds. Trump claims the polls are wrong about his underwater approval rating.

As for Trump's message, it doesn't change much from stop to stop. There are the greatest hits: his past election wins, his One Big Beautiful Bill, and a walk down memory lane from right before he launched the war with Iran when gas prices were cheaper. He teases a $5,000 dividend to every American adult if Republicans win the House and the Senate, an idea he first rolled out at the unconventional Republican midterm convention, but has faced resistance from elected Republicans. On most stops he talks about a specific project or deal he has planned for the state.

On Tuesday, Trump is set to campaign in Greenville, North Carolina. Republican campaign committees have already started canceling ad reservations meant to help Trump's handpicked Republican Senate candidate there, Michael Whatley. It's a sign they see that race as moving out of reach.

Sponsor Message

There's also a congressional district in Eastern North Carolina that was redrawn to favor Republicans as part of Trump's mid-decade redistricting push. It shouldn't be competitive, but it's now rated a toss-up by the Cook Political Report.

"I think it's going to backfire on them this year in every way shape and form," said Anderson Clayton, chair of the North Carolina Democratic Party. "He's trying to drum up any amount of support that he can at the last minute. But I don't think that North Carolinians are going to fall for it again."

World.title: Here's why some people say the 2-day weekend is due for a makeover
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | How old is the two-day weekend?: Cost of Living 9:14 A brief history of the weekend

As the two-day weekend turns 100 years old, some say it's high time for a calendar shakeup.

"Almost nobody alive remembers the time before we had a five-day week and a two-day weekend," said Grace Tallon, co-founder of Work Time Revolution, a Toronto-based consultancy group that helps employers adopt shorter work hours.

Labour historians and advocates for workweek reform point out that much has changed since the two-day weekend became standard about a century ago, depending on where you are in the world.

Tallon notes that only 20 per cent of women were in the workforce at that time. "Now we have mostly dual-income households, yet we still have a situation where we have a five-day workweek that doesn't serve really any family."

Experts also point out that the weekend is a human-made concept that has evolved before and can evolve again.

Grace Tallon, co-founder of Work Time Revolution, a Toronto-based consultancy group that helps employers adopt shorter work hours, says the way we live and work has changed a lot since we last revisited the length of the workweek. (Submitted by Grace Tallon)

How the two-day weekend came about

In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, a long workweek was the norm.

"Basically, if you were working for wages, the regular work week was six days of 10 hours a day," said labour historian Craig Heron, a professor emeritus at York University in Toronto.

"The beginning of the weekend was the Sunday that everyone got off for religious reasons," Heron told Cost of Living host Paul Haavardsrud.

Though Henry Ford is widely credited with instituting a two-day weekend, there's quite a bit more to the story, including decades of work by the labour movement.

Prior to Ford's five-day-week, small groups of workers had achieved similar reforms.

"The most famous group were the printers," Heron said. "They managed to get an eight-hour day by about 1910."

An illustration published in the Canadian Illustrated News shows workers taking part in a Nine-Hour Movement march in Hamilton, Ont., in 1872. The movement pushed for shorter working days and helped spur major changes to Canadian labour law. (Canadian Illustrated News/Library and Archives Canada)

When Ford announced in October 1926 that his factories would move to a five-day week, the company became the first major U.S. employer to do so.

That same month, the American Federation of Labor passed a resolution at its annual congress calling for a five-day week, Heron says.

But it would be a while until the two-day weekend was broadly adopted, including in Canada, he says.

Many workplaces in North America and elsewhere first reduced Saturday work to half a day.

The labour movement grew stronger in the 1940s as the Second World War drove demand for workers, giving unions greater leverage to win shorter workdays through major strikes, he says.

Governments began to take note and legislate accordingly.

In workplaces that adopted policies that reduce hours while maintaining pay through pilots run by the non-profit 4-Day Week Global, participants reported an improvement in their ability to combine paid work with their social lives. (Tint Media/Shutterstock)

Work has changed

Since then, the nature of work has changed significantly, in ways that can affect whether a two-day weekend feels adequate.

"We have a much more fluid kind of work schedule for a lot of people who work electronically, who work at all hours, all times of the day or week, and can be on call anytime," said Heron. "Their cell phone could ring whenever their employer wants them."

While working hours steadily decreased from the late 19th century to the middle of the 20th, they began to increase again after that, says David Henkin, a historian at the University of California, Berkeley and author of The Week: A History of the Unnatural Rhythms That Made Us Who We Are.

The erosion of boundaries between work and personal time has not only increased the amount of work that people do, he says, it has also "decreased the amount of insulation, psychic insulation, that people have from work."

When every weekend is a long weekend

A desire to address that erosion is part of what's fuelling momentum for a four-day workweek.

Tallon is also a former executive director of the non-profit 4-Day Week Global, which conducted four-day-week pilots starting in 2022 , in which hours were reduced while pay remained the same. She says all 41 participating companies in Canada and the U.S. kept the four-day week after the six-month trials ended.

One of them was Praxis, a public relations firm in Toronto.

Meredith Nebel, an account director for public relations firm Praxis, says that since the company moved to a four-day week she's been able to keep her weekends more free for family time because she can get errands, chores and appointments out of the way on Fridays. (Submitted by Meredith Nebel)

Meredith Nebel, an account director for Praxis, says days off are staggered. Colleagues cover her work while she's off on Fridays, "and then I take on their Monday work just to make sure that there's no pause in the workflow."

Nebel says she doesn't think she could go back to a five-day week.

"I have more time with my kids. I have time within my own community. I have more time for my own life and my own desires and just building myself as a human," she said.

Nebel says she uses Fridays to get appointments, household errands and chores out of the way so weekends are free for family time and kids' activities.

Charles Latimer, who works for Greenpeace, says having Fridays off since the organization adopted a four-day week has given him time to volunteer.

"I just started a little kids' basketball program after daycare on Tuesdays," said Latimer, who works remotely from Lund, B.C., about 200 kilometres north of Vancouver.

On Fridays Latimer takes care of administrative tasks for the program and also keeps his four-year-old home from daycare, he says.

Charles Latimer, seen here with his four-year-old daughter and their dog, works as head of strategic integration for Greenpeace, which reduced hours to a four-day schedule. (Submitted by Charles Latimer)

Consultant Grace Tallon says switching to a four-day schedule takes considerable planning. "That could mean that you need to restructure your meetings; that could mean that you need to ensure that everybody has heads-down time, when that previously wasn't respected."

At Praxis, Nebel says it hasn't been a struggle to get the work done in less time.

"Work just seems to expand to fill the time that you give it," she said, "but with the four days there's a natural urgency so we plan more deliberately and we're sharper about what actually needs to get done."

'The week is unnatural'

We tend to think of the week — with its five days of work and two of rest — as set in stone.

But Henkin says the very idea of the week as a whole, let alone the way we divide it, is considerably more arbitrary than the other units humans use to measure time.

"The week is unnatural because it is not actually rooted in any of either the astronomical phenomena that produce things like days or … hours or years, nor are they rooted in the biological rhythms that produce patterns of day and night."

Tallon says that whether a workplace is looking to adopt a four-day week or just rein in long hours, it's about "how you start to respect your own time and how the company starts to respect your time."

"And many of these people then feel, 'I can turn off my notifications in the evening. I'm not gonna look [because] I feel I have to. Because nothing's going to blow up or burn down.'"

World.title: From ‘killing the golden goose’ to better than ever: Has Alberta's relationship with Ottawa changed?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The relationship between Alberta and the federal government has faced its share of political and economic conflict over the years . Some Albertans would argue more than its fair share.

From the drawing of the province’s boundaries to natural resource control to the creation of the National Energy Program to pipeline cancellations and political representation, generations of Albertans have expressed feelings of alienation .

Last year, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith added to the litany of rebukes of Ottawa from Alberta leaders over the years. (Her predecessor, Jason Kenney, once said the federal government was "killing the golden goose".)

After launching a panel tour to hear citizens' frustrations, Smith said, “You know what Ottawa can't help but be fixated on? ... Punishing our energy sector and layering on policies to keep it in the ground."

She made those remarks nearly two months after the Liberals won a fourth-consecutive election under new leader Mark Carney.

Members of the Alberta Next panel gathered for a public town hall meeting in Red Deer at the Westerner Park grounds on July 25, 2025. (Jason Markusoff/CBC)

Fast forward to this fall, with Albertans poised to go to the polls in a referendum that could ultimately lead to a separation vote, and Smith is expressing a very different view.

“I do think Canada is working better than it ever has,” Smith told CBC News , noting she will be voting for the province to stay put.

The remarks follow months of Smith saying that, in her view, working out the differences between Alberta and Ottawa would be the key to quelling separatist sentiment, a blueprint she said is shared by Carney.

WATCH | Premier says Alberta and Canada 'walking together' for first time in a long time: Premier says Alberta and Canada 'walking together' for first time in a long time | Duration closed caption 3:15 At a campaign stop with Prime Minister Mark Carney, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said she and Carney can agree on voting to remain in Canada in the upcoming referendum, but 'there is still more to come' and she is going to vote yes to the nine other questions on the ballot. 'I have bad news for you, prime minister - all of the premiers are interested in talking about immigration reform,' Smith said.

So what changed in the relationship between the province and Ottawa? Is Alberta really in a better place than a year ago? And if so, for how long?

For her part, Smith said that Alberta has “finally” found a government willing to move swiftly on major projects, such as the Pacific Link pipeline , while not “standing in the way” of Alberta developing its resources.

Carney, the premier said, is a “different type of leader.”

“I think he understands the Constitution. I think he respects the constitutional division of powers,” she said. “There’s areas that are federal jurisdiction, and areas of provincial jurisdiction.”

That’s why, the premier argued, Albertans should vote to remain in Canada, with a newfound belief that federation can function fairly.

But those who say the province needs to go its own way to realize its true potential see Carney’s promises as mere window dressing after years of policy that stymied economic growth and personal freedoms.

Constitutional lawyer Keith Wilson argued in favour of Alberta independence at a debate in Calgary held in late May. (New West Video)

“They’re just saying, 'Hey, we’re getting along.' Well, what if they stop getting along?” said Keith Wilson, one of the most prominent leaders in the Alberta separatist movement.

“I am not satisfied to have the future of my children’s success and prosperity hinge upon whether the prime minister and a premier have a good personal relationship.”

No to the nine ('bad laws')

In addition to the proposed Pacific Link pipeline and other federal investments, Smith has praised federal movement around what she calls the “nine bad laws” that she demanded be addressed in order to avoid an “unprecedented national unity crisis.”

As detailed by Smith in March 2025, they were, in brief:

A spokesperson in the premiers’ office said it considers seven of the nine “scrapped or reformed.”

“Investment is soaring and major projects are moving forward again. This is proof of progress and a more collaborative relationship,” Ryan Fournier wrote in an email.

WATCH | Ottawa and Alberta engaged in 'tough collaboration,' says Carney: Ottawa and Alberta engaged in 'tough collaboration,' says Carney | Duration closed caption 2:01 At a campaign stop in Red Deer, Alberta with Premier Danielle Smith, Prime Minister Mark Carney said when the federal and provincial governments are 'open and honest with each other' about challenges, they can 'find solutions.' The two leaders urged Albertans to vote 'no' to a referendum on separation.

The federal government revised those policies amid criticism from some that the moves would claw back environmental protections and concern from others surrounding Indigenous consultation .

Wilson isn’t satisfied with progress to date, citing, among other developments, a recent Alberta Court of Appeal ruling that stated the federal government’s Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional.

“I’m sorry, but this is just … political platitudes, absent substantive action. If the prime minister was serious about these things, he would offer to change equalization,” he said.

“He would announce that he’s going to follow the court decision, and repeal Bill C-69 [the Impact Assessment Act]. Surely, people aren’t this gullible. But maybe they are?”

The Alberta Court of Appeal in Calgary is seen in this file photo. Earlier this month, it ruled the federal government's Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional. (Google Maps)

Heather Exner-Pirot, director of energy, natural resources and environment at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute in Ottawa, said that Canada had a “terrible reputation” for investment due to policies implemented under former prime minister Justin Trudeau.

“The corrections to the ‘nine bad laws’ … those are all meaningful, in that they have attracted investment,” she said.

“You can always say that things aren’t perfect, or there’s things we can still do to improve competitiveness, but I don’t think anyone would have anticipated two years ago that we could be where we are here today.”

Earlier this month, the federal and Alberta governments announced that the proposed Pacific Link pipeline, which would carry one million barrels of oil a day from Alberta to the B.C. coast, had become the first project designated in the national interest. That classification means that federal approvals and regulatory reviews will be fast-tracked.

Prominent separatists, meanwhile, have argued that the Pacific Link pipeline is not a point in Carney’s favour.

WATCH | How much money could the new Pacific Link pipeline cost Canadian taxpayers?: How much money could the new Pacific Link Pipeline cost Canadian taxpayers? | Duration closed caption 24:49 Chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton speaks with Energy Minister Tim Hodgson about the significance of the Pacific Link Pipeline’s national interest designation and how much of the $35-billion-plus estimated price tag Canadian taxpayers could be on the hook for. Then, Alberta Finance Minister Jason Nixon talks through what the pipeline means for provincial unity, ahead of a referendum on separation. Finally, Grand Chief Stewart Phillip from the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs shares his concerns with the pipeline’s condensed environmental review and Indigenous consultation processes.

“This is a nationalized pipeline. Is that really the only way to get something done in Canada, is to have the government do it?” said Cory Morgan, who heads the third-party advertiser Pathway to Independence, in a recent video . “That’s not a good sign, guys.”

Exner-Pirot said government de-risking is necessary for West Coast pipelines given challenges tied to past projects.

After Kinder Morgan halted construction on the Trans Mountain pipeline, the federal government under Trudeau took over, buying the troubled project for $4.5 billion in 2018. The project cost eventually spiralled to $34 billion.

“The particular circumstances of a west coastal pipeline are terrible,” Exner-Pirot said. “I think, [it is] justified for government to de-risk it, and to show that it can be done.”

Heather Exner-Pirot, director of energy, natural resources and environment at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, says changes to laws and regulations under Prime Minister Mark Carney have made Canada more competitive and attractive for investment. (Paula Duhatschek/CBC)

However, Exner-Pirot said many other energy projects, including other pipelines, are moving forward successfully without government subsidies — like LNG Canada's Phase 2 expansion in Kitimat, B.C.

“So, the idea that we’re not building anything else except for this one project with government funding or backing is simply not true.”

Fault lines

In the eyes of the Alberta government, the “nine bad laws” may be well on their way to a resolution under Canada’s new prime minister.

But Carney’s comments tied to the “No to the Nine” campaign drew prompt opposition from the provincial government on Thursday.

"No to the Nine" is a prominent federalist advertising campaign that urges Albertans to reject the nine referendum ballot questions not concerned with separation. Five of those questions deal with immigration, while four are aimed at constitutional reforms, like abolishing the Senate.

At a Thursday event, Carney suggested Albertans should vote “No to the Nine." The premier then posted on X that despite the two finding common ground on many issues, it appeared Carney “had yet to fully understand just how damaging the open-border policies” of his predecessor were.

Ian Brodie, a political scientist at the University of Calgary who was chief of staff to former prime minister Stephen Harper, called Carney’s comments a “miss.”

“The winning federalist campaign here is to acknowledge that Alberta has had a short shrift from Confederation over the last few years, and that changes are needed if the province is going to get a fair deal,” Brodie said on CBC Radio's Calgary Eyeopener .

Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke alongside Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Friday at a brewery in Red Deer, Alta. (CBC)

For his part, Carney said Thursday that he didn’t “need a referendum” to co-operate more with the provinces on immigration.

“The province is closer to the needs of the industries here, where the shortages are,” Carney told Global News , adding the federal government had already taken “control” on changes to immigration.

Despite the potential awkwardness, Carney made a campaign stop with Smith at a brewery in Red Deer on Friday, where he made a point of characterizing the relationship between the two as involving “tough collaboration.”

“In our time working together, the premier has consistently put the most difficult issues on the table, with the intention of finding a common way forward,” Carney said.

The conversations to come

“Ottawa may be 2,000 miles away, but destructive federal policy travels on winged feet and strikes like the wrath of God.”

That’s how Monte Solberg, an Alberta MP from 1993 to 2008 for the Reform Party, Canadian Alliance and Conservative Party of Alberta, characterized the relationship between the West and Ottawa in a 2018 column on alienation written for CBC News.

Today, he’s pushing for the federalist side in the referendum, as part of the Vote to Stay campaign. In his view, now is not the time to separate, as Canada is locked in negotiations with the United States.

“That doesn’t mean that, over time, there shouldn’t be a discussion about how we address some of the unfairness in Confederation,” he said.

As to whether the prime minister is the person who will have that conversation?

“Well, I think it’ll be a priority for the premier [of Alberta], and for some other premiers. They’ll have their chance to make their case that this needs to be addressed,” Solberg said.

“I think there is a potential to do so with this prime minister that there wasn’t with, certainly, Justin Trudeau.”

Voters at a downtown Edmonton polling station are pictured on Oct. 13. (Jack Farrell/The Canadian Press)

For Wilson, who believes in an independent Alberta, none of what’s been offered up can be seen as a win.

In his view, there’s been no offer whatsoever to address what he sees as the “structural unfairness” of how Alberta is treated within Confederation.

“None of what [Smith] is doing is addressing those core issues. I don’t know what’s happened to her. I just don’t,” he said.

Some separatists have argued that Albertans should consider Option 2 — to commence the process to hold a future binding referendum on whether Alberta should leave Canada — so as to preserve leverage in negotiations with Ottawa.

Others say they’re opposed to both options on the ballot.

“What Canada needs — is a middle-ground path into the future — a set of constitutional reforms that restore the legal primacy of provincial governments for policies in health, education and social services,” wrote Ted Morton , an Ed Stelmach-era cabinet minister and one of the authors of the well-known "Alberta firewall" letter, which advocated for Alberta to exit the Canada Pension Plan, among other ideas.

Competing referendum signs line a boulevard in Calgary on Oct. 15. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

Polling has suggested that Carney is the most popular politician in Alberta, ahead of Smith and federal Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre.

Duane Bratt, a political science professor at Calgary's Mount Royal University who has argued for the federalist side at events during the referendum campaign, said it is inevitable, as political gravity kicks in, that the prime minister won’t be able to hang onto that level of support forever.

“There�’s always frictions between the federal and provincial governments,” Bratt said.

“The question is: are we going to see that same friction that we saw in the Trudeau era?”

World.title: It's over: Canada ends England's 41-match unbeaten streak in women's rugby
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

England's unprecedented 41-game unbeaten run was broken by Canada 24-21 and witnessed by the biggest crowd in North American women’s rugby on Friday in Toronto.

Canada, unable to handle England's scrum, trailed 14-5 at halftime and 21-12 after more than an hour and didn't settle a compelling WXV contest until a 78th-minute try by Shoshanah Seumanutafa.

“We really had to grind it out and find a way,” Canada captain Sophie de Goede said. “That's kind of the DNA of our team.”

England suffered its first loss since the 2022 Women's Rugby World Cup final, its only previous defeat in 72 matches since 2019.

“Sometimes the flipped coin doesn't go on the side you want it to go,” England captain Meg Jones said. "It's just the nature of the beast."

England showed vulnerability last month at home where it drew with Canada 26-26, ending its 39-match winning streak. That effort gave Canada confidence for the return match at home, including the availability of world player of the year De Goede, rested from its last match, a loss in France, and wings Asia Hogan-Rochester and Alysha Corrigan after injuries.

The hope drew 18,621 spectators, 7,000 more than the previous biggest crowd for a standalone women’s match in North America. England should have scored first but Claudia Moloney-MacDonald dropped the ball over the tryline.

Then Canada used numbers after a Zoe Harrison yellow card for fullback Savannah Bauder to score in a three-on-one.

England stumbles continued with three turnovers in the Canada 22, two on the tryline. But after Canada lock Laetitia Royer was sin-binned, England powered ahead with tries by Maddie Feaunati and Harrison before halftime.

Canada closed to 14-12 in the second half when Corrigan collected her own grubber kick and celebrated before scoring. But England moved further ahead 21-12 after 12 phases when prop Sarah Bern smashed over.

Canada was plagued by forward passes but stayed calm. A missed penalty touch-finder by England was countered and prop DaLeaka Menin, one of three Canada survivors from its last win over England 10 years ago, plowed over to cut the gap to two again. Another England clearance was returned by Canada from its half and De Goede and Gabrielle Senft lined up Seumanutafa to beat the cover to the left corner flag and cap a milestone night in Canadian rugby.

They go again in Ottawa next Friday.

World.title: What the Ukraine dispute reveals about U.S. control over Starlink
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Earlier this week, Ukrainian officials said they had lost some access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, the satellite communications system operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX.

Musk, CEO of SpaceX, denied any involvement in restricting Ukraine's access, saying that decision would be up to the U.S. government.

Meanwhile, on Friday, U.S. President Donald Trump denied he was involved in the decision to restrict access and said he didn't think Musk was involved either.

Trump's remarks followed a Reuters report that the White House had ordered the restrictions.

Ukrainian officials said this week that military-grade Starlin k terminals s topped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance over Ukrainian territory.

Still, the potential ability of the U.S government to affect the operation of a Starlink-related satellite system may also have raised questions about Washington's ability to influence commerical users of the system.

In Canada, for example, Starlink provides internet access in remote areas and has about 500,000 users.

Here's a look at the U.S. government's relationship with Starlink and Starshield, and the role it plays in each.

A Ukrainian drone operator monitors video feeds and satellite imagery on an array of tablets. Ukrainian officials say restrictions on Starshield have disrupted some drone operations. (Neil Hauer/CBC)

What's the difference between Starlink and Starshield?

Starlink is a Space X's commercial satellite internet network, with more than 11,000 satellites and roughly 13 million subscribers. It is available to businesses and individuals.

Its low-Earth-orbit satellites allow it to deliver faster connections than traditional satellite internet systems.

The network gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how its military operates on the battlefield.

But when Musk and SpaceX became concerned about the commercial system being used for military purposes, the company created Starshield, said Mark Hilborne, an associate professor in the defence studies department at King's College London.

Unlike the thousands of satellites used in the Starlink network, Starshield is limited to around 250, Hilborne said.

It's also a more secure network, is not publicly available and is used specifically for government and military purposes. Its secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals.

WATCH | Ukraine says Starlink restrictions are disrupting military operations: Ukraine says Starlink restrictions are disrupting military operations | Duration closed caption 1:56 Ukraine says restrictions on the military version of Starlink have disrupted its defence capabilities against Russia and prompted questions about whether changes to Elon Musk's SpaceX internet service were politically motivated.

Few countries have access to Starshield, Hillborne said. The U.S. is the main customer, while the United Kingdom and Ukraine also have access. In Ukraine's case, the Pentagon covers the fees and allows the country to use the system.

While Starshield's missions are separate from Starlink's commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield's secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals ‌but rely ⁠on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.

What role does the U.S. government have in Starshield?

According to Musk, the Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S government. That means any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and, ultimately, by the president, he said.

"Mostly, it is used by [the U.S.] and it's for them. And so they probably make the ultimate decisions" regarding its use, Hilborne said.

According to a 2024 Reuters report, the Pentagon has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft ​for missile-warning missions and a spy ​constellation for the National Reconnaissance ⁠Office.

But the relationship between Starshield and the U.S. government is "fuzzy," Craig Douglas Albert, a political science professor and graduate director of the Intelligence, Defense and Cybersecurity program at Augusta University in Georgia, said in an email to CBC News.

This image shows Starlink satellites shortly after being launched into space in 2019. (SpaceX)

SpaceX develops and supplies Starshield through government contracts, meaning the system is privately owned but procured by the U.S. government, Albert said.

"There is a lot on this relationship that is classified and thus, the direct relationship is still unclear," he said.

Does the U.S. government have any control over Starlink?

Again, Albert says, it's not entirely clear.

The U.S can regulate Starlink through licensing requirements and the terms of government contracts governing how the company operates, he said.

However, much of the relationship is classified, limiting public understanding of how much influence the U.S. government has over Starlink, Albert said.

But the U.S. has no direct control over Starlink itself, he said.

What major satellite systems does the U.S. government control?

Major examples would include the Global Positioning System (GPS), a space-based radio-navigation system owned by the U.S. government and operated by the United States Space Force. Its satellites provide services to civilian and military users.

WATCH | The high-stakes race to get Canadian rockets into orbit: The high-stakes race to get Canadian rockets into orbit | Duration closed caption 6:48 Canada is the only G7 country without space launch capabilities and it may soon lose its main ride into orbit with SpaceX planning to phase out the Falcon 9. CBC’s Abby Hughes looks at the high-stakes race to build homegrown rockets and secure the nation’s space sovereignty.

The U.S. Space Force also operates Wideband Global SATCOM (WGS) and Advanced Extremely High Frequency (AEHF) system for military communications, as well as the Space-Based Infrared System ( SBIRS) for advanced missile warning.

"The relationship between satellite technology and the U.S. government exists from everyday consumer and citizen consumption through advanced national security operations," Albert said.

Should Canadians be concerned about U.S. government control over private commercial systems?

Hilborne said that while the U.S. may technically have the capability to turn off such a system in a region of Canada, for example, such a move would likely be resisted by commercial operators.

However, the U.S. government could likely apply leverage to a company like SpaceX to bend to its wishes, he suggested.

Albert added that citizens "should always force accountability of technology that is dual use and has a relationship between citizen consumer consumption and national security."

World.title: In Canada's drone-killing 'Sandbox,' companies compete for a $1M prize
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Suffield Research Centre is in the heart of Alberta's Big Sky country and is also blessed with Canada's sunniest skies, making it the perfect testing ground for one of Canada's most critical areas of innovation: drone and counter-drone technology.

Once the main training ground for the tank crews of the British Army, the British gradually withdrew and left entirely by 2024.

But today, the base is buzzing with activity as militaries urgently rearm with new technologies.

Even the British are back, in smaller numbers for now, and not to drive tanks but fly drones — and shoot them down.

Canada's Department of National Defence this month used Suffield to hold its fourth Counter-Uncrewed Aircraft Sandbox (CUAS), a drone-killing contest with a million-dollar prize for the most promising innovation.

Companies from Canada, Australia, Finland and the U.S. showcased new methods of detecting and intercepting drones, closely watched by members of the Canadian, Dutch, German, British, American and Ukrainian militaries.

WATCH | New drone-defence technology showcased: New drone-defence technology put to the test at Canadian showcase | Duration closed caption 2:15 Dozens of companies from Canada and around the world put their counter-drone technologies to the test at the Suffield Research Centre in Alberta as the government looks to strengthen the country’s defence systems.

All of the armies are there to learn and observe. But the Ukrainians, as the only military at the Sandbox with real-world experience in drone warfare, are also there to teach.

"They're creating the environment that we want to emulate," said Col. Gabriel Doré of the Royal Canadian Air Force. "They're on the battlefield. They're the ones who are innovating the fastest. And they can tell us immediately if something's going to work or not just by looking at it, because they're living it."

Learning from the experts

The conflict in Ukraine has turbocharged the pace of scientific innovation in all forms of drone warfare: aerial, ground-based, marine surface and underwater.

There are now even drones that can transition from underwater to aerial flight.

"We need to be the number one in drones to fight against Russia," said Ukrainian Army Maj. Sergiy Kuzyara.

Kuzyara said those drones include cheap, simple first-person view (FPV) quadcopter drones used on the front lines to marine drones to "deep-strike drones which are reaching Russian refineries or military production plants."

A sign at the Suffield Research Centre, about five kilometres north of Suffield, Alta. (Evan Dyer/CBC)

Kuzyara says his mission in Canada is not only to check out the latest designs, but also "help your producers to understand what's needed at the front line, what direction they need to go to be successful."

Tech that was cutting-edge at the 2022 CUAS Sandbox would already be obsolete on Ukraine's front lines, where jamming is so intense that drone operators have given up almost entirely on radio remote control — opting instead to guide their drones through hair-thin fibre-optic wires trailing from spools many kilometres long.

Some of the technology showcased this year at the Sandbox would not be practical in Ukraine's direct combat zones — although useful for other applications.

Signals jamming influences every aspect of the drone war in Ukraine. Ukrainian Army Lt-Col. Maxim Velychenko says satellite-powered navigation (such as GPS) is also jammed on the front lines.

Kamikaze drones go jet-powered

One example of the frenetic pace of innovation in the drone war: the feared Iranian Shahed drones — fixed-wing kamikaze drones that can travel over 2,000 kilometres — have undergone a recent threatening upgrade.

"We know how to shoot down the Shaheds powered by the internal combustion engines," said Kuzyara. "But they switched to jet-powered and so we need to use something new: jet-powered interceptors or missiles."

The new Shaheds are sometimes mixed with the older kind in what Kuzyara calls a "tricky" manoeuvre to deceive air defence crews — flying together at about 180 kilometres per hour before the jet-powered drones more than double their speed to attack.

Firefighters work at the site of Ukraine's Academy of Sciences building hit by a Russian jet-powered drone strike last month. (Sergiy Chalyi/Reuters)

Paul Ziadé thinks he has the solution.

The CEO of Calgary's North Vector Dynamics has been a regular at the Sandbox. He's designed a metre-long, laser-guided missile with the jet-powered Shahed in mind.

"Our missile does not need to achieve a direct hit on the target," he said. "Similar to many other air defence missiles, all we need to do is get to the proximity of the threat and then the warhead takes care of the rest."

Unlike other air defence missiles, however, this prototype is designed to defeat drones — and is both smaller and cheaper.

In the test witnessed by CBC News, North Vector's missile almost brushed a target drone, considered a kill for a weapon that carries a proximity fuse and uses a warhead to blast a forward-conical explosion.

Having shown its ability to connect with the target, the next round of testing will likely include the warhead.

Cost a critical factor

Weapons already exist that can reliably destroy even a jet-powered Shahed. The problem is their cost.

At the start of the U.S. and Israel-Iran war, the United States and Gulf kingdoms were forced to use Patriot PAC-3 missiles ($5 million Cdn each) and other expensive interceptors to defeat much cheaper Iranian drones.

Ukraine has succeeded in inventing lower-cost interceptors, but jet-powered drones such as the new Shahed and the Geran-5 have forced the use of pricier alternatives.

Cost is critical, says Doré.

"Otherwise it's really easy to send a bunch of drones our way that's going to make us, you know, use very exquisite, very expensive systems," he said.

WATCH | European countries concerned about drone sightings: Suspicious drones are stalking NATO skies with impunity | Duration closed caption 2:04 European powers are on growing alert because of suspicious drones flying over sensitive sites inside NATO territory with seeming impunity. Some analysts and European leaders accuse Russia of staging an intimidation campaign, but Moscow denies any involvement.

"We're going to empty our magazines very rapidly."

Reducing cost-per-shot and ensuring you don't run out of firepower are key goals of drone developers, with all sides expecting to see more drone "swarms" in the future, and greater use of AI in targeting and guidance.

Armin Strobel of St. John's-based StrobelTEK did a PhD thesis on drone swarms in 2010, when it was still an exotic and little-researched subject. Today he is competing in the Sandbox as the designer of a cheap, portable optically guided kinetic missile meant to defeat those swarms.

He told CBC News that fully autonomous attack drones are on the horizon.

"There might be some steps in between, but you'll basically just send out drones and say, 'Look for those targets and take care of them.'"

Kuzyara says larger, fixed-wing drones will increasingly come to resemble missiles, as they speed up to defeat interceptors.

Extra points for new ideas

The Department of National Defence doesn't tell competitors how to neutralize drones. Those who show the most promise in innovation win the prize, say organizers.

Examples this year include an explosive 12-gauge shotgun round from Colt Canada, fitted with a proximity fuse that allows a shooter to kill FPV drones without a direct hit.

Alabama-based SCI Technology has a long, tubular drone with six rotors that carries a net. Nets have been used for a while to entangle drones and make them crash, but SCI's solution is for situations where it's not safe to knock an explosive drone out of the sky because of the presence of people or sensitive infrastructure on the ground.

SCI's AeroGuard fires a net that captures the enemy drone, but the net stays tethered to the AeroGuard, which then carries the captured drone to a safe location.

Australia's AIM Defence, which won first prize in 2024, brought two laser units to the 2026 event.

Jenelle Frewen, the company's director of strategic initiatives, says AIM used its $1-million prize to set up a Canadian division that now employs 10 people. Its laser system has since become more powerful, more accurate and lighter.

"We've had a lot of fantastic support from Canada," she said. "We were originally an Australian company, we're now a joint Australian-Canadian company."

'Obsolete in a couple of weeks'

The Department of National Defence finds it worthwhile to provide a free testing facility and cash prizes because its mission in Suffield has a double purpose.

The first is to find the best counter-drone technologies for the Canadian Forces, which recognize a need to catch up in the fastest-growing area of modern warfare.

The second, though, is to foster a domestic drone manufacturing industry. The Carney government's Defence Drone Initiative is focused on developing capabilities in marine drones, underwater drones, uncrewed ground vehicles, explosive payloads, long-range precision-strike drones and the counter-drone interceptors being tested at Suffield.

That means creating an environment of constant innovation, says Doré.

"Even if we could come up with a perfect solution today, it would probably be obsolete in a couple of weeks," he said. "It's not so much about finding the perfect solution now, it's about finding the right process and having the ability to iterate rapidly."

He expects that Canadian drone companies will soon "be as competitive as any around the world" if the support from the government continues.

Under those conditions, he said "both counter and drone companies should be able to find a market for themselves, and answer the call when it comes to developing a sovereign capability."

World.title: N.S. growers eye new apple export markets amid U.S. trade tensions
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Nova Scotia's apples are poised to reach more overseas tables this year.

The province's fruit growers' association said it's taking steps toward the goal of shipping some of this season's apple harvest to Taiwan.

It marks a new move by Nova Scotian growers to diversify their global markets amid Canada-U.S. trade tensions.

The United States currently accounts for 90 per cent of Nova Scotia's apple exports, according to the Nova Scotia Fruit Growers' Association. While the sector remains untouched by direct tariffs, local growers are seizing the moment as an opportunity.

"We've built a great relationship with the consumers in certain American states and cities," said Emily Lutz, the association's executive director.

" But it is important now more than ever to have alternatives available, and just for other markets to be aware of the quality of fruit that we grow in Nova Scotia."

The move will help growers find a stronger position in case there is a future trade disruption.

Data shared by the association show the province's apple exports to the U.S. exceeded $28 million last year. The U.S. was followed by Vietnam, which imported nearly $750,000 worth of Nova Scotia apples.

Lutz said Vietnam has become Nova Scotia's second-largest apple market after a foothold was established about seven years ago.

Growers are now targeting the Taiwan market this year, while also looking to enter Thailand. Lutz said many Southeast Asian countries do not grow apples, which creates opportunities for fruit producers in Nova Scotia.

Although those countries are closer to Australian and New Zealand producers, Nova Scotia will benefit from having the opposite harvest season.

Emily Lutz said some Southeast Asian countries do not grow apples, which creates opportunities for fruit producers in Nova Scotia. (Paul Légère/Radio-Canada)

In February, the federal government launched the AgriMarketing Program, providing $75 million over five years to agriculture businesses nationwide to find new markets. Out of that, the Nova Scotia Fruit Growers' Association secured $300,000.

Lutz said the funding can support their various market development activities, such as attending international exhibitions and hiring local marketing experts.

Michael Van Meekeren, vice-president of Van Meekeren Farms Ltd. in Lakeville, N.S., said while this year's apple crop is not the largest on record, it is still a bumper season, and having access to new markets is an exciting opportunity for growers.

Van Meekeren said Nova Scotia will prioritize exporting varieties with a strong global competitive edge, such as Honeycrisp and Ambrosia.

He believes exports will not strain local supply, as the Atlantic region has a small population and abundant apple resources.

"We just export the ones that really shine from Nova Scotia," Van Meekeren said. "I think it is the right thing to do for Nova Scotia when we have something that is as good or better than any others in the world."
