World.title: US commerce secretary’s resistance to cutting tariffs stalls trade talks with Mexico
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico’s trade talks with the United States have stalled as a direct result of U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s opposition to tariff cuts, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday.

Citing people familiar with the negotiations, the Journal said talks were at an impasse due to disagreements ​over the U.S. tariffs on vehicles, steel and aluminum from Mexico.

The report said Lutnick has opposed significant cuts to the 25% tariff on Mexican cars and the 50% tariff on steel, aluminum and derived manufactures (finished products made of steel and aluminum). Such levies were imposed by the Trump administration for what it called national security reasons and are administered by Lutnick’s department.

Mexico is on record as citing tariff relief as its top priority in trade negotiations with the U.S.

The Journal traces Lutnick’s intransigence to pressure from U.S. domestic industry, which has told the Trump administration that reducing tariffs would harm businesses and lead to layoffs.

Lutnick is not leading the negotiations with Mexico, but according to the Journal his presence is creating tension with the man who is — U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

It is the second time Lutnick has disrupted advanced negotiations with a North American partner, the report said, apparently referring to Canada. But he has now re-inserted himself into Trump’s trade agenda after being sidelined through most of 2026 as Greer gained more prominence.

Sources told the newspaper that the two countries appeared close to finalizing a deal that would have reduced the U.S. tariffs in exchange for a series of concessions from Mexico.

Mexico had already agreed to suspend for five years the 10% tariff it applied to imports of parts and components intended for vehicle assembly. This concession also seeks to reduce assembly costs, attract investment in new production lines and strengthen supply chains, especially as the automotive industry has been contracting.

Finalizing this bilateral deal would pave the way for further talks on renewing the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, which is currently under review.

Officials from both countries denied that the bilateral talks had stalled. Mexican officials and numerous business executives had expressed optimism about an imminent agreement.

On Wednesday, Mexico’s Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard updated federal deputies about the perceived progress in the bilateral trade talks.

During his meeting with members of the Social Economy and Cooperativism Promotion Committee and the Economy, Commerce and Competitiveness Committee of the Chamber of Deputies, Ebrard told the lawmakers that President Claudia Sheinbaum’s leadership had helped Mexico consolidate itself as the country with the best conditions for accessing the U.S. market.

Just two weeks earlier, after meeting with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer at the National Palace, Ebrard declared that “Mexico is ever closer to reaching new trade agreements with the United States and does not expect to lose the favorable position it maintains with other Washington partners.”

Ebrard was scheduled to meet with the same two legislative committees on Friday.

With reports from The Wall Street Journal, El Universal, Reuters, El Economista, LopezDoriga.com, La Silla Rota and The Latin Times

World.title: Religion in Kenya Explained
World.content:
GUIDES · KENYA

Key Facts — Faith mix Kenya is a majority Christian country with a large Muslim minority. About 85.5 percent of people were Christian and 11 percent Muslim as of 2019, on the government’s estimate, the latest count.

— Churches Non-evangelical Protestants were about 33 percent and Catholics about 21 percent in 2019. Evangelical, African-instituted and Orthodox churches together made up about 32 percent.

— State and faith The constitution says there shall be no state religion. It also creates Kadhis’ courts for Muslim family law.

— Leaders As of 17 October 2026, Archbishop Maurice Muhatia Makumba chairs the Catholic bishops and Archbishop Jackson Ole Sapit leads the Anglicans. Al-Hajj Hassan Ole Naado chairs the Supreme Council of Kenya Muslims, as at 15 October 2026.

— Next vote The general election falls on Tuesday 10 August 2027. Churches and mosques are already courted and are already speaking on political violence.

— Travel The US travel advisory for Kenya stood at Level 2, exercise increased caution, as of 28 July 2026. Lamu, Garissa, Wajir, Mandera and Tana River counties are Level 4, do not travel.

Kenya religion is overwhelmingly Christian, with a large Muslim minority concentrated on the coast and in the north-east. For US readers, faith matters because churches and mosques shape elections, health care, schools and travel safety.

Kenya Religion in Numbers

The latest national count is the 2019 census. The US State Department, in its 2022 report on religious freedom, gives the government’s 2019 estimate as about 85.5 percent Christian and 11 percent Muslim.

Among Christians, non-evangelical Protestants were about 33 percent of the population and Roman Catholics about 21 percent. Evangelical Protestants, African-instituted churches and Orthodox churches together made up about 32 percent.

Hindus, Sikhs, Baha’is and followers of traditional African religions each account for less than 2 percent. The census also found about 755,000 people who said they were atheist or had no religion.

Faith follows geography and ethnicity. Most Muslims live in the north-east and on the coast, and the State Department says ethnic Somalis and Swahilis in the coastal region account for a majority of Muslims.

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “Is Morocco safe? Washington says use increased caution” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

The five largest ethnic groups, the Kikuyu, Luhya, Kalenjin, Luo and Kamba, are predominantly Christian. Our Kenya Population 2026, Ethnic Groups and Faiths guide sets out the wider census picture.

Every share above dates from 2019 and is a rounded State Department figure, so the full KNBS tables may differ by a few tenths of a point. A later count may shift the balance between Protestant, Catholic and Muslim communities.

The Catholic Church: Schools, Hospitals and Bishops

The Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops (KCCB) lists 28 Catholic jurisdictions in the country. They are four archdioceses, 23 dioceses and one military ordinariate.

Archbishop Maurice Muhatia Makumba of Kisumu is the KCCB chairman, with Archbishop Anthony Muheria of Nyeri as vice-chairman. Archbishop Philip Anyolo leads Nairobi and Archbishop Martin Kivuva Musonde leads Mombasa.

The Cathedral Basilica of the Holy Family in central Nairobi (Photo: Bahnfrend, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only — every claim links to its source article. Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesCost of living, safety, visas across Latin America › RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. × Best for expats Cost of living Safest places Easy visas Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

The Church is also a major provider of services. The KCCB says its Catholic Health Department supplies about 25 percent of health care in Kenya through 451 health units.

A national commission set up in 1961 guides religious education in Catholic-sponsored schools. Caritas Kenya, the Church’s development arm, runs humanitarian and social programmes.

The bishops also speak on public life. In a statement of Thursday 16 April 2026 they cited the Shakahola and Kware deaths as proof of weak state surveillance.

They also called bodies found in Kilifi and Kericho deeply disturbing. The statement followed a meeting of the bishops in Karen, Nairobi.

Protestant, Anglican and Evangelical Churches

Protestants form the largest Christian group, spread across older mission churches and newer evangelical congregations. African-instituted churches are churches founded by Africans rather than by foreign missions.

The Anglican Church of Kenya (ACK) says it has 37 dioceses. Archbishop Jackson Ole Sapit has led it since he was elected on 20 May 2016 and consecrated on 3 July 2016.

St Peter’s Anglican Church in Nyeri, central Kenya (Photo: Shyamal L., CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

The National Council of Churches of Kenya (NCCK) describes itself as a family of Christian communions and organisations. It says it was founded in June 1913 at a missionary conference at Thogoto, near Nairobi.

The State Department said in its 2022 report that the new president and deputy president were both tied to evangelical churches. After their September 2022 inauguration the new government held prayer services at State House, and some observers raised concerns about blurring church and state.

Muslims on the Coast and in the North-East

Muslims are about 11 percent of Kenyans, and most live in the north-east and on the coast. There are also significant Muslim communities in parts of Nairobi and in western Kenya.

The Supreme Council of Kenya Muslims (SUPKEM) is a national Muslim organisation with its headquarters in Nairobi. Its National Chairman, Al-Hajj Hassan Ole Naado, issued a communique after a national Muslim leaders forum in the capital on 15 October 2026.

At the forum SUPKEM launched the Ummatic Policy Liaison Directorate, a permanent unit meant to link the Muslim community with ministries and the National Treasury. The leaders said they were willing to strengthen ties with the current government.

The constitution creates Kadhis’ courts under a Chief Kadhi. They decide questions of Muslim law on personal status, marriage, divorce and inheritance, but only when all parties are Muslim.

Kenyan Muslims also travel each year on the Hajj to Saudi Arabia. In June 2026 the Kenya Hajj Mission met at SUPKEM headquarters and opened registration for the 2027 Hajj.

It kept 14 accredited agents, each with at least 300 pilgrims. Saudi authorities have ended Class D tents in Mina, so pilgrims will choose only Class A, B or C.

Lamu Old Town, listed by UNESCO in 2001, has long been a centre of Islamic and Swahili learning. UNESCO names the annual Maulidi festival among its religious functions.

A minaret of the sea front mosque in Lamu, opposite the main jetty (Photo: Ahmedshayo14, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Human rights and Muslim groups said in 2022 that counterterrorism efforts disproportionately affected Muslims, especially ethnic Somalis. Kenyan Somalis and Nubians also reported trouble obtaining national identity cards.

Al-Shabaab, a Somali militant group, has attacked churches, security posts and villages since October 2011, mostly in border areas. Christian Solidarity Worldwide, a UK rights group, lists July 2026 attacks in Mandera County.

One ambush on 28 July killed five counter-terrorism officers. In July 2026 a Kenyan raid in Mandera County killed 11 suspected militants, the group reports.

Other Faiths and People Without Religion

Hindus, Sikhs, Baha’is and followers of traditional religions are small minorities. Indigenous and traditional groups are not required to register, and many do not.

A former MP, Stephen Ndichu, petitioned a court in September 2022 to suspend the registration of Atheists in Kenya, a society of nonbelievers. The society said the case followed its criticism of the First Lady for hosting religious services at State House.

Schools that follow the national curriculum offer religious education in Christian, Muslim or Hindu teachings, plus ethics. In March 2022 the Ministry of Education told schools to stop enforcing hijab bans and forced religious subjects.

What the Constitution and the Law Say

Article 8 of the 2010 constitution says there shall be no state religion. Article 32 protects freedom of conscience, religion, belief and opinion, including the observance of a day of worship.

Article 27 bars the state from discriminating on grounds that include religion, conscience and belief. Article 32 also says nobody may be denied a job or access to an institution because of their belief.

New religious groups, places of worship and faith-based charities must register with the Registrar of Societies, which reports to the Attorney General’s office. Registered bodies may apply for tax-exempt status, including relief on imported goods.

The government lifted a seven-year ban on registering new religious societies in June 2022, the State Department reports. Guidelines issued on 13 July 2022 then required clergy to hold a theology diploma or degree, show tax compliance and win a recommendation from a registered religious society.

The Penal Code makes insulting a religion a misdemeanour with up to two years in prison. Christian Solidarity Worldwide says these provisions are rarely used and should be reviewed.

Faith and Politics Before the 2027 Vote

The next general election falls on Tuesday 10 August 2027, the second Tuesday in August under Article 101. Church and mosque leaders are already speaking on cohesion, hate speech and political violence.

On 8 July 2026 the NCCK General Secretary, the Reverend Canon Chris Kinyanjui, asked the state cohesion commission to tighten action on hate speech. He warned that the 2027 election carries a serious risk of violence.

On 12 June 2026 armed men twice stormed All Saints’ Cathedral in Nairobi during a civic forum on the national budget. Archbishop Ole Sapit and the NCCK condemned the attack, and police said at least two suspects were arrested.

Two of the forum’s organisers, Transparency International Kenya and the Kenya Human Rights Commission, said suspects named a political sponsor. Those claims have not been tested in court, and no alleged sponsor had been charged by late June 2026.

In a statement reported on 14 October 2026 and read at the ACK Synod, Archbishop Ole Sapit condemned abductions as immoral, unethical and unconstitutional. He warned that such acts risk plunging the country into lawlessness ahead of the 2027 election.

The State House church dispute showed the same tension. In July 2025 President William Ruto proposed an 8,000-seat church at State House, and Archbishop Ole Sapit objected to the location.

The Bench of Bishops backed the Archbishop on 11 July 2025, and Muslim leaders asked for a mosque as well. Nairobi’s Catholic Archbishop, Philip Anyolo, voiced concern about perceived bias.

On 28 August 2025 Justice Enock Mwita of the High Court barred permanent religious buildings at official residences until 18 November. The order followed a petition citing Article 8.

Ruto has since defended a chapel in the State House compound, The Star reported on 13 July 2026. He said it would serve staff and be paid for by him and his friends, not by public money.

The Star did not say how far building had progressed. Whether it is the same project that the court paused in 2025 is not stated.

Shakahola and the Debate on Regulating Churches

Shakahola is a forest area near Malindi where investigators found mass graves. Paul Mackenzie, a self-described pastor, was accused of urging followers to starve, and Christian Solidarity Worldwide counts 429 bodies.

A terrorism-related trial over deaths at Kwa Binzaro formally opened on Tuesday 4 August 2026 at the Shanzu Law Courts in Malindi. Mackenzie and seven co-accused face organised criminal activity charges linked to 52 deaths, and two face terrorism-related charges.

About 60 witnesses are expected, including four protected witnesses. The court allowed the prosecution to adopt earlier testimony from 18 witnesses in High Court Criminal Case E006 of 2026.

The accused are presumed innocent unless convicted. Investigators have reported 19 intact graves and five disturbed graves about 62 kilometres from Malindi.

After Shakahola, President Ruto commissioned a taskforce in May 2023 to review how religious organisations are governed. A proposed Religious Organisations Bill in the Senate would oversee theological training, set a code of conduct and require financial reporting.

Many churches oppose the bill and prefer self-regulation through a code of conduct. The government has said it has no intention of regulating religion.

Holidays and Festivals

Article 9 of the constitution names three national days: Madaraka Day on 1 June, Mashujaa Day on 20 October and Jamhuri Day on 12 December. A national day is a public holiday, and our Mashujaa Day 2026: 20 October Holiday, Eldoret, US Visitors guide explains the next one.

Both Islamic festivals of 2026 were declared by gazette notice. The Interior Cabinet Secretary declared Friday 20 March 2026 a public holiday for Idd-ul-Fitr, which ends Ramadan.

A second notice declared Wednesday 27 May 2026 a public holiday for Eid ul-Adha. It appeared in a special issue of the Kenya Gazette dated 25 May 2026.

The Catholic bishops sent Easter greetings in a public statement dated Thursday 16 April 2026. It called for peace, jobs for young people and respect for human life.

What It Means for US Readers

Investors should note that church and mosque networks are large service providers, with Catholic facilities alone supplying about a quarter of health care. Faith leaders also act as early warning voices on election risk, so political risk reviews should follow their statements.

Travellers face a Level 2 advisory, exercise increased caution, issued by the US State Department on 28 July 2026. Level 4, do not travel, applies to Garissa, Wajir, Mandera, Lamu and Tana River counties, with Tsavo National Park excluded, and to parts of Kilifi and the coast north of Malindi.

The advisory says terrorists have targeted places of worship, hotels, markets and transport hubs. It warns that attacks can happen at any time, including around national days and religious holidays.

Expats and diaspora families will find faith groups at the centre of civic life, from health care to election monitoring. A faith group that wants to operate in Kenya generally registers with the Registrar of Societies, and should take legal advice on current rules.

What Is Not Known

No census since 2019 gives religion shares, so current numbers for Muslims, Catholics and evangelical churches are estimates at best. The ACK website gives a diocese count but no membership figure.

It could not be confirmed whether the High Court has ruled on the State House church petition, so its final outcome is open. The timing of any verdict in the Kwa Binzaro trial is also not known.

Neither the timetable nor the final rules of the Religious Organisations Bill have been confirmed. The number of Kenyan pilgrims on the 2026 Hajj has not been confirmed either.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the main religion in Kenya?

Christianity is the main religion, with about 85.5 percent of people as of 2019 on the government’s estimate. Muslims are about 11 percent.

Does Kenya have a state religion?

No, Article 8 of the constitution says there shall be no state religion. Article 170 creates Kadhis’ courts that apply Muslim law to Muslims in family matters.

Where do Kenya’s Muslims live?

Most live in the north-east and on the coast, with communities in Nairobi and western Kenya. The State Department says ethnic Somalis and Swahilis in the coastal region account for a majority of Muslims.

Who leads Kenya’s main churches and Muslim body?

As of 17 October 2026, Archbishop Maurice Muhatia Makumba chairs the Catholic bishops and Archbishop Jackson Ole Sapit leads the Anglicans. Al-Hajj Hassan Ole Naado chairs SUPKEM, and the Reverend Canon Chris Kinyanjui was NCCK General Secretary in July 2026.

What happened at Shakahola?

Investigators found mass graves in the Shakahola forest near Malindi, and Paul Mackenzie was accused of urging followers to starve. A trial over deaths at Kwa Binzaro opened on 4 August 2026, and the accused are presumed innocent unless convicted.

Is it safe to visit Kenya’s churches and mosques?

The US advisory for Kenya was Level 2, exercise increased caution, as of 28 July 2026. It says terrorists have targeted places of worship and rates Lamu, Garissa, Wajir, Mandera and Tana River counties Level 4.

Which religious holidays did Kenya declare in 2026?

The government declared Friday 20 March 2026 a holiday for Idd-ul-Fitr and Wednesday 27 May 2026 for Eid ul-Adha. Both were announced by gazette notice.

World.title: Veritá Poll Puts Flávio at 51%, Lula at 49%
World.content:
The Parliament building in Rabat, where the press council bill was approved in 2026 (Photo: Davide Cesare Veniani, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

BRAZIL · ELECTIONS

Published Saturday, 17 October, 10:55 a.m. ET · Source: Instituto Veritá

Key Facts The country Brazil, Latin America’s largest country, elects its president in a runoff on Sunday 25 October between President Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

What happened On Saturday 17 October, the polling institute Veritá released a national runoff survey with Flávio Bolsonaro narrowly ahead.

The numbers Flávio Bolsonaro has 51.1% of valid votes and Lula 48.9%, a gap of about 2 points.

Margin of error 1 percentage point at 95% confidence, on 15,554 interviews with registration BR-01107/2026.

Fieldwork Interviews ran from Monday 12 to Friday 16 October, so they include the days after the 15 October Datafolha release.

Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

Prediction markets Polymarket gives Flávio Bolsonaro a 76.8% chance of winning the 25 October runoff and Lula 23.5% (17 October, 10:30 a.m. ET). Polymarket puts Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning at 77% and Kalshi at 79% (Lula: 24% and 21% ), as of 17 October, 10:20 am ET ; prices are bets, not polls.

Still open Veritá published valid votes only, and this report found no raw totals, so the share of undecided voters is unknown.

Flávio Bolsonaro leads President Lula by 51.1% to 48.9% of valid votes in a new poll from Instituto Veritá, released on Saturday 17 October. The survey is the latest in the Brazil election 2026 runoff, which is due on Sunday 25 October.

The Veritá poll adds a fresh data point to our Brazil election polls tracker eight days before the vote. Flávio Bolsonaro, senator for Rio de Janeiro, represents the conservative Liberal Party (PL), while Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s president, represents the left-wing Workers’ Party (PT).

What the Veritá Runoff Poll Found

Veritá interviewed 15,554 voters across all 27 Brazilian states from 12 to 16 October, Jornal Razão reported. The institute set the margin of error at 1 percentage point with 95% confidence.

The institute ran the survey on its own initiative and registered it with the electoral court (TSE) as BR-01107/2026, according to Midiamax. The valid-vote result was 51.1% for Flávio Bolsonaro and 48.9% for Lula.

Valid Votes and Why They Matter

Valid votes leave out blank and spoiled ballots, which is how Brazil’s electoral court reports the final result. Pollsters publish this split so that their numbers can be compared with election night.

The gap of about 2 points is roughly twice the stated margin of error of 1 point. Other pollsters use different samples and methods, so one survey does not settle the race.

How It Compares With Datafolha

Datafolha, a major pollster linked to the newspaper Folha de S.Paulo, published a runoff poll on 15 October with Flávio Bolsonaro at 51% and Lula at 49% of valid votes, GZH reported. Veritá’s split of 51.1% to 48.9% sits in the same range.

Veritá’s fieldwork ended on Friday 16 October, a day after Datafolha published its poll. Our tracker lists each survey with its dates so that readers can compare them.

What It Means for US Readers

If you hold Brazilian stocks, bonds or US-listed shares of Brazilian companies, a runoff this close can bring price swings until the result is known. Polls from different institutes can point in slightly different directions, so many investors follow several at once.

If you follow US politics or trade, the winner will shape Brazil’s dealings with Washington for the next four years. A lead of about 2 points is a snapshot of opinion, not a forecast.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, an online prediction market, bettors give Flávio Bolsonaro a 76.8% chance of winning the 25 October runoff and Lula 23.5% (17 October, 10:30 a.m. ET). The “Brazil Presidential Election” market has drawn about US$185.3 million in total bets.

These are bets, not polls, and they can move quickly on new surveys. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Prices are bets, not polls, and can move fast. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

Veritá’s valid-vote figures were published without raw totals in the reports we reviewed, so the share of undecided, blank and null voters is unknown. We also could not confirm how the institute weighted its sample.

It is not known how voters will react in the final week, or how many will turn out on 25 October. Any poll measures opinion on the days of the interviews and does not predict the result.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who leads Brazil’s latest runoff poll from Veritá?

Flávio Bolsonaro leads with 51.1% of valid votes against 48.9% for Lula, a gap of about 2 points. Instituto Veritá released the poll on Saturday 17 October 2026.

How many voters did Veritá interview?

Veritá says it heard 15,554 voters in all 27 Brazilian states between 12 and 16 October. The stated margin of error is 1 percentage point at a 95% confidence level.

Who paid for the Veritá poll?

Veritá carried out the survey on its own initiative, so no newspaper or party commissioned it. It is registered with the electoral court (TSE) under number BR-01107/2026.

What are valid votes in a Brazilian poll?

Valid votes leave out blank and spoiled ballots, which match how the electoral court reports results. Veritá published the valid-vote split, and the Midiamax report did not give raw totals.

When is Brazil’s runoff?

Brazilians vote on Sunday 25 October 2026, eight days after this poll was released. The winner becomes president of Latin America’s largest country.

World.title: Morocco Media Landscape Explained
World.content:
GUIDES · MOROCCO

Key Facts — The media system Morocco media is a mix of state-run broadcasters, palace-linked owners, family-run news sites and a large online audience. The press council, the audiovisual regulator HACA and the courts set the rules.

— Press freedom Morocco ranked 105th of 180 countries in the 2026 press freedom index, a gain of 15 places on 2025. It scored 50.55, in the “difficult” band.

— State broadcasters The public group SNRT runs the state channels and is absorbing 2M and Medi1. The 2M takeover went to the Competition Council in December 2025, and completion is not confirmed as of October 2026.

— Online audience Morocco had 35.5 million internet users in October 2025, or 92.2% of the population. Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Instagram are the main news routes.

— Who governs King Mohammed VI named Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri head of government on 29 September 2026, and her cabinet took office on 16 October 2026.

Morocco media explained: who runs the state broadcasters, who owns the main newspapers and news sites, and how the law and the palace shape what is published. Every figure carries its year and every office-holder is current as of October 2026.

Morocco media is a mixed system in which the state controls the biggest television and radio networks, while private owners and a fast-growing online sector compete for audiences. For US readers it matters because Morocco is a trade and security partner whose news ecosystem is shaped by institutions close to the palace.

In the 2026 press freedom index of the group Reporters Without Borders (RSF), Morocco rose 15 places to 105th of 180 countries. This guide covers broadcasters, newspapers, digital outlets, ownership, regulation and the open questions as of October 2026.

How the System Is Built

Morocco is a constitutional monarchy under King Mohammed VI, who names the head of government after each election. Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri of the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), the largest party after the vote of 23 September 2026, was appointed on 29 September 2026.

Her cabinet was named at a ceremony at the Royal Palace in Rabat on 16 October 2026, with Samir Belfkih as government spokesperson. Broadcasting is overseen by the regulator HACA, the Haute Autorité de la Communication Audiovisuelle, while newspapers answer to the press code and the courts.

Washington says use increased caution” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

The sector has four layers. Each has a different owner and a different degree of independence.

State-run broadcasters: the public group SNRT, which runs the Al Aoula channel and radio networks and is absorbing 2M and Medi1.

The state news agency MAP, Maghreb Arabe Presse, which supplies official copy to every newsroom.

Private print: Arabic-language and French-language dailies and weeklies, many owned by business figures or investment groups.

Online media: news sites, YouTube channels and social platforms, where 78% of surveyed Moroccans got news in 2025.

Aerials and satellite dishes on rooftops in the old city of Fez, where television still reaches homes directly (Photo: Adam Jones, Ph.D., CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Public Broadcasting: SNRT, 2M and Medi1

SNRT, the national radio and television company, is the public broadcaster and took 88% of public media funding in 2017. Its radio networks held a 26.73% audience share that year, according to the Media Ownership Monitor run by RSF and Le Desk.

2M, run by the company SOREAD, reached a 33% television audience share in the same 2017 study. The finance ministry owned 72% of SOREAD and SNI, the royal holding company, owned 20%.

Medi1 is a Tangier-based news broadcaster with television and radio arms. On 16 May 2024 the Competition Council published a notice that SNRT would acquire 100% of the share capital and voting rights of Medi1 TV.

In January 2025 SNRT chief executive Faïçal Laraïchï told a parliamentary committee that SNRT would take full ownership of 2M and Medi1 TV within two months, Morocco World News reported. A plan for a public media holding had been presented to parliament on 25 May 2021 by the then minister Othman El Ferdaous.

On 3 December 2025 the Competition Council published a notice that SNRT had notified the acquisition of 99.99% of SOREAD, the company behind 2M. The notice invited comments until 15 December 2025, and no clearance decision or completion filing was found as of October 2026.

Newspapers and Who Owns Them

Print is split between Arabic-language titles, which were growing in 2017, and French-language titles, which were declining. The Media Ownership Monitor found that Arabic-language owners mostly came from journalism, while French-language shareholders included business and financial leaders.

Businessmen held stakes in five of the nine French-language publications that study examined, including Aujourd’hui Le Maroc, La Vie Éco, L’Économiste and La Nouvelle Tribune. Two of them, Aziz Akhannouch and Moulay Hafid Elalamy, were government ministers in 2017, and Akhannouch led the previous government.

The royal holding company SNI held shares in four media companies in 2017. Three of them ranked among the five largest by turnover.

In June 2026 the project State Media Monitor placed Maroc Soir, publisher of Le Matin and Assahra Al Maghribiya, in its “Captured Private” tier and called its ownership and editorial line palace-aligned. That is an outside classification, and the publisher has not been quoted in the sources reviewed.

Independent titles exist but struggle for money, and advertising tends to favour pro-government media, according to RSF’s 2026 country assessment as summarised by Morocco World News. Lakome, Badil and Enass are named as outlets that keep publishing critical reporting.

Where the Advertising Money Goes

In 2017 television took 39.8% of the advertising market, outdoor posters 29.1%, radio 16.7% and print 13.2%. The same study said advertising was not allocated fairly and recalled boycotts of the magazines TelQuel, Nichane and Le Journal Hebdo in the early 2000s.

Digital News and Social Media

Morocco had 35.5 million internet users in October 2025, or 92.2% of the population, a national digital report found in November 2025. Social media identities numbered 22.8 million, equal to 59.1% of the population.

Facebook’s advertising reach was also 22.8 million in late 2025, and YouTube reached 21.6 million. TikTok reached 16.7 million adults and Instagram 15.1 million.

In the Digital News Report 2025 from the Reuters Institute, 78% of Moroccan respondents got news online and 28% said they trusted most news. For news, 49% used YouTube, 47% Facebook, 32% Instagram, 30% WhatsApp groups and 24% TikTok.

Hespress, founded in 2007, is run by Marocads, owned only by the El Guennouni brothers, and the Media Ownership Monitor calls it Morocco’s most popular news website. The 2025 survey listed Hespress among the online brands with reasonable trust, next to Medi1 and the state channel Al Aoula.

Concern about false information is high, with 54% of respondents worried about telling real from fake news online in 2025. Mohamed Mehdi Bensaid, then minister of youth, culture and communication, cited digital media growth and misinformation as reasons for the 2026 press council bill.

Press Freedom and the Law

RSF ranked Morocco 105th of 180 countries in its 2026 index, published at the end of April, with a score of 50.55. That compares with 120th and 48.04 in 2025.

RSF credited gains in political and security indicators but said economic and legal pressure still weighs on the sector. Its tracker listed no journalists killed or detained in Morocco from 1 January 2026 to late April, as cited by Morocco World News.

Prison sentences for press offences were abolished in 2016. Journalists can still be prosecuted under other laws, such as the Penal Code, and critics of the government can face lawsuits.

The best-known recent case is Hamid El Mahdaoui, editor of the news site Badil. A Rabat court sentenced him on 11 November 2024 to 18 months for defaming Justice Minister Abdellatif Ouahbi, and an appeals court upheld the sentence on 30 June 2025.

Ouahbi kept the justice portfolio in the cabinet named on 16 October 2026. According to RSF’s assessment, reporting on these topics can still bring legal or financial pressure:

The monarchy and religion.

The security services and protests.

Western Sahara.

Corruption.

A café in Tangier with a television on the wall, photographed in November 2015 (Photo: cat_collector, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

The Press Council and Self-Regulation

The National Press Council is meant to let journalists and publishers police their own ethics. Its legal basis has been contested, and the Constitutional Court ruled on an earlier text.

On 24 December 2025 the upper house, the House of Councillors, adopted an earlier reorganisation text after four opposition groups walked out over rejected amendments. In January 2026 the Constitutional Court struck down five of its articles, and the government revised the bill as Draft Law 09.26.

On 4 May 2026 the House of Representatives approved Draft Law 09.26 by 70 votes to 25, and a House of Councillors committee backed it on 15 June 2026 by five votes to three. The law entered into force in July 2026, when a temporary committee took over the council’s duties until elections could be held.

Bensaid said the bill creates a commission to oversee council elections and gives the council more autonomy. Opposition lawmakers objected that using publisher turnover to set representation favours large economic players.

Morocco World News reported that the council would shrink from 19 to 17 members and that more than 130 amendments were tabled at committee stage. Critics say the mix of elections and appointments could skew representation.

Journalists voted for their representatives on 15 September 2026, and on 21 September the new council elected Mokhtar Laghzioui as president by 11 votes to 3. Hanane Rihab was elected vice president with 11 votes.

The Parliament building in Rabat, where the press council bill was approved in 2026 (Photo: Davide Cesare Veniani, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

State and Palace Influence

Influence runs mainly through ownership, money and the courts rather than formal censorship. The Media Ownership Monitor found in 2017 that nine of the 36 companies it studied were linked to the state, the government or the royal family.

Public funding is concentrated in SNRT, and television and radio ratings come from bodies run by coalitions of economic interests. The study said the regulator HACA declined its request for up-to-date broadcast data.

Self-censorship is described as a common result of court cases and doubts about judicial independence. Editors take most care with the monarchy, the security services and Western Sahara.

Government officials describe the press council reform as a step that strengthens independence and ethics. Both views are on the record and can be weighed against the ownership and legal facts above.

What It Means for US Readers

Investors and companies should treat state broadcasters as an official voice and check corporate news against filings and several outlets. Data are patchy, since 16 of 40 media companies surveyed in 2017 published no financial information.

Travellers will find English-language coverage on Hespress English and Morocco World News, while everyday media runs in Arabic and French. The Rio Times language guide explains how those languages divide up in daily life.

Expats who publish commentary should know that defamation cases such as El Mahdaoui’s are brought under the Penal Code. Anyone relying on Moroccan sources should check who owns them, because the state or palace-linked investors hold stakes in many large outlets.

What Is Not Known

It is not confirmed whether SNRT has completed the takeover of 2M and Medi1. The Competition Council notice on 2M dates from December 2025, no clearance decision or completion filing was found, and the detailed ownership monitor dates from 2017.

The cabinet list of 16 October 2026 names Mohamed Mehdi Bensaid minister of Youth, Culture and Sports and lists no communication minister. It is therefore not stated who now carries media policy, a brief that Bensaid held until that date.

Whether the new government will change course on press regulation has not been stated. Survey data on news habits come from online panels and may not reflect Moroccans who are offline.

Frequently Asked Questions

How free is the press in Morocco?

RSF ranked Morocco 105th of 180 countries in 2026, up 15 places from 120th in 2025, with a score of 50.55. The country sits in the “difficult” band, and prosecutions under the Penal Code and financial pressure remain concerns.

Who owns the main television channels in Morocco?

The state controls most of them through SNRT, which runs Al Aoula and is absorbing 2M and Medi1. In 2017 the finance ministry owned 72% of 2M’s operator SOREAD and the royal holding company SNI owned 20%.

What is the most popular news website in Morocco?

The Media Ownership Monitor describes Hespress as the most popular news website in the country. It was founded in 2007 and is edited by Marocads, owned by the El Guennouni brothers.

Where do Moroccans get their news?

In the Digital News Report 2025, 78% of respondents got news online, and YouTube (49%) and Facebook (47%) led among social platforms. Trust in news overall was 28%.

What is Morocco’s National Press Council?

It is the body that lets journalists and publishers regulate their own ethics, and it issues press cards. Law 09.26 reorganised it, and the new council elected Mokhtar Laghzioui as president on 21 September 2026.

Can journalists be jailed in Morocco?

Prison sentences for press offences were abolished in 2016, but journalists can be prosecuted under the Penal Code. Hamid El Mahdaoui received 18 months in November 2024 for defaming the justice minister, and an appeals court upheld it on 30 June 2025.

Sources: Royal Palace statements on the appointment of the head of government, 29 September 2026 and on the new government, 16 October 2026; RSF and Le Desk, Media Ownership Monitor Morocco, November 2017; Morocco World News on the 2026 press freedom index, 30 April 2026; Morocco World News on Draft Law 09.26, May 2026; Hespress on the House of Councillors vote, 24 December 2025; Hespress on the El Mahdaoui appeal, 30 June 2025; Morocco World News on SNRT, 7 January 2025; Competition Council notice on Medi1 TV, 16 May 2024; Hespress, public media holding plan, 25 May 2021; Media Ownership Monitor entry on Hespress; Digital News Report 2025, Morocco, 17 June 2025; national digital report, 8 November 2025; State Media Monitor, Morocco; Competition Council notice on SOREAD, 3 December 2025; RSF country page, Index 2026; Morocco World News on the press council president, 22 September 2026; Morocco World News on the temporary committee, 25 July 2026. All accessed 17 October 2026.

World.title: Colombia Security and Crime Explained 2026
World.content:
GUIDES · COLOMBIA

Key Facts — The country Colombia is a close US security partner that grew 261,000 hectares of coca in 2024, up 3.5% on 2023. Washington kept it on its 2026 list of countries that failed to curb drugs.

— Who is in charge Abelardo de la Espriella, a conservative lawyer, became president on 7 August 2026. In September 2026 he ended peace talks with the ELN guerrillas and said armed groups would get no political status.

— Violence Colombia recorded between 14,038 and 14,780 homicides in 2025, depending on the official count. Killings from January to August 2026 ran about 2% above the same months of 2025.

— Armed groups The ELN has about 6,300 members on official 2025 estimates, and the Gulf Clan about 9,000 on estimates from late 2025. Both are on the US terrorist list, as are the FARC-EP and the Segunda Marquetalia.

— Travel Colombia carries Level 3, Reconsider Travel, on the US advisory scale since 31 March 2026. Arauca, Norte de Santander, Cauca (except Popayán), Valle del Cauca (except Cali) and the strip within 10 km (6 miles) of the Venezuelan border are Level 4, Do Not Travel.

— Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

Colombia security in 2026 mixes falling kidnappings with stubbornly high homicide, extortion and displacement. This guide explains the numbers, the armed groups, the forces that fight them and what to know before you go.

Colombia security matters to Americans because the country grows coca on 261,000 hectares and works closely with Washington against traffickers. A conservative government that took office on 7 August 2026 has ended peace talks with armed groups and promised a harder line.

This guide sets out the crime trends, the main armed groups, the police and army, the hotspots and the safer areas, with every figure dated. It is written for investors, travellers and expats who want a calm, factual picture.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Colombia Crime Trends in Numbers

Colombia counted 14,038 homicides in 2025 in the defence ministry’s open data as of 16 September 2026, up from 13,497 in 2024. The ministry’s first count, reported by El Tiempo, was lower at 13,726, a rate of 25.8 per 100,000 people against 25.6 in 2024.

The forensic institute, Medicina Legal, gave a higher preliminary figure of 14,780 homicides for 2025, against 14,021 in 2024. The counts differ because the ministry tallies only killings it ties directly to violence, El Tiempo noted.

The first quarter of 2026 brought no fall. The ministry’s open data show 3,485 homicides from January to March 2026, up 4% from 3,345 a year earlier, and 9,434 from January to August, up 2% from 9,256.

Extortion also rose, to 2,914 cases in the first quarter of 2026, up about 7% on a year earlier. Massacres, meaning attacks that kill three or more people, numbered 30 with 94 victims by March, and victims rose 32%.

Kidnapping moved the other way in 2026. Preliminary ministry data show 238 victims from January to August 2026, against 434 in the same months of 2025, a fall of 45%.

That fall follows a sharp rise. The ministry’s year-end review called 2025 the worst year in a decade for extortive kidnapping, Publimetro reported.

City figures can differ from the national picture. Bogotá recorded 73 homicides in September 2026, its lowest September count since 2003, La Silla Vacía reported.

Bogotá’s security secretary, César Restrepo, put the capital’s cumulative fall in homicides for 2026 at about 8%. Bogotá, Barranquilla and Medellín all recorded fewer homicides in 2025 than in 2024, El Tiempo reported.

Young adults face the greatest risk. The ombudsman’s office, the Defensoría del Pueblo, put the 2025 rate at 57.61 per 100,000 among people aged 18 to 28, against 23.08 for the whole country.

The ombudsman, Iris Marín, blamed armed groups both inside and outside talks with the government. Her office quoted a national rate of 23.08, lower than the ministry’s 25.8, so every figure here is an estimate.

Who Runs Security Policy in 2026

President Abelardo de la Espriella took office on 7 August 2026. He ended the earlier government’s “total peace” policy and treats all armed groups as terrorists, the research group Security Council Report noted in October 2026.

In September 2026 he announced the end of the talks with the ELN that his predecessor, Gustavo Petro, had left in place. He summed it up as “the false peace is over”, Semana reported, and offered armed groups only submission to justice.

He named retired general Jorge Eduardo Mora López, who has led special forces and intelligence units, as defence minister on 6 July 2026. Mora was still in office in October 2026, after the Senate rejected a censure motion against him on 23 September.

A draft Anti-Terrorism Statute would create a public register of terrorist actors, similar to the US Treasury’s OFAC list. Banks and notaries would have to check it, and the draft sets rules for air strikes within humanitarian law.

As of 9 October 2026 the bill had not reached Congress, Vanguardia reported. Opposition senator Iván Cepeda called it “especially worrying” that the register could impose economic sanctions without a court conviction.

A police customs officer on duty at the Simón Bolívar International Bridge in Cúcuta, on the Venezuelan border, 13 February 2018 (Photo: National Police of Colombia, CC BY-SA 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

In a determination dated 11 September 2026, the US president kept Colombia on the list of countries that “failed demonstrably” on drugs. He also ruled that US aid to Colombia is vital to American interests.

The determination blamed the previous government for the label. It said the president would consider lifting it if De la Espriella’s campaign against coca and cocaine shows progress.

The ELN and the FARC Dissidents

The National Liberation Army, or ELN, is a guerrilla group formed in 1964 that has fought the state for decades. InSight Crime, citing official 2025 figures, puts it at about 6,300 members, including militia and support networks, with about a fifth of them based in Venezuela.

InSight Crime, a research group on organised crime, places the ELN in at least 184 municipalities across 19 departments. It funds itself through extortion, kidnapping, taxes on coca growers and traffickers, illegal mining and border smuggling.

In January 2025 the ELN began an offensive in Catatumbo, a border region of Norte de Santander, against the 33rd Front, a FARC dissident unit. By January 2026 the ombudsman’s office counted 105,203 victims of the fighting, including 101,587 people forced from their homes, Publimetro reported.

Across the country in May 2026, 15,045 people were confined to their homes and 2,799 were displaced, the ombudsman’s office said. Nearly half of those displaced were in Tibú and El Tarra, where dissidents loyal to the commander known as Calarcá fight the ELN, El Tiempo reported.

FARC dissidents are fighters who rejected or abandoned the 2016 peace deal with the former FARC guerrilla army. They are split into rival factions that fight one another and the ELN.

On 12 October 2026 a car bomb near the El Bordo toll on the Pan-American Highway in Cauca wounded three civilians. The army blamed the Carlos Patiño structure, a FARC dissident unit, in a preliminary attribution reported by Publimetro.

Security Council Report also noted a car bomb at a police station on 31 August 2026 that killed one civilian and injured 11 others. It added that late-August air strikes in Guaviare reportedly killed more than 30 people, including five children, an allegation in the UN Secretary-General’s report that we have not independently confirmed.

The Gulf Clan and Other Criminal Gangs

The Gaitanist Self-Defence Forces of Colombia, known as the EGC or Gulf Clan, is among the country’s biggest armed groups, with about 9,000 members on official figures cited by the think tank Ideas para la Paz. The think tank Pares found it present in 302 of Colombia’s roughly 1,100 municipalities, MDZ reported in December 2025.

The group grew out of 1990s paramilitary forces and former members of the EPL guerrillas, and it began in the Urabá region near Panama. Its reported leader is Jesús Ávila, known as Chiquito Malo.

The US State Department designated the EGC a foreign terrorist organisation in December 2025. It followed the ELN, the FARC-EP and the Segunda Marquetalia on the US list, and the move could complicate talks the former government held with the Gulf Clan.

In the north, the Autodefensas Conquistadoras de la Sierra Nevada, or ACSN, hold the mountains above Santa Marta. On 12 October 2026, 41 detainees escaped a holding centre in the city, among them the group’s alleged finance chief, alias Mongolo, El Espectador reported.

The escape came weeks after the ACSN’s armed strike of September 2026, which followed the killing of its alleged second-in-command, alias Cholo. Guards had opened a gate to give an ailing detainee paracetamol, and others used the moment to flee.

Cocaine and the Money Behind the Violence

Colombia had 261,000 hectares of coca in 2024, up 3.5% from 253,000 in 2023, in the UN drugs office survey. The results were published in June 2026.

The Pacific region held 121,612 hectares and Catatumbo 48,739 hectares. Tumaco, on the Pacific coast, was the municipality with the most coca, at about 31,000 hectares.

Coca grew in 180 of Colombia’s 1,122 municipalities, about 16% of the total. Cocaine seizures rose 19% in 2024 to about 889 tonnes, while manual forced eradication fell 54%.

Coca bushes on a forested hillside in Colombia (Photo: Hoyosmunosyolanda, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

Armed groups earn money along the whole chain, from taxing growers to running labs and moving product across borders. InSight Crime says the ELN is directly involved in cocaine production and trafficking, especially along the border with Venezuela.

The White House determination of 11 September 2026 said coca cultivation and cocaine production reached record levels under the previous government. It expects De la Espriella’s campaign to show progress on eradication and on breaking up what it calls narcoterrorist networks.

Police, Army and Their Limits

The National Police sits inside the Ministry of Defence, alongside the army, navy and air force. That structure puts one minister in charge of both the soldiers who fight armed groups and the officers who patrol cities.

About 11,200 soldiers were deployed in Operation Catatumbo as of January 2026, Publimetro reported. Armed groups answer with explosive-laden drones, and the ombudsman’s office counted 394 such attacks between April 2024 and December 2025, Publimetro reported.

Military action has intensified under the new government. InSight Crime recorded that the military bombed an ELN camp between San Calixto and Tibú on 11 August 2026.

The Santa Marta escape of 12 October 2026 showed the limits of the state’s grip. El Espectador said it revived debate on whether authorities can contain criminal groups.

The UN Verification Mission, which monitors the 2016 peace deal, has a mandate that expires on 31 October 2026, and the Security Council is expected to vote on renewal. Congress’s economic committees have backed a 2027 budget that would leave the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, the transitional justice court, about US$87.8 million short of its request.

Hotspots and Safer Areas

Violence in Colombia is local, and the map changes by department. These are the areas that official and press sources name most often in 2026.

Catatumbo, Norte de Santander: the ELN and FARC dissidents fight over coca land and border routes, and the area holds 48,739 hectares of coca.

the ELN and FARC dissidents fight over coca land and border routes, and the area holds 48,739 hectares of coca. Cauca: dissident attacks continue, including the car bomb at El Bordo on 12 October 2026.

dissident attacks continue, including the car bomb at El Bordo on 12 October 2026. Arauca: InSight Crime describes clashes between the ELN and the FARC dissident 10th Front in the Arauca–Apure corridor.

InSight Crime describes clashes between the ELN and the FARC dissident 10th Front in the Arauca–Apure corridor. Pacific coast: the ombudsman’s office listed Buenaventura, Roberto Payán and Linares as emergencies in May 2026, and Tumaco has the most coca of any municipality.

the ombudsman’s office listed Buenaventura, Roberto Payán and Linares as emergencies in May 2026, and Tumaco has the most coca of any municipality. Caquetá and Putumayo: these two departments had the most confinement in May 2026.

these two departments had the most confinement in May 2026. Santa Marta and the Sierra Nevada: the ACSN armed strike of September 2026 and the escape of 12 October 2026 centre on this area.

Safer areas exist, mostly in the big cities, though Cali’s homicides rose from 1,177 to 1,282 in 2025. Bogotá, Barranquilla and Medellín all recorded fewer homicides in 2025 than in 2024, El Tiempo reported.

The main tourist cities, Bogotá, Medellín and Cartagena, lie outside the conflict zones listed above. Street crime still occurs there, and the US advisory says violent crime is common in many areas of Colombia.

Hillside homes in Comuna 13, a Medellín district that visitors now tour (Photo: Bernard Gagnon, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

Civilians, Leaders and the Peace Deal

Indepaz, a Colombian peace research institute, counted 78 massacres in 63 municipalities in 2025, against 76 in 2024. It also recorded 187 social leaders and human rights defenders killed in 2025, up from 173 in 2024.

Indepaz counted 39 signatories of the 2016 peace deal killed in 2025, up from 31 in 2024, Minuto60 reported. The signatories are former FARC fighters who laid down arms.

The ombudsman’s office said at least 500 Colombians a day were displaced or confined in May 2026. The report blamed armed groups that control movement in communities.

What It Means for US Readers

For travellers, Colombia carries Level 3, Reconsider Travel, on the US State Department scale in an advisory dated 31 March 2026. Arauca, Norte de Santander, Cauca (except Popayán), Valle del Cauca (except Cali) and the strip within 10 km (6 miles) of the Venezuelan border are Level 4, Do Not Travel.

The advisory warns that the US embassy sometimes receives reports of US citizens kidnapped for ransom. Visitors should check it before booking and keep to the main cities and tourist routes.

For investors, the Anti-Terrorism Statute is the item to watch. If passed as drafted, its public register would oblige banks and notaries to screen counterparties, which affects US firms with Colombian partners.

Extortion and attacks on roads raise logistics costs outside the big cities. Security policy also shapes US aid, because the September 2026 determination ties any lifting of the drug-failure label to progress on coca.

For expats, daily risk depends mainly on the city and the neighbourhood. Residents should follow local alerts and avoid road travel in Cauca and Catatumbo.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether homicides will fall or rise across 2026, because full-year figures are not out until early 2027. Preliminary counts are often revised, and the defence ministry and the forensic institute use different methods.

It is not known how the Anti-Terrorism Statute will read when it reaches Congress, or whether lawmakers will pass it. Nor is it clear whether the Security Council will renew the UN mission before 31 October 2026.

The true size of the armed groups is uncertain, and a new count of the Gulf Clan is under way. Coca data for 2025 is not yet published, so it is unknown whether the 2024 rise continued.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many homicides does Colombia record each year?

The defence ministry counted 13,726 homicides in 2025 and the forensic institute a preliminary 14,780. The rate was about 25.8 per 100,000 people.

Is Colombia safe for US tourists?

The US State Department rates Colombia Level 3, Reconsider Travel, in an advisory dated 31 March 2026. Most visitors stay in the main cities, which lie outside the conflict zones, but violent crime is common in many areas.

Which armed groups operate in Colombia?

The main ones are the ELN guerrillas, FARC dissident factions, the Gulf Clan and the ACSN in the Sierra Nevada. The US lists the ELN, the FARC-EP, the Segunda Marquetalia and the Gulf Clan as terrorist organisations.

Is kidnapping still a problem in Colombia?

Yes, although it fell in 2026. Preliminary data show 238 victims from January to August 2026, against 434 a year earlier.

Which areas of Colombia should travellers avoid?

The US advisory says do not travel to Arauca, Norte de Santander, Cauca (except Popayán), Valle del Cauca (except Cali) and the strip within 10 km (6 miles) of the Venezuelan border. Catatumbo, the Pacific coast and parts of the Sierra Nevada also see heavy armed-group activity.

What is Colombia’s Anti-Terrorism Statute?

It is a draft law that would create a public register of terrorist groups and people, with asset freezes and rules for air strikes. As of 9 October 2026 it had not reached Congress, and the opposition has criticised its reach.

Sources: US State Department, Colombia travel advisory; Federal Register, Presidential Determination No. 2026-23, 11 September 2026; White House, 2027 Majors List; Security Council Report, Colombia, October 2026; InSight Crime, ELN profile, 12 August 2026; Ministry of Defence, homicide open data, updated 16 September 2026; El Tiempo, homicides 2025; El Colombiano, Medicina Legal homicides 2025, 16 March 2026; El Espectador, defence ministry figures, first quarter 2026; Blu Radio, kidnapping January to August 2026; Publimetro, extortive kidnapping 2025; Publimetro, Catatumbo one year on; El Tiempo, Defensoría displacement May 2026; Blu Radio, youth homicides, Defensoría; La Silla Vacía, Bogotá September 2026; Minuto60, Indepaz 2025 balance; Forbes Colombia, coca survey 2024; Vanguardia, Anti-Terrorism Statute, 9 October 2026; Vanguardia, defence minister, 6 July 2026; MDZ, Clan del Golfo, December 2025; El Espectador, Santa Marta escape; Publimetro, El Bordo car bomb, 12 October 2026; Semana, end of ELN talks. Figures are the latest available and several are preliminary. All accessed 17 October 2026.

World.title: Religion in South Africa Explained
World.content:
GUIDES · SOUTH AFRICA

Key Facts — The country South Africa counted 62,027,503 people in Census 2022. Christians are 84.5% of those who answered the religion question.

— The mix African traditional religion stands at 7.8%, Islam at 1.6%, Hinduism at 1.1% and Judaism at 0.1%. People with no religion are 2.9%, as of the 2022 count.

— The map KwaZulu-Natal is the least Christian province at 74.3%, with the most Hindus (4.2%). The Western Cape has the largest Muslim share at 5.2%.

— The law Section 15 of the Constitution guarantees freedom of religion, and section 31 protects religious communities. Good Friday and Christmas are among the 12 public holidays in 2026.

— The debate A state commission’s committee published a draft framework for church accountability in December 2025, which it calls voluntary self-regulation. Church groups oppose it and have asked the High Court to annul the committee.

South Africa religion explained: who believes what, which churches matter, and where faith meets law and politics. All figures are dated and come from official sources as of October 2026.

South Africa religion is overwhelmingly Christian on paper, yet the country’s faith life is far more varied than that headline suggests. Census 2022 recorded 84.5% Christians, 7.8% followers of African traditional religion, 1.6% Muslims and 1.1% Hindus.

For US readers the practical points are legal and social. The Constitution protects every faith, churches are a political force, and a draft framework for church accountability is a live dispute.

How Many South Africans Follow Each Faith

Statistics South Africa published the religion results of Census 2022 in its Cultural Dynamics report in 2025. The census counted 62,027,503 people in total, and the religion tables cover about 60.2 million with a recorded answer.

Christianity stood at 84.5% in 2022, up from 75.9% in 1996 and 79.8% in 2001. People with no religious affiliation fell from 11.7% in 1996 to 2.9% in 2022.

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “Is Morocco safe? Washington says use increased caution” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

African traditional religion registered 7.8% in 2022, against 0.0% in 1996 and 0.3% in 2001. Islam stood at 1.6%, Hinduism at 1.1%, Jewish faith at 0.1% and other beliefs at 0.3%.

A further 1.9% of answers were undetermined in 2022, down from 9.4% in 1996. Statistics South Africa says that fall may reflect better data collection between censuses.

The 2011 census did not ask about religion, so the series jumps from 2001 to 2022. Anyone comparing trends should keep that 21-year gap in mind.

Where Each Faith Is Strongest

Faith follows settlement history, so the provincial map matters. KwaZulu-Natal has the highest share of African traditional religion at 13.5% and of Hindus at 4.2%.

The Eastern Cape follows on African traditional religion at 11.0%, and Mpumalanga shows 7.7%. The Western Cape has the largest Muslim share at 5.2%, down from 6.9% in 1996.

The Northern Cape, North West and Free State are the most Christian provinces, at 94.3%, 94.6% and 92.2%. KwaZulu-Natal is the least Christian at 74.3%, with the highest traditional and Hindu shares.

Limpopo once had the largest unaffiliated share, at 29.4% in 2001. By 2022 that had dropped to 5.1%, while its Christian share rose from 67.8% to 86.2%.

At least 85% of Black African, coloured and white respondents are Christian. Among Indian and Asian South Africans, 37.1% are Hindu, 33.0% Christian and 24.0% Muslim.

Among Black Africans, 9.5% name African traditional religion, against 0.1% in 1996. Whites are 7.0% of respondents but 12.0% of those with no religious affiliation.

Men are 48.3% of respondents but 61.3% of those with no affiliation. Statistics South Africa’s model gives women an adjusted odds ratio of 0.52 for reporting no religion.

The Narainsamy Temple in Newlands, Durban, a Hindu temple listed as a protected heritage site (Photo: Janek Szymanowski, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons).
