Christian Churches: Mainline, Zionist and Pentecostal

Christianity in South Africa spans Catholic, Anglican, Methodist and Dutch Reformed churches, African-initiated churches and newer Pentecostal congregations. The census tables reviewed here publish broad faiths, not church-by-church counts.

Writing in The Conversation in 2024, theologian Dion Forster of Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam said mainline membership has steadily declined. He said African indigenous churches and neo-Pentecostal churches have grown significantly, without giving membership figures.

The Zion Christian Church (ZCC) is a major African-initiated church, with its headquarters at Moria, about 35 km from Polokwane in Limpopo. Daily Maverick describes two main groupings there, St Engenas and Star.

The St Engenas group is led by Bishop Joseph Lekganyane, and its Easter pilgrimage draws tens of thousands of members, including visitors from Eswatini and Botswana. The 2023 Easter gathering was the first mass service since 2019, after the pandemic.

The Catholic Church speaks through the Southern African Catholic Bishops’ Conference (SACBC). Cardinal Stephen Brislin is its president, as the conference website showed in October 2026.

The Vatican named Bishop Sithembele Sipuka Archbishop of Cape Town on 9 January 2026. Sipuka, previously Bishop of Mthatha, had led the SACBC as president from 2019 to 2024.

Regina Mundi Catholic church in Soweto, Johannesburg, a gathering place in the anti-apartheid era (Photo: Moongateclimber, authorship assumed per the Commons file page, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

African Traditional Religion and the Shembe Church

African traditional religion centres on ancestors, family obligations and community ritual, and many followers also attend church. The census records one answer per person, so overlap between faiths is not visible in the headline numbers.

A Pew Research Center survey, with interviews from December 2008 to April 2009, found South Africa among four countries where over half believe sacrifices to ancestors can protect them. The survey covered 19 sub-Saharan countries, and its findings predate the 2022 census.

The Shembe Church, also called the Nazareth Baptist Church, is based in KwaZulu-Natal. The Sunday Tribune reported in January 2026 that it has more than a million followers in South Africa and neighbouring countries.

Each January its factions walk barefoot to holy mountains, a three-day journey of 50 to 80 km. The eBuhleni faction went to Khenana Mountain in 2026, while the eKuphakameni faction went to Nhlangakazi.

The pilgrimage has seen clashes between factions in the past, and a court order now requires them to schedule walks so as to avoid conflict. The 2026 pilgrimage was described as peaceful.

Islam, Hinduism and Judaism

Muslims are 1.6% of the population, with the highest share in the Western Cape (5.2%) and 1.9% in KwaZulu-Natal. Islam is the faith of 24.0% of Indian and Asian respondents and 6.8% of coloured respondents.

Hindus are 1.1% nationally and 4.2% in KwaZulu-Natal, the highest of any province. The Hindu share among Indian and Asian South Africans fell from 49.9% in 1996 to 37.1% in 2022.

The Juma Masjid mosque on Queen Street in central Durban (Photo: Akidjoh, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

Jewish faith registered 0.1% nationally in 2022, with 0.2% in the Western Cape. Other beliefs, a broad category, reached 0.7% in the Western Cape.

Hindus and Muslims have the highest shares of legally married adults aged 12 and over, at 49.5% and 45.8%. Christians stand at 23.9%, and followers of African traditional religion at 17.5%.

The Divorce Amendment Act, announced as signed by the Presidency on 9 May 2024, recognises Muslim marriages when they end. It defines a Muslim marriage, protects children and sets rules for dividing assets.

Faith and Politics

Politicians have courted South Africa’s churches for decades. Nelson Mandela addressed the ZCC Easter conference at Moria on 20 April 1992 and called apartheid a sin.

He also said that no government should have the right to prescribe religious observance for the country’s citizens. Section 15 of the 1996 Constitution later set rules for religious observance at state institutions.

President Cyril Ramaphosa, leader of the African National Congress (ANC), addressed the St Engenas Easter pilgrimage in 2023 and again in 2024. In 2024 he spoke ahead of the 29 May election, and Julius Malema of the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) also attended.

In January 2026 the Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) president, Velenkosini Hlabisa, joined the Shembe pilgrimage, and the ANC and the newer uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MK) sent good wishes. The IFP is rooted in KwaZulu-Natal, where the Shembe church is based.

The sources reviewed give no data on how congregants vote, so a bloc vote cannot be assumed. The visits do show that parties court the leaders of large faith communities.

The Constitution, Holidays and Religious Observance

Section 15 of the Constitution guarantees everyone freedom of conscience, religion, thought, belief and opinion. It lets state and state-aided institutions hold religious observances only if they follow public rules, are equitable and are voluntary.

Section 15 also allows legislation recognising marriages and personal law under any tradition or religion, if consistent with the Constitution. Section 31 says members of a religious community may not be denied the right to practise their religion and form associations.

South Africa has 12 public holidays under the Public Holidays Act of 1994. Good Friday fell on 3 April 2026, Family Day on 6 April, Christmas Day on 25 December and the Day of Goodwill on 26 December.

No Muslim, Hindu, Jewish or African traditional festival appears on the 2026 public holiday list. Good Friday moves with the church calendar, and in 2027 it falls on 26 March.

The Row Over Regulating Churches

The Commission for the Promotion and Protection of the Rights of Cultural, Religious and Linguistic Communities, known as the CRL Rights Commission, is a state body. It set up a Section 22 Ad Hoc Committee for the Christian sector on 2 October 2025, after allegations of abuse by some church leaders.

The committee published a draft self-regulatory framework in December 2025, which the Mercury reported in March 2026 includes annual financial reporting, written constitutions and vetting of foreign national pastors. The Commission describes it as voluntary, with no state licensing, and says a sector council would award a “Seal of Good Standing” to churches that opt in.

Chairperson Thoko Mkhwanazi-Xaluva said in March 2026 that existing non-profit law already requires constitutions and financial statements. The Commission listed a consultation round in the Eastern Cape for 13 to 17 July 2026.

Thousands of congregants marched in Durban in March 2026 under the South African Church Defenders banner. They demanded that the committee be scrapped and the chairperson removed.

Parliament’s Portfolio Committee on Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs said on 11 February 2026 that religious freedom is protected and congregants must be shielded from abuse. It said it was not yet in a position to comment on the process, and the Church Defenders had asked the Gauteng High Court to annul the committee.

On 16 October 2026 the Commission said it welcomed an ANC statement of 13 October that reaffirmed religious freedom and described the framework as self-regulation, not state regulation. The Commission’s statement does not mention the court case, and its outcome is not known.

How Faith Shapes Daily Life

Census 2022 found that 93.1% of households are single-religion, 3.2% have mixed religions and 3.7% have none. Faith is therefore mostly a shared household identity.

Marriage patterns differ by faith. Among adults aged 12 and over, 69.8% of followers of African traditional religion have never married, against 62.3% of Christians.

Churches shape the annual calendar through Easter pilgrimages and Christmas observance. In 2023 Bishop Lekganyane urged congregants at Moria to stop drug abuse.

The SACBC’s January 2026 plenary, themed Synodality and Mission, named corruption, lawlessness and climate change as concerns. Church bodies thus act as civil-society voices, not only as places of worship.

What It Means for US Readers

Travellers should note that Good Friday, Family Day, 25 December and 26 December are public holidays, so plan around closures. Large pilgrimages gather at Moria around Easter and in KwaZulu-Natal in January.

Investors should watch the church-regulation row, since the draft framework touches reporting by religious non-profits. It has no stated link to listed companies, and the sources reviewed show only a voluntary draft and a court challenge as of October 2026.

US faith groups, missionaries and charities should read the proposal on vetting foreign pastors closely. It was still a draft in October 2026, and whether it would affect visas or registration for foreign clergy is not clear.

Expats will meet a mostly Christian society with sizeable minorities, led by Muslims in the Western Cape and Hindus in KwaZulu-Natal. The state is secular in law, and the Constitution protects every faith.

What Is Not Known

The census tables reviewed do not split Christians by church, so the size of the ZCC, Catholic, Pentecostal and other bodies is unverified. Membership claims made by churches themselves are not audited.

Why African traditional religion rose from 0.3% in 2001 to 7.8% in 2022 is not explained in the report’s headline findings. Changes in question wording and coding could play a part, and the report does not say.

The outcome of the High Court challenge to the Section 22 Committee was not found in the sources reviewed as of October 2026. The sources also do not show whether Parliament will legislate on religious oversight.

The SACBC president was checked on the conference website in October 2026, but the ZCC leader and the CRL chairperson are as reported in 2023 to March 2026. Readers should check the church or commission directly before relying on a name or title.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the largest religion in South Africa?

Christianity, at 84.5% of people in Census 2022. African traditional religion follows at 7.8%, then Islam at 1.6% and Hinduism at 1.1%.

How many South Africans have no religion?

Census 2022 put the share with no religious affiliation at 2.9%, down from 11.7% in 1996. White respondents are 7.0% of the total but 12.0% of the unaffiliated.

What is the Zion Christian Church?

It is a major African-initiated church in South Africa, with its headquarters at Moria near Polokwane in Limpopo. Its St Engenas group, led by Bishop Joseph Lekganyane, draws tens of thousands of members to its Easter pilgrimage.

Does South Africa have an official religion?

No, section 15 of the Constitution guarantees freedom of conscience, religion, thought, belief and opinion. State institutions may hold religious observances only if they follow public rules, are equitable and are voluntary.

Which Christian days are public holidays in South Africa?

Good Friday, Family Day, Christmas Day and the Day of Goodwill are among the 12 public holidays. In 2026 they fell on 3 April, 6 April, 25 December and 26 December.

Are Muslim marriages recognised in South Africa?

The Presidency announced on 9 May 2024 that the Divorce Amendment Bill had been signed into law. It defines a Muslim marriage, protects children and sets rules for dividing assets when such a marriage ends.

Sources: Statistics South Africa, Cultural Dynamics in South Africa, Report 03-01-84, Census 2022 (statssa.gov.za); Census 2022 population count, Polity, 10 October 2023 (polity.org.za); Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, chapter 2 (justice.gov.za); South African Government, public holidays (gov.za); SAnews, Divorce Amendment Bill signed into law, 9 May 2024 (sanews.gov.za); Parliament of South Africa, COGTA committee on religious freedom, 11 February 2026 (parliament.gov.za); SACBC, plenary and executive (sacbc.org.za); Fides, appointment of the Archbishop of Cape Town, 9 January 2026 (fides.org); Pew Research Center, Tolerance and Tension, 2010 (pewresearch.org); South African History Online, Mandela at Moria, 20 April 1992 (sahistory.org.za). Reporting from Daily Maverick, 1 April 2024 and 10 April 2023 (Moria); Sunday Tribune, 4 January 2026 (Shembe pilgrimage); The Mercury, 17 March 2026 (CRL Rights Commission); Dion Forster, The Conversation, May 2024 (repost). CRL Rights Commission, Section 22 Christian sector and media statement of 16 October 2026 (crlcommission.org.za). All accessed 17 October 2026.

World.title: Cuba Geopolitics Explained 2026
World.content:
GUIDES · CUBA

Key Facts — The island A one-party Communist state 145 kilometres (90 miles) from Florida, a BRICS partner country and, since 29 January 2026, a US national-emergency target.

— US pressure Executive Order 14380 (29 January 2026) declared a national emergency, and its oil-supplier tariffs were ended on 20 February 2026. Order 14404 (1 May 2026) created a sanctions list that named Miguel Díaz-Canel on 4 June 2026.

— Russia and China A Russian tanker brought about 730,000 barrels on 31 March 2026. China has sent rice and solar equipment by ship in 2026.

— Europe The EU is reviewing its 2016 cooperation agreement. The European Parliament voted 283 to 199 on 18 June 2026 to urge its suspension.

— UN scorecard On 29 October 2025 the UN General Assembly backed ending the US embargo by 165 votes to 7, with 12 abstentions.

— Prediction markets Polymarket gives an 8.5% chance that Miguel Díaz-Canel is out as Cuba’s leader by 31 December 2026 (17 October, 9:12 a.m. ET). It gives 11.5% for a US strike on Cuba by that date.

— Power Index Cuba ranks 14th of 14 in Cuba ranks 14th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 22.5 points (October 2026 edition).

Cuba geopolitics explained: which powers press, feed or court Havana in October 2026, and what each of them wants. Every claim carries its date and a named source.

Cuba geopolitics in 2026 is a contest over a fuel-starved island 145 kilometres (about 90 miles) south of Florida. Washington is squeezing it, Moscow and Beijing are keeping it afloat, and Europe is questioning its own deal with Havana.

For US readers it matters because the pressure runs through American law, American ports and American tariffs. This guide covers the United States, Russia, China, the European Union, Mexico, the Gulf states, Turkey, India and BRICS.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Cuba ranks 14th of 14 with 22.5 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (53); weakest: economic weight (0). Alignment group: Closer to Beijing. Some pillar data are incomplete for Cuba; see the index notes. WatchNo sovereign rating; economy contracting (-3.8%); incomplete data (‡). See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The United States Sets the Terms

No other state shapes Cuba’s choices as much as the United States. The embargo dates from the early 1960s, and Washington has held the Guantánamo Bay naval station since a 1903 lease that Havana disputes.

On 29 January 2026 President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14380, declaring a national emergency over Cuba. It let the President set extra tariffs on goods from any country that supplies oil to the island, directly or through intermediaries.

Commerce would find whether a country supplies oil, State would recommend, and the President would decide. Executive Order 14389 of 20 February 2026 then ended the extra duties under that order, although the national emergency remains.

The US Embassy in Havana overlooking the Malecón seafront, reopened as an embassy in 2015 (Photo: Bjen78, CC BY 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

A second order, number 14404, followed on 1 May 2026. It created a sanctions list covering Cuba’s energy, defence, mining, financial services and security sectors.

It also reaches foreign banks that handle significant transactions for listed persons. The Treasury told non-US firms to finish winding down existing dealings with GAESA, the military-run business group, by 5 June 2026.

The Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control listed GAESA under the new order on 7 May 2026. On 4 June 2026 it added President Díaz-Canel, his wife Lis Cuesta Peraza and the Revolutionary Armed Forces ministry.

On 15 October 2026 the Treasury added a Havana bank, Banco Internacional de Comercio, to the same list. New regulations that took effect on 30 September 2026 ended group people-to-people travel and US bank accounts for independent Cuban entrepreneurs.

Talks are the other half of the picture. On 5 October 2026 Cuba’s chargé d’affaires in Washington, Lianys Torres Rivera, said the two sides keep channels of communication but hold no formal negotiations.

President Trump said in late September 2026 that Secretary of State Marco Rubio was deep into negotiations, and a State Department spokesperson said talks were ongoing. Havana calls its political system a red line and says it will not negotiate it.

Military action is a stated worry rather than a declared plan. No US government announcement of an operation against Cuba had been confirmed as of 17 October 2026.

Oil, Mexico and Venezuela Redraw the Map

Cuba relies heavily on imported petroleum, and Venezuela and Mexico were among its suppliers. That supply chain broke in January 2026.

Venezuelan cargoes stopped after the US operation of early January 2026 that removed Nicolás Maduro from power. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said on 27 January 2026 that Mexican shipments had paused, calling it a sovereign decision.

Pemex, the Mexican state oil company, had shipped nearly 20,000 barrels a day to Cuba from January to 30 September 2025. Shipments fell sharply after Secretary of State Rubio visited Mexico City in September 2025, according to energy analyst Jorge Piñón.

On 30 March 2026 Sheinbaum said Mexico has the right to send fuel to Cuba, whether as aid or commerce. She gave no date for a new cargo and stressed a humanitarian motive.

Mexico matters because it is close to Cuba and a major US trading partner. Every Mexican decision on Cuban oil is therefore also a trade question with Washington.

Russia Supplies Oil and Seeks Business

Russia is Cuba’s oldest great-power partner and the only state to have delivered a large oil cargo in 2026. The tanker Anatoly Kolodkin entered Matanzas Bay on 31 March 2026 carrying about 730,000 barrels.

A tanker enters Havana Bay beneath the old fortifications, a reminder that Cuba depends on seaborne fuel (Photo: Guillaume Baviere, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

President Trump said he had no problem with Russian oil reaching the island and let the ship through on humanitarian grounds. Analysts estimated the cargo covered nine to ten days of Cuba’s diesel demand.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova called Cuba “our closest friend and partner in the Caribbean” on 1 April 2026. Energy Minister Sergei Tsivilev said on 2 April that a second vessel was being loaded.

Cuba’s energy minister, Vicente de la O Levy, said on 22 April 2026 that the Russian oil would last only until the end of April. Russia’s ambassador, Viktor Koronelli, promised on 8 May 2026 that Moscow would keep supporting Cuba.

Business ties run through an intergovernmental commission, which met for the 23rd time in St Petersburg on 1 April 2026. CiberCuba reported that it agreed investments above US$1 billion and let Russian firms manage Cuban industrial sites, including vehicle assembly.

At the St Petersburg International Economic Forum on 4 June 2026, Cuban Deputy Prime Minister Óscar Pérez-Oliva Fraga offered Russian companies energy, refining and transport projects. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Chernyshenko said Russia would keep investing despite US sanctions.

China Builds Solar Parks and Sends Rice

China helps Cuba with food, solar power and diplomacy rather than with oil. CiberCuba reported on 26 March 2026 that the ship Loyalty Hong had reached Havana with 15,600 tons of Chinese rice.

CiberCuba described that cargo as part of a 30,000-ton donation announced in January 2026. It named no official source for the figure, so treat it as reported rather than confirmed.

CiberCuba reported that Chinese ambassador Hua Xin said in early October 2026 that Beijing will keep backing Cuban energy projects. The outlet, citing grid reports, said solar output peaked at 562 MW on 29 September 2026.

Against that, CiberCuba cited the state grid operator’s forecast of a shortfall of about 2,040 MW at peak demand on 2 October 2026. Solar power fades at dusk, just when Cubans switch on the lights.

Four battery systems of 50 MW each are planned, but in early October 2026 only the Cotorro unit was confirmed working, CiberCuba reported. Batteries are the missing link between daytime sun and evening demand.

Beijing says it opposes unilateral sanctions and backs Cuban sovereignty. The terms of Chinese credit, Cuban debts to China and any security cooperation are not public, so this guide does not claim any.

The European Union Questions Its Own Deal

Europe is Cuba’s main Western partner and is now rethinking the relationship. The EU and Cuba signed a Political Dialogue and Cooperation Agreement in December 2016.

On 20 May 2026 EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas told the European Parliament the agreement was under review and had not delivered the expected results. She said the EU does not finance the Cuban state and that a negotiated reform is better than a collapse.

On 18 June 2026 Parliament voted 283 to 199, with 85 abstentions, for a resolution on repression in Cuba. It urged suspension of the agreement and EU sanctions on Díaz-Canel and GAESA executives.

Parliament’s resolution does not bind the Commission or the Council of the EU. As of 17 October 2026 we found no decision by either body to suspend the agreement.

Brussels keeps sending aid alongside the pressure. Brussels Signal reported on 23 July 2026 that the Commission committed 10 million euros (about US$11.3 million) more for medicines, food and water repairs.

That conversion uses the European Central Bank reference rate of 1.1253 dollars to the euro on 16 October 2026. Japan, a distant partner, gave food worth US$1 million through the World Food Programme on 16 October 2026, including 425 tons of rice, CiberCuba reported.

The UN Vote and the BRICS Bid

The annual UN General Assembly vote on the US embargo is the clearest scorecard of Cuba’s friends. On 29 October 2025 it passed with 165 votes in favour, 7 against and 12 abstentions.

In 2024 the tally was 187 in favour, with only the United States and Israel against. The seven opponents in 2025 were the United States, Israel, Argentina, Hungary, Paraguay, North Macedonia and Ukraine.

The José Martí Memorial in Havana’s Plaza de la Revolución, the political heart of the Cuban state (Photo: Arturo Pardavila III, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

Twelve states abstained, including Costa Rica, Ecuador and Morocco. In Latin America the shift came from Argentina and Paraguay voting against and from Costa Rica and Ecuador abstaining.

As of September 2026 Cuba is a BRICS partner country, a status short of full membership. Other partners include Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam.

At the 18th BRICS summit in New Delhi in September 2026, Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla said Cuba wants to become a full member. India’s External Affairs Minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, met him on 12 September 2026 and called the talks useful.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on 14 September 2026 that Russia supports Cuba’s aspiration to join the group’s work, CubaNet reported. BRICS decides by consensus, and no timetable or member agreement on Cuban admission has been announced.

The Gulf, Turkey and Other Partners

Saudi Arabia is the Gulf state with the clearest footprint in Cuba. The Saudi Fund for Development is financing a King Salman Mosque in Old Havana, budgeted at about US$9.3 million, 14ymedio and CiberCuba reported in late September 2026.

The fund has financed seven other Cuban projects in health, sanitation and infrastructure worth about US$193.3 million, the outlet said. A mosque does not ease fuel shortages, and no start date has been published.

Little is public about the United Arab Emirates or Qatar in Cuba. No 2026 deal from either has been confirmed.

Turkey’s Karadeniz Holding supplies floating power plants through its Karpowership unit. A contract signed in October 2018 began at 110 MW and had grown to 300 MW by November 2021, El Toque reported in 2022.

Whether the barges still run at that scale in October 2026 is not confirmed, and payment terms were never published. No 2026 Turkish government statement on Cuba is confirmed either.

What It Means for US Readers

Investors face secondary-sanctions risk, because foreign banks and firms that deal with listed Cuban entities can be sanctioned under Executive Order 14404. Oil and shipping companies should note that the oil-supplier tariffs under Executive Order 14380 were ended on 20 February 2026, but the emergency and sanctions remain.

Tourist travel by US persons remains barred by US law, and since 30 September 2026 group people-to-people trips no longer qualify under a general licence. Travellers who completed a trip-related transaction before that date may be grandfathered.

Cuban-American families and entrepreneurs should know that US banks must block funds held in accounts opened for independent Cuban entrepreneurs under the old authorisation unless the Treasury licenses them. Accounts for Cuban nationals in Cuba remain available, but funds must be remitted to Cuba.

Expats and exporters should expect the rules to keep moving. The Treasury added Cuba designations on 7 May, 18 May, 4 June, 6 August and 15 October 2026.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket gives an 8.5% chance that Miguel Díaz-Canel is out as Cuba’s leader by 31 December 2026 (17 October, 9:12 a.m. ET). That market has about US$752,000 in volume, and the price fell 2.5 points over the past week.

The market for a US strike on Cuba by 31 December 2026 stands at 11.5%, with about US$5.4 million traded. Contracts for a strike by 31 January and by 31 March 2026 both closed without one.

A separate market on a US invasion of Cuba in 2026 stands at 7.5% on about US$3.6 million in volume, up 3 points in a week. A US-Cuba economic deal by 31 December 2026 is priced at 12.5%, but only about US$33,000 has traded.

These prices are bets, not polls, and they move on news within minutes. They show what traders expect, not what will happen.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

Several May 2026 reports said a second Russian tanker turned away from Cuba, and we have not confirmed the outcome or when Russia will deliver again. Nor is it known how much Cuba owes China or on what terms.

It is unclear whether Washington will use another tool to penalise countries that supply oil to Cuba, now that the Order 14380 duties have ended. The two governments describe the US-Cuba contacts differently, so their content is unconfirmed.

Cuba’s BRICS bid has no timetable, and the 2026 UN vote date and tally are not yet public. The output of the Turkish power barges and Cuba’s 2025 trade shares by partner are also unconfirmed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which countries support Cuba most in 2026?

Russia and China are its most visible backers, with a Russian oil cargo on 31 March 2026 and Chinese rice and solar help. Cuba’s energy minister said the Russian oil would last only until the end of April 2026.

What US sanctions apply to Cuba as of October 2026?

The national emergency declared by Executive Order 14380 of 29 January 2026 remains, although its oil-supplier tariffs were ended on 20 February 2026. Order 14404 of 1 May 2026 created a sanctions list that includes GAESA and President Díaz-Canel, and new Treasury rules took effect on 30 September 2026.

What does the United States want from Cuba?

The January 2026 order alleges Russian and Chinese intelligence and defence ties, links to Hezbollah and Hamas, and repression of political opponents. Havana calls its political system a red line and says it will not negotiate it.

Is Cuba a member of BRICS?

As of September 2026 Cuba is a BRICS partner country, not a full member. Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla said in New Delhi that Cuba wants full membership, and Russia has voiced support.

How did countries vote at the UN on the Cuba embargo?

On 29 October 2025 the General Assembly voted 165 to 7, with 12 abstentions, to call for an end to the embargo. The United States, Israel, Argentina, Hungary, Paraguay, North Macedonia and Ukraine voted against.

Does the EU still have an agreement with Cuba?

Yes, the 2016 Political Dialogue and Cooperation Agreement remains in place, but the EU said on 20 May 2026 that it is under review. The European Parliament voted on 18 June 2026 to urge its suspension.

Can Americans travel to Cuba in 2026?

US law bars tourist travel, and since 30 September 2026 group people-to-people trips no longer qualify under a general licence. Travellers should check Treasury rules before booking.

World.title: Egypt Media Landscape Explained
World.content:
GUIDES · EGYPT

Key Facts — The country Egypt has about 118.4 million people as of 2025. Its state broadcasters, biggest newspapers and largest private media group are covered below.

— Press freedom Egypt ranks 169th of 180 countries in the 2026 press freedom index, with a score of 24.92. It was 170th in 2025.

— Who owns what A 2019 survey of 41 national outlets found the state held 36.6% of them through two state media authorities. The largest private group is widely linked to the General Intelligence Service.

— The regulator The Supreme Council for Media Regulation is chaired by Khaled Abdelaziz as of September 2026. The president appoints the heads of the three bodies that run the sector.

— Journalists in jail Between 18 and 25 journalists were behind bars in October 2026, depending on the count. Six staff of one investigative site were arrested from 28 September 2026, and prosecutors ordered them held on 7 October.

— Online audience About 98.2 million Egyptians were online at the end of 2025, and Facebook reached about 51.6 million of them.

Egypt media explained: who owns the newspapers and channels, who regulates them, which outlets are blocked and how Egyptians get news online. The guide is dated October 2026.

Egypt media is shaped by the state and by owners close to it. Reporters Without Borders (RSF) ranked Egypt 169th of 180 countries in its 2026 press freedom index.

That shapes what Egyptian news can show, who profits from its airwaves and how risky it is to report from Cairo. This guide maps the state outlets, private groups, regulators and independent voices as of October 2026.

It matters to US readers because most of what they read about Egypt passes through this system. Every figure below carries its date.

Who Controls What Egyptians Read and Watch

RSF calls the system closed, saying pluralism is almost non-existent in Egypt. It adds that virtually all media are “directly controlled by the state, the intelligence agencies or a handful of wealthy, influential businessmen”.

The Media Ownership Monitor, an RSF project, surveyed 41 of the most popular national outlets and published its findings in January 2019. It found that the state held 36.6% of them through the National Media Authority and the National Press Authority.

The Egyptian Media Group held a further 12.2% and the Falcon Group 4.9%, both tied to intelligence services in that study. Intelligence services were linked to 12 of the surveyed entities, including eight broadcasters.

The study is nearly eight years old, so its percentages are a baseline rather than a current count. Later changes in ownership are described below.

A newspaper stand in Cairo in 2008, selling Arabic dailies, magazines and foreign papers (Photo: zolakoma, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

State Media from Maspero to Al-Ahram

Egyptian Radio and Egyptian Television are state-owned, and so are the channels Al Oula, Al Thaniya and Nile News. The Media Ownership Monitor also lists the Egyptian Media Production City, the satellite operator Nilesat and the Middle East News Agency as state assets.

RSF names Al-Akhbar, Al-Ahram and Al-Gomhuriya as the three most popular state-owned national newspapers. The state press houses also include Dar El Tahrir, Akhbar Al Youm, Dar Al Hilal, Rose Al Yousef and Dar Al Maaref.

The 2019 study said state media had piled up debts over decades and were not profitable. A 2018 law lets the president and the executive choose the heads of the two state authorities, who in turn appoint editors across state institutions.

Enterprise reported that decrees of November 2024 named Ahmed El Moslemany chairman of the National Media Authority. The same decrees renewed Abdel Sadeq El Shorbagi at the National Press Authority for four years, and Egyptian press reports of 10 September 2026 described El Moslemany meeting United Media Services’ new board.

RSF reported in September 2026 that Chinese state media had opened two regional newsrooms in Cairo. It added that Al-Gomhuriya agreed in April 2026 to co-publish with the Qingdao Daily Newspaper Group.

The Regulators and the 2018 Laws

Three 2018 laws, numbered 178, 179 and 180, let the president appoint the heads and some members of the media bodies. RSF noted this in its January 2019 release on the ownership monitor.

The Supreme Council for Media Regulation, known as the SCMR, was created in 2017 and enforces the Press and Media Regulation Law, No. 180 of 2018. Its chairman is Khaled Abdelaziz, a former youth and sports minister who replaced Karam Gabr under a November 2024 decree.

On 14 September 2026 the SCMR ordered outlets, websites and social platforms to stop featuring the wife of football coach Hossam Hassan. It also summoned three channels over their coverage of his private life.

The 2019 study recorded the council stopping programmes, investigating television hosts and fining outlets. It also said the council had banned publications for allegedly violating “the values of society and the State”.

Foreign reporters need a permit from the State Information Service, which RSF says is headed by Alaa Youssef. The 2019 study said the service had refused permits to some journalists and threatened others.

RSF says a 2018 law explicitly authorises surveillance of social media accounts with more than 5,000 followers. It adds that journalists are often charged with belonging to a terrorist organisation or disseminating false information.

The Private Groups and Who Owns Them

The biggest private group is United Media Services, also known as the Egyptian Media Group. The State Media Monitor, a research project, said in June 2026 that it runs more than 40 subsidiaries and is Egypt’s largest media group.

Its owner is Eagle Capital Financial Investments, which took control in December 2017. The State Media Monitor says independent reporting links the group to the General Intelligence Service.

Mada Masr reported in December 2017 that Eagle Capital is a private equity fund owned by that service. It said the fund was headed by Dalia Khorshid, a former investment minister.

Its holdings, as listed by the State Media Monitor in June 2026, cover television, print, radio and streaming. The main ones are below.

Television: ON, CBC, Al-Hayah, DMC, Al Qahera News and Extra News.

Print and digital: Youm7, Al-Watan, Sout Al-Ouma, Ain, DotMasr and Q News, launched in October 2024.

Radio: On Sport FM, Radio Hits, Shaabi FM, Mega FM, Nagham FM and Radio 9090.

Production and streaming: Watch iT, Synergy, Media Hub, POD, Presentation and United Sports.

Leadership has changed often, with Tamer Morsi chairman from February 2018 and Tarek Nour appointed in December 2024. The State Media Monitor says Mohamed El-Saadi became acting chairman in April 2026, but Egyptian press reports of 10 September 2026 described a new board, so the post may have changed.

The group is not short of political tests. In July 2025 it ended its contract with presenter Lamis El Hadidy after her ON programme went off air, which press freedom groups described as retaliation.

In December 2025 its outlets announced they would stop covering social media and TikTok influencers. The State Media Monitor says detailed financial statements are not public, and a 2021 plan to list a minority stake on the Egyptian Exchange had not happened by mid-2026.

The 2019 study said Al Shorouk and Al Masry Al Youm were owned by wealthy businessmen. It said Al Dostor and Al Bawaba had owners with political interests, and Al Nahar TV a prominent businessman.

Independent and Blocked Outlets

RSF says Mada Masr, an independent news site, has been inaccessible in Egypt since 2017. The 2019 study counted about 100 news websites blocked since May 2017, including the sites of RSF and the monitor itself.

The sharpest recent case is Matsada2sh, an investigative fact-checking site founded in 2018. Police arrested all six members of its newsroom over two to three days from 28 September 2026, in home raids and street arrests.

Human Rights Watch named them as Abdallah Qadry, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Islam Barakat, Omar Helal, Mohamed Mahmoud and Mohamed Adel. It said the Interior Ministry had not identified any specific criminal charge.

The Interior Ministry accused the site of spreading false content and linked it to the banned Muslim Brotherhood. The Committee to Protect Journalists says the ministry called it an unlicensed, foreign-run page.

Founder Abdelrahman Mansour rejects the accusation. He told the Committee to Protect Journalists that the site has “no affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood”, and the Egyptian Press Syndicate condemned the arrests.

On 7 October 2026 the Public Prosecution ordered all six held in pretrial detention while it investigates, Egyptian Streets reported. The statement listed no charges or detention length, and defence lawyers say no court has yet seen the case.

Other cases are older. RSF and 14 other organisations called on 23 July 2026 for the release of editorial cartoonist Ashraf Omar, who had been detained for two years.

There have been releases too. RSF counts the freeing of journalist Alaa Abdel Fattah and blogger Mohammed Ibrahim Radwan among landmark releases, and credits pressure from activists, unions and the international community.

Cameras and placards at a 2007 protest by Egyptian press photographers against police harassment in Cairo, cropped to remove faces (Photo: Hossam el-Hamalawy, CC BY-SA 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

Press Freedom Rankings and Jailed Journalists

In RSF’s 2026 index Egypt ranked 169th of 180 with a score of 24.92, up from 170th and 24.74 in 2025. Its sub-scores ranked 168th on politics, 167th on the economy, 162nd on law, 169th on society and 163rd on security.

RSF’s live barometer showed 18 journalists detained in Egypt on 17 October 2026 and none killed since 1 January 2026. Its statement of 30 September 2026 counted the six Matsada2sh reporters plus 18 other detainees, or 24 in all.

The Committee to Protect Journalists put the number at 25 on 2 October 2026. Counts differ because each group defines who is a journalist and when a detention counts.

Social Media and the Online Audience

Egypt had about 118.4 million people in 2025, according to the World Bank, and 113.2 million mobile subscriptions in 2024. The World Bank puts internet use at 74.6% of the population in 2024.

DataReportal, which compiles digital audience figures, counted 98.2 million internet users, or 82.7% of the population, at the end of 2025. The two series use different methods, so they should not be mixed.

DataReportal’s advertising-reach estimates for late 2025 show where the audience sits. They are not counts of active users.

Facebook: about 51.6 million.

YouTube: about 49.3 million.

TikTok: about 48.8 million adults.

Instagram: about 21.7 million.

Snapchat: about 20.6 million.

X: about 4.64 million.

Older surveys show how fast habits shift. The 2019 study found that 77% of Egyptians used television for news.

Newspaper readership had fallen from 25% in 2013 to 16% in 2017. The number of newspaper and magazine titles fell about 40% between 2011 and 2017.

The state treats social platforms as part of the media. Law No. 180 of 2018 applies to websites and social platforms, and RSF says accounts above 5,000 followers can be put under surveillance.

Apartment blocks on the Zamalek waterfront in Cairo at night (Photo: Vyacheslav Argenberg, CC BY 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

What It Means for US Readers

For readers, the first rule is to check who owns a source. The 2019 study found state or intelligence-linked owners behind just over half of the surveyed outlets.

For investors, the main private media group is not listed, and its financial statements are not public. State media were described in 2019 as indebted and unprofitable, so there is little public data on which to value the sector.

For journalists, researchers and visitors who publish online, the risks are concrete. Foreign reporters need State Information Service permits, and Egyptian colleagues face arrest, blocked sites and charges of spreading false news.

Independent Egyptian reporting often reaches US readers only through foreign outlets or social media. That makes the Matsada2sh arrests, which removed an entire newsroom, a signal about how much of Egypt’s own reporting can continue.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the six Matsada2sh journalists will be formally charged or freed. The Public Prosecution ordered pretrial detention on 7 October 2026 without publishing charges or a detention length, and no later ruling has been found.

Egypt’s full media ownership is not public. The State Media Monitor says United Media Services does not publish detailed financial statements, and the 2019 study found no public media-consumption survey.

Counts of jailed journalists differ between monitors, so the true figure is uncertain. This guide found no later change at the regulators named in November 2024, but it could not confirm the National Press Authority head from a 2026 source.

Frequently Asked Questions

How free is the press in Egypt?

RSF ranked Egypt 169th of 180 countries in its 2026 index, with a score of 24.92. It says pluralism is almost non-existent and that independent outlets are censored and targeted by prosecutors.

Who owns Egypt’s biggest private media group?

United Media Services is owned by Eagle Capital Financial Investments, which took control in December 2017. Mada Masr reported then that Eagle Capital is owned by the General Intelligence Service.

Which Egyptian newspapers are state-owned?

RSF names Al-Akhbar, Al-Ahram and Al-Gomhuriya as the three most popular state-owned national newspapers. The state press houses also include Dar El Tahrir, Akhbar Al Youm and Rose Al Yousef.

Who regulates the media in Egypt?

The Supreme Council for Media Regulation, chaired by Khaled Abdelaziz as of September 2026, enforces Law No. 180 of 2018. The president appoints the heads of the regulator and of the two state media authorities.

Is Mada Masr blocked in Egypt?

RSF says Mada Masr has been inaccessible in Egypt since 2017. The 2019 Media Ownership Monitor counted about 100 news websites blocked since May 2017.

How many Egyptians use social media?

DataReportal counted 98.2 million internet users in Egypt at the end of 2025 and 51.6 million social media user identities in October 2025. Facebook reached about 51.6 million, YouTube 49.3 million and TikTok 48.8 million adults, as advertising-reach estimates.

World.title: Uruguay in Latin America, Its Role, Weight and Alliances
World.content:
GUIDES · URUGUAY

Key Facts — The country Uruguay is a South American republic of about 3.4 million people in 2025, wedged between Argentina and Brazil. Its capital, Montevideo, hosts the Mercosur secretariat.

— The economy As of October 2026, the 2026 forecast is US$95.2 billion in output, or US$27,339 per person, the highest of 19 Latin American countries in the IMF table, Guyana aside. Growth is forecast at just 1.3%.

— Regional seats Uruguay chairs Mercosur, the South American customs union, until December 2026. It also holds the rotating presidency of CELAC, the Latin American and Caribbean forum, for 2026 and 2027.

— Trade Goods exports reached US$13.49 billion in 2025, a ten-year high, and China took about 26% of them. The United States has applied a 12.5% tariff on many Uruguayan goods since 24 July 2026, with beef and pulp exempt.

— Who is who President Yamandú Orsi leads a centre-left government of the Broad Front (Frente Amplio) coalition. Mario Lubetkin is foreign minister.

— Power Index Uruguay ranks 7th of 14 in Uruguay ranks 7th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 45.9 points (October 2026 edition).

— What it means for you US investors face a small, open economy with a new US tariff on some exports. US travellers face a Level 2 State Department advisory for crime.

Uruguay is small in people and money, yet it holds a larger place in Latin America’s clubs than its size suggests. This guide sets out its weight, its seats, its disputes and its partners as of October 2026.

The Uruguay continent story is one of a small country with an outsized voice. It has about 3.4 million people, yet it hosts the Mercosur secretariat in Montevideo and chairs both Mercosur and CELAC in 2026.

For US readers, Uruguay matters as a stable democracy that trades with everyone and now faces a new US tariff. The Nasdaq-listed online marketplace MercadoLibre also gives Montevideo as its business address in its US filings.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Uruguay ranks 7th of 14 with 45.9 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (88); weakest: future resources (23). Alignment group: Hedging. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Figures come from the International Monetary Fund’s October 2026 outlook, the World Bank and Uruguayan ministries, with money in US$. Daily news is in the Rio Times Uruguay section, and our guides to the Southern Cone neighbourhood and to the Uruguayan economy go deeper.

Uruguay’s Weight in Numbers

The World Bank counts about 3.38 million people in Uruguay in 2025, and it is the smallest of the 19 Latin American countries compared here. Its forecast GDP for 2026 is US$95.2 billion, a modest figure beside Brazil and Argentina.

Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

Brazil’s economy is about 28 times larger than Uruguay’s, and Argentina’s is about 8 times larger. The five Mercosur States Parties together produce about US$3.6 trillion in 2026, and Uruguay supplies about 2.6% of it.

Income per person is where Uruguay stands out. At US$27,339 in 2026 it tops the 19 countries, ahead of Costa Rica at US$21,282, Panama at US$20,877 and Chile at US$19,961.

Measured at purchasing power, Uruguay’s US$39,008 per person ranks second among the 19, behind Panama at US$47,129. Only Guyana, which this comparison leaves out, earns more per person in South America.

Growth is the weak spot in Uruguay’s story. The IMF forecasts 1.3% for 2026 and 2.4% for 2027, against 5.0% for Panama and 3.3% for Costa Rica in 2026.

Uruguay lives off trade. Exports of goods and services were 27.1% of GDP in 2025, and goods exports reached US$13.49 billion, the highest level in ten years.

Container cranes at the port of Montevideo, the gateway for Uruguay’s beef, pulp and soy exports (Photo: Falk2, CC BY-SA 3.0 de via Wikimedia Commons).

RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only — every claim links to its source article. Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesCost of living, safety, visas across Latin America › RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. × Best for expats Cost of living Safest places Easy visas Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Beef brought in US$2.68 billion in 2025, or 20% of the total, followed by pulp at US$2.31 billion and soybeans at US$1.42 billion. China bought about US$3.49 billion, roughly 26% of all goods exports and the largest single share.

How Uruguay Compares With Its Peers

Uruguay’s strongest case is institutional rather than economic. Freedom House scored it 97 out of 100 for 2026, ahead of Chile at 95, Costa Rica at 91, Argentina at 85 and Brazil at 73.

Transparency International’s 2025 index scored Uruguay 73 and ranked it 17th of 182 countries, down three points from 2024. Chile scored 63, Costa Rica 56, Argentina 36, Brazil 35 and Panama 33.

The World Bank puts Uruguay’s Gini index, where a lower number means more equal incomes, at 40.0 in 2024. That is below Argentina at 42.4, Chile at 43.0, Costa Rica at 45.5 (2025), Panama at 49.7 and Brazil at 50.3.

Chile and Costa Rica are Uruguay’s nearest peers in stability, and our guides to their roles allow a direct comparison. Neither is a full member of Mercosur, the customs union Uruguay helped found in 1991.

Mercosur, the Home Base

Mercosur is the customs union that Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay founded with the Treaty of Asunción in 1991. The treaty placed its administrative secretariat in Montevideo, where it sits in the Mercosur building.

The Mercosur building in Montevideo, seat of the bloc’s administrative secretariat (Photo: Igna, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

The 68th Mercosur summit on Tuesday, 30 June 2026, in Luque, Paraguay, listed five States Parties, including Bolivia. Chile, Ecuador, Panama, Colombia and Peru were listed on its agenda as associated states.

At that summit Uruguay took the rotating presidency from Paraguay for six months, until December 2026. President Orsi named implementation of the recently concluded trade agreements as its main priority.

The interim trade agreement with the European Union has applied provisionally since 1 May 2026. The full agreement still awaits the European Parliament, which asked the EU Court of Justice for an opinion in January 2026.

Foreign Minister Lubetkin told Euronews in July 2026 that he did not know whether Parliament would vote in 2027 or 2028. He added that Uruguay plans to host the first EU-Mercosur trade forum in December 2026.

Under former centre-right president Luis Lacalle Pou, a push for a bilateral China deal caused friction with Mercosur partners. In May 2025 Orsi said any such deal should involve the whole region, and EFE reported that Uruguay no longer sought one alone.

Montevideo also hosts ALADI, the Latin American Integration Association, created by the Treaty of Montevideo of 12 August 1980. Its website lists 13 members, from Argentina and Mexico to Cuba and Venezuela.

CELAC and the Wider Region

On Saturday, 21 March 2026, in Bogotá, Colombia’s President Gustavo Petro handed the rotating presidency of CELAC to Orsi. CELAC, the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States, is a political forum with no common market.

Orsi listed food security, the energy transition, disaster-risk management, higher education and productive development as priorities. He also called for joint action against organised crime and for support for stability in Haiti.

Orsi said CELAC would coordinate support for a Latin American or Caribbean candidate for UN Secretary-General. He named no candidate or country.

Uruguay has supplied regional leaders before, such as former foreign minister Luis Almagro. He became secretary general of the Organization of American States on 26 May 2015 and won a second term on 20 March 2020.

Orsi leads a centre-left government but courts leaders of other camps, including Argentina’s Javier Milei, Chile’s José Antonio Kast and Bolivia’s Rodrigo Paz. El Observador wrote on 8 September 2026 that Milei’s government has backed Uruguay’s bid to join the CPTPP.

Argentina and Brazil, the Two Giants Next Door

Argentina and Uruguay share the Uruguay River under a 1975 statute and a joint commission known as CARU. The Salto Grande dam, shown below from the Argentine bank, stands on the same river.

The Salto Grande dam on the Uruguay River, seen from the Argentine bank (Photo: Dario Alpern, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

Their best-known dispute ended at the International Court of Justice after Argentina filed a case on 4 May 2006 over pulp mills. On 20 April 2010 the court found Uruguay had breached procedural duties but not substantive environmental ones.

A newer row concerns a green-hydrogen and e-fuels plant planned by HIF Global at Paysandú. On 3 September 2026 Lubetkin told Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno that Uruguay would relocate it after Argentine objections to a site near Colón.

The project is worth about US$5.3 billion, which would make it the largest investment in Uruguay’s history. The new site is a 48-hectare plot owned by the state oil company Ancap.

On Monday, 21 September 2026, Orsi met Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in New York during the UN General Assembly’s high-level week. They discussed border cooperation, including a planned binational bridge over the Jaguarão River, but no signed deal or timetable was reported.

Lula thanked Uruguay for letting Brazil use the surplus of its beef export quota to China. Both countries sell beef to China, which makes the favour a notable one.

China, the United States and Europe

China has been Uruguay’s largest trading partner for 14 years, Euronews reported in July 2026. Europe is the largest investor and the United States leads in services, it added.

Lubetkin put it plainly: “We work with China, with the United States and with the European Union.” He said Uruguay is not choosing sides.

Uruguay XXI, the export promotion agency, ranks China first for 2025 goods exports, then Brazil, the European Union and the United States. Sales to the United States grew almost 30% that year, while sales to Brazil fell 15%.

Since Friday, 24 July 2026, the United States has charged Uruguay a 12.5% tariff on many goods, up from 10%. It followed a US inquiry into forced-labour import bans, and the economy ministry says 77.5% of 2025 exports are exempt, including beef and pulp.

Lubetkin said in June 2026 that nobody had explained the reasons to Uruguay, and he noted that exports to the United States kept growing. A meeting between Orsi and President Donald Trump was on the agenda then, with no date set.

Uruguay’s foreign ministry also lists Mercosur trade agreements with Singapore and with EFTA, the European Free Trade Association. Together with the EU deal, they widen the markets Uruguay can reach without leaving the customs union.

The CPTPP Bid and the Pacific

On 21 November 2025, in Melbourne, Uruguay won the no-objection of all CPTPP members, the step that opens accession talks. The CPTPP, or Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, has 12 members, including Chile, Mexico, Peru, Japan, Canada and the United Kingdom.

Chile chairs the accession working group, which first met on 13 May 2026. Uruguay is writing a compatibility study of every chapter, and Vice Foreign Minister Valeria Csukasi said there was no doubt it could meet the commitments.

Ámbito, a business news site, estimated in May 2026 that Uruguay could join around 2027 if it follows Costa Rica’s timetable. That is an estimate, not an official date.

What It Means for US Readers

US investors face a small, open economy with 1.3% forecast growth for 2026 and a 12.5% US tariff on some exports. MercadoLibre, listed on Nasdaq under the ticker MELI, gives Montevideo as its business address in its US filings.

The State Department rates Uruguay Level 2, exercise increased caution, in an advisory issued on 28 July 2026. It cites violent crime, most common in Montevideo, Canelones, Maldonado and Rivera.

US importers will find Uruguayan beef, pulp and oranges exempt from the new 12.5% tariff, while soy, honey and chemicals are not. Exporters are meanwhile looking to the EU deal and the CPTPP for new markets.

What Is Not Known

No official CPTPP accession date was published in the sources reviewed, and the European Parliament has not set a vote on the EU deal. Lubetkin himself said he could not say whether it would come in 2027 or 2028.

It is also unclear how the 12.5% US tariff will affect farm and forestry exports over a full year. The ministry’s exemption figure covers 2025 sales, not 2026.

Whether an Orsi and Trump meeting will happen, and what it would deliver, is not known. The government said in June 2026 that it was on the agenda without a date, and we found no later confirmation.

The final site and schedule for the HIF plant are not settled, and Argentine legal actions may continue. Argentina’s government reportedly does not know how many are still open.

Frequently Asked Questions

How big is Uruguay compared with the rest of Latin America?

About 3.38 million people lived in Uruguay in 2025 according to the World Bank, and the IMF forecasts a US$95.2 billion economy for 2026. That is modest beside Brazil or Argentina, yet its US$27,339 income per person is the highest of 19 Latin American countries in the IMF table, Guyana aside.

What is Uruguay’s role in Mercosur?

Uruguay is a founding member and hosts the bloc’s administrative secretariat in Montevideo. It holds the rotating presidency from 30 June to December 2026 and has made implementing new trade deals its main priority.

Does Uruguay lead CELAC?

Uruguay took over the rotating presidency of CELAC from Colombia on Saturday, 21 March 2026, in Bogotá. President Yamandú Orsi named food security, the energy transition and the fight against organised crime among his priorities.

Who is Uruguay’s biggest trading partner?

China, which bought about US$3.49 billion of Uruguayan goods in 2025, roughly 26% of the total. Brazil ranked second, the European Union third and the United States fourth.

How does the US tariff affect Uruguay?

The United States has charged a 12.5% tariff on many Uruguayan goods since 24 July 2026, up from 10%. Uruguay’s economy ministry says 77.5% of 2025 exports to the United States are exempt, including beef and pulp.

Is Uruguay safe for US travellers?

The State Department rates Uruguay Level 2, exercise increased caution, because of crime, in an advisory issued on 28 July 2026. Crime is most common in Montevideo, Canelones, Maldonado and Rivera.

When could Uruguay join the CPTPP?

All members agreed to start accession on 21 November 2025, and the working group first met on 13 May 2026. The sources reviewed give no official entry date, and one business outlet estimated around 2027.

World.title: Mopan Technical High School’s Agri-Business students seek support to grow production and build young entrepreneurs
World.content:
Mopan Technical High School’s Agri-Business students seek support to grow production and build young entrepreneurs

By Zoila Palma: Mopan Technical High School’s vibrant Agri-Business Department is cultivating more than chickens, eggs and vegetables; its students are developing practical skills and entrepreneurial ideas that could contribute to Belize’s agricultural sector and national development.

The enthusiastic students are seeking financial assistance and business partnerships to improve the presentation and packaging of their products.

Currently, they sell their produce to the community using regular plastic bags and hope to acquire more suitable packaging for their eggs, chickens and other agricultural products to give them a more professional appearance.

Beyond improving packaging, the students have proposed an exciting initiative: establishing a dedicated Mopan Tech Market Day, when the school would open its doors to the community, allowing residents to purchase products directly from the students. The initiative would provide an opportunity to showcase their work, strengthen their entrepreneurial skills and connect the school’s agricultural production with local consumers.

The students say they have the willingness, dedication and hands-on experience to continue working the soil, raising poultry and improving the quality of their products. What they need now is the support and resources to take their efforts to the next level.

Mopan Technical High School is therefore inviting businesses, entrepreneurs and potential partners to collaborate with its Agri-Business Department through financial assistance, packaging supplies, equipment or other forms of support. Such partnerships would help students strengthen their practical training while developing products that can compete in the marketplace.

Supporting these students means investing in young Belizeans who are eager to learn, produce and build their future through agriculture.

Businesses and individuals willing to partner with Mopan Technical High School can help transform the students’ ideas into opportunities that benefit both the school and the wider community.

World.title: Building Futures together: Mopan Technical High School seeks community support for meaningful projects
World.content:
Building Futures together: Mopan Technical High School seeks community support for meaningful projects

By Zoila Palma: Mopan Technical High School is seeking support for several projects aimed at improving the school environment, enhancing safety and creating better conditions for students and teachers.

As the institution continues to strengthen its vocational and technical education programs, it is also encouraging community members, businesses and other stakeholders to contribute to initiatives that can make a lasting difference in the lives of students.

Among the projects identified is the construction of a new concrete roundabout entrance to improve access to the campus. During the rainy season, the entrance becomes muddy and nearly impassable, creating challenges for students and teachers entering the school grounds.

Belizean Studies teacher Casi Sagastume explained that the vision is to develop a concrete entrance that creates a more welcoming appearance while improving safety for students, staff and visitors.

In addition, Mopan Technical High School is also seeking equipment for its Food and Nutrition Kitchen, sporting equipment and improved infrastructural works for its football field and basketball court.

The proposed improvements reflect the school’s commitment to creating a better learning environment and addressing practical challenges that affect the school community.

Principal Dr. Katie Jones and Mopan Technical High School is inviting individuals, businesses and organizations to consider supporting its projects and becoming part of the institution’s continued development. Dr. Jones expressed gratitude to valued stakeholders and reiterated that meaningful partnerships in education will empower and enable students with the skills needed for a competent, qualified and skilled workforce.

Community support can help turn these plans into reality while giving students an improved environment in which to learn, develop practical skills and prepare for their future careers.

Giving back to the community means investing in the next generation.

Through partnerships and contributions, stakeholders have an opportunity to help Mopan Technical High School advance meaningful projects that benefit students, educators and the wider community.

Those interested in supporting Mopan Technical High School’s projects and investing in students’ futures are encouraged to call 823-2028 and join the school’s efforts in building brighter futures together.

World.title: Building skills, Shaping futures! Mopan Technical High School champions Vocational Education
World.content:
Building skills, Shaping futures! Mopan Technical High School champions Vocational Education

Breaking Belize News journalist Zoila Palma was recognized as a valued stakeholder of Mopan Technical High School during the institution’s first-ever Stakeholder Dinner 2026, in appreciation of her continued support and efforts to promote the school’s programs and achievements.

Palma expressed pride in receiving the recognition, noting her personal connection to the institution, where her daughter, Zabrina, is a student. “I am proud and honored to be recognized as one of Mopan Technical High School’s valued stakeholders at its first-ever Stakeholder Dinner today!” she shared.

A strong advocate for vocational and technical education, Palma commended Principal Dr. Katie Jones, Vice Principal Andrew Arnold, the administration, staff, educators and partners in education for their dedication to preparing students for meaningful careers. She emphasized the importance of practical training in fields such as agriculture, tourism and hospitality, carpentry, welding, engineering and other essential professions.

“These are the practical, hands-on skills Belize needs to continue growing,” Palma stated, highlighting the role of vocational education in equipping young people with skills that can translate into employment and contribute to national development.

Palma reaffirmed her commitment to promoting vocational and technical skills in Belize, thanking the school’s leadership and partners for their continued efforts to develop a skilled workforce. She noted the importance of preparing future business and tourism professionals, strengthening the agricultural sector and training qualified professionals across various industries.

“Investing in vocational education means investing in our young people, empowering them with the knowledge and skills to build meaningful careers and contribute to our nation’s development,” Palma said.

Palma congratulated Mopan Technical High School on the milestone and reaffirmed her commitment to supporting the institution and advocating for vocational and technical education as valuable pathways for students to develop practical skills, build careers and help shape Belize’s future.

World.title: BBN Journalist recognized for supporting Mopan Technical High School
World.content:
BBN Journalist recognized for supporting Mopan Technical High School

Breaking Belize News journalist Zoila Palma was recognized as a stakeholder of Mopan Technical High School during the institution’s first stakeholder dinner last night, in appreciation of her continued efforts to promote the school’s programs and achievements.

Principal Dr. Katie Jones thanked Palma and Breaking Belize News for highlighting the institution’s initiatives, including its recent participation in the “I am Agriculture” video competition, where Mopan Technical High School secured second place.

During her remarks, Palma commended Dr. Jones, the school’s administration and educators for their dedication to students and the development of technical and vocational education. She encouraged educators to continue promoting, supporting and advocating for vocational and technical studies, emphasizing that students have different learning styles and abilities and should have opportunities to pursue educational paths that suit their strengths.

Palma, who also manages Palma’s Lumber & Supplies, shared how vocational training can translate into meaningful employment opportunities. She noted that one of the company’s recent interns is a proud graduate of Mopan Technical High School who initially visited the business during Career Week while studying carpentry.

His experience led to him being hired by Palma’s Lumber & Supplies, demonstrating how technical education can help bridge the gap between classroom learning and the workforce.

Palma expressed pride in being part of the Mopan Technical High School family and pledged to continue supporting and promoting the institution and its programs.

She highlighted the importance of recognizing vocational education as a valuable pathway for students to develop practical skills, pursue careers and contribute to Belize’s development.

World.title: Mopan Technical High School hosts first-ever Stakeholder Dinner, seeks support for new projects
World.content:
Mopan Technical High School hosts first-ever Stakeholder Dinner, seeks support for new projects

By Zoila Palma: Mopan Technical High School hosted its first-ever stakeholder dinner last night, recognizing valued stakeholders who have supported the institution and seeking additional assistance for projects aimed at improving the school’s facilities and student programs.

The event provided an opportunity for the school to acknowledge the contributions of its stakeholders while sharing its plans for continued development and the resources needed to enhance the learning environment for its students.

Among the projects for which the school is seeking support is the construction of a new concrete roundabout entrance to improve accessibility and enhance the campus entrance. During the rainy season, the entrance becomes muddy and nearly impassable, creating challenges for students and teachers accessing the school.

Belizean Studies teacher Casi Sagastume explained that the vision is to create a concrete entrance that offers a more welcoming appearance while improving safety and accessibility for students, teachers, and visitors.

The institution is also looking to acquire new kitchen equipment for its Food and Nutrition students, install air-conditioning units in its science laboratories, and obtain sporting equipment for its school teams.

Through the stakeholder dinner, Mopan Technical High School hopes to strengthen its partnerships with individuals, businesses and organizations that can contribute to its continued growth.

The school emphasized the importance of collaboration in providing students with improved facilities, practical learning opportunities and the resources needed to excel academically and beyond the classroom.

World.title: Flood alert issued across Belize as heavy rainfall threatens rivers and low-lying areas; 2 – 4 inches of rain possible over some areas
World.content:
Flood alert issued across Belize as heavy rainfall threatens rivers and low-lying areas; 2 – 4 inches of rain possible over some areas

By Hugh O’Brien: A flood alert across Belize has been issued as additional rainfall is expected to affect the country over the weekend.

According to the National Meteorological Service (NMS) in the Ministry of Sustainable Development and Climate Change, rainfall forecasts of “2 – 4 inches are possible over portions of Belize during the next four days”.

Residents in low-lying, flood-prone and riverside communities especially are advised to remain alert and to closely monitor official weather and flood updates as conditions may change rapidly.

During periods of heavy rainfall, the NMS advises caution “near rivers, streams, low-level crossings and other flood-prone areas” and residents are advised “to not attempt to cross flooded roads or waterways”.

According to the NMS, “several rivers are currently at normal or below-normal levels”. However, additional rainfall could cause smaller streams and tributaries to rise quickly, while larger river systems may respond more gradually as rainfall accumulates. Particular attention is being urged for rivers that are already elevated or approaching bankfull levels.

In its latest weather forecast, the NMS reported that in the north, rivers are near or below normal. In the west, the Mopan River, in particular, has shown a moderate increase in water level, but remain near or below normal. The Belize River is “above normal levels at More Tomorrow” but further downstream toward the coast, and at the Crooked Tree Lagoon, levels are below normal.

In the south, the Sittee River is rising toward bankfull levels and is a cause for concern for increased flooding. The Gales Point Lagoon, Moho River, Temash River and Sarstoon are rising above normal levels

Despite the current conditions in the nation’s rivers, the NMS warns that further rainfall could lead to rapid changes, particularly in smaller waterways and areas that are already vulnerable to flooding.

The NMS says it will continue to monitor rainfall and river conditions and that the flood outlook may be updated if forecast conditions or field observations change.

World.title: Police seek public’s help to identify two-year-old girl found in Belize City
World.content:
Police seek public’s help to identify two-year-old girl found in Belize City

UPDATE: The 2-year-old girl has been reunited with her parents.

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Belize Police Department is appealing to the public for assistance in identifying a two-year-old girl who was found on Carissa Street in Belama Phase Two, Belize City, on Friday, October 16, 2026.

Crime Stoppers Belize has circulated a photograph of the child in hopes that someone will recognize her and help authorities establish her identity and locate her family.

Police have not yet disclosed the circumstances under which the child was found or whether any parent or guardian has come forward.

Anyone who recognizes the child or has information that could assist police is urged to call 615-5179, contact Crime Stoppers anonymously at 922, use the P3 Tips app, or visit the nearest police station.

The Belize Police Department confirms that information submitted through Crime Stoppers can be provided anonymously.

World.title: Man accused of torching Hotchandani family’s $485,000 vehicles still without attorney as arson case heads to High Court
World.content:
Man accused of torching Hotchandani family’s $485,000 vehicles still without attorney as arson case heads to High Court

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Nearly two years after three luxury vehicles belonging to businessman Bob Hotchandani and his son were destroyed in a suspected arson attack, the man accused of setting them ablaze is still without an attorney as his case moves toward trial in the High Court.

Twenty-four-year-old Manuel Anthony Moralez appeared unrepresented before Justice Candace Nanton on Friday for a case management conference involving three counts of arson.

When questioned about legal representation, Moralez told the court that he intended to secure an attorney and would try his best to do so if granted additional time.

Justice Nanton agreed to adjourn the matter until March 15, 2027, giving Moralez approximately five months to obtain legal representation. However, she warned that if he remains unrepresented by then, the court will have to proceed with setting a trial date.

Moralez, a construction worker from Sandhill Village, was charged with three counts of arson in December 2024 following a fire that destroyed three vehicles parked outside the Hotchandani family residence on Barrack Road in Belize City.

The vehicles included a 2022 Cadillac Escalade valued at $250,000 and a 2023 Audi Q7 valued at $150,000, both belonging to 75-year-old businessman Bob Hotchandani. A Chevrolet Silverado pickup truck valued at $85,000, belonging to his son, Sunjay Hotchandani, was also destroyed.

According to earlier reporting by 7News, police said three men arrived at the property by boat shortly before 5:00 a.m. on December 22, 2024, poured a flammable substance on the vehicles and set them on fire before escaping by boat.

Surveillance cameras reportedly captured the attack, and police subsequently identified Moralez as one of the alleged perpetrators.

At his initial arraignment, prosecutors opposed bail, citing the substantial value of the destroyed vehicles, the surveillance evidence and concerns that Moralez could interfere with the investigation or face retaliation from other persons allegedly involved. He was subsequently remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

The case has since been committed to the High Court for trial, but proceedings remain stalled while Moralez attempts to secure legal representation.

Moralez’s next court appearance is scheduled for March 15, 2027.

World.title: DIRTY COWARDS
World.content:
Police personnel at the scene where one of their colleagues was fatally shot and another left with lifethreatening injuries in the Five Miles area of St Catherine on Friday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

THE police have identified one of three men killed in a firefight in the Five Miles area off the Sligoville main road in St Catherine, Friday morning, during which gunmen used a child to draw cops closer before opening fire, killing one law enforcer.

He is Malique Hussey, otherwise called Mal Boss, from Spanish Town, St Catherine, with connections in Five Miles.

According to the police, Hussey was a known associate of a high-risk target identified as Kenroy Willis, who operates out of the St Andrew North Police Division and is wanted for four murders.

Up to news time the police had not determined the identities of the other two men who were fatally shot in the gun battle which also resulted in the death of Corporal Trevoy Shaw, who was assigned to the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s (JCF) Special Operations Unit, and the injury to a constable who, up to press time, was in hospital in critical condition.

A third cop suffered minor injuries, not gunshot-related, during the incident.

A 10-year-old child was also shot in what Jamaica Observer sources say was a deliberate attack by Hussey, who was her father.

According to the police, about 5:15 Friday morning members of its Special Operations Unit went in search of Willis, Hussey, and their cronies.

On arrival, the police were met with gunfire by men who had barricaded themselves in a house with a woman and three children, including a monthsold baby.

During the stand-off the men indicated that they wanted to surrender, and used one of the children to signal their willingness to lay down their illegal firearms.

“I can confirm that a child was held out the door, and it was declared that they were willing to surrender, and when the police approached, seeking to retrieve the child, fire was opened upon those policemen,” senior communications strategist at the Jamaica Constabulary Force Dennis Brooks told journalists metres from the shooting scene.

“The gunmen shot from behind the child, which placed the police in a precarious position, even in accessing the building, because of the presence of children,” Brooks said.

He explained that they were met by heavily armed men, and a woman declared from inside the building that she and two children were inside.

The woman, the injured 10-year-old, and the baby were allowed to leave the building by the gunmen, who kept a child inside the house as they continued to fire at the cops who were supported by members of the Jamaica Defence Force.

According to Brooks, the men manipulated the presence of the children in the house and the police’s willingness to accept their surrender, pretending to wave the ‘white flag’ multiple times.
