“It is the intention of the police on every operation to bring persons to justice, place them before the court, and so it is not our intention to proceed marauding into a building — whether or not there are children and women in there.

And if there is an indication, even the slightest indication, that they are willing to surrender then we are going to engage that possibility,” Brooks said.

He lamented the death of the corporal who was trying to retrieve the child, describing it as heartbreaking.

“I left several policemen and women in tears in Kingston because they knew him well… He was promoted to the rank of corporal about a month ago, which speaks to his own dedication and the recognition of his work.

“I mean, imagine at this time he is just enjoying this new development in his career, and he is [the] pride of his family in this moment, and for his life, his light to be put out in such a manner in seeking to make this country a safer place — it is heartbreaking,” Brooks said.

The pain of Shaw’s colleagues was palpable at Spanish Town Hospital as news spread that two of their colleagues had been rushed there with gunshot wounds.

It became worse when it was confirmed that he had died while the constable had been rushed into surgery.

Shortly after 10:00 am a policeman was seen leaving the hospital’s Accident and Emergency Department (A&E), with sources indicating that he was the person who had suffered the non-gunshot-related injury.

The cop appeared to be in some discomfort as he limped towards a police vehicle parked on the grounds of the hospital.

The vehicle was quickly surrounded by other cops.

Shortly after 11:00 am, people who appeared to be related to the shot cops stormed onto the facility, with cries of grief, as they sought to enter the A&E Department seeking answers.

About five minutes later a black police vehicle raced onto the compound, with cops carrying what appeared to be the bodies of the three slain criminals.

For a minute chaos unfolded as several people hurried to the van to observe what was happening.

But this curiosity was stopped in its tracks by police personnel, who chased away civilians trying to capture videos or photos.

In his immediate reaction to the attack on the men and women under his command, Police Commissioner Dr Kevin Blake, who visited the scene, described the gunmen as murderous.

He said while death is always a possibility for a cop, “We prepare, we equip, so that every single member after an operation goes home to his or her family safe and injury-free.

Unfortunately this morning, that hope and that preparation was shattered.” Blake told the police on the scene that the best way to honour their fallen comrade would be to remain relentless.

“Because we are who we are, because we would rather take them in to face the court, we lost a member… let not that define how we operate going forward,” said Blake.

“I know it is a tough time, and for the colleagues of the officer killed and the officer injured, I understand,” added Blake.

The attack on the police was condemned by political representatives during Friday’s sitting of the Senate, human rights group Jamaicans For Justice, and several other organisations

World.title: Clarendon power shift stalled by court order
World.content:
Member of Parliament for Clarendon Central Delroy Williams (left) and May Pen Mayor Joel Williams (second right) celebrate with JLP supports after special sitting of the Clarendon Municipal Corporation on Friday at which an ex parte interim injunction was tabled which blocked the PNPs efforts to take over leadership of the corporation

THE People’s National Party (PNP) says it plans to challenge a Supreme Court injunction that has stalled its bid to take control of the Clarendon Municipal Corporation.

PNP senior councillor in the corporation Scean Barnswell has also questioned how the injunction was handled at the corporation, claiming it was not entered in its registry, and raised doubts about whether it had been properly served.

The dispute emerged at a special meeting of the corporation on Friday, where councillor for the May Pen North Division Tanyalee Williams formally made the switch from the Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) to the PNP, giving the Opposition party a 12-10 majority in the 22-member council.

The switch had created an opening for the PNP to seek the removal of Mayor Joel Williams and Deputy Mayor Clivalee Mundle and elect replacements backed by the new majority.

However, the meeting was halted after the mayor said an ex parte interim injunction prevented the council from dealing with the matter.

In a statement issued on Friday, the PNP described the injunction as “profoundly anti-democratic”.

The PNP said its legal challenge is intended to allow the meeting to continue and the relevant resolutions to be considered.

Earlier, during the special meeting, Barnswell also raised concerns about how the injunction reached the corporation, questioning whether it had been formally recorded and properly served.

“Chairman, let the record reflect that we have asked the question of how the document has been received at the municipal corporation? We have a registry that logs all external correspondence that comes to the CEO.

It is logged into the registry and I just want to place on record that there is no indication of this document being logged into the council’s registry,” he said.

Barnswell later told reporters that the document appeared to have been presented without the usual procedures being followed.

“There was no signature on the document by the…judge who would have seen it.

There was no official seal or stamp on the document itself, [and] while we respect the court’s decision, we just want to highlight some of the things which we have a problem with the document, no signature, no file date, no official seal or stamp, and it was just a courtesy copy that was sent to us.

So… our attorney is vetting it some more, and they will advise further as to how we proceed,” added Barnswell.

CEO of the corporation Rowhan Blake told councillors during the meeting that he was served in his capacity as the defendant and had attended court at 9:05 Friday morning.

Blake said he then circulated the decision to councillors by email, using the same method through which he normally sends minutes and other correspondence.

He said the order restrained the corporation, its councillors and officers from considering, debating or voting on agenda items two to five, which were the ones that covered the proposed changes to the corporation’s leadership.

The mayor relied on the order to stop the meeting from proceeding.

But PNP councillors disputed his handling of the adjournment, arguing that the decision to end the meeting should have been put to a vote and decided by the majority.

Councillor Romain Morris (PNP, Mocho Division) referred to the Local Government Act and called on the corporation’s CEO to guide the meeting on how it should proceed.

“Mr CEO please note this meeting was not adjourned properly.

The motion of adjournment, Mr Chairman, is a question and is set out in the Local Government Act section 32(J) and with that said, Mr Chairman, it must be adhered to… With that being said the chairman is no longer in his seat, [and] I am going to ask if we can elect a member among ourselves to continue with the remainder of the meeting from the majority,” questioned Morris.

His intervention followed the mayor’s repeated attempts to end the meeting, citing the injunction.

The PNP councillors maintained that the decision to adjourn should have been put to a vote and decided by the majority, rather than the mayor declaring the meeting over.

As the dispute continued, Morris suggested that the councillors remaining in the chamber elect someone from their majority to continue with the meeting.

However, JLP councillors disputed that approach, maintaining that the mayor had already adjourned the meeting and that the council could not proceed in his absence.

PNP councillors continued to challenge the handling of the adjournment and called on Blake to advise them on the way forward, but Blake and the mayor subsequently left the chamber, even as the PNP members maintained that the meeting had not been properly adjourned.

The dispute over the adjournment added to the disagreement over the injunction, with the PNP unable to proceed with the planned leadership changes despite its new 12-10 majority.

Mayor Williams, speaking with the media after the meeting, defended his decision to seek court intervention.

“We are seeking to get clarity as it relates to the Section 16 of the Local Government Act… They are the ones who are playing political football with the people’s business, not us on this side.

We’re always serious about getting the people’s business done in the parish of Clarendon and [by] extension across Jamaica.

That’s what we’re here for, not to play games,” declared the mayor.

He declined to discuss Williams’s decision to leave the JLP, saying: “She’s on the other side and I don’t wish to speak on her.”

World.title: New custos commits to St Elizabeth’s post-Melissa recovery
World.content:
New custos rotulorum for St Elizabeth Bernard Henry gets a kiss from his wife Verna after he received his Instrument of Appointment from Governor General Sir Patrick Allen on Thursday. (Photos: Garfield Robinson)

BUSINESSMAN Bernard Henry has vowed to build on the work of predecessors as he moves into the role of custos rotulorum for St Elizabeth.

Henry received his Instrument of Appointment from Governor General Sir Patrick Allen, after taking the Oath of Allegiance and the Oath of Office during a ceremony at King’s House on Thursday.

He replaces Beryl Rochester who served 12 years as custos rotulorum for the parish.

“This is a humbling office; I’m very fortunate.

We have had an acting custos who was tremendous so we want to make sure that we work to continue to build on what our former custos, Honourable Beryl Rochester, put in place, and the custodes before, and also what Acting Custos Stevon Sheriffe… did.

So my role is really for us to build from there,” Henry told the Jamaica Observer following the ceremony.

According to Henry, the role is even more significant following the devastation caused by Hurricane Melissa last year.

“To be able to step into this role at this time, when we are in the process of rebuilding our parish, is significant.

And so we want to make sure that we operate with humility, that we are there to help, to add value, and to rebuild St Elizabeth.

“We are a very proud parish and we are a resilient people.

We want to show off who we are and what we do, and we want to make sure that the people who are hurting, we are there to lift them up — especially the youth,” Henry added.

The Category 5 storm, which hit Jamaica on October 28, 2025, left many residents of St Elizabeth scrambling to rebuild their lives, but Henry remains optimistic about the future of the parish.

“I’m hoping that we will get the support that we need to rebuild even better than what we had before.

I see the devastation but I’m also looking for the silver lining, and the silver lining is that we will be able to build back even better.

That’s what I see.

That’s what I want to support.

And so St Elizabeth people, we will come again,” Henry said.

In his address, Governor General Sir Patrick Allen charged Henry to execute the role with sound judgement, objectivity, and the ability to command public confidence.

“You will be my representative in St Elizabeth, and that means that you will support the administration of justice, provide leadership to the network of justices of the peace, and encourage civic participation.

I welcome your intention to improve access to the justices of the peace in St Elizabeth, to maintain meaningful engagement with communities, and encourage opportunities for our young people,” said Sir Patrick.

“Such priorities are especially pertinent as St Elizabeth continues its recovery and renewal.

You have spoken of the importance of listening, learning, and seeking wise counsel.

I encourage you to remain guided by these principles, recognising that the distinction of public office rests ultimately upon the honour with which its responsibilities are discharged,” added Sir Patrick.

The governor general said Henry’s long-standing investment in education, institutional governance, and national development has earned the businessman his confidence.

“He has demonstrated the vision and discipline required to establish enterprises, navigate complex responsibilities, and forge enduring partnerships.

However, his contribution to St Elizabeth extends beyond commercial enterprise.

“As inaugural chairman of the St Elizabeth Community Development Foundation, and through its involvement with the St Elizabeth Homecoming Foundation, he has helped to foster cooperation and advance the interests of the parish.

These experiences assume relevance as he undertakes the responsibilities of custos rotulorum,” said Sir Patrick.

World.title: Changes coming for Miss Jamaica World pageant
World.content:
The 23 finalists competing in the 2026 Miss Jamaica World pageant

Changes will be implemented for this year’s staging of the Miss Jamaica World beauty pageant.

At a sashing exercise and the Beach Beauty Fast Track competition held at the Jamaica Pegasus hotel in New Kingston on Tuesday night, Dahlia Harris, of the Miss Jamaica World Organization, gave an insight into how the new titleholder will be selected.

“Forty per cent of each contestant’s overall assessment will come from her performance throughout the training and development programme, while 60 per cent will come from the judges’ assessment.

Why have we made this change? Because we believe that how a young woman conducts herself throughout the journey is just as important as how she performs when she steps in front of the judges,” Harris told the Jamaica Observer.

“We want to reward punctuality, participation, discipline, deportment, commitment, and a willingness to learn.

We want contestants to understand that professionalism is not something you switch on when the spotlight comes on.

It is demonstrated in how you show up, how you treat people, how you respond to challenges, and how seriously you take the opportunities presented to you.

The crown should represent more than a performance on one evening; it should reflect the character, consistency, and commitment demonstrated throughout the competition.

And we believe this revised assessment structure will help us achieve exactly that.” Instead of a Top 10, a Top 12 will be selected and comprise the winners of the 5 fasttrack competitions; namely, Beach Beauty, Talent, Fitness Challenge, Top Model, and Beauty with a Purpose.

There will also be five judges’ selections and, for the very first time, the Head-to- Head and Multi-Media challenge winners.

“The Challenge events are, therefore, more extensive this year.

The Head-to-Head Challenge, for example, has already selected a top 10 based on their Round One performance and, on Thursday, October 15, they will compete in the semi-final and final rounds.

The judges will select a Top 5 and the public will select a People’s Choice winner, who will join them to complete a Top 6,” said Harris.

At Tuesday night’s event, the 23 finalists were sashed by their respective sponsors.

Afterwards, the Beach Beauty Fast Track competition took place, with Seana’Kay Wright, who is sponsored by Southdale Hardware and Glass Supplies, taking first place.

First runner-up was Matea Mahal Smith, Miss Aveeno, while medical doctor Samantha McLeod, Miss Island Smiles, was named second runner-up.

Ironically, at the recent Fitness Challenge, held at the Emancipation Park in New Kingston, Smith was declared the first-place winner and Wright was her first runner-up.

The coronation of Miss Jamaica World 2026 is scheduled for November 1 at Karl Hendrickson Auditorium, Jamaica College.

World.title: From Spanish Town dreams to Broward County honour
World.content:
D’Angel receives the key to the city of Tamarac from Marlon Bolton, Tamarac’s vice mayor during the Red Gala event in Florida last week.

WHEN dancehall artiste D’Angel received word that she would be honoured with the key to the City of Tamarac, Florida, the tears came before she could fully comprehend the magnitude of the moment.

And, as if that were not enough to process, she arrived in Florida to learn that she would also receive the key to Broward County. The double honour overwhelmed her. “I couldn’t hold back my tears of joy. I was like, ‘God, this is all you,’ ” she recalled.

For the woman who describes her journey in music as one of fighting, overcoming, and enduring more lows than highs, the recognition was more than a ceremonial milestone. It was an unexpected acknowledgement of the work she has put into her career and the resilience she has had to summon along the way.

The artiste, whose given name is Michelle Downer, said she had not realised the extent to which her efforts were being noticed, but was grateful for the recognition. “I never knew anyone was paying attention to what I’ve been doing because it has been a rough journey of fight and overcoming.

But look at me now, just a girl from Spanish Town who had big dreams,” she said. “I’m very grateful and thankful to be honoured outside my country in such high standard. Getting the key to the City of Tamarac and Broward County is mind-blowing.

I’m still processing it.” For D’Angel, the honour represents more than personal achievement, it speaks also to the weight she believes she has carried on behalf of Jamaicans through her music and charitable work.

That sense of responsibility is central to how she views the recognition. It also reinforces the importance of how she conducts herself and represents her country on the international stage.

“I definitely will continue to represent and live up to my honour through my music and deportment, because I’m not only representing my country, I’m now representing a city and a state I was not born in,” she said.

“I have to do my best…” D’Angel continued: “I had a lot of highs and lows moments, more lows than highs, but it never stopped me from pursuing my dreams…

I know I was born for greatness, and no naysayer could ever abort my destiny.

With every moment I had to overcome, I became stronger, more focused, and resilient.” Her ability to keep moving forward, she explained, has been shaped by the people and beliefs that have anchored her through difficult periods.

Among her strongest influences are her mother and her son, whom she identifies as the driving forces behind her life. Their influence helped her to keep going, even when the odds seemed stacked against her.

“I never felt like quitting. Yuh mad?” she said, laughing off the suggestion. “One thing my mom always tell me, never let anyone rejoice over me, so that alone kept me going.

Also, my son, who’s the driving force of my life.” Music itself has also served as a source of encouragement. Knowing that her work has strengthened others has reinforced her belief that she has a purpose to fulfil.

“My music also gave me strength, because I see where it strengthens others as well, so I know I’m purpose and I belong here,” she said. “Is only one Angel, so I had to carry my cross and let God do the rest.” That faith has become increasingly important to her approach to life and career.

D’Angel said that, while she has always worked hard to advance her ambitions, she has recently become more intentional about praying, relinquishing control over outcomes, and placing greater trust in God.

“I’m always working overtime, but since lately I start praying harder and leave everything in God’s hand, and the proof is in the results,” she said.

“Sometimes you have to let go and let God.” The latest honour, she believes, is not the end of the journey, as her work is not finished, “Once you believe in yourself and be authentic, everything else will be added and the world will respond,” she said.

World.title: No letting go
World.content:
MONTEGO BAY, St James — A man who reportedly refused to accept it when the woman was ready to end the relationship has found himself before the court facing charges of assault occasioning bodily harm.

Andre Edwards appeared in the St James Parish Court, before Judge Natiesha Fairclough-Hylton on Wednesday, to answer the charge which stems from an incident on August 28 when the woman visited his home in Norwood, St James, reportedly to collect money.

According to the allegations, the two became embroiled in an argument during which the woman expressed her intention to end the relationship.

Edwards allegedly refused to accept the decision, and the confrontation escalated when he began squeezing her neck.

A physical struggle followed during which Edwards allegedly pushed the complainant to the ground and strangled her with a cord.

She managed to break free and made her way to the police station to report the incident.

The woman reportedly suffered pain, swelling, and bruising to her throat and right eye.

Edwards was subsequently arrested and charged.

When cautioned by the police he reportedly denied the allegations and said, “Officer, yuh nuh si di woman deh a liar? Mi nuh wah nutten fi do wid da woman deh.” Judge Fairclough-Hylton extended his bail and set November 11 for the matter to be mentioned again.

World.title: More schools benefit from Seprod’s Nutri+Milk initiative
World.content:
Diana Taffe-Myrie, principal of Whitfield Primary and Infant School, shares a moment with students following the first delivery of Nutri+Milk. The school is set to receive 2,400 units of milk throughout the 2026/2027 academic year as part of Seprod’s ongoing school nutrition initiative.

SEPROD’S Nutri+ Milk has expanded its school nutrition initiative to six additional schools across Jamaica, committing a further 30,000 units of milk to support young learners throughout the 2026/2027 academic year.

Building on the initiative launched at Naggo Head Infant School in September, the expansion will benefit students at Galilee Early Childhood Development Centre in Kingston, Seaforth Primary School in St Thomas, Anchovy Primary School in St James, Black River Primary and Infant School, and Burnt Savannah Primary School in St Elizabeth, and Whitfield Primary and Infant School in St Andrew.

Through the year-long commitment, Anchovy Primary School will receive 9,600 units of Nutri+Milk, followed by Black River Primary and Infant School with 7,200 units, and Burnt Savannah Primary School with 6,000 units.

Seaforth Primary School, Galilee Early Childhood Development Centre and Whitfield Primary and Infant School will each receive 2,400 units.

The monthly supply will strengthen the schools’ breakfast and nutrition programmes, helping to ease the financial burden on parents while providing students with consistent access to nutritious milk throughout the academic year.

“It is a pleasure to see the Nutri+Milk initiative continue to grow and reach more schools and communities across Jamaica,” said Deidra Grey, brand manager for Nutri+Milk, in a media release.

“We recognise the important connection between good nutrition and a child’s ability to learn, focus and participate in the classroom.

By providing consistent support throughout the academic year we hope to make a meaningful difference in the everyday lives of students while also easing some of the financial pressure on parents and school administrators,” added Grey.

She noted that the expansion forms part of Seprod’s wider commitment to supporting 20 schools across Jamaica throughout the 2026/2027 academic year through its Nutri+Milk brand, reflecting the company’s continued investment in initiatives that promote childhood nutrition, education and overall well-being.

The initiative was first introduced at Naggo Head Infant School in Portmore, St Catherine on September 4, with a commitment of 6,000 units of Nutri+Milk for the academic year.

Together with the six additional schools, this brings the total planned contribution to 36,000 units of milk across seven schools, providing sustained nutritional support to young learners.

In welcoming the donation Alecia Henry, guidance counsellor at Seaforth Primary, said: “We are truly grateful to Seprod and Nutri+Milk for this generous initiative.

Proper nutrition plays a vital role in a child’s ability to concentrate, learn and perform well in school.

“This contribution will not only support our students’ nutritional needs but also ease the financial burden on many families.

As a school, we are pleased to be part of an initiative that prioritises the health, well-being and academic development of our children,” said Henry.

World.title: ‘PURPLES’ RISE!
World.content:
Kingston College players celebrate winning the ISSA Walker Cup football final after receiving the trophy from ISSA President Keith Wellington (second right) and KFC Brand Manager Andrei Roper (fourth right) at Stadium East on Friday. Kingston College defeated Mona High 2-1 in the final. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

KINGSTON College (KC) won a record 10th Walker Cup title with a come-from-behind 2-1 win over Mona High at Stadium East on Friday.

Goals by Rasheed Payne, in the 60th, and Kamaul Patterson (75th) turned around the fortunes of KC after Skylar McFarlane had given Mona a 16th-minute lead. It was a deserved victory for the “Purples”, once again showing resilience after falling behind.

They are now the most successful team in the history of the Walker Cup which was started in 1961. Kingston College won their first title in 1963 and followed that up in 1964 and 1965.

The North Street giant last won the Walker Cup in 2016 but had to wait another 10 years as governing body ISSA changed the format that ruled out the top teams. But in 2026 the format was once again changed that allowed the leading teams and KC truly obliged.

In front of a packed venue, Mona started the brighter as they pressed KC well not allowing the slick moving KC to play their passing game. But KC almost got the scoresheet as a deflected shot crashed onto the upright.

Then Mona stunned KC players and their large crowd support when McFarlane fired home after he was teed up by Sean Leighton. The half ended with Mona in the ascendancy but that changed on the resumption as KC went out with more intent.

Mona seemed set up to attempt to maintain the one-goal advantage for the next 45 minutes, a move that helped KC as they pressed forward searching for that equalising goal.

And it came on the hour mark. Payne, who was pulling the strings in the middle of the park, scored a beautiful free kick from 25 metres when the ball cannoned into the underside of the bar amd dipped over the goal line.

The momentum was clearly with KC, and top scorer Deshawn Byfield could have given them the lead from the penalty spot, but his shot crashed into the upright in the 71st minute.

KC’s second goal came five minutes later when captain and man of the match Patterson fired home, his shot looping over the goalkeeper.

Mona tried to get back on level terms but appeared to struggle to get out of the defensive mindset, and KC were able to comfortably hold on for the historic victory.

It’s the first title of the schoolboy season, with KC on course to also win the Manning Cup, Champions Cup and Olivier Shield. Byfield and Franklyn Mitcham of Mona High shared the Golden Boot with four goals each.

World.title: Starlink restrictions in Ukraine a ‘planned operation’, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy waits for Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson ahead of their bilateral meeting on the sidelines of a European Union summit at the EU headquarters in Brussels on October 16, 2026. | Olivier Hoslet/ AFP via Getty Images

The Ukrainian president called an executive order from U.S. President Donald Trump an “American sanctions blackout.”

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia is looking to create a blackout across Ukraine, amid attacks on energy infrastructure and the waiver of U.S. sanctions on Moscow.

“Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating. Pressure is needed to stop this,” he said on Telegram.

“An American sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, monetary rewards for [Russian President Vladimir] Putin: all of this only encourages him to keep striking,” he added.

World.title: Violent clashes across France as more groups join student protests
World.content:
More than 160 people had already been arrested across the country by midday, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez’s office told reporters.

Students, farmers and members of the Yellow Jacket movement, among others, were slated to take to the streets on Saturday in a “convergence of struggles” to protest raising living costs, sluggish wages and deep disagreements with the government.

The government was expecting “a fairly large turnout,” Nuñez said on Friday.

Saturday’s demonstrations originated in the student protests that began last month with school blockades and calls for better studying conditions, more teachers and more funding. The movement has since spread nationwide — and become a political issue as the campaign for next year’s presidential election heats up.

The government has struggled to deal with the crisis — which Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu described as “urban violence” — and is hoping the student movement will now fade because of a two-week school holiday that started Friday evening.

“The mobilization is marked by a very strong involvement of the ultra-left movement, which is only looking to cause disorder,” Nuñez’s office said Saturday, adding that the minister reiterated his “instructions of utmost firmness” to local prefects and police forces.

World.title: Spain’s far left fails to unite ahead of November vote
World.content:
The Broad Front is made up of Sumar, the current junior partner in the Socialist-led government, the Catalan Comuns, the Communist-led United Left and Más Madrid. Some smaller local parties have also joined the ticket. The lead candidate for prime minister will be Ada Colau, the former mayor of Barcelona.

Sumar, the dominant force in the alliance, has seen its vote share more than halve since 2023, to 5%, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls.

Although Podemos has only been polling at 3%, its full involvement in the Broad Front would have meant a greater overall share of seats for the far left, according to analysts.

The PSOE has been trailing the conservative People’s Party and would need a strong performance by parties to its left in order to keep Sánchez in office. The more likely scenario, polls show, is that the PP will be able to form a majority with the far-right Vox, whose support has been rising.

“The Spanish left is caught up in a game of thrones that demobilizes [voters],” said Irene de Miguel, coordinator of Podemos in the western region of Extremadura, as the deadline loomed.

World.title: EU leaders clash over migration, Ukraine and budget in Brussels — but delay big decisions
World.content:
Speaking to journalists during a packed news conference, Ukraine’s wartime leader urged his European counterparts to come up with a financial plan or risk facing an unprecedented migration crisis with “20 million Ukrainians” fleeing to Europe.

“The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion more from you — for defense, for weapons, and for our resilience,” Zelenskyy said. “This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back.”

But two diplomats told POLITICO that capitals would continue exploring a range of options to meet Kyiv’s needs, including a potential further loan from the EU.

Luc Frieden and Emmanuel Macron speak ahead of a round table during the EU summit in Brussels on Oct. 15, 2026. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images

A debate over whether to mobilize some €300 billion in Russian frozen assets to help Ukraine is a case in point. Nearly a year after EU leaders rejected using the assets amid objections from Belgium, France and Italy, several countries have asked for the option to be revisited, and top EU diplomat Kaja Kallas had said frozen assets would be on the table when leaders met in Brussels.

But after hours of talks about Ukraine, “nothing has changed,” said Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. “The money is not lost but in my belief nothing has happened since we had the discussion last time.”

“In the short term, money to support Ukraine must come from other sources than the frozen assets,” he concluded.

World.title: EU faces growing pressure to plug Ukraine’s Starlink gap
World.content:
"It is unacceptable for Ukraine’s defense — and therefore Europe’s security — to depend on the goodwill of a single American billionaire or on Donald Trump’s decisions," French centrist Member of the European Parliament Christophe Grudler told POLITICO.

Ahead of Thursday's high-level meeting, European lawmakers had been calling on the EU executive to fast-track Kyiv's access to satellite capabilities already pooled under the bloc’s Govsatcom program — which gives participating governments secure communications capabilities.

Negotiations between the EU executive and Ukraine over this access have been ongoing since March, with no breakthrough. Norway and Iceland secured such an agreement earlier this year.

"What I don’t understand is why the European Commission and the Member States have not done everything possible to quickly reach an agreement that would allow Ukraine to benefit from it," added Christophe Grudler, who wrote to EU leaders.

He also called on them to speed up work on IRIS² — the EU’s in-house, planned satellite network and full-fledged match to Starlink, which is only expected to come online in 2030.

Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed in a statement that it is "currently in talks with Ukraine to fully associate" the country with the EU's Govsatcom program. "The war in Ukraine shows that our security also depends on space. And the EU has been doing quite a lot. We are ready to support Ukraine where we can support Ukraine," he added.

World.title: 21 things we learned at the EU leaders’ summit
World.content:
1) Energy stole the show right out of the gate

The summit’s first major clash came Thursday morning, with EU leaders split over whether to delay ETS2, the bloc’s second phase of carbon pricing, to address high energy prices, triggering a three-hour-long standoff.

Italy and Greece joined the Visegrád Four — Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia — in calling for a delay, a push rejected by the majority of countries.

The debate dragged on, delaying lunch (spare a thought for our hungry leaders!) and leading to the cancellation of a press conference on Thursday night.

2) Budget negotiations are a marathon…

Negotiations on the bloc’s next long-term budget were expected to be one of the summit’s most contentious topics. But they were a nothingburger, with most leaders repeating positions they have held for months. The summit brought them no closer to a breakthrough.

Many countries, of course, want a smaller budget, with Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson telling reporters that his country is “not an ATM for the EU.”

Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, meanwhile, said he had no choice but to be frugal at the European level, arguing he is used to tightening his belt at home because his wife is Dutch. Think of Bart next time your Dutch friends ask you to pay them back for that coffee.

World.title: In Europe’s tech capital, Irish labor unions are booming amid AI-driven layoffs
World.content:
Ireland's lucrative tech sector has been rattled by waves of AI-driven layoffs — and the country's fledgling tech union has seen an exponential spike in sign-ups from workers who are worried about their future.

There’s an “awakening” happening right now among workers in Ireland’s tech sector, and a growing “awareness that they’re not bulletproof,” said Sinéad Gibney, a social democrat lawmaker who previously worked for Google.

“I do think what we will see is that parts of roles will be automated, which means that people will be competing more heavily for the same roles," she said. "They won't have the same labor power and therefore we're going to see a drop in quality of work, we're going to see more zero-hour contracts, in more places than we already see it.”

The labor movement brewing in Ireland, where many of the world's tech giants have their EU bases, is part of a wider trend among tech workers globally, who have seen their work disrupted by rapidly evolving AI.

Rise in layoffs

Ireland’s dedicated union for tech workers, the Digital and Techworker Alliance (DATA), has seen a five-fold increase in membership since it was first founded in 2023.

In its first year and a half of existence, membership hovered around 270 people. In the past year-and-a-half, it's jumped to more than 1,350 members, DATA organizer John Bohan told POLITICO. He added that this number tends to spike around layoffs and other actions.

World.title: Scottish government set to drop opposition to new oil and gas fields
World.content:
The Scottish government — led by the SNP since 2007 — released a draft energy strategy in 2023 which set out its “presumption against” new oil and gas fields in the North Sea.

That draft strategy is “out of date,” one senior Scottish government official said. They said a new strategy, expected by the summer, will not contain this wording. A second person with knowledge of the policy said the new strategy will “reflect the world as it is.”

The shift in policy comes with the U.K. government widely expected to give the go-ahead to the Jackdaw gas field next week.

While the Scottish government has little power over the granting of new licenses for projects such as Jackdaw or the Rosebank oil field — where a decision is expected to come separately and at a later date — it has an important symbolic role, and can apply pressure to the U.K. government to approve licenses.

SNP politicians at the party’s conference in Aberdeen privately admitted the stance on Jackdaw has hurt the party electorally.

The party passed a resolution at its conference Friday which stated that the “utilisation of domestic production” of oil and gas is “clearly preferable to importation”. This was seen as a further softening of the position of the SNP — which governed in a quasi-coalition with the anti-exploration Scottish Greens until as recently as 2004.

World.title: Portugal sees protests over cost of living and housing crisis as demonstrations sweep Europe
World.content:
Several housing rights movements are joining trade unions affiliated with the CGTP union federation in demonstrations across Portugal on Saturday, as a series of cost-of-living protests sweeps Europe.

 

The union confederation has called for protests under the slogan: "Higher wages, better pensions, and public services. Against the rising cost of living. A new course for Portugal!"

Rallies are planned in Porto, Coimbra, and Lisbon.

The deepening cost-of-living crisis is affecting much of Europe, driven by rising prices and fuel costs and shortages of affordable housing, and has prompted thousands of people to take to the streets to make their voices heard.

"Faced with the rising cost of living, housing and fuel, even a basic shopping basket has reached an exorbitant price," a CGTP spokesperson told SICN in Coimbra on Saturday morning.

In Porto, the march set off from Praça da Batalha at around 10:30 am and is due to end in Praça D. João I, where protests against the housing crisis have been held throughout the week.

"We are continuing with our people's assembly, with the backing of ordinary citizens, independently of any party. People come from different groups, but we are not institutionally tied to any of them. This outcry is the result of abuse of authority and a way of saying 'enough of this crisis'," Pedro Manuel, one of the organisers of the protest in the city, said on Friday.

"There are those who want to drag us into debating other issues," the Left Bloc's José Manuel Pureza told the Associated Press. "But what people are demanding that we discuss is the right to housing for everyone."

"Those whose rent is getting ever more expensive, those whose mortgage is increasingly hard to fit into the family budget. That is what we are talking about, that is why people have been protesting, always peacefully, always peacefully," he added.

Related Dozens reportedly injured in police crackdown on Portugal housing protest

In Coimbra, the rally began outside Portugal dos Pequenitos and is expected to end in Praça 8 de Maio, in front of the city hall.

In the capital Lisbon, thousands of people are expected for a march scheduled for 14:30 pm local time, starting in Cais do Sodré and finishing in Rossio. However, the mayor of Lisbon has warned that, although he considers it "a just cause," the protests must take place "within the law."

Speaking to the Lusa news agency, CGTP general secretary Tiago Oliveira said the demonstrations were taking place because of the "brutal increase" in housing prices and in the cost of living.

Oliveira also warned of the growing "degradation of public services" and said it was an opportunity for citizens "to fight against the government's policies."

It comes as major cost-of-living demonstrations in France on Saturday turned violent as protesters clashed with riot police.

World.title: Hungarian PM Péter Magyar says Zelenskyy unlikely to visit Budapest later this month
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said he did not expect Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to visit Budapest later this month, despite having extended an invitation to Kyiv.

 

More than 100 politicians have been invited to state ceremonies on 23 October to mark the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution.

However, in an interview with 444.hu published on Saturday, Magyar said he thought Zelenskyy's attendance was unlikely, even though Russian President Vladimir Putin had not been invited.

It comes after Magyar and Zelenskyy said at the EU summit in Brussels on Friday that they could meet again later this year.

"Either I will travel to Kyiv and from there we will go together to Beregszász, or the president will come to Budapest and from there we will go to Beregszász," Magyar said.

In post on X following their Brussels meeting, the Hungarian PM said he had expressed his "full solidarity" with Ukraine as it continues to battle Russia’s ongoing invasion.

He added that the pair had agreed to "continue talks at ministerial level, with a special focus on improving the situation of minorities in both countries" and that they believed it was "in both countries’ interests to build a new foundation for our political and economic relations."

Zelenskyy's deputy chief of staff had told Euronews earlier this week that the Ukrainian leader had been invited to Budapest for the 23 October commemorations amid efforts to reset relations between Kyiv and Budapest after years of diplomatic disputes that have repeatedly obstructed Ukraine's path towards EU membership.

"We have received an invitation. On 23 October, an event will be held to mark the 70th anniversary of the Hungarian Revolution," Zhovkva said. "The President of Ukraine has received an invitation to attend. We shall see."

World.title: Pope Leo XIV leaves hospital following lung operation
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV has reportedly left hospital following surgery to remove a cancerous growth from his lung.

 

The AFP news agency reported that the 71-year-old pontiff was met with cheers and applause from people gathered outside the hospital as he made his way out.

He had been cleared for discharge from hospital earlier on Saturday, the Vatican had announced.

"Following the doctors’ assessment this morning, Pope Leo XIV will be discharged today from Gemelli Hospital, where he was hospitalised for surgery on his right lung," a statement from the Vatican press office said.

"He will leave the hospital in the early afternoon and return to the Vatican. Tomorrow, he will lead the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment," it added.

Doctors said the decision had been made after blood tests and a chest X-ray confirmed he was fit to be discharged.

Chicago-born Leo had been recovering in Rome's Gemelli hospital since undergoing the operation on Tuesday.

The Vatican said earlier this week that the "lower lobe of the right lung was removed" during the procedure, whilst also confirming a diagnosis of a "pulmonary adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the pre-operative tests."

"The Holy Father was in the operating room for about 3 hours, and the duration of the operation itself was around 90 minutes. The surgery was successful and there were no complications," it added.

On Thursday, doctors said a chest X-ray had shown "good recovery" of the affected lung.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | October 17th, 2026 – Midday
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Super tanker ablaze after striking mine in Strait of Hormuz, IRGC says
World.content:
A super tanker has caught fire after striking a sea mine in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Saturday.

 

In a statement shared via Iranian state media, the IRGC's navy said a tanker carrying more than two million barrels of oil struck a mine whilst "attempting to pass through an unauthorised route" in the Strait, causing a "massive explosion" and a "fierce fire." It is unclear exactly where the incident took place.

Iran's Fars news agency posted a video appearing to show the vessel ablaze.

The IRGC navy accused the tanker of having turned off its positioning and radar systems in an effort to evade detection.

"The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and the consequence of defying Iranian regulations in the Strait of Hormuz is burning in the fire of trust in the terrorist US army," the IRGC navy added in its statement.

The Strait of Hormuz is a crucial gas and oil transit chokepoint that has been at the heart of tensions between Washington and Tehran since the Iran war broke out in late February.

Iran effectively cut off the passage, which usually carries around 25% of the world’s seaborne oil trade, following US and Israeli strikes on the country, prompting the US to impose a naval blockade on Iranian ports.

The US military has repeatedly pushed back on claims that the IRGC has control of the Strait, saying commercial vessels have continued to transit the region "despite unwarranted IRGC aggression."

Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of US Central Command (CENTCOM), said in an update on Friday that US forces were working with regional allies and partners in the shipping industry to help protect vessels navigating the Strait.

"Let me be clear, the Strait of Hormuz is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran," he said. "It remains open for business."

World.title: North Korea says it tested new AI-powered torpedo system
World.content:
North Korea said on Saturday that it had tested a new AI-powered torpedo system as it continues a wave of recent weapons demonstrations.

 

The country's KCNA state news agency reported that the test involved the "super-speed, precisely guided" Zam-2.0 torpedo system, which it said uses artificial intelligence to aid with target detection and guidance.

The report said the test had verified the weapon's propulsion systems.

It comes after North Korea also tested two types of underwater-launched strategic cruise missiles on Wednesday as part of what is believed to be a push to bolster its naval capabilities. The missiles are thought to have been fired from a submarine.

North Korea has also carried out a number of ballistic missile tests in recent weeks as it seeks to build up its arsenal amid growing tensions with neighbouring South Korea.

In August, US President Donald Trump told reporters that North Korean leader Kim Jong-un had "57 very powerful nuclear weapons" as he once again touted the pair's relationship.

"You know what, the fact that I get along with him, that's a good thing not a bad thing," Trump said, adding that Pyongyang's nuclear arsenal should "never" have been allowed to happen.

Trump said at the time that he intended to meet with Kim later this year, although he gave no further details on the plan.

The president also claimed earlier this month that he was preventing a war between North and South Korea "on a constant basis."

World.title: No money for Ukraine and EU budget cuts: What could a Le Pen victory mean for the EU?
World.content:
Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally, is seeking to become France’s next president on a hardline anti-EU platform, pledging to cut the country’s contributions to the EU budget and end funding for Ukraine.

 

On Ukraine, Le Pen has repeatedly pledged to end financial assistance. Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Wednesday, she said that if elected, France could only sustain funding for six months because of the “perilous” state of its public finances.

“This funding will stop, and it is a matter of honesty to tell [Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy] the truth,” she told Euronews.

Zelenskyy hit back in an interview with the Financial Times on Thursday. “The price to pay is not as high as the value of people’s lives,” he said. “That is why I think Ms Le Pen is not fully familiar with certain details.”

He added that, if Le Pen were elected president, she should have access to “the most powerful European system that works”, stressing that Ukraine’s battlefield experience could benefit European countries.

Le Pen has also called for an end to EU sanctions against Russia, while saying France could continue training Ukrainian troops and supplying military equipment to Kyiv.

Her comments signal that Le Pen is prepared to take a hardline stance, pledging to end French funding for Ukraine in a position similar to that of US President Donald Trump.

Her stance also contrasts sharply with that of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who is often compared to Le Pen but has advocated continued support for Kyiv.

Speaking in the Italian Senate on Wednesday ahead of an EU summit in Brussels, Meloni delivered a forceful defence of Ukraine’s right to self-defence.

“Supporting Ukraine is not an alternative to peace, it’s what makes it possible,” Meloni said. “The peace we want is one that is sustainable, just and also safeguards Europe and our interests.

“Therefore, the position of this government will not change: support for Ukraine, pressure on Russia and Euro-Atlantic unity.”

‘France’s support for Ukraine goes far beyond aid’

“France’s support for Ukraine goes far beyond aid alone. It is primarily diplomatic,” Elie Tenenbaum, director of the French Institute of International Relations’ Centre for Security Studies, told Euronews.

He highlighted France’s leading role in initiatives such as the Coalition of the Willing, launched alongside the United Kingdom, as well as other mechanisms that “help keep Ukraine afloat”.

These include the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan (USL), whose implementation and disbursement depend on the political backing of major countries, including France.

Tenenbaum stressed that cuts to EU-level funding would have a greater impact on Ukraine than a reduction in France’s bilateral aid.

“If France were not only to stop providing bilateral aid and contributing to the EU budget, but also to actively oppose these kinds of mechanisms, then the entire framework of European assistance to Ukraine would be put at risk.”

According to figures from the German think tank Kiel Institute, France has committed an estimated €27 billion to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. This includes €7.9 billion in bilateral aid and €19 billion through European mechanisms.

Germany remains Europe’s largest provider of aid to Ukraine in absolute terms, having pledged more than €50 billion since February 2022, well ahead of France, Italy and the Netherlands. Relative to GDP, however, Denmark and Estonia provide the highest levels of bilateral aid.

Cutting France’s contributions to the EU budget

With six months to go before France’s presidential election, Le Pen is campaigning on a platform centred on tighter immigration controls, greater national sovereignty and measures to tackle the cost-of-living crisis, as rising fuel prices fuel public discontent.

Her party has backed capping France’s net contribution to the EU budget at €5 billion a year, down from €8 billion, according to figures published by the French Senate. Such a move would mark a departure from recent years, during which France’s contributions have generally increased, despite annual fluctuations.

Under President Emmanuel Macron, France has backed a larger EU budget, unlike countries such as Germany, which favour tighter spending limits. Paris has also called for new EU own resources, meaning additional sources of revenue beyond member state contributions.

Although France is a net contributor to the EU budget, it also receives substantial funding for its farmers through the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP).

“France stands out among the major contributors as it is the only one that has so far supported an ambitious EU budget,” Eulalia Rubio, a senior research fellow at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.

She said Le Pen’s proposals reflected a “lack of understanding” of EU institutions.

“Spending varies slightly every year, so you can’t say, ‘We’re only going to pay €5 billion every year from now on’,” she commented.

Rubio warned that if France overcame the legal obstacles to cutting its contributions, other member states would have to make up the shortfall. Such a prospect could prove particularly contentious given that France is the largest recipient of farming subsidies.

On Wednesday, France’s National Assembly rejected the National Rally’s proposal to unilaterally reduce the country’s contributions to the EU budget for 2027, instead backing the government’s planned level of funding.

Thierry Chopin, an adjunct professor of European studies at Sorbonne University, said a National Rally victory could mark a break with France’s traditional role as a driving force within the EU and with the “intellectual contributions championed by Paris” in recent years, which had gained traction in response to global events.

Chopin pointed to France’s role in promoting European sovereignty, strategic autonomy in defence and trade protection measures. However, he said France’s influence had waned during Macron’s second term as its economic credibility declined.

“This credibility was not particularly strong to begin with, but it has worsened given the country’s budgetary situation, public debt and the difficulties facing its public finances. And then, once again, there are political considerations, because the executive branch has been weakened,” he said.

EU budget for 2028-2034

Speaking to the Financial Times on Wednesday, Le Pen described efforts to reach an agreement on the EU’s 2028-2034 budget by the end of 2026 as "anti-democratic."

She accused the European Commission of undermining “democratic processes” by advancing the budget ahead of elections in France, Spain, Italy and Poland.

Ahead of the vote, Macron has moved to secure key positions, including at the central bank, by appointing allies. On Thursday, the French president told EU leaders during a closed-door meeting that Paris favours reaching a deal this year.

Beyond the timeline, Le Pen is also focused on the substance of the EU budget. Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, she said she hoped to “build new coalitions” with like-minded parties to challenge what she described as an anti-growth mindset in Brussels.

She also suggested that the European Central Bank (ECB), led by Christine Lagarde, should revise its mandate to give greater weight to economic growth. The ECB is independent and its primary mandate is to maintain price stability.

Experts told Euronews they are sceptical that member states would support another major overhaul of EU fiscal rules following the sweeping reform of the Stability and Growth Pact in 2024.

“In my view, member states show little appetite for another major reform,” Andreas Eisl, a senior research fellow in European economic policy at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.

He added that “future changes are likely to involve reinterpretations of the existing rules rather than a fundamental overhaul of their legal foundations”.

Le Pen has repeatedly criticised EU regulations and standards, describing them as “regulatory hell” or a “regulatory shantytown”, and has pledged to strip them back to the bare minimum. Such an approach could undermine the bloc’s legal framework if adopted across member states.

“Obviously, if every member state does this, the EU can no longer function as a union based on the rule of law,” Chopin said.

The National Rally leader has also vowed to “stop” the European Green Deal, the EU’s flagship programme to cut emissions and achieve climate neutrality by 2050.

Le Pen argues that the Green Deal undermines economic growth. She has also proposed abolishing institutions such as the European Committee of the Regions (CoR), an advisory body representing local and regional authorities involved in implementing EU policies, including climate measures.

“The dismantling of the European Green Deal is already underway. If Marine Le Pen were to be elected, this would only be further accentuated, according to certain analyses,” Phuc-Vinh Nguyen, head of the Energy Centre at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.

Maria Tadeo contributed to this report

World.title: Trump signs executive order waiving new Russia sanctions package
World.content:
US President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order to waive a new package of sanctions and tariffs on Russia shortly before it was due to take effect, telling Congress it was in the US' national interest.

 

Trump had signed the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026" into law in September in a push to increase pressure on the Kremlin and the Russian economy.

The legislation - named in honour of the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, who championed the measures - had sought to impose sanctions on Russian government and military officials, major banks, and vessels in Russia's shadow fleet. It also provided for duties on Russian goods and goods from certain countries continuing to buy Russian oil and gas.

Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev has called the decision to put the sanctions on hold a "significant and truly historic moment," adding that the package could have "brought economic cooperation between Russia and the US to a complete standstill."

Trump's move comes amid his increasing criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

It also follows a controversial announcement from Trump, who is gearing up for the US' midterm elections, earlier this month on a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Russia to release large flows of diesel into global markets in an effort to bring down fuel prices.

"It was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social account. "Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel."

Zelenskyy in Brussels

The Ukrainian leader has been in Brussels this week, where he has been meeting with European leaders to discuss the ongoing war.

Taking questions from the media on Friday, Zelenskyy was asked whether he felt he had been made a "scapegoat" for Trump's "own problems" ahead of November's midterms.

He gave a wry smile and said: "This is my answer."

Addressing the US-Russia diesel deal, Zelenskyy added that Ukraine "can’t accept diesel deals, because gas deals will come next."

"I’m absolutely sure of that," he said. "After gas, sanctions will be lifted on other things. It will eventually extend to the banking system, specific individuals, and the chemical industry. And there are risks around the frozen assets. If I don’t defend that through diplomacy – who will do it for us?"

World.title: Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea
World.content:
A wave of deadly attacks on cargo ships in the waters of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania has jolted the alliance into calling an emergency meeting on Black Sea security. Yet any move to send NATO ships hinges on Turkey reversing its steadfast refusal to allow warships into the Black Sea.

Advertising

Thursday saw two chemical tankers struck by drones close to a Romanian port.

It follows two similar attacks in Bulgarian waters in the past week. More than 20 sailors have been killed or remain missing.

“The war has come in full force to the Black Sea now,” said Yoruk Isik, a maritime analyst who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. “With the change in technology compared to the beginning of the war, drones really disrupted maritime traffic.”

According to Isik, the latest attacks underscore the growing spread of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. “Russian ports and Ukrainian ports are heavily targeted, but now even in NATO waters ships are getting hit, in Bulgarian waters, Romanian waters.

“We are at a point where there is no safe place.”

The latest strikes targeted vessels along a key Ukrainian shipping route, casting Russia as NATO’s prime suspect as Moscow intensifies its assault on Ukrainian trade.

After meeting on Thursday with the leaders of Bulgaria and Romania, both NATO members, Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the military alliance would “continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed”.

Romanian President Nicușor Dan said NATO would hold a crisis meeting next week to discuss the situation.

Gatekeeper to the Black Sea

NATO could deploy air defence systems against drones to protect Bulgarian and Romanian waters.

But any deployment of naval ships will depend on NATO member Turkey, which controls access to the Black Sea through the Turkish Straits under a long-standing international treaty, the 1936 Montreux Convention.

Since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Ankara has blocked entry of Russian and Ukrainian warships or military vessels belonging to NATO members without a Black Sea coast, arguing for a diplomatic solution.

In recent weeks the Turkish government has sought to broker a ceasefire on commercial shipping, without success. Isik claims that failure, coupled with the latest escalation in attacks, is increasingly calling into question Ankara’s reliance on diplomacy alone.

“Either they’re going to have a breakthrough and the Kremlin is going to de-escalate, or Ankara is going to accept the reality that there needs to be a more credible force here – bigger vessels have to come,” the analyst said.

He pointed out that the navies of Romania and Bulgaria are not equipped to handle such an operation alone, with Cold War-era ships nearing the end of their lifespan.

“So Turkey's engagement is key to any successful NATO planning in the Black Sea.”

Russian leverage

Despite Turkish-owned cargo ships coming under attack in recent weeks, and Turkey’s deep reliance on Black Sea trade, Ankara has so far kept its powerful navy on the sidelines.

International relations expert Huseyin Bagci, of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University, says Turkey fears an escalation in the conflict and will be wary of allowing NATO ships into the Black Sea.

“I do not think the government would dare,” said Bagci. “Probably the government considers this a provocation to drag Turkey into the war... Turkey is afraid of getting involved in the Black Sea against Russia, this is somehow a trauma in the Turkish mind.”

Moscow also retains powerful leverage over Ankara, he suggested.

Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom is about to complete a multi-billion-dollar nuclear power station in Akkuyu, southern Turkey. Ankara sees it as vital to the drive to reduce its heavy dependence on imported energy. “It is illogical to oppose Russia now while you let the Russians complete the nuclear plant,” said Bagci.

Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies

Ankara also knows that letting NATO vessels in while barring Russian warships could provoke Moscow into contesting Turkey’s prized status as the gatekeeper to the Black Sea.

However, retired Turkish diplomat Selim Kuneralp, an expert on the Montreux Convention, warns Turkey’s control over Black Sea access is likely already in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s sights.

“This has probably had an impact on Russia’s ability to conduct the war, and I doubt that Putin is very happy with the situation,” said Kuneralp. “So if he were to win the war, there is a very strong risk that he will take the initiative of saying: ‘this is unacceptable and we want to have free passage of warships from now on, regardless of whether there is a war’.”

As a signatory, Moscow has the right to call for a revision of the Montreux Convention every five years.

For centuries, Russia fought repeated wars with the then Ottoman Empire for control of the Turkish Straits. In the early years of the Cold War, even Joseph Stalin tried his hand, but the United States intervened and thwarted him.

Now Ankara walks a tightrope between Moscow and its NATO partners to avoid a resurrection of those historical rivalries.

World.title: China's influence in the gaming industry is growing
World.content:
Home to more than 700 million gamers, China is the world's largest gaming market — but it's also one of the most tightly regulated. The effects reach far beyond China, impacting players around the world.

In a dark underground hideout, dim light spills from a handful of oil lamps. A comrade fiddles with a rifle. A red flag hangs on one of the roughly hewn stone walls, bearing a hammer and sickle on a white star — the symbol of the ChineseWorkers' and Peasants' Red Army. Weapons are scattered on the ground. One is picked up, and soon the action moves into the snowy forest, where gunfire erupts among the trees.

Such a scene could fit in a new installment of "Call of Duty," the popular first-person shooter game that transports players to battlefields past, present, and future. But it is actually from "The Defiant." The game is currently being developed by the Chinese studio Hoothanes Technology in Hangzhou. It tells the story of Chinese forces fending off the Japanese army in the 1930s and 1940s.

Developer Connor Xu tells DW the weapons featured in the game are unique. They were used only in Asia and are therefore unfamiliar to many Western players, he says. The same goes for the story, which Xu says has never before been told in a video game.

Game developer Connor Xu wants to tell stories from Chinese history Image: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

"The Defiant" is also designed to appeal to an international audience. In just a few years, China has emerged as a major player in the global gaming industry despite strict regulations, censorship and a former ban on video game consoles.

Gaming is part of everyday life in China

More than 700 million people in China regularly play video games. According to market research company Newzoo, most consider gaming an important part of their lives. Many use games to stay in touch with friends.

"Games make life more interesting," developer Xu says. "I can try different roles, different stories, different characters, because we only have one life to live, but we can play a role in another story. That's really attractive, I think, to Chinese users."

'Honor of Kings' is largely unknown outside China, but it's one of the country's most popular games Image: Tencent/Level Infinite/TiMi Studio Group

People in China primarily play games on PCs and smartphones, while consoles are much less common. There are historical reasons for that: While gamers in Europe and North America debated whether PlayStation or Xbox was the better console in the early 2000s, the devices were not officially sold in China between 2000 and 2014. Chinese authorities said the restrictions were intended to protect children and teenagers from becoming addicted to gaming.

Limits on gaming time and extensive controls

Minors in China are currently allowed to play online games for no more than three hours a week. There are no such limits for adults, but gaming is subject to strict controls. Anyone who wants to play must register using their real name and a personal identification number. That effectively allows the state to track who plays what and when, as well as whom they communicate with.

There is also a gray area that the Chinese government appears to tolerate. Some players log in using VPNs, giving them access to games that are not officially available in China. Some younger players use their parents' accounts to get around the limits on gaming time.

The Chinese role-playing game "Genshin Impact" bears visual and gameplay similarities to "The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild" Image: Cognosphere/miHoYo/HoYoverse

Despite its strict controls on underage gamers, China has become increasingly receptive to video games in general, having recognized the industry's enormous economic potential. Early on, games released for Chinese players often appeared to be copies of Western titles. At the same time, Chinese tech companies such as Tencent and NetEase invested in numerous Western gaming companies.

No license? No sales in China

One distinctive feature of the Chinese market is its licensing system. "Unlike a lot of the other big video games markets in the world, China has a tightly regulated and licensed official video games market," George E. Osborn tells DW. The journalist advises NGOs and governments on video games and spoke at the Gamescom congress. In his book "Power Play," he describes how authoritarian states use video games to pursue political objectives.

The strategy game 'Heroes of Might and Magic III Remake' is currently being developed by Ubisoft's studios in Chengdu and Shanghai Image: Ubisoft

The rule for all games in China is simple: No license, no sales. "That system essentially forces developers who want to release their video games to go through multiple layers of approval from China's Ministry of Propaganda, Ministry of Culture," Osborn says.

Strict criteria for video games

Games are prohibited from containing material that threatens China's unity, sovereignty or territorial integrity, among other restrictions. Pornographic content and gambling are also banned. Games may not incite crimes that threaten national security or spread information authorities believe could disrupt public order.

"The whole point around this criteria is that it's deliberately designed to be pretty vague," Osborn says. Whether a game violates the rules is a matter of interpretation. Sometimes games are altered even after release. In the 2025 action role-playing game "Wuchang: Fallen Feathers," for example, enemies based on famous Chinese figures from the Ming Dynasty suddenly could no longer be killed. Instead, they would collapse from exhaustion.

Chinese culture is an international hit

The Chinese action role-playing game "Black Myth: Wukong" became an unexpected international hit in 2024. By then, it was clear Chinese developers could do more than cater to the domestic market — they could create successful games for a global audience as well. The game was inspired by the 16th-century Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West."

The video game 'Black Myth: Wukong' became an international hit Image: Game Science Interactive Technology Co

Osborn sees nothing wrong with bringing Chinese culture to audiences around the world. The question, he says, is how much the state actually intervenes in the games themselves. "I think in general, video game players are actually quite deeply skeptical of these kinds of things. They are generally very good at spotting when someone might be selling to them or someone might be propagandizing. And so I think if it's too obvious, it won't work," he says.

The problem of self-censorship

Because of the licensing system, Western developers also have to comply with government requirements if they want to sell their games in China. And they do want to, Osborn says, because the market is too big to ignore. "But I think when you start thinking about the potential impact this has on creative standards around the world, I think it's really important that developers ask themselves the question of what will we or won't we compromise on here?"

He fears the real danger lies in self-censorship. That could lead developers, for example, to leave queer characters out of their games. That would represent a major step backward, he says, because games help many people explore their identities.

China is not the only country where games are modified to comply with national regulations. In Germany, for example, symbols that violate the country's constitution, such as the swastika, may not be shown in games unless the game in question explicitly contributes to the country's culture of remembrance. Depictions of extreme violence also have to be removed from German versions.

History from a Chinese perspective

Glorifying violence is prohibited in China, too, yet Xu's team is still allowed to develop a war game. How does this add up? Xu explains it this way: "I think in this game, the most important thing is not violence. The most important thing is to tell history."

Xu says the team is committed to delivering a historically accurate product. Whether it succeeds will be for historians to judge.

This article was translated from German and edited by Sarah Hucal.

World.title: Pope Leo leaves hospital after cancer surgery
World.content:
Four days after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo left the hospital in Rome. His doctors said he was well enough to return home.

Pope Leo XIV left the Gemelli hospital in Rome on Saturday afternoon. He returned to the Vatican four days after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.

The 71-year-old pope walked unaided to his car and stopped to speak with well-wishers outside the hospital.

"I am better, thank you," Leo XIV said as he was driven away in a black SUV. Leo XIV entered the Vatican ten minutes after leaving the hospital.

After conducting blood tests and imaging scans of his chest, the pope's doctors said he was well enough to return home.

Currently, Leo is undergoing physiotherapy to help him breathe more easily.

What to know about Pope Leo XIV's lung cancer To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What do we know about the Pope's health?

On Tuesday, Leo XIV had the lower lobe of his right lung removed after doctors identified a nodule suspected to be cancerous. The surgery confirmed that he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

The doctors said his surgery was successful and complication-free. However, they have not yet disclosed the size of the tumor or if the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes. These factors are key in determining the prognosis.

The diagnosis of the relatively young and energetic pontiff, elected in May 2025, came as a shock. It raised questions about the future of his papacy as he deals with the illness.

On Sunday, Leo is expected to lead weekly prayers with pilgrims in St. Peter's Square at noon (10:00 a.m. GMT), which will be his first public engagement since his surgery.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez
