World.title: Azerbaijan's FX reserves 6-fold exceed total reserves of Armenia and Georgia
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 17. Azerbaijan holds a leading position in the South Caucasus in terms of the volume of its strategic foreign exchange reserves, which are six times greater than the total reserves of Armenia and Georgia. According to data from the State Statistical Committee of Azerbaijan, the country's strategic foreign exchange stood at $89.38 billion as of September 30, 2026. This amount is about 19.8 times greater than the country's external public debt of $4.51 billion. In a regional comparison, Azerbaijan's strategic reserves are about 10.9 times larger than Georgia's international reserves, reported at $8.17 billion in September, and 13.4 times larger than Armenia's foreign exchange of $6.66 billion.

This disparity highlights the scale of Azerbaijan's financial buffer. Its strategic reserves encompass both the foreign exchange of the Central Bank of Azerbaijan (CBA) and the assets of the State Oil Fund (SOFAZ). This extensive asset base strengthens the country's capacity to meet external payment obligations and maintain financial resilience amid global economic shifts.

Azerbaijan’s strategic reserves stand out in region

The volume of Azerbaijan’s strategic foreign exchange is significantly higher than the official reserve figures for Armenia and Georgia. According to data from the National Bank of Georgia, the country’s international reserves stood at $8.17 billion in September 2026, while the Central Bank of Armenia reported its country’s foreign exchange at $6.66 billion. In comparison, Azerbaijan’s strategic reserves of $89.38 billion are nearly 10.9 times greater than Georgia’s figure and 13.4 times greater than Armenia’s.

One significant reason for this difference lies in the composition of Azerbaijan's strategic reserves. The country's figure encompasses not only the official foreign exchange of CBA but also the assets of SOFAZ. Therefore, when making comparisons, it should be noted that Azerbaijan's strategic reserves reflect a broader base of sovereign financial assets.

According to figures disclosed by the CBA Chairman, Taleh Kazimov, Azerbaijan's strategic reserves exceed its GDP and are sufficient to cover approximately 41 months of imports of goods and services. Furthermore, the fact that these reserves are 3.5 times larger than the M2 money supply serves as an indicator of the scale of the foreign currency buffer within the country's financial system.

The capacity to finance imports over an extended period enhances the country's room for maneuver in the face of shifts in foreign trade and international financial markets. This scale of strategic reserves demonstrates that Azerbaijan possesses substantial financial resources to meet external payment obligations and maintain economic stability.

Central Bank reserves and State Oil Fund assets complement financial buffer

Two key components, the CBA’s foreign exchange reserves and the assets of SOFAZ, play a significant role in the formation of Azerbaijan’s strategic reserves.

According to the CBA, its foreign exchange reserves stood at $15.36 billion as of October 1, 2026. This represents an increase of $62.1 million (0.41%) compared to September 1, and an increase of $4.05 billion (35.8%) compared to October 1, 2025. Thus, a growth of over $4 billion has been recorded in the CBA’s foreign exchange reserves over the course of one year.

Meanwhile, the assets of SOFAZ amounted to $72.6 billion at the end of the first half of 2026. The fund’s assets are significant in terms of accumulating and managing energy revenues, safeguarding the state’s long-term financial capabilities, and building an asset base for future generations.

Although these two components perform distinct functions, together they form the foundation of Azerbaijan’s extensive financial resources. The CBA’s reserves are significant in terms of external payments and currency liquidity, while the assets of SOFAZ facilitate the long-term management of energy revenues.

Current account surplus strengthens the external financial position

In addition to the scale of strategic reserves, the volume of foreign currency entering the country is a key indicator of financial stability. Data on Azerbaijan’s balance of payments for the first half of 2026 indicate a positive balance in the country’s external financial position.

According to CBA, the current account surplus reached $4.7 billion, or 12.4% of GDP. This is more than double the $2.3 billion surplus recorded during the same period in 2025. While the oil and gas sector posted a current account surplus of approximately $9 billion, the non-oil and gas sector recorded a deficit of $4.3 billion. In the first half of the year, the average realized price of Azerbaijani oil, at $94.5 per barrel, representing a 33% growth compared to the same period of the previous year, bolstered export revenues. During this period, commodity exports amounted to $14.3 billion, while imports totaled $8.1 billion, resulting in a $6.2 billion surplus in commodity trade.

These figures clearly demonstrate the role of the energy sector in shaping the country’s external financial capacity. Revenues generated from energy exports enable the accumulation of strategic reserves, support public finances, and provide resources for economic development.

At the same time, the expansion of the non-oil and gas sector creates further opportunities to strengthen the existing financial base. In the first half of 2026, non-oil and gas exports reached $2 billion, while the surplus in transport services amounted to $941 million. These indicators highlight the potential to further increase the contribution of non-oil sectors to foreign currency inflows.

Expansion of budget revenues enhances economic opportunities

Another factor strengthening Azerbaijan's financial position is its budget indicators. According to data released by the Ministry of Finance, revenues for the consolidated budget in the first 6 months of 2026 amounted to 24.4 billion manat ($14.3 billion), while expenditures totaled 19.8 billion manat ($11.6 billion). This resulted in a surplus of 4.58 billion manat ($2.69 billion), equivalent to approximately 7% of GDP.

The non-oil and gas sector also plays a significant role in the structure of state budget revenues. During the first 6 months, receipts from this sector reached 10.98 billion manat ($6.4 billion), accounting for 57.3% of total state budget revenues, an increase of 6.8% compared to the same period of the previous year.

The expansion of non-oil and gas revenues contributes to the strengthening of the state's financial base and increases the contribution of various economic sectors to budget revenue. Sustaining these results is important for directing the opportunities created by Azerbaijan's strategic reserves toward broader economic development goals. According to the Ministry of Finance’s medium-term forecasts, the share of the non-oil and gas sector in GDP is expected to reach 82% by 2030. For that period, nominal GDP is projected to be 169.1 billion manat ($99.47 billion), while non-oil and gas GDP is forecast at 138.6 billion manat ($81.5 billion). The average annual real growth rate for non-oil and gas GDP is projected to be 4.4%.

The ratio of public debt to GDP is forecast to reach 19.5% by the end of 2026 and 20.4% by the end of 2030.

These figures highlight the importance of aligning debt policy with strategic reserves and budgetary capacity. Furthermore, directing borrowed funds toward productive projects can contribute to supporting economic growth and future budget revenues.

Assets of SOFAZ create long-term financial opportunities

The assets of SOFAZ constitute one of the core components of Azerbaijan’s strategic reserves. The fact that the fund held assets worth $72.6 billion by the end of the first half of 2026 demonstrates that energy revenues have been transformed into a significant financial resource.

Managing the fund’s assets is crucial not only for preserving existing reserves but also for safeguarding financial capacity for future periods. To this end, the long-term management of energy revenues, the generation of investment returns, and the planning of transfers to the state budget play a vital role.

In the Ministry of Finance’s baseline scenario for 2027-2030, the average annual price of oil is assumed to be $65 per barrel. Based on this scenario, the assets of SOFAZ are projected to reach $73.9 billion by 2030.

This approach highlights the importance of employing prudent assumptions when planning for energy revenues over the long term. Azerbaijan’s extensive strategic reserves and the assets held by the fund enable the state to strike a balance between addressing current financial needs and preserving resources for future generations.

Azerbaijan's financial superiority creates basis for future development

Azerbaijan's strategic foreign exchange of $89.38 billion, the low level of foreign public debt compared to this amount, the possibility of financing imports for about 41 months and the current account surplus are the main advantages of the country's financial position. These indicators show that Azerbaijan has large financial resources in the South Caucasus and significant maneuvering opportunities against foreign economic changes.

A comparison with the reserves of Armenia and Georgia clearly reveals the scale of Azerbaijan's financial buffer. Azerbaijan's advantage is related to the wider sovereign financial base, which is formed due to both the CBA's foreign exchange reserves and the assets of SOFAZ.

At the next stage, it is of particular importance to turn this advantage into wider opportunities for economic development. Increasing non-oil and gas exports, promoting productive investments, diversifying budget revenues and effectively managing the assets of the State Oil Fund can further strengthen the financial position of Azerbaijan.

Thus, Azerbaijan's strategic reserves are not only an indicator of current financial stability, but also an important resource for future economic development. Targeted management of these resources and expansion of the non-oil economy can strengthen the long-term foundations of the country's financial dominance in the South Caucasus.

World.title: Iran, Türkiye discuss Gulf and Strait of Hormuz issues
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 17. Issues concerning the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz have been discussed between Iran and Türkiye.

This was stated in a statement by the Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs following the meeting between Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, held on the sidelines of the 52nd session of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) in Baghdad, Iraq, on October 17.

During the meeting, the Iranian minister briefed his Turkish counterpart on current developments.

The parties noted the importance of strengthening cooperation and coordination among Muslim countries and exchanged views on utilizing the capabilities of the OIC to combat issues such as Islamophobia.

They also held discussions regarding bilateral relations and regional developments, including the Palestinian issue.

The next escalation in U.S.-Iranian relations began on July 8. On that day, for the first time since the signing of the memorandum between Washington and Tehran, U.S. forces launched a series of strikes on Iranian territory, allegedly in response to an attack on a merchant ship in the Strait of Hormuz. On the same day, U.S. President Donald Trump announced the suspension of the ceasefire with Iran. In response, Tehran began striking U.S. targets located in Bahrain, Jordan, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE, and Oman. As a result of the conflict, maritime trade in the Strait of Hormuz came to a standstill.

World.title: Iran supports safe cargo transport via Strait of Hormuz - minister
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 17. Iran supports the safe conduct of shipping and cargo transport in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi said at the 52nd session of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in Baghdad, Iraq, on October 17.

This was reflected in a statement by the Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

"The Strait of Hormuz is vital for the energy and trade of the majority of member states of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation. Until February 28, 2026, the Strait remained fully open and secure. Since that date, following military airstrikes by the U.S. and Israel against Iran, it has not been possible to restore security. It’s impossible to return maritime security to a normal state when a country is subjected to bombardment, threats of destruction, and a blockade," he noted.

The Iranian minister recalled that, with the mediation of Pakistan and the support of Qatar, Iran and the U.S. signed the ‘Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding' on June 17. Under the fifth provision of this memorandum, Iran is required to take the necessary measures to facilitate the safe passage of vessels. In this regard, Iran immediately initiated technical discussions with the Sultanate of Oman to fulfill this obligation. Within two weeks, about 60% of vessel traffic was restored. However, actions taken by the U.S. side hindered the implementation of the memorandum, and the established mechanisms for resolving misunderstandings were not followed.

Araghchi also noted that over the past two years, Iran has engaged in negotiations in good faith. However, instead of diplomacy, it has repeatedly faced military aggression. This has created deep distrust regarding the initiation of new negotiations, absent reliable guarantees that such events will not recur. Nevertheless, Iran has kept the door to dialogue open. A specific seven-day plan has been presented to the U.S. side via Qatar, indicating that, provided the necessary conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz could be opened, and the passage of vessels could return to normal within seven days. The choice now rests with the U.S. side.

The next escalation in U.S.-Iranian relations began on July 8. On that day, for the first time since the signing of the memorandum between Washington and Tehran, U.S. forces launched a series of strikes on Iranian territory, allegedly in response to an attack on a merchant ship in the Strait of Hormuz. On the same day, U.S. President Donald Trump announced the suspension of the ceasefire with Iran. In response, Tehran began striking U.S. targets located in Bahrain, Jordan, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE, and Oman. As a result of the conflict, maritime trade in the Strait of Hormuz came to a standstill.

World.title: Azerbaijan's Fuzuli celebrates city day with concert program (PHOTO)
World.content:
FUZULI, Azerbaijan, October 17. A concert program was organized in Fuzuli city to mark Fuzuli City Day on October 17, Trend’s Karabakh bureau reports.

The concert, held at the secondary school No. 1 named after Mirzo Ulugbek in Fuzuli, featured performances by soloists from the Azerbaijan State Academic Philharmonic, Honored Artist and Fuzuli resident Nizami Abdullayev, Aghabala Abdullayev, and a dance ensemble.

The event began with the playing of the National Anthem of Azerbaijan, followed by a minute of silence in memory of the martyrs.

The concert program included works by Azerbaijani composers, examples of national music, vocal and instrumental performances, and traditional national dances.

The event highlighted Fuzuli’s cultural life and the promotion of national music and the art of dance.

A series of public and cultural events are being organized in the city to mark the City Day. The events are being held through the joint efforts of the Special Representation of the President of Azerbaijan in the Aghdam, Fuzuli, and Khojavand districts, and the Ministry of Culture of Azerbaijan.

The purpose of the events is to commemorate the anniversary of the liberation of Fuzuli, preserve national and spiritual values, organize meaningful leisure time for the city's residents, and share the joy of the occasion with families who have returned to their native lands as part of the Great Return.

World.title: Pope Leo leaves hospital for Vatican four days after lung cancer surgery
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV has left hospital in Rome to return to the Vatican following surgery for lung cancer four days ago.

The 71-year-old walked unaided to his waiting car, stopping to speak to well-wishers outside Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Saturday afternoon.

Pope Leo walks ahead of Stefano Margaritora, his lead surgeon. (Reuters: Yara Nardi)

His doctors had earlier said he was well enough to return home after they carried out the latest blood tests and chest imaging.

The pope, who had an operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, will hold his first public engagement since surgery on Sunday when he leads weekly prayers with pilgrims in St. Peter's Square.

Pope Leo has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.

Priests and followers pray the Rosary in front of the statue of the late Pope John Paul II outside Gemelli Hospital. (Reuters: Vincenzo Livieri)

The diagnosis was cause for shock after the pope was elected only in May 2025, raising questions about the future of his papacy as he deals with the illness.

The pope's doctors have said his surgery was completed successfully, without complications.

They have not yet disclosed the size of the tumour or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, both key factors in determining prognosis.

Reuters

World.title: Burning buildings and tear gas mark 29th day of French student protests
World.content:
Protesters clashed with police across France during nationwide rallies over education and the cost of living, as the country heads towards a presidential election.

In Paris, police fired a water cannon and tear gas after hundreds of protesters — most wearing face masks and some setting off fireworks — confronted them at several locations on Saturday.

The tourist office in Lyon was set on fire on Saturday, and offices of French broadcasters CNews and Europe 1 in Paris had windows broken when protesters threw projectiles, French media reported.

"We're taking the Bastille," one demonstrator shouted in Marseille as masked protesters rammed the door of the mayor's offices with security barriers.

The cry is a reference to the 1789 storming of a fortress during the French Revolution.

Protesters scuffle with police during a demonstration against rising living costs in Paris on Saturday. (AP: Emma Da Silva)

Several then entered the town hall, one spray painting an anarchist "A" symbol on an inside wall, before police intervened.

"We're here to protest the deplorable resources allocated to education and against police brutality," said Aude, a masked student who did not give her surname.

Thousands of demonstrators converged for a march through Paris, cutting main roads and prompting authorities to close metro stations in the centre.

Mounting weight on government

The protests are piling pressure on President Emmanuel Macron's government after weeks of student demonstrations turned violent.

The country's Yellow Vest movement, which staged street protests against Mr Macron's government eight years ago over planned fuel tax hikes, had called for the "yellow and youth" demonstrations.

More than 600 demonstrations were planned across France, according to a website set up by organisers.

More than 32,000 protesters took part in some 140 actions nationwide outside Paris shortly after midday on Saturday and police detained more than 160 people nationwide, a source at the interior ministry told AFP.

A masked protester holds a French flag in front of French CRS riot police amid clashes at Place de la Nation. (Reuters: Yves Herman)

In Paris, where authorities have banned protests around government buildings, the Champs-Elysees shopping avenue and train stations, police detained around 60 people on Saturday morning.

Grief from police action

There has been public criticism over the police's perceived disproportionate response.

In the western city of Rennes, around 20 people set up a barricade using trash bins and large pallets on the outskirts of a shopping mall.

Christophe, a 47-year-old carpenter and former Yellow Vest protester who did not give his surname, said he was indignant after seeing what he viewed as police brutality against teenagers in recent weeks.

"We've reached the point where the repression is targeting our own children," he told AFP.

A protester holds a French flag during a demonstration against rising living costs in Lyon on Saturday. (AP: Laurent Cipriani)

"At the end of the month, I have nothing left. Prices are going up but wages aren't," said Franck, a civil servant in his forties who would not give his surname.

Franck was protesting in the central town of Gueret with around 300 people, a quarter of them high school students.

"We can't take it anymore, we're suffocating," he added.

Fuel price hike

Around 45 per cent of French people are worried about the cost of living and inflation, according to a survey of 2,000 people published earlier this month.

Purchasing power in France has dwindled since 2024, while the price of fuel has soared since the start of the US-Iran war earlier this year.

The eurozone's second largest economy is struggling to reign in its public debt, projected next year to reach more than 120 per cent of GDP, which is double the EU limit of 60 per cent.

Economists say significant debt reduction will come only with major reforms, such as sharply curtailing France's generous pension system.

President Macron on Friday evening called "for calm and respect", adding the right to protest went hand in hand with "respect for people and property".

Jean-Luc Melenchon (right) leader of French far-left opposition party marched in a demonstration by French high school and university students. (Reuters: Sarah Meyssonnier)

France's far-left and far-right parties have both capitalised upon the unrest.

Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the far-left France Unbowed party, has backed the student protests and marched in one demonstration.

Marine Le Pen, who leads in opinion polls for the presidential race, has positioned her National Rally party on the side of the police.

AFP

World.title: Starlink speed restrictions ground interceptors as Russian strikes batter Ukraine
World.content:
Ukraine is now unable to use its interceptor systems against Russian drone attacks because of a Starlink speed restriction, president Volodymyr Zelenskyy says.

He said any restrictions would have been set by the US military and US President Donald Trump.

Mr Zelenskyy told reporters in a WhatsApp media chat Ukrainian officials had been told the restrictions were linked to technical issues, adding he was discussing it with US officials.

He said Ukraine had tested Starlink on European Union territory and encountered no such problems there, with the system operating at higher speeds.

Earlier this week Ukraine experienced similar issues, with Starlink owner Elon Musk responding by insisting his firm had nothing to do with the speed limits.

Starlink is a vital battlefield communications tool and determine the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel. (Reuters)

Kyiv says Moscow carried out a 'massive' energy strike

President Zelenskyy said Moscow had carried out a massive strike on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, targeting more than 15 sites across the country.

"The sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia's strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences," he said.

Ukraine's air force said Russian forces launched four cruise missiles and 332 attack drones overnight.

Mr Zelenskyy previously said Ukraine wasn't receiving forewarning of ballistic missile strikes from intelligence partners. (Reuters)

All of the missiles and 289 of the drones had been suppressed or destroyed, it said.

Russia's heavy bombardment of the power grid ahead of winter has been an annual feature of the war, aimed at wearing down Ukraine's appetite for the fight by denying civilians heat and running water.

Ukrainian officials have warned that Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for more attacks in the coming months.

Trump pauses sanctions

President Zelenskyy has also urged supporters to speak out in defence of new US sanctions against Russia, hours after Mr Trump signed an executive order pausing a sweeping package of restrictions targeting the Russian economy.

The White House decision has further raised fears Ukraine could be left exposed to Moscow's escalating assaults.

The relationship between Ukraine and the US has been strained following the announcement the US would buy diesel from Russia. (AP: Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

Mr Zelenskyy described Mr Trump's move to put sanctions on hold as unfortunate, but did not directly criticise the US leader despite deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington in recent days.

North Korea and Russia open first road bridge to deepen ties Ukraine is worried the road bridge could be used to conceal military personnel and weapons in vehicles, rather than a trade route.

"A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Mr Zelenskyy wrote.

He also expressed hope that the new sanctions could be revived.

"This Act could have helped enormously — and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters," he said.

Critics say Trump's decision helps Putin

Named after late South Carolina Senator Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fuelling Russia's against Ukraine.

The bill had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.

President Trump personally signed the legislation last month, two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation.

The president told Congress that the pause was in the national interest but gave no further details.

Senator Richard Blumenthal, who co-drafted the bill, said in a statement Mr Trump was turning his back on "the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies."

"These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," Mr Blumenthal said.

Mr Trump's unexpected decision comes a week after he stunningly said the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.

Trump's threats to Ukraine It is hard to see Donald Trump's shifting position on Ukraine as a clear strategic change, and not one driven principally by soaring fuel prices ahead of the US mid-term elections.

Mr Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter".

The decision has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine — without making a difference to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Mr Trump's war on Iran.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Wallaroos not content with simply being 'better versions' of themselves
World.content:
Among Siokapesi Palu Sekona's many impressive qualities as Wallaroos captain is her uncompromising approach.

Wallabies outclassed by All Blacks The Wallabies fall to the All Blacks for the 13th straight time, as their trans-Tasman rivals record a convincing 43-21 win in Sydney.

As such, it does not come as a shock to learn she feels the Wallaroos still have much room for improvement following their dominant 56-12 win over Scotland in this afternoon's Global XV Series Test.

The eight-tries-to-two victory did not represent a complete performance in Palu Sekona's eyes, which should serve as music to the ears of Wallaroos supporters.

Why?

It shows the Wallaroos are setting the highest possible standards for themselves.

"We still know there is room for improvement and we definitely know what to do to clean that up," Palu Sekona said.

Wallaroos skipper Siokapesi Palu Sekona put in a solid shift on both sides of the ball. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The Wallaroos defeated Scotland 30-10 three weeks ago in Edinburgh during their three-Test swing through Great Britain and France as part of the Global XV Series.

The victory snapped a six-match losing streak but left Wallaroos players and coaches dissatisfied.

It was a sign of the Wallaroos' quickly developing harder edge, which Palu Sekona wants carried through to the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup.

"We knew we could put together a better performance," she said.

"Ultimately results and scores are what people look at. But if we want to break down our rugby, there are so many things to clean up.

"From discipline, to our ruck, to the accuracy of our set-piece. There are things we can continue to work on."

Wallaroos set bar high

The Wallaroos, ranked seventh in the world, are starting from behind scratch when compared to teams such as England and New Zealand.

Both enjoy the benefit of being full-time programs, with their respective governing bodies making a wise move to invest in the women's game.

The Wallaroos are still semi-professional, but a shift to full-time status — as part of an integrated program alongside the women's sevens squad — is in progress.

There is no doubt the Wallaroos' rate of improvement will be accelerated once they go full-time in the lead-up to the World Cup, which Australia will host.

"We don't want to only be the better versions of ourselves," Palu Sekona said.

" We want to be the best in the world. "

Winger Amelia Whitaker scored a double in the Wallaroos' victory. (Getty Images/Corbis: Steve Christo)

The Wallaroos' makeshift coaching team, under the leadership of Rugby Australia's director of women's high performance Tim Walsh, has had a positive influence on the playing group.

Sione Fukofuka will take over as head coach next year and work alongside Walsh, who enjoyed tremendous success in charge of the Australian women's sevens squad.

Like Palu Sekona, Walsh was not completely satisfied with the Wallaroos' display against Scotland.

But he saw enough to know they are heading in the right direction.

"I think it was another step forward, for sure," Walsh said.

The Wallaroos will complete their 2026 Test season when they meet Scotland in Canberra on Friday night.

World.title: World Cup heartbreak for Kangaroos half as Tonga notches first win over England
World.content:
Mitchell Moses will miss the remainder of the Rugby League World Cup, after being ruled out of the Kangaroos' title defence with a lower leg injury that continues his representative misery.

The Parramatta playmaker suffered the injury during Australia's 24-22 win over New Zealand in the tournament opener on Thursday night in Sydney.

He attempted to play on but eventually left the field less than two minutes into the second half.

Meanwhile, England's hopes of reaching the World Cup semi-finals are already on life support after suffering a 30-12 loss to world No.5 Tonga in their blockbuster showdown in Perth.

Moses was injured during the Kangaroos' World Cup opener against New Zealand. (Getty Images: Matt King)

While initially believed to be a calf issue or a hairline fracture, scans following the match revealed Moses had suffered an unspecified "high-grade muscle tear", meaning his World Cup campaign is over.

It's a blow to the Kangaroos, who are already missing Nathan Cleary with a serious leg injury, with Moses the Kangaroos' strongest last-tackle kicker.

Moses switched allegiance to play for Australia at this tournament after captaining Lebanon at the 2022 World Cup.

In Perth, Tonga produced a defensive masterclass in its four-tries-to-two victory over England.

The result put Tonga in the box seat to reach the semis, with games against Lebanon and Samoa to round out the group stage.

England's World Cup campaign is already on life support after Tonga's statement win in Perth. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

In contrast, world No.3 England have been left on the brink of elimination — even if it wins its remaining two games against France and PNG.

Under the confusing group stage system employed for the World Cup, only two teams from across pools B and C will progress to the last four.

If England finish on the same number of wins as Tonga, then Tonga will go through given they won Saturday's head-to-head battle.

World Cup opener a reminder of Australia's glory days There was a time when Test matches were rugby league's biggest, best and bloodiest spectacles, and last night's World Cup opener between Australia and New Zealand was a reminder of those days.

Should England and Samoa end up with the same number of wins, the tiebreaker will be which nation has the better points-for-and-against differential.

Samoa opened its campaign with a 78-4 smashing of France, leaving England needing to post some massive wins in its remaining two games to stay alive.

Stefano Utoikamanu opened the scoring in the 24th minute when he found a hole in England's defence to stroll over untouched.

A pair of Isaiya Katoa penalty goals extended the margin to 10 points by half-time, with England left to rue a series of fumbles and near misses.

England started the second half full of steam, resulting in a team-lifting try to AJ Brimson in the 46th minute.

But in a game where hard work was king, it was a slice of fortune that ended up giving Tonga a vital edge with Haumole Olakau'atu scoring the first of his two tries after he soccered the ball into an opponent's arm and then gathered the bouncing rebound.

And when Tuimoala Lolohea's neat dribble found Tolutau Koula in the corner to make it 22-6 in the 58th minute, it was as good as game over.

The win was a powerful statement from Tonga, whose only previous taste of international success against England came in 2019 when they beat Great Britain.

In Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea's men's side earned a gritty 42-18 win over Lebanon hours after the country's women's team had dispatched France 58-4.

Veteran Rhyse Martin began his farewell tournament in style, scoring a try and going perfect from seven conversions against a dogged Lebanon outfit.

His try with nine minutes left on the clock finished off the Cedars, who were fading in humid conditions.

But Lebanon never stopped trying, with fullback Jacob Kiraz (207 metres) and winger Tony Frances (292 metres) constant threats in attack, while Wests Tigers stalwart Alex Twal led the defence with 48 tackles.

Winger Naomi Kelly crossed four times in the women's game as the Orchids ran in 12 tries to one.

England ended the day's women's action in comprehensive fashion against Wales, with Connie Boyd and Anna Davies both scoring hat-tricks in the 70-6 rout in Perth.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Yagera woman Jayda Allen Bonner remembered at Melbourne vigil
World.content:
WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the name and image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of their family.

Hundreds have gathered in Melbourne to pay tribute to a young Indigenous woman killed at an inner-suburban apartment complex last weekend.

A smoking ceremony was held in honour of 21-year-old Jayda Allen Bonner, who was remembered as "a beautiful soul" by her mother and aunt.

Jayda Allen Bonner, 21, was described by her aunt as a "gentle soul with a heart of gold". (Supplied)

This week, a 31-year-old man was charged with murder and appeared briefly in the Melbourne Magistrates Court.

Police say he was known to Ms Allen Bonner.

Supporters of the Bonner family then marched to Victoria's Parliament to demand changes to domestic violence procedures and reform to better prevent violence against women.

Ms Allen Bonner's mother, Jade Allen, took part in the vigil, wearing a t-shirt emblazoned with an image of her daughter and the phrase 'Justice for Jayda'.

Many attendees carried 'Justice for Jayda' posters in memory of the 21-year-old woman. (ABC News)

"Jayda loved her family fiercely. She had a heart of gold — she would do anything for anybody," Ms Allen said.

"I want everyone to stand up and stop keeping all of this quiet.

"I want to make sure Jayda's name isn't forgotten. She was one-of-a-kind."

Jade Allen and Kellie Carter Bell urge Australians to do more to prevent violence against women. (ABC News)

Ms Allen Bonner's aunt Kellie Carter Bell said all Australians need to do more to speak out against violence against women.

"We're living with wars behind our doors," she said.

"We need recognition, we need people to understand what this stuff looks like.

"The question should be: What can I do to help (victim-survivors) get out safely?"

Questions raised over police response

Antoinette Braybrook, chief executive of Melbourne-based Aboriginal family violence service Djirra, said the 21-year-old's death was "devastating".

She said it was "outrageous" and "shocking" that Ms Allen Bonner could "fall through the cracks".

Ms Allen Bonner's family has previously said the young woman had made a complaint to police about her safety which she later withdrew.

Her family has also said they tried to contact police themselves, but were told that because Ms Allen Bonner was an adult, there was nothing they could do.

Ms Braybrook said that wasn't true.

Antoinette Braybrook says the police response leading up to the death must be investigated. (Supplied)

"They have the power to investigate violence in the home and initiate their own intervention orders and charge people; my question is, why didn't they do that?"

Ms Braybrook added that it was not uncommon for women experiencing violence to withdraw their complaints to police, even if they were still in danger.

Speaking generally, she said women experiencing violence might be pressured into doing so or be threatened with further violence by their abusers.

"The perpetrator has absolute control, power and control over her in that situation," Ms Braybrook said.

"It's a consistent issue in our work."

While Djirra was now in contact with the young Yagera woman's family, Ms Braybrook said given the history of concern for Ms Allen Bonner's safety, it was "extremely disappointing" police or other authorities had not connected her with the service before her death.

"That's one of the concerns that we have as a specialist Aboriginal community-controlled organisation working on the frontline of Aboriginal women and children's safety," she said.

"I am just at a loss — I sit at the table, many tables, with police, with corrections, with courts and others, talking about how we can improve the safety of women.

"When things like this happen to women, it just makes those talks that we participate in all of the time seem like a joke."

A Victoria Police spokesperson said the death of a young woman in Carlton on October 10 was suspicious.

"The investigation is being led by the Homicide Squad," the police spokesperson said.

"As part of investigations, Victoria Police will thoroughly examine any interactions between police and the victim in the lead-up to her death.

"We are unable to comment further while the investigation remains ongoing."

World.title: 13-year-old arrested in Narrabeen Lagoon 'sexual touching' probe
World.content:
A 13-year-old boy has been arrested in connection with reports of multiple women being "sexually touched" allegedly by a man on an e-bike in Sydney's Northern Beaches.

The incidents, which number six to date, took place between October 1 and October 12 in broad daylight while the women were walking or running at Narabeen Lagoon and in the surrounding bushland.

The arrested teenager attended Mona Vale Police Station on Saturday evening and is assisting police with their enquiries, a NSW Police statement said.

The incidents took place between October 1 and October 12 in broad daylight. (ABC News)

Police have increased patrols on walking trails surrounding the lagoon.

In an update on Saturday afternoon, Superintendent John Duncan said it was alarming that women were being harassed.

"We take these matters very, very seriously," he said.

"In consultation with State Crime Command and the Sex Crime Squad, we've got a number of overt and covert activities.

"We have a number of our uniformed and plain-clothed officers in the area."

Most of the alleged offending occurred between 4pm and 6pm.

In some cases several incidents occurred on one day.

Police believe just one person is involved, but are "keeping their options open".

"I'd imagine that person, or their families or friends, will actually know who that is," Superintendent Duncan said.

"And we encourage them to come forward and help with our investigations."

'Rode away on an e-bike'

The first reported incidents happened on October 7 and October 8.

"In each incident, a male allegedly approached women on walking trails, sexually touched them and then rode away on an e-bike," police said in a statement.

"In one of the incidents, the man also made inappropriate sexual comments."

The first incidents reported to police took place on walking trails near the lagoon. (ABC News)

After a public appeal for information on October 12, police received an additional three reports — one dating back to the first of that month.

The woman alleged she was approached by a man near South Creek Road at Wheeler Heights about 4.30pm and allegedly sexually touched before he rode away on an e-bike.

On October 12, in two separate incidents between 5pm and 5:30pm, two women reported being sexually touched by a male riding an e-bike.

There have been no reports since then, Superintendent Duncan said, but he feared there may be more cases.

"We do believe that there are probably more victims out there that may have some information or may have been a victim of this particular crime," he said.

"And we'd like them to come forward and contact either Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or Dee Why Police Station."

Anyone with dashcam footage is also urged to contact police.

World.title: More teens arrested over alleged assault of 15yo boy
World.content:
Two more teenagers have been arrested over an alleged group assault in the western Victorian town of Stawell earlier this month.

Police say a 15-year-old-boy was attacked by a group of teenagers near the intersection of Wakeham and Doye streets about 5:45pm on October 5.

They allegedly stole his shoes and clothing before running away.

The boy was taken to hospital but has since been released.

On Saturday, police said a 14-year-old boy had been charged with several offences, inlcuding recklessly causing injury, while a 16-year-old girl was also expected to be charged.

It follows the arrests of two 15-year-olds and a 14-year-old on Tuesday. They were charged with affray, robbery, recklessly causing injury, and theft.

They will appear in the children's court at a later date.

A spotlight on security

The incident comes as community pressure grows on the Northern Grampians Shire Council to install CCTV in police-identified crime hotspots at Stawell.

The alleged assault has renewed the conversation about public safety in Stawell. (ABC News: Sarah Mullins)

After the three initial arrests made earlier this week, Mayor Karen Hyslop said the council's policy had not changed "for now", but "priorities can be re-evaluated".

She said council had looked into "the financial cost and privacy concerns", and found CCTV installation would involve "allocating hundreds of thousands of dollars from the budget".

But Stawell resident Jessica Lees, who, alongside two other mothers, ran an online survey earlier this year to collect data in support of cameras being installed, was not happy with that response.

She said more than 300 people filled out the survey and had questioned why the council had not explored every option, including available state government grants for the cameras.

"If other councils across Victoria can find ways to fund CCTV, why can't we?" she asked.

World.title: Western Sydney Airport makes play for premium travellers
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Western Sydney Airport makes play for premium travellers Chris Zappone October 18, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. In a bid to promote itself as option for premium travellers, Western Sydney Airport has revealed details of its international lounge one week before commercial flights are scheduled to start. An artist’s rendering of the Western Sydney airport international lounge will reflect the colours of the Blue Mountains. The 80-seat mezzanine-level facility, set to open next month, will initially serve Singapore Airlines passengers travelling through Australia’s newest airport. Designed by COX Architecture, The Rayleigh Lounge aims to establish the airport’s credentials with the all-important sector premium traveller, passengers willing to pay more for front-of-cabin seating, better food, and higher quality flying experiences. Digitally rendered images provided by the airport show the space featuring dedicated seating and dining areas, a bar, an open kitchen, and three private shower suites to support the needs of solo travellers, families, and groups.



WSI is the first new full-scale international airport to open in Australia in over half a century. It will begin serving domestic passengers on October 25 when Jetstar launches operations, followed by Air New Zealand’s first international flight the next day. Singapore Airlines flights connecting WSI to Singapore Changi Airport will begin on November 23, by which time the lounge – operated by air services provider dnata – is scheduled to open. An artist’s render of the dining area in the new The Rayleigh Lounge at Western Sydney International. “Ahead of our inaugural flight, we are working closely with our airport partners to deliver a seamless, premium ground experience for our customers,” said Singapore Airlines regional vice president Foo Chai Woo. “We look forward to welcoming travellers at Western Sydney International Airport and introducing them to the world-class service for which Singapore Airlines is known.” Singapore Airlines, second only to Qantas in the number of international flights service Australia, won the Skytrax 2026 World’s Best Airline award last month.



Premium travel, involving business class seats (and above) as well as priority boarding and luxurious lounges, has emerged as a growing, and profitable segment for aviation sector, following the end of the COVID-19 lockdowns in 2022. Australia’s existing capital city airports, including Sydney Kingsford Smith, have extensive dedicated airlines lounges. The bar. The mezzanine-level lounge will initially accommodate 80 people. In keeping with the airport’s western Sydney location, the design of the WSI international lounge has been selected to reflect the colours of the surrounding Cumberland Plain and Blue Mountains. “From the moment passengers walk in, we want them to see and feel that they’re in Western Sydney,” said COX Architecture partner Brooke Lloyd. With its location on the mezzanine level, the lounge will offer views across the airfield to the Blue Mountains. While the airport expects modest traffic initially, its infrastructure is built to scale up as demand increases. The airport’s curfew-free schedule is expected to spur competition with Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport, even as WSI’s initial focus centres heavily on leisure travel and visiting friends and relatives.



WSI chief executive Simon Hickey noted that as more airlines join WSI and passenger numbers grow, The Rayleigh Lounge will expand alongside them. The international lounge “will open ahead of the holiday period, giving our international travellers an outstanding start to their journey from Western Sydney to the world,” he said. At 80 seats, the lounge is roughly half the size of a standard airline lounge in a major hub. However, plans are in place to expand its capacity to 130 seats as foot traffic grows. Related Article Aviation Fiji Airways to feed tourism boom through Western Sydney Airport “It’s good to see they have allowed room to expand and almost double the lounge’s footprint,” Executive Traveller editor-in-chief David Flynn told this masthead, “because that could be needed as more international airlines join the WSI roster”. Singapore Airlines will initially operate an Airbus A350 featuring 40 business class seats on the route. “Given the lounge has an 80-seat capacity, if every business class seat is sold, the lounge will already be at 50 per cent capacity,” Flynn noted. Access will be available to Singapore Airlines business class passengers, as well as KrisFlyer Gold, Star Alliance Gold, and PPS Club members.



“I wouldn’t say the lounge would be empty by any stretch, but it’s certainly not going to be standing room only at this stage,” said Flynn. Dnata director Burt Sigsworth said his company will bring “dnata’s international experience in airport hospitality and food service to The Rayleigh Lounge, while working with local producers to give the offering a strong connection to Western Sydney.” The highly anticipated $6 billion airport will launch services with Qantas, Jetstar, Air New Zealand, Singapore Airlines, VietJet, and Fiji Airways. At launch, Jetstar will operate up to 14 weekly flights between Western Sydney and Melbourne, daily flights to the Gold Coast (increased from four weekly to meet demand), and three weekly flights to Brisbane. World.title: Put this quirky European ski resort (and its pies) on your radar now
World.content:
InspirationEurope Put this quirky European ski resort (and its pies) on your radar now Steve Madgwick October 18, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

My luggage slides past me, bound for my “forest house” aboard a human-drawn, metal-framed sled that looks like it was made in a shed by an eccentric, pragmatic tinkerer. I shuffle from the cable-car station to the Hotel Waldhaus in two minutes, powder snow puffing from my boots. Not a single internal combustion engine has been fired up in my name since I left Zurich Airport for Aletsch Arena, a triple village Swiss Alps ski resort cloistered away in the southern canton, or state, of Valais. A handful of anxiety-inducing tight train connections – perhaps only possible in Switzerland or Japan – deliver me to Bettmeralp Talstation, where the hydro-electric-powered cable car swooshes me up, over a sliver of Rhone River, into Bettmeralp. The scenic route to the top of Aletsch Arena on the Eggishorn gondola. Aletsch Arena AG Helicopter or hiking notwithstanding, this is the only way for travellers to reach the hamlets of Bettmeralp, Riederalp and Fiescheralp because these snow-globe-esque Bernese Alps villages are car free. If not for the falling snow and low clouds, I’d already be snapping shots of a couple of Swiss Alps celebrities: the Matterhorn (well south-west) and Jungfrau to the north. Aletsch Arena’s ski lifts and dapperly groomed trails have a Swiss-train-network quality to them. Fanning upwards from Bettmeralp, the clinically logical piste layout makes it easy to swoop down into and back out of Riederalp, gondolas soaring over snow-dolloped chalets. It’s actually challenging to get lost here, although one particularly tantalising forest run flows all the way down to the valley floor, finishing between villages. A five Swiss francs ($9) taxi ride will rectify your “mistake”.



The south-facing (sun-facing, when it’s out) ski area is beginner- and intermediate-focused. The terrain, relatively mild by Swiss standards, is peppered with a healthy smattering of approachable and family-friendly terrain parks and snow-cross courses, with easy plans Bs if you want to chicken out. 



I slide into Hotel Alpfriden for premature après, resting my Aperol Spritz on al fresco wine barrels. “Good evening altogether,” toasts my host, David, even though it’s early afternoon. Apparently, a local bishop once tried to ban day-drinking here so the day-drinkers simply redefined the meaning of evening. Don’t let the name put you off trying Valais’ signature savoury pie. iStock Shouts of “santé” and “ciao” rise above the après hubbub, a soundtrack of early ’90s bangers and the occasional buzzing snowmobile. The Valais German dialect is patently flavoured by its geography – France, 60 kilometres west; Italian mountains in plain sight southwards. Unlike glamour-puss resorts like St Moritz (80 kilometres east), most of Aletsch Arena’s visitors seem local, more or less, as you might expect of a place so far off the radar that it’s rarely a first-choice ski town for foreigners. It’s also a place still unapologetically comfortable in its own skin. Related Article Opinion

Europe The 50 things we love about travel in Europe (and the five we don’t) Ben Groundwater Travel writer I over-confidently schuss back to Hotel Waldhaus, settling into my Holz100 room, a design made from a quarter of local timbers, with dowels replacing nails and glue. I love the panoramic-window alcove, the 1980s-spec rotary phone and the turn-down Swiss chocolates. Daniela Berchtold’s family has owned the hotel since 1955, a couple of years after the cable car was built, pre-resort days. Before that, farmers would walk up their cows to graze on summer pastures, leaving before winter snows settled.



The ingredients for Waldhaus’s cholera pie are grown in the same “hippy” organic way that Daniela’s parents have always done; heaving with garden potatoes, apples and onions. Every household has a different recipe for this dish, the unappetising name for which is either linked to families making-do during the pandemic, or Chola or Cholu (Valais German for coal), as the pastry was baked on coals, depending on which story you choose to believe. When I depart Bettmeralp, the human-powered sled slides my luggage back to the cable car. Snow falls, heavier now, settling on the storybook Chapel of Maria zum Schnee (Mary of the Snows). People walk their fluffy dogs, ski into the store for local cheese, and drag their hyperactive kids out of snowdrifts. Back on the train, these car-free days already seem like make-believe. DETAILS Hotel Waldhaus Bettmeralp has rooms from 230 Swiss francs ($400). See waldhaus-bettmeralp.ch/en; an eight-day Swiss Travel Pass, with unlimited travel by train, bus and boat, costs from 665 Swiss francs. World.title: Seven must-do experiences on one of the world’s greatest harbours
World.content:
InspirationAsia Seven must-do experiences on one of the world’s greatest harbours Jenny Hewett October 18, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. With its historic ferries, dazzling viewpoints and award-winning dining spots, Hong Kong’s harbour sets the stage in this pulsating Asian city. Here are seven highlights. Ride the tram to the highest peak on Hong Kong Island The Victoria Peak tram is the easy way to get to the best views of the city. iStock Victoria Peak, or Tai Ping Shan as it’s known to locals, is both a lofty viewpoint and test of character. Many hike their way above Hong Kong’s skyscraper forest for those iconic views over the glittering harbour, but the air-conditioned, glass-roofed, historic Peak Tram is a much less intimidating option. The electric funicular railway opened in 1888 as the first in Asia and was originally steam powered. See thepeak.com.hk Hop on the Star Ferry to Kowloon



Hong Kong’s legendary ferries have been operating since 1880. 



See ancient treasures in the West Kowloon Cultural District The M+ gallery, West Kowloon Cultural District, Hong Kong. Housing both the modern art M+ Gallery and Hong Kong Palace Museum, this cultural district in Kowloon comprises 40 hectares of public open space and museums displaying modern and ancient Chinese art. On display at the Hong Kong Palace Museum are more than 900 pieces on loan from the Palace Museum in Beijing’s Forbidden City, including ornate musical clocks, sets of seals, traditional board games and 13th century porcelain. See hkpm.org.hk Eat Michelin-starred dim sum at Lung King Heen Enjoy Michelin-star dining at Lung King Heen. This is their steamed lobster and scallop dumpling. iStock



Not only did this venue’s baked pineapple bun with barbecued pork and pine nuts propel this venue to Michelin-star status (currently two), its dining room is front row to the action on Victoria Harbour. Four Seasons Hong Kong’s flagship restaurant was the first Chinese restaurant in the world to earn three Michelin stars back in 2009. It offers weekday and weekend dim sum, tasting menus and elevated Cantonese a la carte options, such as marinated pork knuckle in sand ginger sauce. See

fourseasons.com Related Article Asia Inside the spectacular property just named the world’s best hotel Watch the city twinkle from Tsim Sha Tsui The neon skyline over Victoria Harbour is impressive from most angles, but especially so at night from Tsim Sha Tsui during an electrical storm. Ride the elevator 18 floors up to hip northern Chinese restaurant Hutong in Kowloon to watch lightning and thunder turn Hong Kong Island and its surrounding peaks into a cinematic masterpiece. The limelight is only briefly stolen by the signature Peking duck, which is set on fire and spun around like a tornado by a chef directly at the table. See hutong.com.hk Ride a junk boat at sunset in Victoria Harbour



No icon is more symbolic of Hong Kong’s roots as a fishing village than the traditional Chinese wooden junk boats with red sails bobbing around its deep-water harbour. This is one of the last remaining places where you can set sail on the authentic vessels. The 70-year Dukling junk boat offers tours around the harbour, while replica AquaLuna runs nightly sunset cruises that include drinks and outdoor lounge areas. See dukling.com.hk; aqualuna.com.hk The writer travelled with the assistance of Hong Kong Tourism Board.

World.title: Pope Leo to leave hospital on Saturday, four days after lung cancer surgery
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropePope Francis Pope Leo to leave hospital on Saturday, four days after lung cancer surgery Nicole Winfield and Paolo Santalucia Updated October 17, 2026 — 10:24pm ,first published October 17, 2026 — 9:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Rome: Pope Leo is expected to leave hospital on Saturday afternoon (Rome local time) following surgery for lung cancer, the Vatican said, after blood tests and chest imaging found him fit to return home four days after his operation. The 71-year-old pontiff, who has not been seen in public since a procedure on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, will also hold his first public engagement since surgery on Sunday. He will lead weekly prayers with pilgrims in St. Peter’s Square at midday. This picture, released by the Vatican on Friday shows Pope Leo XIV celebrating Mass at the hospital in Rome, where he is recovering from surgery. Vatican Media via AP Pope Leo XIV gave strong indications on Friday (Rome time) that he was recovering well from lung cancer surgery and was very much in charge of running the Catholic Church, speaking on the phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin, meeting with top aides and celebrating Mass in a makeshift hospital chapel.



The Vatican said that during the call with Putin, “The Holy Father expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, and called for a ceasefire to allow the delivery of food and medical assistance, and the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population.” The statement added that Leo “reaffirmed the Holy See’s commitment to promoting dialogue and peace”. The Gemelli Hospital in Rome. Getty Images Putin voiced support for “the Vatican’s intention to help create conditions for ensuring the safety of the local population and facilitating the delivery of essential supplies”, and an agreement was reached to coordinate efforts in this regard, the statement said. Also on Friday, the Vatican released the first images of Leo since his lung cancer surgery on October 13, showing him standing up at the altar in green vestments, as doctors said that tests confirmed his “continued improvement”.



Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed after doctors identified a suspected cancerous nodule. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. “His post-operative recovery allows him to carry out his normal daily activities completely on his own,” said a medical update signed by Leo’s personal physician Dr Luigi Carbone and the head of thoracic surgery, Dr Stefano Margaritora. Pope Leo XIV pictured in St Peter’s Square on October 7. AP Photo/Andrew Medichini The Vatican had originally estimated a weeklong hospital stay, and had cancelled his audiences through Tuesday. Even as questions swirled about the future of Leo’s young pontificate, there were signs on Friday that it was all systems go. The Vatican published the names of journalists accredited to fly on Leo’s plane with him during his November 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. Leo’s ability to make the trip has been in question since his diagnosis, and the Vatican can change the plans at any time. But the posting of the media list signalled that at least on an organisational level, the trip was going ahead.



Doctors are still awaiting the results of tests to understand the precise molecular and genetic makeup of the cancer, whether it has spread beyond the lobe and whether any further treatment is necessary. World.title: AFLW round 10: Daisy Pearce reaches a ‘big decision’; Cats annihilate the Eagles in Perth
World.content:
The Cats have leapt to the top of the AFLW ladder (even if only temporarily) with a 53-point domination of the Eagles on their home Perth deck, 8.18 (66) to 1.7 (13).

Only wastefulness in front of goal prevented an even more commanding win for Geelong, who staggeringly kept the Eagles goalless until the game’s final minutes.

It was a day to forget for Lucia Painter and the West Coast Eagles. AFL Photos

Most telling was Geelong’s ability to punish West Coast on turnover – dominating that statistic 49 points to just two.

Newly re-signed Eagles coach Daisy Pearce would surely have been left scratching her head at just how emphatically her side was wiped off the park.

Georgie Prespakis continued her run of dominance with 39 disposals, six clearances and six tackles, while her teammates Nina Morrison, Amy McDonald and Mikayla Bowen finished with 27 touches apiece.

Pope Leo left hospital in Rome on Saturday afternoon to return to the Vatican following surgery for lung cancer four days ago.

“I am better, thank you,” the pope said as he was driven away in a black SUV.

Pope Leo leaves hospital followed by surgeon Stefano Margheritora. AP Photo/Andrew Medichini

His surgeon, Dr Stefano Margaritora, head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli Hospital, accompanied him to the hospital door as he was formally discharged.

The 71-year-old waved to well-wishers outside as he walked to the waiting vehicle. He briefly stopped when a teenage girl presented him with a homemade papal doll.

World.title: Western Sydney Airport makes play for premium travellers
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Western Sydney Airport makes play for premium travellers Chris Zappone October 18, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In a bid to promote itself as option for premium travellers, Western Sydney Airport has revealed details of its international lounge one week before commercial flights are scheduled to start. An artist’s rendering of the Western Sydney airport international lounge will reflect the colours of the Blue Mountains. The 80-seat mezzanine-level facility, set to open next month, will initially serve Singapore Airlines passengers travelling through Australia’s newest airport. Designed by COX Architecture, The Rayleigh Lounge aims to establish the airport’s credentials with the all-important sector premium traveller, passengers willing to pay more for front-of-cabin seating, better food, and higher quality flying experiences. Digitally rendered images provided by the airport show the space featuring dedicated seating and dining areas, a bar, an open kitchen, and three private shower suites to support the needs of solo travellers, families, and groups.



WSI is the first new full-scale international airport to open in Australia in over half a century. It will begin serving domestic passengers on October 25 when Jetstar launches operations, followed by Air New Zealand’s first international flight the next day. Singapore Airlines flights connecting WSI to Singapore Changi Airport will begin on November 23, by which time the lounge – operated by air services provider dnata – is scheduled to open. An artist’s render of the dining area in the new The Rayleigh Lounge at Western Sydney International. “Ahead of our inaugural flight, we are working closely with our airport partners to deliver a seamless, premium ground experience for our customers,” said Singapore Airlines regional vice president Foo Chai Woo. “We look forward to welcoming travellers at Western Sydney International Airport and introducing them to the world-class service for which Singapore Airlines is known.” Singapore Airlines, second only to Qantas in the number of international flights service Australia, won the Skytrax 2026 World’s Best Airline award last month.



Premium travel, involving business class seats (and above) as well as priority boarding and luxurious lounges, has emerged as a growing, and profitable segment for aviation sector, following the end of the COVID-19 lockdowns in 2022. Australia’s existing capital city airports, including Sydney Kingsford Smith, have extensive dedicated airlines lounges. The bar. The mezzanine-level lounge will initially accommodate 80 people. In keeping with the airport’s western Sydney location, the design of the WSI international lounge has been selected to reflect the colours of the surrounding Cumberland Plain and Blue Mountains. “From the moment passengers walk in, we want them to see and feel that they’re in Western Sydney,” said COX Architecture partner Brooke Lloyd. With its location on the mezzanine level, the lounge will offer views across the airfield to the Blue Mountains. While the airport expects modest traffic initially, its infrastructure is built to scale up as demand increases. The airport’s curfew-free schedule is expected to spur competition with Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport, even as WSI’s initial focus centres heavily on leisure travel and visiting friends and relatives.



WSI chief executive Simon Hickey noted that as more airlines join WSI and passenger numbers grow, The Rayleigh Lounge will expand alongside them. The international lounge “will open ahead of the holiday period, giving our international travellers an outstanding start to their journey from Western Sydney to the world,” he said. At 80 seats, the lounge is roughly half the size of a standard airline lounge in a major hub. However, plans are in place to expand its capacity to 130 seats as foot traffic grows. Related Article Aviation Fiji Airways to feed tourism boom through Western Sydney Airport “It’s good to see they have allowed room to expand and almost double the lounge’s footprint,” Executive Traveller editor-in-chief David Flynn told this masthead, “because that could be needed as more international airlines join the WSI roster”. Singapore Airlines will initially operate an Airbus A350 featuring 40 business class seats on the route. “Given the lounge has an 80-seat capacity, if every business class seat is sold, the lounge will already be at 50 per cent capacity,” Flynn noted. Access will be available to Singapore Airlines business class passengers, as well as KrisFlyer Gold, Star Alliance Gold, and PPS Club members.



“I wouldn’t say the lounge would be empty by any stretch, but it’s certainly not going to be standing room only at this stage,” said Flynn. Dnata director Burt Sigsworth said his company will bring “dnata’s international experience in airport hospitality and food service to The Rayleigh Lounge, while working with local producers to give the offering a strong connection to Western Sydney.” The highly anticipated $6 billion airport will launch services with Qantas, Jetstar, Air New Zealand, Singapore Airlines, VietJet, and Fiji Airways. At launch, Jetstar will operate up to 14 weekly flights between Western Sydney and Melbourne, daily flights to the Gold Coast (increased from four weekly to meet demand), and three weekly flights to Brisbane. If you’ve ever seen the tag “Official Hotel Partner” linking a hospitality chain to a major sporting event and thought, “What does that mean for me?”, then the 2027 Rugby World Cup might just be the time to find out.

IHG Hotels & Resorts is making an expanded play for Australian travellers, with major investment in its luxury hotels and the arrival of a new brand.

An artist’s impression of the revitalised Atrium Bar at Intercontinental Brisbane.

In Brisbane, the former Hilton, a Harry Seidler-designed landmark on Queen Street Mall, is undergoing a multimillion-dollar transformation into InterContinental Brisbane. The Woods Bagot redesign includes a revitalised atrium, new restaurants including an Argentinian grill, new room schemes, a new Club InterContinental lounge and expanded wellness facilities. The hotel remains open during works, scheduled to finish by early 2028.

Meanwhile, an agreement with developers Salter Brothers will see Melbourne’s riverside Crowne Plaza become an InterContinental, with a rooftop restaurant, club lounge and bathhouse. InterContinental Melbourne The Rialto will be transformed into Regent Melbourne by 2030, returning the ultra-luxury brand to Australia after 28 years.

World.title: Put this quirky European ski resort (and its pies) on your radar now
World.content:
InspirationEurope Put this quirky European ski resort (and its pies) on your radar now Steve Madgwick October 18, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

My luggage slides past me, bound for my “forest house” aboard a human-drawn, metal-framed sled that looks like it was made in a shed by an eccentric, pragmatic tinkerer. I shuffle from the cable-car station to the Hotel Waldhaus in two minutes, powder snow puffing from my boots. Not a single internal combustion engine has been fired up in my name since I left Zurich Airport for Aletsch Arena, a triple village Swiss Alps ski resort cloistered away in the southern canton, or state, of Valais. A handful of anxiety-inducing tight train connections – perhaps only possible in Switzerland or Japan – deliver me to Bettmeralp Talstation, where the hydro-electric-powered cable car swooshes me up, over a sliver of Rhone River, into Bettmeralp. The scenic route to the top of Aletsch Arena on the Eggishorn gondola. Aletsch Arena AG Helicopter or hiking notwithstanding, this is the only way for travellers to reach the hamlets of Bettmeralp, Riederalp and Fiescheralp because these snow-globe-esque Bernese Alps villages are car free. If not for the falling snow and low clouds, I’d already be snapping shots of a couple of Swiss Alps celebrities: the Matterhorn (well south-west) and Jungfrau to the north. Aletsch Arena’s ski lifts and dapperly groomed trails have a Swiss-train-network quality to them. Fanning upwards from Bettmeralp, the clinically logical piste layout makes it easy to swoop down into and back out of Riederalp, gondolas soaring over snow-dolloped chalets. It’s actually challenging to get lost here, although one particularly tantalising forest run flows all the way down to the valley floor, finishing between villages. A five Swiss francs ($9) taxi ride will rectify your “mistake”.



The south-facing (sun-facing, when it’s out) ski area is beginner- and intermediate-focused. The terrain, relatively mild by Swiss standards, is peppered with a healthy smattering of approachable and family-friendly terrain parks and snow-cross courses, with easy plans Bs if you want to chicken out. 



I slide into Hotel Alpfriden for premature après, resting my Aperol Spritz on al fresco wine barrels. “Good evening altogether,” toasts my host, David, even though it’s early afternoon. Apparently, a local bishop once tried to ban day-drinking here so the day-drinkers simply redefined the meaning of evening. Don’t let the name put you off trying Valais’ signature savoury pie. iStock Shouts of “santé” and “ciao” rise above the après hubbub, a soundtrack of early ’90s bangers and the occasional buzzing snowmobile. The Valais German dialect is patently flavoured by its geography – France, 60 kilometres west; Italian mountains in plain sight southwards. Unlike glamour-puss resorts like St Moritz (80 kilometres east), most of Aletsch Arena’s visitors seem local, more or less, as you might expect of a place so far off the radar that it’s rarely a first-choice ski town for foreigners. It’s also a place still unapologetically comfortable in its own skin. Related Article Opinion

Europe The 50 things we love about travel in Europe (and the five we don’t) Ben Groundwater Travel writer I over-confidently schuss back to Hotel Waldhaus, settling into my Holz100 room, a design made from a quarter of local timbers, with dowels replacing nails and glue. I love the panoramic-window alcove, the 1980s-spec rotary phone and the turn-down Swiss chocolates. Daniela Berchtold’s family has owned the hotel since 1955, a couple of years after the cable car was built, pre-resort days. Before that, farmers would walk up their cows to graze on summer pastures, leaving before winter snows settled.



The ingredients for Waldhaus’s cholera pie are grown in the same “hippy” organic way that Daniela’s parents have always done; heaving with garden potatoes, apples and onions. Every household has a different recipe for this dish, the unappetising name for which is either linked to families making-do during the pandemic, or Chola or Cholu (Valais German for coal), as the pastry was baked on coals, depending on which story you choose to believe. When I depart Bettmeralp, the human-powered sled slides my luggage back to the cable car. Snow falls, heavier now, settling on the storybook Chapel of Maria zum Schnee (Mary of the Snows). People walk their fluffy dogs, ski into the store for local cheese, and drag their hyperactive kids out of snowdrifts. Back on the train, these car-free days already seem like make-believe. DETAILS Hotel Waldhaus Bettmeralp has rooms from 230 Swiss francs ($400). See waldhaus-bettmeralp.ch/en; an eight-day Swiss Travel Pass, with unlimited travel by train, bus and boat, costs from 665 Swiss francs. See switzerland.com; swisstravelpass.com The writer travelled as a guest of Switzerland Tourism.

World.title: Olivia Dean concert stopped due to sound issues
World.content:
Olivia Dean was forced to stop her sold-out concert at Western Springs Bowl on Saturday night due to sound issues.



Dean was playing to more than 40,000 people at the revamped venue as part of her Art of Loving Live tour.



RNZ executive editor Jeremy Rees, who was at the concert, said Dean played three songs to a jubilant crowd, before leaving the stage, saying the sound needed to be "reset".



"We're looking at an empty stage at the moment and it's a real disappointment for people who had been looking forward to the Olivia Dean concert for a long, long time,” Rees said.



At 9.30pm, a stage manager announced the sound at the stadium was being reset.



Rees said the first few songs sounded very good, although Dean's voice cut out in places.



"The crowd were right into it and singing along and happy, and then just as I say, she said she had to stop. She improvised for a moment, talking about love and her latest album, while people were trying to fix the sound."



The concert restarted just after 10pm, with Dean apologising to the crowd and saying the show would not be cut short, before launching into a song.

World.title: Bledisloe Cup: Josh Moorby's try double highlights All Blacks' game of two halves
World.content:
Picking just one of the seven All Blacks tries that best summed up their 43-21 victory over Australia in a masterclass in cohesive attack and decision making in Sydney on Saturday was difficult - but Josh Moorby's second five-pointer might be it.

After a bruising run by second-five Timoci Tavatavanawai - a late replacement following the withdrawal, before kickoff, of Jordie Barrett - the ball found left wing Moorby, who showed it to Wallabies right wing Max Jorgensen and halfback Ryan Lonergan, and went over untouched.

Ultimately, that converted score was the All Blacks' final points of an extraordinary afternoon in front of 73,000 at Accor Stadium, as the Wallabies, swept again in the Bledisloe Cup for the sixth successive year, finally found something.

The home side had the better of the second half - helped by the fact the All Blacks played the final 12 minutes shorthanded - and five minutes with just 13 players - due to debutant Chay Fihaki's yellow card for a high tackle and, before that, replacement hooker Samisoni Taukei'aho's injury, which left them with no more players on the bench.

The visitors were scoring at almost a point a minute, when Damian McKenzie's conversion for Moorby's second try went over and - led by skipper Codie Taylor, loose forward Peter Lakai and a rejuvenated Beauden Barrett, who also scored a double - Dave Rennie's men looked as good as they have all year.

They committed to backing up last weekend's victory at Eden Park and, perhaps inspired by the bright afternoon sunshine, played with a continuity and skill that blew the Wallabies away in the first half.
