They did it despite Jordie Barrett's calf problem, which ruled him out hours before kickoff, and fellow midfielder Quinn Tupaea's head injury within two minutes of the start.

Despite a very much reshuffled line-up, the intensity with which the All Blacks went about their work was almost as impressive as their short-passing game, which showed an incredible appreciation for time and space against a Wallabies team determined to right the wrongs of last weekend.

Beauden Barrett also had a try double against Australia. www.photosport.nz

The All Blacks had four tries in the space of 14 minutes, Moorby, Beauden Barrett, Lakai and Rieko Ioane - on for Tupaea - all finishing scores that highlighted their killer instinct.

Lock Jeremy Williams' reply for the Wallabies was only a blip, as the All Blacks made the most of Williams' yellow card for offside after the re-start for Wallace Sititi to over from a scrum and Barrett putting an exclamation on the half with an intercept try from 70m out.

"I thought we were awesome in that first 40 - just backing ourselves and playing what was in front of us - but the second 40 was a bit different," Taylor said afterwards.

Counterpart Harry Wilson said: "I'm gutted. When you give a team like the All Blacks a headstart, it's tough... we're going to have to improve a lot."

Australia fought back with two tries to one in the second half, but this was a devastating loss for them in their final home game of the year. Their next home test is in Perth on Anzac Day, 2027.

Unfortunately for them, their opponents are the All Blacks.

Wing Will Jordan's absence in the second half may spark concerns about a potential injury and Shannon Frizell's leg issue after he come into the test off the bench may also be a problem.

As Taylor hinted, the second-half performance may come under some scrutiny by Rennie and company, but maintain such intensity is difficult, when the game is all but over at halftime, and after last weekend's second-half performance at Eden Park, it was a reminder that if this team get it right, they can be devastating.

All Blacks 43 (Beauden Barrett 2, Josh Moorby 2, Peter Lakai, Rieko Ioane & Wallace Sititi tries; Damian McKenzie 4 conversions) Australia 21 (Jeremy Williams, Tom Wright & Filipo Daugunu tries; Ryan Lonergan 2 conversions, Declan Meredith conversion)

World.title: Shorthanded All Blacks too strong for Wallabies in Bledisloe Cup sweep
World.content:
The All Blacks ended the game with just 14 fit players, as they beat the Wallabies 43-21 in the second Bledisloe Cup test in Sydney.

The visitors scored seven tries to the hosts' three to claim back-to-back wins over Australia.

Midfielder Quinn Tupaea left the field for an HIA, after hitting his head on the ground early in the match and didn't return, with Rieko Ioane coming on to take his place.

Both sides started well, but the All Blacks struck first through wing Josh Moorby, who scored out wide, after a period of attack in the Wallabies 22. First-five Damian McKenzie was unsuccessful with the conversion.

The visitors were soon in again, with fullback Beauden Barrett stepping over for a try, after a nice break from flanker Peter Lakai.

McKenzie was unable to add the extras, with the All Blacks leading 10-0 nearing the 20 minute mark.

Peter Lakai of New Zealand goes over to score. www.photosport.nz

Lakai was rewarded for some good support play, taking a short ball from halfback Cam Roigard to barge over for the All Blacks' third try. McKenzie nailed the sideline conversion to make it 17-0 to New Zealand.

The All Blacks' next try was superb, with some slick handling and good running lines putting Ioane in the clear, before the replacement back beat the last defender to help the visitors extend their lead to 22-0.

Australia had barely had the ball, but they looked good when they had it, and lock Jeremy Williams scored their first try, after some nice attacking play inside the All Blacks 22. The conversion was successful to make it a 15-point game at 22-7 to the All Blacks.

Williams was then yellow-carded, after being penalised with the All Blacks hot on attack, leaving the Wallabies a man down for the last 10 minutes of the first half.

The All Blacks made the most of the numerical advantage and scored on the next play, with No.8 Wallace Sititi storming over from the back of the scrum. McKenzie added the extras to push their lead out to 29-7.

The Wallabies then went on the attack and were making inroads into the All Blacks defence, when Barrett intercepted an Australian pass and sprinted 70 metres to put a dagger in the home side's hearts just before halftime. McKenzie kicked the extras for a 36-7 lead at the break.

Beauden Barrett of New Zealand dives over to score. www.photosport.nz

A big break from midfielder Timoci Tavatavanawai led to another try for Moorby, who sold a dummy to two Australian defenders, before trotting over the line. McKenzie's conversion was good to put the All Blacks ahead 43-7.

Replacement back Chay Fihaki came off the bench for his All Blacks debut and made a nice break, before not quite connecting with an attempted grubber kick.

The All Blacks had made 14 linebreaks by the 53rd minute and continued to stretch the Wallabies defence, although the hosts were also hard to handle with ball in hand and they scored next through fullback Tom Wright, who had been impressive all game.

The conversion was successful to cut the All Blacks lead to 43-14 with about 25 minutes remaining.

The Wallabies cut that lead to 43-21, with Filipo Daugunu scoring a try for the hosts, and the All Blacks then went down to 14 men for the final 11 minutes of the match, due to too many injuries.

They then had Fihaki yellow-carded for a high tackle, but managed to hold on for a 43-21 victory for 13 straight wins over Australia.

The All Blacks had already retained the Bledisloe Cup, after winning last week's first test at Eden Park 50-19.

Recap all the action with our live blog below:

World.title: Orchids and Kumuls pile on tries in respective World Cup victories
World.content:
The Papua New Guinea Orchids started their 2026 Rugby League World Cup campaign on a high, with a convincing 58-4 win over France in Port Moresby on Saturday afternoon.

Playing their first-ever world cup game at home, at Santos National Football Stadium, in their first international against France, the Orchids ran in 12 tries in total - four to winger Naomi Kelly, who scored one in the first 35-minute spell before adding three in the second half.

In the process she also equalled the record for the most tries in a single match by any PNG Orchids player.

The previous record was held by Belinda Gwasamun, who scored four tries against Brazil during the 2022 Women's Rugby League World Cup.

Tia Molo, Shelly Long and Fleur Ginn got a double each against France.

The Orchids led 32-0 at halftime, with six tries recorded in the first 35 minutes.

Relna Wuruki-Hosea of the Canberra Raiders notched the first try for the home side in the seventh minute, with a powerful run from a scrum outside the French 10-metre zone.

North Queensland Cowboys' Emily Veivers converted the goal kick to give the Orchids an early 6-0 lead.

Hooker Ua Ravu at dummy half led their attacks, with Cynthiah Peters at seven directing play.

Captain Elsie Albert was a powerful runner up front.

France attacked from their line in a good set in the 12th minute and won a penalty on the PNG 30-metre line.

Dummy half Cristina Song directed their attacks as forwards Elodie Pacull, Perrine Monsarrat, Stacy Bessiere and Leila Bessahli started gaining valuable metres with their strong forward drives upfield.

That resulted in a close drive for the corner flag but it ended in a knock-on close to the PNG line.

Shellie Long ran through the French defence to score the Orchids' second try, followed by Paramatta Eeels Fleur Ginn, who stepped her way through a gap, dummied and ran in to score between the posts after the PNG team attacked from the restart.

Tia Molo claimed the team's fourth try in the 24th minute, before Naomi Kelly finished off wide out for the Orchids five minutes later, after Molo stepped inside two players to leave Kelly free out wide. Veivers kicked the goal and PNG were up 28-0.

Former Wallaroos rugby union player Ivania Wong then showed her speed out wide on the right and ran back in between the posts to score.

PNG Orchids led 32-0 after the first 35-minute spell.

Closed off

France went straight to attack from the restart and their persistence was rewarded when Manon Samarra went over after playmaker Lisa Diraison set up the attack.

The try was the only one the visitors managed in the game as PNG responded and closed off the game, with a dominating second half performance, running in six more tries.

Kelly kicked off their scoring in the second spell, after the Orchids varied their play with Ginn and Peters going through the defensive gaps to set her up.

Then it was Ginn who picked up a loose pass and ran through the French defensive line to score between the posts again for her second try.

Veivers' goal kick gave them a 42-4 lead.

Replacement Essay Banu combined well with captain Albert as the two big forwards kept the momentum on through the middle of the field.

With 20 minutes to go Molo went over to score her second from a penalty, after Albert was stopped on the line. Molo picked up from the ruck and dived over for the 46-4 lead.

Then it was Kelly's turn again for her third try with 18 minutes to go. She received the pass from Molo, who had chased Peters' grubber towards the corner flag.

The Orchids then capped off their afternoon with Kelly's fourth try before Long crashed over in the right corner for the team's 12th try of the afternoon.

Captain Elsie Albert said the team had prepared well for the game and the tournament.

"It was a great win, in front of the home crowd," she said.

"I thought we had a good preparation leading up to this game and I thought everyone went out there and did what we exactly needed to do.

"It's great to be back home playing and to get a win in front of the home crowd."

PNG Orchids coach Craig Sandercock said post-match it was a great game and a good start to their campaign.

"I was really pleased," he said.

"They've trained so hard. Really pleased for them and having the crowd support - it was fantastic."

PNG Kumuls Facebook

Kumuls also victorious

It was the first of a double-header in Port Moresby, with the PNG Kumuls paying Lebanon also on Saturday afternoon.

The PNG Kumuls made it a double win for the home teams, defeating Lebanon 42-18.

The side scored seven tries to Lebanon's three, and open their campaign on a high, in front of their vocal local fans.

The Kumuls scored tries through Gairo Voro, Robert Derby, Nixon Putt, Finley Glare, Epel Kapinias, Ryse Martin and Bailey Biondi Odo.

Martin added the other points through his boots.

Lebanon got their three tries from Abbas Miski, who got two, and Tony Sukkar.

World.title: Thieves targeting trailer tyres in Bay of Plenty
World.content:
Thieves in the Eastern Bay of Plenty are targeting trailer tyres to use in street racing.

Police are urging trailer owners to secure their wheels after a spate of thefts, including at a local club where six trailer wheels were stolen recently.

Police said the thefts were indiscriminate, opportunistic, and could be deterred with vigilance.

They suggested storing trailers out of sight or behind locked gates, as well as properly securing wheels with padlocks and heavy-duty chains.

World.title: Guam on high alert as Typhoon Champi strengthens, ports shut
World.content:
Typhoon Champi has intensified into a category 2 storm as it approaches the Mariana Islands, prompting Guam to shut its commercial port and forcing flight cancellations across the neighbouring Northern Marianas.

Guam governor Lourdes Leon Guerrero placed the island under its highest typhoon readiness condition at 1pm Saturday local time, ordering residents to remain indoors as Champi threatens to strike as a powerful category 3 typhoon early Sunday.

Authorities have also ordered residents in southern coastal and flood-prone areas to evacuate, with six emergency shelters designated across the island.

The US National Weather Service said Champi had sustained winds of 100 miles per hour (about 161km) Saturday afternoon and could strengthen further before passing just south of Guam.

National Weather Service warnings are available here.

The US Coast Guard has placed Guam's commercial port under its highest heavy weather restriction, suspending all cargo and vessel operations.

Port general manager Rory Respicio said preparations were complete, with gantry cranes secured and shipping containers lowered to protect them from destructive winds.

In the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, the Commonwealth Ports Authority said airports on Saipan, Tinian, and Rota remained open under its latest advisory, although several flights had been cancelled.

United Airlines cancelled flights for Sunday and Monday, while Star Marianas Air suspended its Sunday inter-island services.

Seaports across the Northern Marianas were also operating under weather-related restrictions, with further limitations expected.

CNMI governor David Apatang has placed Rota under Typhoon Condition II, while Saipan and Tinian remain under Condition III.

Rota could experience winds of up to 80 miles (129km) per hour, with stronger gusts, while Saipan and Tinian are forecast to experience tropical storm conditions.

The Weather Service has urged residents throughout the Marianas to seek safe shelter before sunset Saturday, with the worst conditions expected Sunday morning.

World.title: General practitioner called out of retirement to staff undermanned Horowhenua clinic
World.content:
A doctor has been called out of retirement to a Horowhenua clinic, where the last remaining general practitioner resigned last month.

Levin's Taitoko Health has announced that Dr Andy van de Vyver will return to the clinic for five months, after retiring last year.

Dr van de Vyver served the community for 40 years at the clinic, previously known as Masonic Medical Centre.

Commenters on the clinic's Facebook announcement reacted positively to the news, welcoming him back.

One comment read: "I jumped out of my chair when I got this email! We have certainly missed you.

"On the other hand, your retirement has been very well deserved, and I'm sad you have to leave that to come back and help, so I'm glad for you that it is only 5 months!

"And thank you... it means so much to so many of us."

Sources with experience working at the clinic have told RNZ his retirement was the start of difficulties at the clinic and of the "intense environment of burnout".

Since his retirement, a dozen staff have left or given notice, including four GPs, among whom was the last remaining GP for the clinic, where 4500 patients were enrolled.

World.title: Cruise ship passengers to be charged $20 less for travelling to and from NZ
World.content:
Cruise ship passengers will be charged $20 less for travelling to and from New Zealand.

Customs Minister Casey Costello announced Friday changes to the Border Processing Levy, which was forecast to recover $124.3 million in Customs' border processing expenses in 2026/27.

From 1 July 2027, arriving cruise passengers will pay $7.20, down from $27.14. Departing passegers will pay 71 cents, up by 3 cents.

New Zealand Cruise Association chief executive Jacqui Lloyd said the announcement was "incredibly helpful going forward" as one step towards helping the industry.

Lloyd said the cruise industry was responsible for one in 10 tourists coming to the country.

But she said cruise lines were limiting the number of New Zealand port calls, bringing fewer passengers as a result.

Customs Minister Casey Costello. RNZ/Marika Khabazi

She said there were several factors contributing to the decline, such as difficulty in getting slots for docking in Sydney - where cruises often start and finish.

"And so it does mean that there's a reduction in port calls around New Zealand as itineraries get shortened because they need to leave Sydney and get back to Sydney at a certain time."

Another issue was cost: Lloyd estimated it could cost $650,000 for a ship with 3000 passengers to do about eight port calls around New Zealand in government and port fees.

"There are Maritime New Zealand fees going into every single port in New Zealand. There is also [an] oil pollution levy for every single port in New Zealand that is through Maritime New Zealand. You've also got a broader border levies, which we've just been discussing around Customs and MPI [Ministry for Primary Industries].

"And then the ports also, of course, will be charging to berth in each of their ports. Also, many do a per passenger fee, but they're also charging for security, gangways, staffing, bollards, all sorts of things that need to happen for the operation for a ship to come into a port."

She said New Zealand had been viewed as one of the most expensive places for cruise lines to visit.

But Lloyd said work between government and ports would bring about positive change.

New Zealand Cruise Association chief executive Jacqui Lloyd. Supplied / NZ Cruise Association

"We've had some great news out of Maritime New Zealand who are holding their levies for the next few years. MPI are doing the same. We also have Customs now with their new rates."

She clarified that new government departments' rates had not been set solely for the benefit of the cruise industry, but that they were beneficial.

It might also take a few years for the benefits to appear, as cruise lines booked their itineraries years in advance, so companies wouldn't be lured back instantaneously, she explained.

She said this kind of cross-agency collaboration was necessary for the industry's future.

"It's been ... [good] to really open the dialogue between all the sectors and really make sure that people aren't operating in silos and create some good discussion and awareness on what any kind of change, how that might affect other parts of the sector."

But ultimately, what was needed, she said, was certainty.

"The cruise lines need certainty for planning. They need to know when there is going to be an increase in costs or a change in regulation and they need to know early so that they can put that into their budgets and their planning for future deployment.

World.title: 'Terrible to watch': Ohope Wins euthanased after fall in Caulfield Cup
World.content:
New Zealand mare Ohope Wins has been euthanased after a fall in the Caulfield Cup that also included 2025 Melbourne Cup winner Half Yours.

With about 200 metres to go in the 2,400m race, which was won by Gavin Bedggood's Kingswood, Half Yours was in the middle of the pack when there appeared to be contact with Kings Valley.

Half Yours went down hard, sending jockey Mark Zahra into the turf, with Ohope Wins also coming down after Jye McNeil was unable to avoid the fallen McEvoy Racing product.

Racing Victoria Stewards later confirmed Ohope Wins, from Chris Waller Racing, was euthanased by the on-course veterinarian.

Jye McNeil on Ohope Wins in the mounting yard before the Caulfield Cup. (Getty Images: Vince Caligiuri)

"The mare was unable to be saved due to the nature of the injury sustained," a Racing Victoria (RV) statement read.

"RV extends its condolences to Yulong, the owners of Ohope Wins, her trainer Chris Waller and their stable staff who cared for the horse and are deeply saddened by their loss."

Yulong and Waller released a statement, saying "few words can express our current emotions".

"Ohope Wins was a true star of the turf, but to the people who looked after her everyday, she was so much more," the statement read.

"She was brave. She was kind. She was full of character, but more importantly, she was loved.

Ohope Wins won the Oaks at Randwick in April. (Getty Images: Vince Caligiuri)

"Our hearts go out to all involved throughout her career, especially those who cared for her on a daily basis."

Half Yours, the defending Caulfield Cup victor, got up and eventually crossed the finish line without a jockey.

The stewards said Half Yours would undergo a "thorough veterinary examination" after falling in "a racing incident", which would be subject to an inquiry.

Half Yours got up and crossed the line without a rider. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Half Yours returned to his stall, while stewards said Zahra and McNeil were both "conscious and alert" and transported to hospital for further assessment.

Trainer Tony McEvoy said after the race that Half Yours had suffered some abrasions but looked OK, all things considered.

"That was terrible to watch," McEvoy said.

"The horse, he's got a couple of lacerations, he seems bright, he seems composed in himself.

"He's got a laceration under his arm, he's got a laceration on a hind leg. They look superficial."

The final race of the day at Caulfield was delayed.

World.title: Cats underline AFLW premiership credentials as Crows snap Suns' winning run
World.content:
Geelong has underlined its AFLW premiership credentials with a 53-point rout of West Coast in Perth.

Midfielder Georgie Prespakis (39 disposals, six tackles, five clearances) was at her dominant best as teammate Mikayla Bowen (27 disposals) also impressed in the 8.18 (66) to 1.7 (13) victory.

In Adelaide, the Crows boosted their hopes of a finals appearance with victory over Gold Coast, while Brisbane and the Western Bulldogs also claimed victories as the competition's top eight continued to take shape on Saturday.

The Eagles challenged early at Leederville Oval but had to wait until late into the fourth quarter to kick their first major of the afternoon, with Isabella Lewis slotting from a forward-half stoppage.

The Cats boasted eight different goalkickers and Prespakis registered a career-high 13 score involvements as Geelong finished the day in first.

Former leader North Melbourne can reclaim top spot with victory over Essendon on Sunday.

Earlier, Adelaide moved back into the finals frame after ending Gold Coast's six-game winning run.

Sisters Niamh (right) and Grace Kelly (left) combined for an early Adelaide goal. (Getty Images: Sarah Reed/AFL Photos)

Led throughout by Irish sisters Grace (three goals, 12 disposals) and Niamh Kelly (two goals, 20 disposals), and 18-year-old Chloe Bown (one goal, 25 disposals) in the final quarter, the Crows scored back-to-back wins for just the second time this season in a 10.3 (63) to 7.11 (53) win.

The bad news for the Crows was the loss of influential midfielder Maddi Newman who went down twice with a knee injury.

She stayed down after a non-contact incident midway through the third quarter and got subbed off to have her left knee strapped before coming back onto the field.

Later in the term, she was hit hard by Gold Coast's Charlie Rowbottom and was carried off again, later appearing on the sidelines on crutches with ice on the back of her knee.

The win left the Crows eighth on the ladder with five wins and five losses, equal on points with Hawthorn, and four points ahead of Fremantle, West Coast, Port Adelaide and Richmond, although the Dockers have a game in hand.

And the Suns fell out of the league's top four just hours later, with the Western Bulldogs notching a convincing 30-point win over Carlton at Princes Park.

Midfielder Mikala Cann was among the Bulldogs' best with 27 disposals and a goal, while key forward Emma McDonald kicked two majors in her side's 8.8 (56) to 3.8 (26) victory.

The victory saw the Bulldogs leapfrog both the Blues and the Suns into fourth, as Carlton fell to a first defeat in four games.

The Bulldogs are now tied on competition points with North Melbourne and Melbourne in second and third, respectively — although the Kangaroos are yet to play in Round 10.

In Ipswich, Port Adelaide's hopes of pushing into finals contention took a hit with a 16-point loss to Brisbane.

The victory ended a five-game losing streak for the Lions, who were led by midfielders Isabel Dawes (16 disposals, one goal), Sophie Conway (19 disposals, one goal) and Alexandra Anderson (24 disposals).

Conway was especially electric in the opening quarter, reaching the first break with 15 disposals and a goal, as her side made its way to a 5.4 (34) to 2.6 (18) victory, just its third of the season.

The defeat means the Power remains four competition points and percentage from the finals places.

World.title: Wallabies outclassed as All Blacks continue Bledisloe Cup domination
World.content:
The Wallabies have slumped to a 13th straight defeat to the All Blacks, with their trans-Tasman rivals recording a convincing 43-21 victory at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

The result meant the All Blacks swept the two-Test Bledisloe Cup series, having thrashed the Wallabies 50-19 at Auckland's Eden Park a week ago.

A dominant first half from the visitors set up this afternoon's win.

They scored six tries to one to lead 36-7 at half-time, before extending their lead to 43-7 shortly after the break when winger Josh Moorby completed a double.

To the Wallabies' credit, they refused to give up.

Tom Wright and Filipo Daugunu crossed the stripe for the home side, but the two converted tries only served to limit the damage on the scoreboard.

Filipo Daugunu crossed for one of the Wallabies' second-half tries. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Alongside Moorby, All Blacks veteran Beauden Barrett touched down for a brace of tries, with his second coming after a 70-metre dash to the line.

The Wallabies had high hopes before the back-to-back Bledisloe Cup Tests, but they are forced to return to the drawing board.

Coach Les Kiss and his squad will now turn their attention to their remaining Nations Championship Tests in the UK.

They play England (November 9, AEDT), Scotland (November 16) and Wales (November 22).

The Wallabies will have to wait until next year's historic Anzac Day Test in Brisbane to face the All Blacks again.

The Wallaroos were too strong for Scotland to post a second straight Test win. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Earlier on Saturday, the Wallaroos scored a massive 56-12 win over Scotland to kick off the quadruple header.

It is the Wallaroos' second straight win over the Scots, and they will meet again in Canberra on Friday night.

Meanwhile, the world champion Australian women's sevens team fell to New Zealand in their preseason match, 21-12.

In the men's sevens match, which was also a preseason fixture, Australia drew 19-19 with Fiji.

It is the first time all four of Australia's national rugby teams have appeared on the same match-day schedule.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: 'Decision next year': Nawaqanitawase keeps Wallabies options open
World.content:
Mark Nawaqanitawase is refusing to rule out turning his back on Australia for next year's home Rugby World Cup as a three-nation tug-of-war for the cross-code super talent escalates.

While Wallabies captain Harry Wilson and coach Les Kiss have no doubts Nawaqanitawase will be wearing the gold jumper at the 2027 global showpiece, the player himself is keeping his options open.

The in-demand winger's manager this week suggested Nawaqanitawase may choose to represent Fiji, to honour his father's heritage, or Italy, who the dual international is also eligible for through his grandmother.

Still only 26, the prospect of Nawaqanitawase defecting from Australia had seemed improbable.

Under World Rugby laws, if he chose to switch allegiances, following 11 Test appearances for Australia in 2022-23 before enjoying a hugely successful two-year stint in the NRL, the dual international would not be allowed to wear the Wallabies jumper ever again.

Wallabies in awe of Nawaqanitawase It was not just the 80,000 spectators, nor the millions of TV viewers in Australia, who were left in awe of Mark Nawaqanitawase's performance in the NRL grand final.

Representing Fiji or Italy could appear a more appealing scenario in the twilight of his career, but not his pomp.

However, the newly-crowned NRL premiership winner took to social media yesterday to reveal he had yet to make any decisions about his playing future beyond a looming two-year, $3 million stint in Japan under former Wallabies coach Robbie Deans.

"I just thought I would jump on here as there has been a lot of speculation on my future," Nawaqanitawase posted on Instagram.

"My only focus right now is moving to Japan in a couple of weeks and connecting with my new team at Saitama Wild Knights.

"I will weigh up my options and make a decision next year on my international future.

"Love, Marky."

After taking in the Kangaroos' thrilling Rugby League World Cup win over New Zealand on Thursday night with Nawaqanitawase in Sydney, Wilson is confident the free agent will be playing for Australia next year.

"I don't have to convince him," Wilson said ahead of the Wallabies' second Bledisloe Cup clash with the All Blacks in Sydney today.

" I played junior Wallabies with him, played Wallabies with him, saw him last night supporting the Kangaroos, so I think it's pretty obvious who he wants to play for. "

Coach Kiss is also optimistic about the 2023 Olympic sevens star opting for a Wallabies return next year.

"I think there's no doubt that he wants to be back in the game for us, that's for sure," Kiss said.

"We'll continue our conversations and go from there. I'm not going to speak on his behalf at all. But we know where he wants to play."

AAP

World.title: Tattoo artist brings queer joy to AFLW pride jumper
World.content:
When it comes to elite sporting teams, some adopt roaring tigers or bucking horses on the guernseys, but sometimes a "fruity" dolphin works best.

The playful design for the Gold Coast Suns' Pride Round guernsey, by Sunshine Coast tattoo artist Mady Peters, is bringing fun, and maybe some luck, to the Queensland AFLW side.

Ms Peters's design features a rainbow football boot, which she says highlights the support of the LGBTQIA+ community for women's football, as well as a carabiner, a symbol historically associated with the women-loving-women community.

She said the colours and characters reinforced Pride Round's message of self-expression.

Mady Peters, also known as Pokey Pokes, in her tattoo studio. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Nykayla Dux)

"It just came from a place of joy," Ms Peters said.

" I think that's everything that the Pride Round kind of stands for — this celebration and to show up authentically and as yourself. "

Among the more light-hearted illustrations is a dolphin holding a non-binary flag.

"I believe dolphins are a bit fruity," Ms Peters said.

Peters, Mithen and Lynch all shared the same vision for the 2026 Pride Guernsey: queer joy, self-expression, and a little bit of silliness. (Facebook: Gold Coast Suns)

The Sunshine Coast artist said she hoped Pride Round would help queer people relish and celebrate their identities.

"There is a world that still exists where people would rather not be here than be themselves, and that's so sad to see," she said.

Her work has won the endorsement of Mitch Brown, who last year became the AFL's first past or present player to openly come out as part of the LGBTQIA+ community.

Gold Coast Suns AFLW players Lily Mithen and Katie Lynch worked with Ms Peters to develop the guernsey.

LGBTQIA+ community 'in the fabric' of AFLW

Mithen said the team wanted the design to reflect their individual personalities.

"Katie and I are a bit loud and fun and silly and we wanted that to be felt through the jumper," she said.

Mithen said helping design the guernsey was an important way to honour the LGBTQIA+ community, which she said had been "woven into the fabric of the AFLW from the very beginning".

"[The AFLW has] always been a place where people have been really free to be themselves," she said.

Lily Mithen says Pride Round celebrates everyone’s individual strengths. (Supplied: Gold Coast SUNS)

For Lynch, her connection to football began playing with "the boys" at the age of four and grew into an enduring love of the game and a place where she felt accepted.

She said many in the AFLW had grown up knowing they "maybe did see themselves doing things a little differently", and that shone through in their sport.

Lynch said it was important to acknowledge a "very brave and courageous group" continuing to challenge perceptions of the LGBTQIA+ community in sport, including in the men's competition.

Head of AFLW at the AFL Players Association Julia Chiera said she could remember feeling like the "odd one out" as the only young girl playing football in her community, before finding a sense of belonging at Melbourne's Darebin Football Club as an adult.

Chiera said women's football had provided a welcoming environment for many queer people at the community level well before the national competition began.

She said football had historically attracted many queer women and gender-nonconforming people because of their "fearlessness" to challenge social expectations.

"It felt empowering to be amongst women who loved football and didn't really care if it was not socially acceptable for women to play sport," she said reflecting on her time at Darebin.

Julia Chiera says the AFLW’s culture of authenticity and acceptance extended beyond sexuality and is celebrated year-round in the women’s league. (Supplied: AFL Players’ Association)

However, Chiera said more work was needed to improve inclusion in the men's game, which did not have a dedicated Pride Round.

She said meaningful support for the LGBTQIA+ community required clubs, players, administrators and supporters to demonstrate genuine inclusion throughout the season and behind closed doors, rather than relying on a single round.

Ms Peters said she hoped the guernsey would bring the Gold Coast side the same good luck for their second and final game of Pride Round 2026 after the Suns won their first match last week.

"I knew it was lucky. I put lucky vibes into it," she said.

The Gold Coast Suns will wear the Pride guernsey for a final time against the Adelaide Crows in Adelaide on Saturday afternoon.

World.title: Dees dismantle Tigers to seal AFLW finals series berth
World.content:
Melbourne has secured a spot in the AFLW finals series after dismantling Richmond with ease in Pride Round.

Last night's 14.10 (94) to 5.2 (32) win was a return to form after the Demons' surprise first-ever AFLW loss to Gold Coast the previous week.

The defeat to the Suns was front of mind for Demons coach Tom Wilson ahead of the Tigers clash at Melbourne's Princes Park.

"We understood last week was far from our best performance," Wilson said before the first bounce.

"We thought around the ball we probably got a bit of a lesson in that space.

"Contest is going to be really important. (Richmond) having Monique Conti and Ellie McKenzie in there, it's a real weapon for them."

Conti returned to the field for the first time since an Achilles injury in round three and wasted no time getting to work.

Within seconds of the first bounce, the club's seven-time consecutive best-and-fairest winner won the centre clearance for the Tigers.

It was a welcome return given Richmond's struggles this season to win the loose ball. The Tigers rank second-last in the competition for contested possession.

But despite Conti's return, and Richmond ruck Poppy Kelly dominating with 23 hit-outs, the Demons won the centre contest time and again through Olivia Purcell and Tyla Hanks.

The pair heeded coach Wilson's call, with each picking up more than 30 disposals and a combined 13 clearances.

Their dominance set up Melbourne's 47 inside-50s to Richmond's 18, and spelled a long night for the Tigers' defence.

Ryleigh Wotherspoon kicked four goals to give the Demons some reassurance ahead of a finals series in which they may be without lead goal kicker Mia Austin, who has undergone throat surgery and does not yet have a set return date.

"We've got a lot of forwards that can kick goals, and even the mids can come through and kick goals, and so we're well supported and well balanced," Wotherspoon said after the game.

"We're pretty unstoppable."

AAP

World.title: Jillaroos lived up to their end of the bargain, but fans need to follow
World.content:
Seeing the Jillaroos in action is a rare privilege — a collection of the best women's rugby league players in the world, in the sport's global showpiece, on home soil.

The three-time defending champions opened their World Cup at Western Sydney Stadium with a flexing 40-0 win over Samoa, in a campaign that should engage and excite Australians and the vast diaspora of the other competing nations.

While that was the case for the earlier men's game between Samoa and France, with 13,174 fans, mostly representing western Sydney's large Samoan community, they left in large numbers at the end of that game.

And there were very few supporters — Samoan or Australian — left by the end of the women's clash, in a disappointing sight for an event of this stature.

A strong contingent of fans turned up to watch Samoa's men play France. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

This is not a new dilemma for women's sport. When and where to play, whether to have double headers, how best to engage existing fan bases and draw in new ones?

Women's State of Origin has been a good example of elevating the women's game in its own way, standing separately to the men's series, often in smaller venues, but packing them with passionate fans who are there only to watch the women. And drawing big numbers on TV too.

The World Cup presents a different challenge, with Australia currently in a league of its own on the field and another trophy considered by many as a fait accompli.

But the world is starting to catch up, and as the tournament progresses over the next month, it would be a shame for the event to go under the radar.

Rugby League World Cup live The all-conquering Jillaroos begin their women's Rugby League World Cup campaign against Samoa. Follow live.

Jillaroos coach Jess Skinner summed it up simply afterwards.

"Let's get around women in sport, right? All women in sport, and particularly this Rugby League World Cup. We've got a lot of talented women across all of the teams," she said.

"Stay and support that and the growth. Something really cool is happening in this generation of sport with our ladies, and you're going to miss it.

"There's history making moments over this World Cup, no doubt, and want to see our fans, particularly in the green and gold, to be a part of that. But also just in general, come and have a look."

The Jillaroos will play England and Wales in their next pool games. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Samoa coach Frank Pritchard suggested the late 8pm kick off didn't help, and the women were keen to play before the men.

"Our fans and our supporters will always stick through it and and stay there," he said.

"I've seen a lot of blue jerseys out there. We had plenty of support, that's for sure."

Jillaroos captain Isabelle Kelly was less concerned with the crowd, than with ensuring the Jillaroos achieve what they set out to at this tournament. And all signs point to a four-peat.

Jillaroos just warming up

It was a straightforward win for the Australians, who were not at their ruthless, rampaging best, but instead showed they are warming to the task, and will likely ignite as the tournament progresses.

Five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher had an impressive first outing in the green and gold. She was player of the match on debut, continuing the form that saw her guide the Sydney Roosters to the NRLW Premiership.

"Her kicking game was amazing. And she took her opportunities when she had them as well," Skinner said.

"So couldn't get better than that in a World Cup debut for the Jillaroos, become part of a legacy piece, and you get player of the match. So really proud of her."

Olivia Kernick made crucial gains through the middle, Tamika Upton pulled the strings in bursts without being at her fully devastating best, and Jaime Chapman, Julia Robinson, and Jess Sergis surged as needed, with all seven tries scored by different players.

Olivia Kernick was one of the Jillaroos' standouts. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

There were scrappy moments though, times where Samoa's defence jolted, and the visitors found ways to cut through the Australians when going direct.

Freedom Crichton Ropati's bone cruncher on Tiana Penitani Gray in the dying minutes was a highlight, epitomising Fetu Samoa's dedication to valiantly protecting their line, even with the result long gone.

Leading 28-0 at half time, the Jillaroos were restricted to just two tries after the break.

Overall, it was an effort that was enough for the Jillaroos to be content, without being complacent, and for Samoa to find light at the end of the tunnel, rather than wallowing in darkness.

"We spoke about pride in the jersey and what it takes to be here, sea of blue, effort on effort, and definitely showed that in the second half," Pritchard said.

"That second half proved to us that competing and staying in the fight is more than just a footy game."

Starting to see it

Athletes often speak of the honour of representing their country and their family on the world stage.

But for many of the Pasifika nations competing at this tournament, filled with players from the diaspora in Australia and New Zealand, it hits a little different.

Fetu Samoa's players say it has meant a lot to be at the World Cup for the first time since 2008. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

As with the men, tears streamed down the faces of the Fetu Samoa players during the national anthem.

And they continued afterwards, not of disappointment, but of deep understanding of what it means to be here.

"What our ladies are doing for our young girls at home with sport in general, especially rugby league, is massive," Pritchard said.

"It's something that our girls can gravitate towards."

It was an especially meaningful game for Evania Isa'ako, who has previously represented Australia.

"For me, it was not just coming and playing and putting on this jersey; it was being able to learn [about the culture]," she said.

"So off the field, culturally, everything that we've done. All the work that Frank's put in behind the scenes… outsourced people to come in and teach us, that's the really important stuff behind the scenes that people don't see."

They might not see it yet, but come the end of the tournament, maybe there'll be more eyes watching.

World.title: Proteas urged to wear down Australia's bowling machines in second Test
World.content:
South Africa have vowed to do better at wearing Australia's bowlers down in the second Test, desperate to rebound after the batters' meek surrender in Durban.

The Proteas are set to welcome back pace ace Kagiso Rabada for Sunday's second Test in Gqeberha, after he terrorised Australia on the last tour in 2018.

But the hosts have pointed to their batting as the biggest bridge that must be mended between the two sides after the series-opening 214-run defeat.

Aiden Markram was the only Protea to pass 50 in the Test, with seven others scoring between 30 and 49 across both innings.

That prompted coach Shukri Conrad to claim he was "pulling the very last strands out of his hair" as he axed both Tristan Stubbs and Kyle Verreynne.

South Africa number three David Bedingham spoke of the relentless nature of Australia's attack on Friday, with Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon offering little reprieve.

But with the three Tests in this series essentially being played back-to-back, he stressed the importance of putting work into the Australian bowlers.

"It's just about trying to take them to 80 overs, 100 overs, 120 overs," Bedingham said.

"And then, I know they're machines, but everyone gets tired eventually. Well, hopefully…

"When Kesh (Maharaj) and Simon (Harmer) were batting around the 68th over in the first innings, I'm not saying they were tiring, but the ball was a lot softer.

"It looked a lot easier. So if we could have maybe been four, five down there, then maybe the game would have a different angle."

Meanwhile, Rabada looks almost certain to play, as the Proteas fight to avoid their first home series defeat since England toured in 2019-20.

Rabada's record of 58 wickets at 21.39 is the second best of any quick against Australia this century, behind only Jasprit Bumrah.

He was the Proteas' arch-villain in the 2018 series, colliding with Steve Smith after taking his wicket in Gbqerha (then Port Elizabeth) and only avoiding a ban on appeal.

Kagiso Rabada missed the first Test against Australia with a hamstring tear, but he looks set to return in Gqeberha. (Getty Images: Sameer Ali, file photo)

Rabada has steamed in at South Africa training this week, showing no signs of the hamstring tear that sidelined him for through the ODIs and first Test.

"He's massive for us," Bedingham said.

"It looks like he's quick again, he's sharp.

"Even if you look back last year in the World Test Championship final, he took nine wickets against Australia.

"Against any team he plays against, he's ready. Hopefully, come this next Test, he takes nine or 10 wickets; that would be quite nice."

Batters Marques Ackerman and Matthew Breetzke are expected to come in at St George's Park, with Ryan Rickelton to take gloves from Verreynne.

AAP

Tech.title: Jad Abumrad loves a butterfly knife and a good springy pillow
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

It’s hard to overstate Jad Abumrad’s impact on the podcasting world. He created and hosted Dolly Parton’s America and Fela Kuti: Fear No Man, two Peabody Award-winning shows that offered unprecedented looks at the lives of two of the most important music icons of the last century.

Before that, though, he created Radiolab, an experimental NPR show that leaned heavily on creative sound design and eventually helped redefine what a podcast could be. In the early days of podcasting, shows were often just a couple of people talking at each other at a table (some still are), or lazily repackaged radio broadcasts. Radiolab instead told deeply reported stories in themed episodes with original music and cinematic sound effects that helped enhance the storytelling. And often, the sounds and music were created by Abumrad himself.

Abumrad retired from Radiolab in 2022, leaving it in the capable hands of Latif Nasser and Lulu Miller. But he’s been plenty busy since then, not only producing Fear No Man, but also composing for film, theater, and dance, and serving as a distinguished research professor at Vanderbilt University.

Despite his intimidating resume, however, he’s a man of simple pleasures who collects an ungodly amount of audio plug-ins and loves the satisfying clack of a butterfly knife.

What is your most indispensable tool?

My pillow. I need a flat, springy pillow, and I don’t understand this new hotel / airbnb trend towards giant fluffy pillows that wreck your neck for a week (I’m that age). So, a good travel pillow. In terms of digital tools: it’s rare to say you love a calendar app, but I truly love Fantastical. It takes the most annoying task in the world — scheduling a meeting with many busy people — and makes it actually fun. In terms of digital audio tools: I am addicted to audio plugins and have a thousand too many, but the one I come back to over and over is a little granular synthesis app called Granite. It’s 15 years old at this point, but it’s just so musical. I’ve used it to score dozens of OG Radiolab pieces.

Which is the most underappreciated?

I think indoor plumbing is wildly underappreciated. I have a whole talk I give about the miracle of indoor plumbing.

What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?

Alfred. It’s a super lightweight do-everything replacement for Apple’s built-in Spotlight. Like Raycast but without the annoying AI features.

What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?

I wish I could eliminate all the buzzes and dings. In fact, I wish there were a button that could turn my smartphone into a very dumb phone, because I only need it to be smart a few minutes a day.

What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar?

My tab bar is boring and functional: NYT, Ground.News, the Vanderbilt Library resource page (which links to Nexis and all the journals), ESPN.

How many tabs do you have open right now?

14, but today has been a big research day.

Which social media platform do you use the most (if any)?

I use Instagram sometimes. I used to be active on Twitter and had a decent following, pre-Elon, but then they changed the login process, and I got locked out. I never could get back in and stopped wanting to.

What is your happy place online?

Bandcamp, Andrew Huang’s YouTube channel.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

A tie between my Motorola flip phone from 1997 and a butterfly knife I saved up for a decade earlier. Snapping open and shut the phone satisfied some deep, restless urge, and the same was true for the rotational flourish of the wrist involved in opening and closing the knife.

Which was the most disappointing?

Muse brainwave headset.

What game do you have the fondest memories of?

Around the same time as the butterfly knife, I used to save up quarters all week and then run to the local Kroger and play Donkey Kong. I was never good. But I do have a distinct memory of one time getting to a new level, barrels flying everywhere. I remember the depths of that adrenaline rush.

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

People walking their dogs while looking at their phones. Maddening.

What is one thing you wish you had created?

The soundtrack to Birth. Alexandre Desplat is a shape-shifting genius, and that movie, in addition to being peculiar and amazing, has one of the most haunting scores ever.

What creation are you most proud of?

My children. I was, of course, only a co-creator. My partner Karla might say no, more of a production assistant.

Which are you least proud of?

I feel fondly towards a lot of my early music and stories. They were what I needed to make at the time. But I’m glad the bulk happened before the internet became the permanent archive, so they’ve been conveniently lost to time.

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?

Richard Nodell, my longtime work coach slash therapist slash pal, once told me: “Your job is not to know where you’re going but to lead the search” ... wise words.

What is your current obsession?

The Finnish composer Kaija Saariaho (who somehow made the orchestral sound like storms passing over fields) and UK dubstep, the dark underground grimy amalgam of garage, drum n bass, 2-step and Jamaican dub that preceded the American variant sometimes not-wrongly called “bro-step.”

What do you do when you need to focus?

I meditate for two minutes and then brick my phone.

What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?

I set up some gamelan strips on a table in my room, and I bang on those when I need a reset.

When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?

I go places without my phone all the time. But then again, I have an Apple Watch, so it probably doesn’t count.

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

My son and I bought an original pressing of John Coltrane’s Blue Train about a month ago.

What do you think is worth splurging on?

Food and music.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

“In a world of noise, one man heard the signal.”

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

Tech.title: SpaceX’s ambitious, expensive gamble to replace AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon
Tech.content:
Today, I’m talking with Walter Piecyk, a partner and analyst at LightShed Partners who covers tech, media, and telecom, about SpaceX’s recently announced plan to become a major wireless carrier.

Last week, SpaceX agreed to buy a big chunk of low-band spectrum to expand the Starlink network, spectrum that’s been traded around the telecom business for decades now. SpaceX’s ambitious plan is to use that spectrum to help build “the world’s most advanced mobile network.”

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

Combined with news that the FCC approved the deployment of 15,000 next-gen Starlink satellites and the company’s previous agreement to purchase close to $20 billion worth of EchoStar spectrum last year, it’s now clear SpaceX is serious about competing with AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile.

I’ve covered the telecom business for a long time, and I’ve always known that these companies can say they want to do something until they run into the harsh reality of how expensive it is to actually do it. The telecom graveyard of pivots, bad ideas, and failed acquisitions is vast.

Walt has been closely monitoring SpaceX’s acquisition, and he’s correctly predicted that the company was headed in this direction for months now. So I wanted to dig into whether SpaceX can pull this off, why Walt thinks the existing telecom giants have really fumbled their response to SpaceX’s growing threat, and what happens when Elon Musk’s rocket company jumps headfirst into a business everyone loves to hate.

Okay: LightShed Partners’ Walter Piecyk on SpaceX’s plan to expand into mobile. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Walter Piecyk, you’re a partner and a tech, media, and telecom analyst at LightShed Partners. Welcome to Decoder.

Thanks for having me. I’m looking forward to it.

I’m excited to talk to you. I feel like we’ve been tweeting or posting around each other for many, many years, but I’m a telecom nerd at heart. I’ve been covering the space for ages. SpaceX is going to make a big splash. It’s going to be the fourth major mobile carrier in the United States and maybe the world. It bought some spectrum to do it.

It’s EchoStar spectrum by way of private equity. It is at once very simple and also very complicated. Give us the state of the state. SpaceX bought 800 Mhz spectrum for $8 billion. They spent nearly $20 billion already on separate EchoStar spectrum. What is SpaceX trying to do here?

It’s definitely complicated, but maybe less complicated than trying to figure out how to put a data center out in space and making that work. Or something on the moon. But they don’t typically want to own spectrum and spend for spectrum. If you think about how Starlink was built, satellite companies don’t typically pay for spectrum. And then as the business evolved and as they saw the opportunity in telecom, they purchased some spectrum initially from EchoStar.

The feedback they got from investors at that time was very positive and they said, “Wait a minute, you should do more here.” This is a trillion-dollar enterprise value business in the US alone. Obviously they have global aspirations both for Starlink as well as what they’re doing with this mobile telephone service. So they bought more. They went back to EchoStar. That’s a key thing to pay attention to, in that they bought some spectrum and then they went back and bought some more.

Because with a lot of things that Elon Musk does, he learns as he goes. He bought the spectrum, got feedback, talked to people in telecom, and bought some more spectrum. Then we didn’t hear from them for a while. Now, you have this thing that happened last week where they bought some more spectrum, and I can go through the history of it if you care, but it’s long, wonky telecom stuff. This was originally the Nextel spectrum, if you remember that company.

I do. Actually, I do want you to go through the history because I think the telecom business is best understood as a bunch of lobbyists trying to make everything more complicated than it should be. Yes, spectrum auctions are complicated and what spectrum is good for what is deeply tied to the physics of the radio spectrum and all that.

But here it’s the 800 MHz spectrum from the Nextel service, the old push-to-talk, walkie-talkie service that Sprint had to divest as part of the deal to get sold to T-Mobile. They’ve been trying to sell it for ages. They sold it to this company, Grain Management. They’ve been sitting on it, and when Starlink showed up, Elon bought it. Nobody else wanted it. What did he see in the spectrum that no one else did?

When you realize that you need to build a terrestrial network to support what you’re doing with satellites, because satellites work fine if you’ve got your dish on the top of your house and you’re getting your broadband, but when you’re trying to connect with a phone that doesn’t have the same type of power or you’re going inside a home, you’re going to need better coverage.

Sirius Satellite also has supplementary towers. There are not that many of them, but sometimes when you get out of Sirius coverage, you will connect to a tower. When they bought that EchoStar spectrum and then got FCC approval, and if you looked into those details of that FCC approval and what was required, you would see that they can’t do this by satellites alone. There had to be terrestrial.

Then SpaceX, as Elon is wont to do, tries to send some diversions like, “We’re going to do Femtocell, we’re not going to do macrocell, this, that, and the other thing.” But they realized that they were going to build a terrestrial network. Now they finally realized, “If I’m going to offer mobile service, I need some form of a terrestrial network.”

At the same time, the telcos are not going to help them out. They’re not going to give them a wholesale agreement. Then when they go back and say the companies that had the lowest churn, what is the fundamental value you need in a terrestrial network? It’s low-band spectrum. Why? It travels further, you can get better coverage, and you have that connectivity.

So getting this low-band spectrum piece was just an important part, not to make the satellites work better, but to actually give them the spectrum assets that they need to build a terrestrial network. That’s why the stocks reacted, because people finally came to terms with the fact that Elon is actually going to build a terrestrial network.

I’m less interested in the stock and more interested in just the cost structure of how this works. If I rewind my brain to being a baby blogger at Engadget 100 years ago, the FCC told all the TV networks they had to stop broadcasting on 700 MHz and we were going to run an auction.

Verizon and AT&T bought big chunks of 700 MHz spectrum and that’s what 4G is built on. That’s the low-bandwidth spectrum that you’re talking about. It goes everywhere. This was a big victory that we reallocated 700 MHz, and 800 MHz was sitting right there the whole time. This is the Nextel spectrum. If it is so valuable, why wasn’t there a market for it until Elon showed up just now?

It was part of this transaction. T-Mobile ended up having to sell it because the government said, “If we’re going to allow you to take out the fourth competitor, which was Sprint, then in order to enable another fourth competitor out there, we need to have you guys give up some of your low-band spectrum.”

Part of the deal that T-Mobile and Sprint had with the government was that they would sell it to EchoStar. Why? Because Charlie Ergen, CEO of Dish at the time — it’s EchoStar now — was going to be the fourth competitor. This was the rationale that they gave in terms of the approval of the transaction. Dish needed low-band spectrum. The problem is Ergen went about his business, he was trying to build a network, and then he just couldn’t afford to buy that.

They had the rights to buy. Then at that point when Ergen failed on the bid to come up with the dollars to buy that spectrum, it enabled T-Mobile and actually forced them to put it up for auction. Now, your question: Why didn’t someone else show up then? Again, from SpaceX’s standpoint, as I mentioned at the start of this podcast, their strategy has been evolving over time.

In terms of the other telcos, they can’t really use it. There are some limitations that they have. But in hindsight, maybe Verizon or AT&T should have bought this 800 MHz spectrum for whatever it was, let’s call it $8 billion. They’re probably losing more in enterprise value over the concerns of what’s happening with SpaceX than what it cost them just to buy it in what’s known as foreclose. They basically just take it, even if they don’t use it or do whatever they need to meet those build out requirements and stop SpaceX from having unnecessary assets. I don’t think even these companies were taking Elon seriously and thinking that he would actually build the network.

Do you think that’s colored by the failure of Dish? We covered the promises of Dish Network to build a fourth wireless carrier in this country so closely. Their attempt was predicated on some amount of technology innovation.

They were going to build this thing called an O-RAN network, which had a more competitive supplier base instead of just Nokia or Siemens or whoever, and they were going to run it on AWS and that was going to reduce costs. Man, eventually they supported one Motorola handset in Vegas and even that was backstopped by AT&T. They literally could not do it. These promises never came true. Dish is a different company and Charlie Ergen’s a different CEO and their ability to just throw money at a problem until it’s solved is very different from Elon.

But if they couldn’t innovate to make a cheaper, faster network, what’s the evidence that Starlink can stand up an entire terrestrial network at a cost basis that allows them to compete selling service to consumers, while they’re also standing up an entire network in space? Because that feels like adding up a lot of cost.

I’m going to go back even deeper than that. Remember when Sprint was struggling, Masayoshi Son from SoftBank was claiming the same thing. They were going to cut their CapEx to nothing and they were going to use these small cells. They innovated how wireless was going to get delivered. That failed. Obviously, they had to get bailed out through the purchase when T-Mobile bought Sprint effectively for just the spectrum.

That network got completely decommissioned. To your point, Dish got a network built, but they couldn’t resonate in the market. The difference between Dish and SpaceX is Elon’s ability to get customers. That’s where Dish truly failed. They built the network. The network worked fine. They had the wholesale agreements that they needed.

I’ll push back on you a little bit there. I have a very funny email from a Dish PR person from several years ago where they said, “We’d like to issue a correction to your story. Our network does exist.” That was the level that they were competing at, where they had to insist to us that the network was real, even though we could not find it in our tests in the various cities they claim.

Maybe there was a network, they built some amount of network, but they had not built anything that competed at the national scale with the big three.

Absolutely. It’s not like your phone. The phone that I was using, I had an iPhone that it was mostly going to roam onto the AT&T and T-Mobile wholesale agreements that existed. The theory is you get the customers, you have a go-to-market strategy, and then you backfill the network. This is probably going to be something similar.

You can even go back to when John Legere first took over T-Mobile. They had a crappy network, and then Legere promised, “We’re going to build it,” taking on customers saying that the network was great before the network was great. Then it caught up because they actually finally got the Germans, Deutsche Telekom, to give them the money to invest in the network.

The same thing can happen here where SpaceX will sell something that’ll probably rely on other assets that are out there, even if the telcos themselves are circling the wagons. They have the satellites for certain benefits in terms of coverage and then they can build the capacity over time. The point is it’s going to take time. You can’t just turn on a network overnight and start selling service on that.

This has always been my framework of how to think about telecom companies. You can try to run the network cheaper or you can run some kind of different technology to make that cheaper. Or you can just spend and have the best network, which was the Verizon strategy for years and years and years.

Then you’ve got to acquire and manage your customers. That was the T-Mobile strategy. That was John Legere. He was just nicer to people than AT&T was, and he picked up a lot of customers and that drove some investment.

Then you’ve got to get some devices. You have to have the iPhone. We can set that aside because it feels like that era of competition is over. We’re not doing exclusive devices anymore. But those are the two. I’m just looking at the network here. It does not seem to me, from the outside, that Starlink is proposing to build a cheaper network.

It feels like they’re proposing to build a vastly more expensive network because they need the satellites. They’re going to launch 15,000 more satellites to support this network. Then they’re going to build a terrestrial network by investing in spectrum on the ground and building some set of base stations.

Then they’re going to have to convince one of the big three to let them roam over as some sort of mobile virtual network operator (MVNO). The big three do not want to do that. So they’re going to overcharge them for that. I’m just stuck at that being a lot of cost, even if you’re Elon Musk and you can make some set of people buy whatever you’re selling.

The third thing you said is obviously the most challenging. That’s the tent and the pole that prevents you from launching services sooner rather than later. But without necessarily getting a wholesale agreement, there might be other ways. Roaming agreements exist out there. There are roaming partners that exist that these telcos still rely on. It’s very expensive. It’s not something you can build a high-margin business on, but it perhaps provides an entry to the market sooner rather than later.

As Apple has pitched in terms of satellite connectivity, some people are in the middle of the Utah desert texting because they’re injured. There’s value there. But it’s the soccer field. We have, maybe not in the cities, but in the suburbs, plenty of areas that the telcos have effectively given up on trying to provide coverage because of NIMBY-ism, meaning people just don’t want these cell sites. This satellite coverage can give you not just this basic text messaging that Apple has been doing through the Globalstar constellation, but a true cellphone-type experience.

So that’s a positive. The second differentiation is the fact that these telcos have 60 percent earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) margins. So there’s a lot of fat there that can be eaten off of, that when you’re selling other services in terms of Elon, like home broadband, maybe this becomes an entree in terms of pushing Grok and people’s usage. You don’t necessarily need 60 percent margins, in this case, for him to justify building this network.

They also talk about other data connectivity that these satellites are going to enable. Again, in the current constellation, you need a lot of power and you need a dish. But if you don’t have that, if you have the cell phone-type power, then the internet of things (IOT) and other types of opportunities that exist there become another revenue opportunity that they look at.

It’s just funny. The IOT story — that’s what all these companies promised us about 4G. That’s what they all promised us about 5G. There’s something about this business that just rhymes every time. They’re going to do self-driving cars and robot surgery. I’m confident we’re going to hear about self-driving cars and robot surgery when it comes to Starlink and Tesla and Optimus.

There’s something about these applications for next generation networks that just recurs, and we hear about them all the time. Then I think about our consumer audience at The Verge, and they want long battery life and fast service and [connectivity] all the places they go. I’m not sure how that squares with your phone is going to connect directly to a satellite in the middle of a soccer field. There’s something about that that also seems challenging.

It’s just the performance if your phone does connect to the satellite on the soccer field and it works. A lot of the things that people said wouldn’t work on Starlink in terms of airplanes or even getting customer-premises equipment (CPE) down below a certain price, they’ve delivered on. Obviously, Elon sometimes delivers on them a little later than some of his initial optimistic promises, but they ultimately get delivered on.

There is the ability with these new constellations to give you that type of connectivity on these spaces. Is that enough to differentiate with consumers? I don’t know. The telcos have attacked this by saying, “No one cares about our direct-to-device (D2D) services.” Well, your D2D services are not good. It’s just sending basic text messages. What they’re talking about is giving you that blanket coverage where you get what you expect from your cell phone wherever you go.

That’s fine, but you still have to give it to the person in the middle of the building where their cell phone works today and provide the volume at a cost that is going to be attractive to that consumer. So those are longer-term things that are going to require some amount of terrestrial network build. Then the question is: how much? A lot of the attacks that have been out there have been referencing $100 billion, $200 billion. I get that. Why?

Telcos each spend $10 billion to $15 billion a year, but they are maintaining massive customer bases. To get that initial network up where you have that usage, where you use that low-band spectrum to get into buildings, is not those types of numbers. You’re probably talking like $10 billion, $15 billion for that initial build in terms of CapEx.

The dynamic there is really interesting. I’m just thinking about AT&T when the iPhone came out. The network immediately got overloaded because there was a surge of customer demand that took four years to truly resolve. Part of that resolution was just putting the iPhone on the other carriers.

How do you think that will play out for Starlink here? Because right now, Starlink customer service is not the best in the industry. Their actual service, people love it. And then when they need customer service, it’s a bunch of automated systems and people complaining on Reddit. So there’s some challenge there if you’re running a consumer business at this scale.

For consumer businesses, think about all the advertising that’s done. The fulfillment, dealing with the phones, phone subsidies, and that’s a big part of the financing. How many customers are we talking about? So for the amount of spectrum that they have now in the network that I’m talking about for $10–$15 billion, you’re not taking 50 percent share overnight. I don’t think that would be that expectation from day one.

But then the theory of telco is that when you do that initial CapEx build, you have your initial spectrum purchases — $10, $20, maybe $30 billion — another $10 or 15 billion in terms of CapEx. If you are successful and you do get that five or 10 million customers, the opportunity to invest more happens. If you go back to the old days when the cable view of wireless was going to be, “We’re going to get these MVNOs. We’re going to drive the wireless companies into the dirt and then we’re just going to buy them.”

That happened in at least one European market, and that was the cable bull thesis that was occurring. You could have the same bull thesis emerge from the SpaceX bulls here where they’re going to say, “We’ll get those first five or 10 million customers. We’ll drive them into the ground. Verizon’s going to be so desperate for any type of revenue because their revenue declined. They’re just going to hand them a wholesale deal and then they’ll start selling spectrum. There’s going to be a spectrum auction with the FCC.”

You can see how the narrative can build based on, “An initial CapEx that’s not that big, get in the market, and then if it’s successful, we start investing more.”

Let’s talk about the terrestrial network for one more turn. I heard you throw a little water on the idea that they’re going to build femtocells. That is what Elon and Gwynne Shotwell have been saying — that they don’t need to build the traditional kind of terrestrial network that AT&T and Verizon and T-Mobile have, where you have a lot of fiber back haul, the big sites that require all kinds of zoning permits and everything. That they can basically just put small cell stations next to Starlink dishes, put them anywhere they want, and blanket the world with them. And Starlink itself will be the backhaul.

I sense some problems with this. Starlink is not 100 percent reliable all the time. If you have a network that is not 100 percent reliable all the time, you’ve got some problems, so maybe you have to backstop it somehow. But you don’t think that’s what they’re doing. You think they’re going to build a regular terrestrial network.

I’m sure that’ll be a part of it, but you need macro towers for that type of coverage and penetration and power. Not to explain physics to SpaceX, they probably know it better than anybody, but what you’ll see is as they talk more about this low-band spectrum that they purchase, when we get on the conference calls of these tower companies, you’re going to find out that you’re going to see a lot of those antennas show up on towers.

It’s just natural. You can talk about femtocells, but it’s hard to see that the network’s going to get built without macro towers.

One of the weirder aspects of the telecom industry, as it’s constituted in the United States right now, is that cell carriers own some of their towers and operate some of their towers. And then there are these crazy third parties that literally have names like TowerCo that operate a bunch of the other towers.

Are those captured? Do you think SpaceX can get deals with those companies, or are they beholden to their big partners?

These are huge real estate investment trusts (REITs). American Tower is the biggest one. It’s probably one of the largest companies in this. When you consider any REITs, there are other companies out there. They have these towers. They have space in many cases where basically SpaceX can just go and get an additional antenna. It’s a lot easier to do that now than when the wireless companies were initially building this stuff and having to erect their own towers.

In addition, EchoStar is going through a bankruptcy. They have a lot of radios that could be used, that could be bought on the cheap, that could expedite SpaceX’s entrance in the market. They haven’t shown interest in that yet. The EchoStar bankruptcy process hasn’t yet concluded, but EchoStar can still be a potential partner here by selling them radios that are already on towers.

You’ve lifted the amount of time. Those radios use the spectrum that SpaceX is purchasing, so it can be a quick fix for them to enter the market. Who knows if they do that? They may have their own view like Masayoshi Son did on how to build this new cheap network.

Is there a way to read this as just they’re slowly buying EchoStar or whatever EchoStar tried to do?

EchoStar has some remaining spectrum that Verizon really needs. At this point, there is some strategic sense to just buy EchoStar outright — because EchoStar is getting stock that was issued to them at a discount. If you’re buying them, you’re effectively buying in your own stock.

You don’t have to issue the cash to the company and you’re getting whatever cash proceeds that EchoStar is getting from some of its spectrum sales. They can actually get incremental cash on the balance sheet and buy their stock in. We’ll see if that plays out. By the way, then you don’t have to also deal with Dish, which sometimes can be challenging.

T-Mobile’s in the mix here. I want to talk about Verizon, you’ve mentioned them several times, but T-Mobile is Starlink’s current partner for direct-to-device cell connectivity. Are they just getting rocked? Are they going to be a part of this? How’s that going to work?

If you think about the start of that, that was former T-Mobile CEO Mike Sievert up on stage with Elon announcing this thing and everyone’s very happy. Then Deutsche Telekom decided it needed a different CEO at some point. You had that transition where Mike retired and you brought in a new CEO, and there might just be a different view on how that relationship works.

I’m guessing that it’s been very frustrating for SpaceX to deal with them and certainly they would probably want to avoid any exclusivities going forward. They may need to if they want to sign one of these wholesale agreements that we talked about before.

It just seems like, as you mentioned, SpaceX and Starlink went after a little bit of the consumer market here. They bought some spectrum. They got a good reaction to it. Now they’re going to go after the whole thing and their existing telecom partner is thrown by the wayside.

If you look at the three big telecoms in the United States, they are circling the wagons. They’re saying this is never going to work. They’re never going to sign the MVNO agreements. They’re putting together their own satellite pool. There’s something here where they are panicked by the existence of meaningful competition in a way that does not usually happen in telecom.

Yeah, I agree with that. I don’t know if it’s SpaceX leaving them or T-Mobile leaving SpaceX, but that relationship which started out so happy with the old CEO is certainly not positive. T-Mobile executives have been throwing shade at SpaceX incessantly over the past couple of months. They formed a joint venture (JV) together.

It reminds me of when fixed wireless first hit the cable market and Chris Winfrey talked about it derisively as “cell phone internet” and played it down. Ultimately, that’s what’s really bit them and why cable stocks are in the position they’re in today, given the amount of customers that they’re losing to cell phone internet.

There are some similarities now in terms of how these executives are downplaying what they can do. Is it going to be costly? Is it going to be complex? Sure. But so is Terafab and so are so many other things. So is making an autonomous vehicle or catching a rocket with chopsticks. That’s the reality that they have to deal with. Investors have seen what this management team has done before in other areas and are just applying it here. Whether that’s fair or not, time will tell.

I’m actually very curious about that because I know you cover the company and I know you cover the industry. There’s some part of SpaceX that is just a meme stock. People love Elon. There’s some part of Tesla where it’s not valued like a car company, it’s valued like a software company, even though it is very much a car company. We’ve yet to see where the software multiples might come from for Tesla.
